### [1] [FailSAE: Towards Interpretable Failure Prediction for Vision-Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04276)
*Jie Ma,Zongxi Liu,Yi Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpretable failure prediction in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). The method formulates failure prediction as classification over sparse SAE latent activations and uses a three-stage training pipeline that maintains interpretability while improving failure prediction accuracy. The approach outperforms baselines and enables concept-level analysis of failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models like CLIP are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, making failure prediction critical. Existing methods (confidence scores, auxiliary classifiers) are effective but lack interpretability. The authors investigate SAEs to provide interpretable failure prediction that can explain why failures occur.

Method: 1) Formulate failure prediction as a classification task over sparse SAE latent activations
2) Three-stage failure-aware training pipeline:
   - Stage 1: Train SAE on VLM representations
   - Stage 2: Train failure classifier on SAE latents
   - Stage 3: Fine-tune SAE with failure-aware loss to maintain interpretability while improving failure prediction

Result: 1) Outperforms all evaluated baselines in failure prediction
2) Failure-aware training encourages SAE latent directions to capture more class-specific concepts
3) Concept-level analysis reveals failure representations shift from class-specific to ambiguous/style-related concepts
4) Learned SAE latent directions can support runtime failure recovery

Conclusion: Sparse Autoencoders provide an effective interpretable framework for VLM failure prediction. The three-stage training pipeline successfully balances interpretability and predictive accuracy. The approach enables concept-level analysis of failure modes and supports runtime recovery, making it suitable for high-stakes VLM deployments.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have achieved strong performance across multimodal tasks by aligning visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space. As VLMs are increasingly used for high-stakes domains, failure prediction becomes critical for risk-aware deployment and human intervention. Existing failure prediction methods typically rely on confidence scores or auxiliary classifiers. Although these methods are effective on predicting VLM failures, they provide limited interpretability. In this work, we investigate the use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpretable failure prediction in VLMs. We formulate failure prediction as a classification task over sparse SAE latent activations and introduce a three-stage failure-aware training pipeline that encourages the learned latent directions to remain interpretable while becoming more informative for failure prediction. Our experiments show that the resulting framework outperforms the evaluated baselines in failure prediction. Further analysis suggests that failure-aware training encourages SAE latent directions to capture more class-specific concepts. We also use the SAE to provide a concept-level analysis of how model representations change during failures, revealing a shift from class-specific concepts toward more ambiguous or style-related concepts. Finally, we explore how the learned SAE latent directions can support runtime failure recovery.

</details>


### [2] [When Seeing Overrides Knowing: Visual Dominance and Deferral-Based Method for Personalized Safety in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04281)
*Edward Sun,Yuchen Wu,Zixian Ma,Eric Hanchen Jiang,Yijia Xiao,Xiaoyuan Yi,Ranjay Krishna,Wei Wang,Jindong Wang,Aylin Caliskan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses personalized safety in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) deployed in high-stakes settings, where models may give unsafe responses for users with unknown context. The authors introduce MPS-Bench, a benchmark with 5,181 scenarios across 12 high-risk domains with hidden user profiles. Evaluating 8 frontier VLMs reveals they rarely seek missing context (86-99% direct response rate) and score poorly on personalized safety (max 2.6/5). Analysis identifies "visual dominance" - a two-stage mechanism where visual information suppresses textual risk signals during multimodal fusion. The proposed solution, PRISM, is a lightweight input monitor achieving 0.978 AUC and dominating the safety-utility Pareto frontier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical safety gap in VLMs deployed in high-stakes settings (medical, emotional, situational contexts). Current VLMs may provide responses that appear reasonable generally but are unsafe for specific users whose context is unknown to the model. This represents a novel problem of "personalized safety" in multimodal systems that hasn't been adequately studied.

Method: The authors develop MPS-Bench, a benchmark with 5,181 scenarios from 584 real-world images across 12 high-risk domains, each paired with hidden user profiles. They evaluate eight frontier VLMs on this benchmark. To understand failure mechanisms, they analyze multimodal interactions and identify visual dominance through causal interventions. Based on the identified two-stage mechanism, they propose PRISM - a lightweight input monitor using bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when deferral is needed.

Result: The evaluation reveals significant safety failures: VLMs respond directly 86-99% of the time rather than seeking missing context, and none exceeds 2.6/5 on personalized safety. Analysis identifies visual dominance - visual information enters text representations early and suppresses textual risk signals during multimodal fusion. The two-stage mechanism involves visual affect being transferred to the text stream in early layers and then shaping final decisions, making late-stage remediation unreliable. PRISM achieves 0.978 AUC and strictly dominates the safety-utility Pareto frontier across all tested models.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that current VLMs have a fundamental safety flaw in personalized contexts due to visual dominance during multimodal fusion. The proposed PRISM approach successfully addresses this by using bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when queries require deferral, achieving strong performance (0.978 AUC) while maintaining safety-utility balance. This represents an important step toward safer deployment of VLMs in high-stakes applications.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, where a response that is reasonable in general may still be unsafe for a particular user whose medical, emotional, or situational context is unknown to the model. We study this problem of personalized safety in multimodal systems and introduce MPS-Bench, a benchmark of 5,181 scenarios from 584 real-world images across 12 high-risk domains, each paired with a hidden user profile. Evaluating eight frontier VLMs, we find that they almost always respond directly (86-99%) rather than seek missing context, and none exceeds 2.6/5 on personalized safety. To understand why these failures arise, we analyze multimodal interactions and identify visual dominance: visual information enters text representations early and suppresses textual risk signals during multimodal fusion. Causal interventions reveal a two-stage mechanism in which visual affect is first transferred into the text stream in early layers and then shapes the final decision through this altered text representation, making late-stage internal remediation unreliable. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose PRISM, a lightweight input monitor that uses bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when a query is likely to require deferral. PRISM achieves 0.978 AUC and strictly dominates the safety-utility Pareto frontier across all tested models.

</details>


### [3] [Step Back to Move Forward: Reflection-Aware Preference Optimization for Visual Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04282)
*Junlong Wu,Jiuzhou Lin,Jia Sun,Boheng Zhang,Huaiqing Wang,Dewen Fan,Houde Liu,Qianqian Gan,Fan Yang,Tingting Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RA-GRPO is a new reinforcement learning-based preference alignment framework for diffusion models that improves generation quality by incorporating "backward" reflection during optimization. It introduces Diffusion Reflection (using a weak estimator to guide latent states toward higher-probability regions of the data manifold) and Counterfactual Path Synthesis (distilling rectified trajectories into the policy without inference overhead).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models have become dominant for visual generation tasks, but existing policy gradient-based RL methods for preference alignment explore inefficiently and are vulnerable to local optima that degrade semantic faithfulness and visual realism. The field needed a more stable approach to align generative models with human preferences while mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization.

Method: The method introduces two key components: (1) Diffusion Reflection, which rectifies intermediate sampling trajectories by inverting the diffusion process with a weak estimator, guiding latent states toward higher-probability regions of the true data manifold; (2) Counterfactual Path Synthesis, which implicitly distills these rectified trajectories into the policy, enabling the model to internalize search-based exploration benefits without inference-time overhead. The approach is architecture-agnostic and integrates with standard pipelines.

Result: Extensive experiments on T2I (text-to-image) and T2V (text-to-video) models demonstrate that RA-GRPO significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization.

Conclusion: RA-GRPO presents a promising direction for stable preference alignment in diffusion models. The method's architecture-agnostic nature and seamless integration with standard pipelines suggest broad applicability. By addressing the limitations of inefficient exploration in policy gradient methods, this work advances the practical deployment of human-preference-aligned generative models.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become the mainstream paradigm for modern visual generation and have substantially advanced multimedia content synthesis, especially in text-to-image and text-to-video tasks. To further align such generative models with human preferences, reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown strong potential as a post-training strategy. Nevertheless, existing policy gradient-based methods often explore inefficiently, making them vulnerable to local optima that may degrade semantic faithfulness and visual realism. To address these challenges, we present Reflection-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO), a new RL-based preference alignment framework for diffusion generative models. The core idea is to improve "forward" generation by incorporating "backward" reflection during optimization. We first introduce Diffusion Reflection, which rectifies intermediate sampling trajectories by inverting the diffusion process with a weak estimator, guiding latent states toward higher-probability regions of the true data manifold. Furthermore, we introduce Counterfactual Path Synthesis to implicitly distill these rectified trajectories into the policy, enabling the model to internalize the benefits of search-based exploration without incurring inference-time overhead. Extensive experiments on T2I and T2V models demonstrate that RA-GRPO significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization. The method remains architecture-agnostic and integrates seamlessly with standard pipelines, suggesting a promising direction for stable preference alignment.

</details>


### [4] [Joint Alignment and Distillation for Video Generation via Sample-Guided Distribution Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04283)
*Jiuzhou Lin,Junlong Wu,Fei Zuo,Huan Ouyang,Dewen Fan,Boheng Zhang,Huaiqing Wang,Jia Sun,Fan Yang,Houde Liu,Kehai Chen,Min Zhang,Tingting Gao,Han Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DM-Align is a unified single-stage optimization framework that combines distribution matching-based distillation with preference alignment for video generative models, eliminating the need for multi-stage RL training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-based preference alignment methods for video generation suffer from prohibitive computational costs when applied before distillation, while applying RL after distillation leads to model collapse. Current workflows treat RL and distillation as disconnected stages, causing inefficiencies.

Method: DM-Align extends the standard Distribution Matching framework by deriving two complementary gradient directions: one for distillation (minimizing gap between real and fake models) and another for preference alignment (using distributional gap from preference pairs or intra-group exploration, inspired by DPO and GRPO). These gradients are synergistically combined in a single-stage optimization.

Result: Comprehensive experiments across multiple foundational video models show that DM-Align robustly enhances both distillation quality and preference alignment, consistently outperforming standalone variants and sequential two-stage pipelines.

Conclusion: The proposed sample-guided framework successfully eliminates the need for multi-step reward evaluation and complex ODE-SDE conversions inherent in traditional RL approaches, providing a more efficient and effective solution for aligning video generative models to human preferences.

Abstract: Aligning video generative models to human preferences heavily relies on Reinforcement Learning (RL), which suffers from extensive computational overhead. Existing workflows typically treat RL and distillation as disconnected stages: applying RL before distillation incurs prohibitive computational costs, whereas applying RL after distillation frequently leads to model collapse. To overcome these limitations, we propose a unified, single-stage optimization framework grounded in Distribution Matching (DM). In the standard DM framework, distillation updates the model via a gradient direction that minimizes the gap between the real and fake models, guiding generations toward clarity and high fidelity. Building upon this, we introduce DM-Align, which derives a complementary gradient direction to guide the model toward human-preferred samples. Inspired by DPO and GRPO, our method leverages the distributional gap -- formulated from either preference pairs or intra-group exploration -- to directly construct this preference-guided gradient. By synergizing these two gradient directions, our approach eliminates the need for multi-step reward evaluation and complex ODE-SDE conversions inherent in traditional RL. Comprehensive experiments across multiple foundational video models demonstrate that this sample-guided framework robustly enhances both distillation quality and preference alignment, consistently outperforming both standalone variants and sequential two-stage pipelines.

</details>


### [5] [Compact Neural Appearance Models for Efficient Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05255)
*Florian Hahlbohm,Jorge Condor,Linus Franke,Martin Eisemann,Marcus Magnor*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper compares spherical appearance models for 3D Gaussian Splatting, introducing a neural implicit alternative that reduces per-primitive appearance storage from 192 to 28 bytes while improving quality and optimization speed by 1.3x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of Spherical Harmonics (SH) in 3D Gaussian Splatting: high storage/memory overhead from SH coefficients, and band-limited basis restricting angular detail.

Method: 1) Compare SH with recent spherical appearance models in same optimized pipeline; 2) Introduce implicit representation using compact per-primitive latent codes decoded by tiny shared MLP; 3) Fuse forward/backward passes into differentiable CUDA rasterizer; 4) Provide portable WebGL viewer for laptop/mobile GPUs.

Result: Neural representation is most compact (192→28 bytes per primitive), 1.3x faster optimization, improves reconstruction quality. Recent spherical models offer strongest overall quality-efficiency trade-off. Analysis reveals appearance parametrization affects geometry recovery and expressive models absorb non-static scene content.

Conclusion: Neural implicit representation with per-primitive latent codes + shared MLP provides best quality-efficiency trade-off. Framework and analysis offer practical guidance for SH replacement beyond image metrics alone.

Abstract: Explicit primitive-based radiance fields such as 3D Gaussian Splatting typically model view-dependent appearance using low-order spherical harmonics (SH). Although efficient to evaluate, SH coefficients dominate per-primitive storage and memory traffic, while their band-limited basis restricts angular detail. We present a thorough, end-to-end comparison of SH and recent spherical appearance models and introduce an implicit alternative that decodes compact per-primitive latent codes using a tiny shared MLP. We integrate all models into the same optimized pipeline, fusing their forward and backward passes into a differentiable CUDA rasterizer and provide a portable WebGL viewer for laptop and mobile GPUs. Our evaluation across reconstruction quality, memory use, and optimization and rendering performance shows that recent spherical models offer the strongest overall quality-efficiency trade-off. Our neural representation is the most compact model evaluated and, compared to third-degree SH, reduces the per-primitive appearance footprint from 192 to 28 bytes, accelerates optimization by 1.3$\times$, while improving reconstruction quality. We further analyze how appearance parametrization shapes optimization, identifying differences in recovered geometry and the tendency of expressive models to absorb non-static scene content. Together, our framework and analysis provide practical guidance for replacing SH beyond what image metrics alone can capture.

</details>


### [6] [The microscope is the mask: privileged views and labels from a cryo-ET forward model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04325)
*Bogdan Toader,Kiarash Jamali,Tanmay A. M. Bharat,Sjors H. W. Scheres*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CARNIVAL is a self-supervised model for protein annotation in cryo-electron tomography volumes that uses simulated data with forward model-based augmented paired views and privileged information from simulation to achieve superior performance on real tomograms without finetuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cryo-ET volumes suffer from limited tilt angles and severe corruption from the measurement operator, making protein annotation challenging. Existing methods lack effective use of simulated data and privileged information during training.

Method: Two key innovations: (1) Forward model-based augmented paired views integrated into LeJEPA self-supervised framework for invariance objective; (2) Using simulation-derived protein positions and identities to inform model architecture and loss function, localizing semantic information at protein positions in dense feature volumes.

Result: CARNIVAL outperforms state-of-the-art contrastive learning model on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms (benchmark dataset with multiple protein types and two processing types) without any finetuning.

Conclusion: Forward model-based data augmentation and exploitation of privileged information from simulation significantly improve transferability from simulated to real cryo-ET data for protein annotation tasks.

Abstract: We explore the use of simulated data for training a model for protein annotation in crowded cryo-electron tomography volumes reconstructed from images collected at limited tilt angles and severely corrupted by the measurement operator. Firstly, we leverage the corruptions imposed by the forward model to generate domain-specific augmented paired views of the exact same scene for an invariance objective integrated into the LeJEPA self-supervised training framework. Secondly, we use additional information from the simulation pipeline such as the positions and identity of proteins in the simulated volumes to inform the architecture of the model and the loss function, so that semantic information is localised at protein positions in the resulting dense feature volume. The resulting model, CARNIVAL, is evaluated without finetuning on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms, using a benchmark dataset containing multiple protein types and two tomogram processing types. We show that CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art model trained using a contrastive objective on simulated data but without forward model-based paired views or privileged information.

</details>


### [7] [UniMate: One Unified Model to Animate Diverse Skeletons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05415)
*Linzhan Mou,Jiahui Lei,Zhiyang Dou,Chenyue Cai,Chaoyue Song,Adam Finkelstein,Szymon Rusinkiewicz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UniMate is a unified foundation model for synthesizing articulated motion for arbitrary skeletons from rigged 3D assets and text prompts, without per-skeleton fine-tuning. It uses a topology-aware diffusion transformer with graph-aware attention, spectral RoPE, and topological conditioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motion generation bottleneck exists because existing learned animators are topology-constrained—they rely on category-specific templates or require per-skeleton fine-tuning and reference motions at inference. This limits scalability and generalization.

Method: UniMate introduces a topology-aware diffusion transformer with three key mechanisms: (1) graph-aware attention bias using pairwise joint relations and geodesic distances; (2) spectral rotary position embedding generalizing RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees via graph Laplacian; (3) global topological conditioner attention-pooled from rest-pose skeleton. Trained on UniML3D dataset (13,006 motion sequences across diverse creature types).

Result: UniMate outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in quality, generalization, and efficiency. Supports zero-shot cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, and text-guided editing.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates that a unified foundation model can generate high-quality articulated motion for arbitrary skeletons from text prompts without per-skeleton optimization, enabling scalable animation asset creation.

Abstract: Recent advances in automatic rigging now deliver animation-ready 3D assets at scale, yet generating the motion to drive them remains a bottleneck. Existing learned animators are topology-constrained: they rely on category-specific templates or require per-skeleton fine-tuning and reference motions at inference. We present UniMate, a unified foundation model that synthesizes articulated motion for arbitrary skeletons from a rigged 3D asset and a text prompt, with no test-time optimization or per-skeleton retraining. UniMate introduces a topology-aware diffusion transformer, which integrates skeletal topology into attention via three mechanisms: (1) a graph-aware attention bias from pairwise joint relations and geodesic distances; (2) a spectral rotary position embedding generalizing RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees via the graph Laplacian; and (3) a global topological conditioner attention-pooled from the rest-pose skeleton. We also curate UniML3D, 13,006 motion sequences spanning bipedal, quadrupedal, avian, marine, insectoid, serpentine, and articulated rigid objects with unified canonicalization and text pairing. Trained on this dataset, UniMate outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in quality, generalization, and efficiency, and supports zero-shot cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, and text-guided editing. Our project page is available at https://linzhanmou.com/unimate/.

</details>


### [8] [Object Concepts Emerge from Motion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04348)
*Boshi Li,Xiaohui Wang,Xiaoyang Wu,Zhichao Li,Ya Yang,Naiyan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A biologically inspired visual pretraining framework that learns object-centric representations from raw videos using motion boundaries as supervision. The method uses optical flow and clustering to generate pseudo-instance masks, which train a single-image encoder via pixel-level pairwise metric learning. Achieves superior performance on geometry and instance-sensitive tasks across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual pretraining methods capture semantic categories but fail to preserve the identity and coherence of individual instances. The authors seek to learn object-centric representations that maintain instance-level information, which is crucial for physical-world perception tasks.

Method: 1) Use motion boundaries from optical flow as object-level grouping signals
2) Generate pseudo-instance masks through off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering
3) Train a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning
4) Apply Motion-Verified Self-Training to expand supervision from 195M to 421M frames
5) Distill representations into Swin backbones (up to Swin-H)

Result: The resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance on monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks.

Conclusion: Motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining without requiring human annotations or camera calibration.

Abstract: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

</details>


### [9] [AdaptVPR: Route-Aware Hard Positive Generation for Robust Visual Place Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04369)
*Shunpeng Chen,Jingyi Zhang,Changwei Wang,Shengpeng Xu,Yukun Song,Xingtian Pei,Jinzhou Lin,Li Guo,Shibiao Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AdaptVPR addresses Visual Place Recognition (VPR) domain shift problems by generating same-place hard positives through a route-aware generative augmentation framework. It uses three complementary generation routes (Global Appearance, Local Occlusion, Dual) with VPR-oriented verification to create 160K verified synthetic samples, achieving up to 9.2% R@1 improvement on benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual Place Recognition suffers from robustness degradation due to domain shifts from illumination, weather, seasonal changes, and dynamic occlusions. The limited appearance diversity of same-place images in existing training data is a key contributing factor.

Method: AdaptVPR uses a vision-language model to parse scene attributes and estimate editing feasibility, with a rule-based scheduler determining generation routes. Three complementary routes: (1) Global Appearance Route for weather/illumination/time-of-day changes; (2) Local Occlusion Route inserting dynamic occluders; (3) Dual Route combining both perturbations. A VPR-oriented verification scheme based on geometric consistency and appearance diversity evaluates candidates, with feedback-based refinement for Local and Dual routes.

Result: Constructed AdaptCities dataset containing 160K verified synthetic same-place hard positives. Experiments across multiple VPR baselines and vision foundation backbones show consistent gains on standard benchmarks and substantial improvements under challenging domain shifts, with R@1 gains of up to 9.2%.

Conclusion: The route-aware generative augmentation framework with VPR-specific verification effectively addresses domain shift challenges in VPR, providing a scalable solution for generating diverse training data that improves robustness across various environmental conditions.

Abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) localizes a query image by retrieving database images of the same or nearby place, yet its robustness is often degraded by domain shifts arising from illumination, weather, seasonal changes, and dynamic occlusions. One contributing factor is the limited appearance diversity of the same place in existing training data. To address this issue, we propose AdaptVPR, a route-aware generative augmentation framework that constructs same-place hard positives for robust VPR training. AdaptVPR first uses a vision language model to parse scene attributes and estimate editing feasibility, while a rule-based scheduler determines the generation route according to editability scores and risk constraints. The generation process is decomposed into three complementary routes: the Global Appearance Route introduces global scene changes in weather, illumination, and time of day; the Local Occlusion Route inserts plausible dynamic occluders; and the Dual Route combines both types of perturbations to produce more challenging appearance shifts. Each generated candidate is evaluated using a VPR-oriented verification scheme based on geometric consistency and appearance diversity, reducing the risk of structural drift while ensuring sufficient appearance variation. Global candidates are generated once and rejected if verification fails, while Local Occlusion and Dual candidates use verification feedback for limited prompt refinement and regeneration. Using this framework, we construct AdaptCities, containing 160K verified synthetic same-place hard positives. Experiments across multiple VPR baselines and vision foundation backbones show consistent gains on standard benchmarks and substantial improvements under challenging domain shifts, with R@1 gains of up to 9.2%. The source code and data resources are publicly available at https://github.com/chenshunpeng/AdaptVPR.

</details>


### [10] [Where Appearance Fails, Geometry Recognizes: A CAD-Free 3D Shape Prior That Complements Vision Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04381)
*Chenxi Tao,Seung-Kyum Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses object recognition in robotics without labeled training sets or CAD models by using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to reconstruct objects from short scans, creating per-class shape prototypes that are fused with frozen DINOv2 image features. The approach achieves comparable recognition to CAD models and shows that geometry provides significant gains on shape-distinctive objects, with modest but consistent gains on textureless industrial parts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is recognizing specific objects in manufacturing and service robotics without labeled training sets or CAD models. Traditional methods rely on CAD models which are often unavailable, while 2D capture provides no shape prior and frozen foundation features fail on geometrically similar, low-texture industrial parts. The authors investigate whether a short object-centric scan can provide recognition value beyond captured images.

Method: The approach involves three main steps: (1) Reconstruct each object using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) from RGB-D depth, (2) Summarize the reconstruction into a per-class shape prototype, (3) Fuse the geometry-based features with frozen DINOv2 image features. The study evaluates on T-LESS (textureless industrial parts) and HOPE (shape-distinctive household objects) datasets, testing recognition performance under various conditions including partial occlusion.

Result: Key findings: (1) Geometry from 3DGS and CAD gives comparable recognition (tied on HOPE, within 1.6 points on T-LESS); (2) On shape-distinctive objects (HOPE), geometry alone reaches 0.920 vs image-only 0.832, with fixed-weight fusion at 0.872; (3) On shape-confusable textureless industrial parts (T-LESS), fusion improves from 0.560 to 0.591; (4) The prior rescues more image failures than breaking successes, and benefit grows under partial occlusion; (5) 3DGS renderings don't help the image side; (6) Frozen-feature recognition is nearly lighting-invariant (within 2.5 points).

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that short object-centric scans can recover recognition value comparable to CAD models without requiring actual CAD. The benefit is governed by shape recognizability—significant for distinctive shapes, modest but consistent for confusable textureless parts. The geometry prior is complementary and particularly valuable under partial occlusion. The value lies in geometry itself, not rendered pixels. The scope is limited to recognition, not pose estimation.

Abstract: Recognizing specific objects onboarded without a labeled training set recurs across manufacturing and service robotics, yet the conventional renderable prior, a computer-aided-design (CAD) model, is often unavailable. Two-dimensional capture supplies no shape prior, and frozen foundation features fail on geometrically similar, low-texture industrial parts. We ask what a short object-centric scan buys for recognition beyond the captured images themselves: each object is reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), summarized into a per-class shape prototype, and fused with frozen DINOv2 image features. First, the scan recovers the recognition value of CAD without CAD: geometry from RGB-D depth (on T-LESS), 3DGS, and CAD gives comparable recognition (tied on HOPE, within 1.6 points on T-LESS); 3DGS is only a convenient route to a point cloud. Second, the payoff is governed by how recognizable the shape is: on shape-distinctive household objects (HOPE) geometry alone reaches 0.920 versus image-only 0.832, a ceiling below which fixed-weight fusion (0.872) sits. On shape-confusable textureless industrial parts (T-LESS) the gain is modest but consistent (0.560 to 0.591 fused, above both single signals). Third, the prior is complementary, not uniformly additive: it rescues far more image failures than it breaks successes, and its benefit grows under partial occlusion. Finally, the worth lies in geometry, not rendered pixels: 3DGS renderings do not help the image side, and frozen-feature recognition is nearly lighting-invariant (within 2.5 points). The study is scoped to recognition, not the BOP pose benchmark.

</details>


### [11] [What Moves? Localized Motion Representations for Compositional Scene Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04383)
*Frank Fundel,Malek Ben Alaya,Thomas Ressler-Antal,Stefan Andreas Baumann,Björn Ommer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces a promptable localized motion representation for videos that produces persistent embeddings for user-specified regions defined by spatial masks. Unlike previous methods that crop images or mask features after encoding, this approach processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on the queried region, preserving global context while isolating local dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world dynamics are compositional, with multiple entities moving simultaneously in shared scenes. However, existing video representations encode motion globally without capturing localized motion for individual entities. Current approaches either crop inputs or mask features post-hoc, which discards the context needed to interpret motion relative to camera motion and scene layout.

Method: The proposed method introduces a promptable localized motion representation that processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on user-specified regions defined by spatial masks. This produces temporally consistent, region-addressable embeddings that isolate local dynamics while retaining global context.

Result: The approach enables object-level motion transfer for controlled composition of dynamic scenes, and supports localized action classification in multi-actor videos. It improves controllability and outperforms global representations localized through cropping or post-hoc masking.

Conclusion: The proposed promptable localized motion representation successfully addresses the limitation of global motion encoding by producing region-specific embeddings that maintain temporal consistency and preserve global context. This approach outperforms alternative localization methods (cropping, post-hoc masking) in both generative control (motion transfer) and discriminative tasks (action classification).

Abstract: Real-world dynamics are inherently compositional: multiple entities move simultaneously within a shared scene, each exhibiting distinct motion patterns. Yet most existing video representations encode motion globally, without explicitly capturing localized motion for individual entities. Crucially, motion is defined relative to a global reference frame, including camera motion and scene layout. However, localized embeddings are often computed from cropped images or obtained by masking features after encoding, discarding the context needed to interpret motion. To address this, we introduce a promptable localized motion representation that produces persistent embeddings for user-specified regions defined by spatial masks. Rather than cropping the input or masking features, our model processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on the queried region. This yields temporally consistent, region-addressable embeddings that isolate local dynamics while retaining the global context required for disambiguation. We demonstrate object-level motion transfer, enabling controlled composition of dynamic scenes. Beyond generative control, our embeddings support localized action classification in multi-actor videos. Across both tasks, our approach improves controllability and outperforms global representations localized through cropping or post-hoc masking. Project Page: https://compvis.github.io/WhatMoves

</details>


### [12] [FAVE: Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding for Efficient Fine-Grained Visual Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04392)
*Amitangshu Mukherjee,Kaushik Roy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAVE introduces a foveated adaptive visual encoding approach that processes selected regions at high resolution while maintaining native geometry, addressing the trade-off between computational cost and fine-grained visual understanding. When integrated with FastVLM, it improves TextVQA by 1.60 points and GQA by 1.31 points with minimal token overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual encoders face a fundamental trade-off between costly full-image high-resolution processing and compact global encoding that weakens local detail evidence. The authors are inspired by human active vision and aim to separate "where to look" from "what to encode", focusing on efficiently encoding selected regions at high acuity.

Method: FAVE (Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding) is a lightweight variable-resolution Vision Transformer (ViT) that encodes externally selected regions at high acuity while preserving native geometry. It uses a controlled small-object regime with oracle ground-truth crops to isolate the encoding problem. Integration with FastVLM combines local tokens (max 16) with global visual tokens while keeping the original global pathway and language model frozen.

Result: On ImageNet objects with native max side of 96 pixels, FAVE improves Top-1 by 9.4 points over fixed-resolution ViT with 12.7× lower FLOPs. In FastVLM integration: TextVQA improves by 1.60 points with 3.3× TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B; GQA attribute questions improve by 1.31 points over FastVLM-1.5B, narrowing the gap to FastVLM-7B.

Conclusion: Selectively allocating high-acuity local capacity provides an efficient complement to broader global representations and model scaling for fine-grained understanding of small objects, text, and attributes. The approach demonstrates that combining foveated local encoding with global representations achieves better efficiency-accuracy trade-offs than simply increasing resolution or backbone capacity.

Abstract: Fine-grained visual understanding depends on local detail, yet visual encoders face a trade-off between costly full-image high-resolution processing and compact global encoding that can weaken such evidence. Inspired by human active vision, we separate where to look from what to encode. We focus on the latter and introduce FAVE (Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding), a lightweight variable-resolution ViT that encodes externally selected regions at high acuity while preserving native geometry. We first isolate this encoding problem using oracle ground-truth crops in a controlled small-object regime. On ImageNet objects with a native maximum side of 96 pixels, FAVE improves Top-1 by 9.4 points over a fixed-resolution ViT on the same crop window with 12.7 times lower FLOPs. Increasing global resolution or backbone capacity does not recover the same operating point. We then integrate FAVE as a complementary local branch in FastVLM. Its local tokens are combined with FastVLM's global visual tokens, while the original global pathway and language model remain frozen. With at most 16 additional local tokens, FAVE improves TextVQA by 1.60 points and achieves a 3.3 times controlled TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B. On GQA attribute questions, it improves FastVLM-1.5B by 1.31 points, extending the benefit beyond text while narrowing the gap to FastVLM-7B. Together, these results show that selectively allocating high-acuity local capacity provides an efficient complement to broader global representations and model scaling for fine-grained understanding of small objects, text, and attributes.

</details>


### [13] [ICM-Bench: Person-Level Identity Reasoning in Multimodal Agents with Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04438)
*Shidu Ren,Yunze Liu,Xing Liu,Chi-Hao Wu,Enmin Zhou,Junxiao Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ICM-Bench is the first benchmark designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. It contains 839 synthetic clips (141 minutes) with 1,217 questions about 6 recurring adults in a one-year life album. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves 74.0% overall accuracy but drops to 60.3% on long-term identity profile questions, revealing current systems struggle with person-centric reasoning over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering but fail to isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. There's a need to specifically evaluate how well agents can link recurring faces, voices, names, person-associated objects, events, and social relations to consistent identities over time.

Method: The researchers developed a theme-configurable pipeline that generates video collections and associates each question with target identities and traceable supporting evidence. They compared three types of systems: direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems on 1,217 open-ended questions about six recurring adults.

Result: Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%. However, its performance drops significantly to 60.3% on questions that require long-term identity profiles. The benchmark reveals that current systems can recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.

Conclusion: Current multimodal agents, despite achieving reasonable overall performance, struggle with identity-centric reasoning over long time horizons. The gap between overall accuracy (74.0%) and long-term identity profile accuracy (60.3%) highlights a fundamental limitation in maintaining and reasoning about consistent person identities across extended video memories. ICM-Bench successfully isolates this capability gap for future research.

Abstract: Long-horizon multimodal agents should remember not only what happened but also who participated. This capability depends on linking recurring faces, voices, names, person-associated objects, events, and social relations to consistent identities over time. Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering, but they do not isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. We introduce ICM-Bench (Identity-Centric Memory Benchmark), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. The benchmark contains 839 synthetic clips spanning 141 minutes and 1,217 open-ended questions about six recurring adults in a one-year life album. A theme-configurable pipeline generates the video collection and associates each question with its target identities and traceable supporting evidence. We compare direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%, yet its score falls to 60.3% on questions that require long-term identity profiles. The results show that current systems recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.

</details>


### [14] [Segmentation of the aorta in 4D flow MRI using 4D convolutional kernels and learning from sparse annotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04439)
*Hinrich Rahlfs,Julio Garcia,Chiara Manini,Markus Hüllebrand,Sebastian Schmitter,Sarah Nordmeyer,Titus Kühne,Heiko Stern,Christian Meierhofer,Andreas Harloff,Sebastian Kelle,Alexander Lenz,Peter Bannas,Jeanette Schulz-Menger,Ralf F Trauzeddel,Anja Hennemuth*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A fully automated 4D U-Net for aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI, using parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernels and sparse 4D labels derived from 2D expert contours, achieves high accuracy (Dice 0.927 internal, 0.911 external) and generalizes across multicenter, multivendor data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI is essential for reproducible hemodynamic assessment but is limited by scarce dense annotations and high computational demands. Current methods either require extensive manual annotation or fail to capture temporal context effectively.

Method: Developed a fully automated 4D (3D+time) U-Net using: (1) parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernels to capture temporal context; (2) sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines (avoiding need for dense 4D annotations). Training: 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors. Evaluation: internal test set (32 scans) and external post-contrast set (30 scans from different site, protocol, and annotator).

Result: 4D U-Net achieved Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), outperforming: 3D U-Net (0.919/0.847), static PC-MRA (0.893), and registration-based propagation (0.808). Differences were small in systole but pronounced in diastole. Excellent agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, wall shear stress, and diameters (ICC ≥0.954 internal, ≥0.980 external).

Conclusion: The method provides reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes well across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data. The model is publicly available.

Abstract: Automated aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI is essential for reproducible hemodynamic assessment but is limited by scarce dense annotations and high computational demands. We developed a fully automated 4D (3D+time) U-Net for segmenting the ascending aorta, arch, and proximal descending aorta, using a parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernel to capture temporal context and sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines, thereby avoiding the need for dense 4D annotations. Training comprised 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors, with evaluation on an internal test set (32 scans) and an external post-contrast set (30 scans; different site, protocol, and annotator), compared against frame-wise 3D networks and two semi-automatic references. Against time-resolved annotations, the 4D U-Net achieved Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), versus 0.919/0.847 for the 3D U-Net, 0.893 for static PC-MRA, and 0.808 for registration-based propagation; differences were small in systole but pronounced in diastole. Agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, axial and circumferential wall shear stress, and diameters was excellent (ICC >=0.954 internal, >=0.980 external), while semi-automatic references performed worse. The method thus provides reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data. The model is publicly available.

</details>


### [15] [Topology-Aware Training and Spatial Diagnostics for Fiber Bundle Segmentation in Tracer Histology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04454)
*Joselyn Romero Avila,Kyriaki-Margarita Bintsi,Ermias Habte,Julia F. Lehman,Suzanne N. Haber,Anastasia Yendiki*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper compares topology-aware loss functions (BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, Topograph) for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. It reveals that detection metrics alone are insufficient, and introduces Excess32 to measure oversegmentation. BCE-Dice achieved highest Dice, while Topograph had lowest β0 error and fewer false positives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual annotation of histological data is labor-intensive, and existing automated segmentation methods rely on pixel-overlap losses (BCE, Dice) without exploring topology-aware loss functions for this task.

Method: Compare four segmentation methods (BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, Topograph) using a frozen DINOv3 foundation model backbone on macaque tracer histology data. Introduce Excess32 metric to measure spatial accuracy beyond traditional detection metrics.

Result: BCE-Dice achieved highest Dice score; clDice achieved highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap; Topograph had similar Dice to BCE-Dice, lowest β0 error, and fewer false positives. Betti-Topograph union raised sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933 but worsened FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34.

Conclusion: Detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality; topology-aware methods like Topograph offer complementary advantages; Excess32 is a valuable spatial diagnostic for quantifying oversegmentation.

Abstract: Anatomic tracer studies reveal how axon bundles project from an injection site, branch into smaller groups of axons, and course through the brain to reach their destinations. Histological data from such studies provide anatomical reference information for validating diffusion MRI tractography. However, manual annotation of the histological data is very labor-intensive, and although automated segmentation methods have been proposed, they rely mainly on pixel-overlap losses such as BCE and Dice; topology-aware loss functions have not been studied for this task. We compare BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, and Topograph for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. To our knowledge, this is the first exploration of foundation-model features for this task. BCE-Dice achieved the highest Dice, while clDice achieved the highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap. Topograph had similar Dice to BCE-Dice, the lowest $β_0$ error, and fewer false positives than BCE-Dice and Betti matching. Fiber bundle segmentation methods are typically evaluated with a permissive rule that counts a bundle as detected given any overlap with the prediction. We show this rule does not capture oversegmentation, and that per-section TPR can be inflated by empty sections assigned perfect recall. To quantify this, we introduce Excess32, a spatial diagnostic measuring predicted pixels outside a 32-pixel tolerance band around annotated bundles. In validation, a Betti-Topograph union raises sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933, but worsens FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34. These results show detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality.

</details>


### [16] [VISTA: Dense Multi-Label Classroom Coding with Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04550)
*Andrew Franck,Brendan Ng,Ben Fitzgerald,Zane Derrod,Chris Cianci,Chris Craney*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces VISTA, a video benchmark for multimodal foundation models using the COPUS classroom observation protocol (24-code multi-label instrument). The baseline achieves 80.1% restricted macro accuracy, outperforming zero-shot (74.9%) by 5.2 percentage points on three held-out chemistry lectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video-language benchmarks are typically constructed without published reliability statistics, leaving the noise floor of the construct unknown. The authors argue that multimodal benchmarking would benefit from methods developed in research communities that have invested in reliability strategies, using COPUS as a case study - a well-established observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature.

Method: The authors recast COPUS as a video benchmark providing: (1) a 24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across 50-90 minute lectures, (2) an externally validated vocabulary, and (3) established per-code reliability targets. They propose VISTA, a baseline that: (1) runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, (2) refines per-window outputs with a lightweight MLP head trained on the frozen backbone, and (3) max-pools predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. Annotations come from a 5-person human-evaluator panel consensus matrix as reference.

Result: On three held-out chemistry lectures, VISTA achieves 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant (5.2% improvement). The largest residual errors occur on visually similar instructor codes and on rare audio-dependent codes. Three systematic failure modes are characterized: (1) audio-partial observability, (2) fine-grained group-work discrimination, and (3) long-tail recall.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates the value of adapting established observation protocols from education research as video benchmarks for multimodal models. The benchmark provides structured labels, external validation, and reliability targets. The authors release benchmark tooling, prompts, and baseline code to facilitate future research on understanding multimodal model capabilities in educational settings.

Abstract: Video-language benchmarks are usually constructed by the dataset authors without published reliability statistics, leaving the noise floor of the construct unknown. We argue that multimodal benchmarking benefits from methods taken from research communities that have already invested in strategies to ensure reliability. We illustrate the case with the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS): a 24-code multi-label observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature. We recast COPUS as a video benchmark for multimodal foundation models, where it provides a dense set of structured labels (a 24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across a 50-90 minute lecture), an externally validated vocabulary, and established literature that provides a per-code reliability target based on human evaluators. Annotations in our evaluation corpus are produced by a 5-person human-evaluator panel whose consensus matrix is our reference. We propose VISTA, a baseline that runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, refines its per-window outputs with a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) head trained on top of the frozen backbone, and max-pools the resulting predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. On three held-out chemistry lectures, VISTA reaches 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant, with the largest residual errors on visually similar instructor codes and on rare audio-dependent codes. We characterize three systematic failure modes (audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, long-tail recall) and release the benchmark tooling, prompts and baseline code at https://github.com/ajfranck/VISTA.

</details>


### [17] [DART: Depth-as-Target Pretraining for Surgical Vision Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04555)
*John J. Han,Adam Schmidt,Muhammad Abdullah Jamal,Jie Ying Wu,Omid Mohareri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DART introduces RGB-D pretraining for surgical vision foundation models by adding a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective to DINOv2, using pseudo-labeled depth maps from off-the-shelf models. This method improves representations without requiring depth at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision foundation models (VFMs) are valuable in data-scarce domains like surgery, but current self-supervised pretraining uses only RGB images, ignoring readily available complementary signals like depth maps. Natural-image VFMs transfer poorly to surgery while scene geometry is rich and informative.

Method: DART builds on DINOv2 with a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective applied to masked iBOT patches, supervised by pseudo-labeled depth. Depth is used only during pretraining; fine-tuning and inference remain RGB-only.

Result: Pixel-level reconstruction head improves representation quality. Depth is more effective than alternative dense signals (e.g., Canny edges). DART outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines across 8 surgical benchmarks (segmentation, depth estimation, image-level recognition), improving dense prediction and image-level understanding.

Conclusion: Freely available geometric pseudo-labels can strengthen foundation model pretraining without extra labels or added inference cost, pointing toward stronger backbones for surgery.

Abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) are valuable in data-scarce domains such as surgery, where a single pretrained backbone can provide rich representations for many downstream tasks. Yet the dominant self-supervised pretraining paradigm uses only RGB images, leaving readily available complementary signals, such as depth maps, unused. This is a particular missed opportunity in surgery, where natural-image VFMs transfer poorly while the scene geometry is rich and informative. With strong off-the-shelf models now able to produce pseudo-labeled dense depth for any image corpus, we hypothesize that such signals can be folded into pretraining to learn better representations. We present DART, an RGB-D pretraining recipe that builds on DINOv2 with a simple modification: a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective applied to masked iBOT patches, supervised by pseudo-labeled depth. Depth is used only during pretraining, so fine-tuning and inference remain RGB-only. We find that this pixel-level reconstruction head improves representation quality rather than disrupting it. We further show that depth, which encodes scene geometry, is more effective as a target than alternative dense signals such as Canny edges, confirming that the gains stem from depth rather than added supervision alone. Across eight surgical benchmarks spanning segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition, DART outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines, including a vanilla DINOv2 trained on identical data, improving dense prediction while also strengthening image-level understanding. More broadly, DART shows that freely available geometric pseudo-labels can strengthen foundation model pretraining without extra labels or added inference cost, pointing toward stronger backbones for surgery.

</details>


### [18] [Dual-Part Multi-Lateral Branched Network for Multi-Class Segmentation in Cardiovascular Catheterization Angiograms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04590)
*Olatunji Omisore,Ahmed Elazab,Ali Shahidinejad,Fariza Sabrina*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes MLBNet, a dual-part neural network architecture for multi-class segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization images. The model uses multi-lateral encoder blocks for feature extraction and multi-head decoder branches for class-aware segmentation of guidewire, catheter, vessels, and background.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing catheterization image processing methods focus on binary segmentation, but clinical applications require simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures (guidewire, catheter, vessels, background). The authors address the need for fast, accurate, and explainable segmentation models for multi-structure catheterization scenes.

Method: The proposed MLBNet architecture consists of two parts: (1) Multi-lateral encoder blocks with lateral branches for repeated feature extraction to learn diverse shared representations; (2) Multi-head decoder branches with class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties. The model was trained and evaluated on multi-class segmentation angiogram data from phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal models.

Result: The dual-part models effectively separated guidewire, catheter, vessels, and background pixels into their respective classes with high probability. All models demonstrated high overall accuracy in distinguishing the dominant background class from foreground structures.

Conclusion: The MLBNet architecture successfully performs multi-class segmentation in catheterization scenes, achieving high accuracy in separating multiple structures. The dual-part design with lateral encoder branches and multi-head decoders enables class-aware segmentation suitable for cardiovascular catheterization applications.

Abstract: Catheterisation image processing requires segmentation models that are fast, accurate and explainable. While most of the existing studies usually focus on binary segmentation, there is a recent demand for simultaneous segmentation of multiple structures found in catheterization scenes. In this study, a dual-part MLBNet architecture is designed with multi-lateral encoder blocks and multi-head decoder branches for class-aware segmentation in cardiovascular catheterization scenes. Lateral branches in the encoder enables repeated feature extraction to learn diverse shared representations, while multiple decoder heads are used to introduce class-skewed branches that specialize in different structural properties in catheterization scenes. To analyze the performances of the dual-part MLBNet architecture, several multi-class segmentation angiogram data obtained during cardiovascular catheterization in phantom models, synthetic human-simulated aorta, and animal model are used for model training and evaluation. Results obtained showed the dual-part models could effectively separate guidewire, catheter, vessels and background pixels to their classes of memberships with high probability. The results demonstrate that all models were able to distinguish the dominant background class from foreground structures with high overall accuracy.

</details>


### [19] [Hidden In Plain Gaze: Gaze Representations as Privacy Controls for Utility and Re-identification Risk in XR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04592)
*Cory Ilo,Brendan-David John,Doug A. Bowman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether choosing different gaze data representations can serve as a lightweight privacy control in intelligent extended reality (XR) systems, before applying formal privacy mechanisms. Using the egocentric HoloAssist dataset, three representations (raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, and engineered eye-movement features) are compared under matched model capacity for task utility (action recognition) vs. privacy leakage (user re-identification).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Eye and head tracking in XR systems can infer user intent and attention, but also reveal biometric identity. The authors seek to explore whether representation choice alone can provide privacy protection at the feature extraction stage, without needing additional perturbation or formal privacy mechanisms.

Method: The study compares three gaze representations under matched model capacity: (1) raw gaze coordinates, (2) spatial attention heatmaps, and (3) engineered eye-movement features. They evaluate on action recognition (task utility) and closed-set user re-identification (privacy leakage) using the HoloAssist dataset with 206 identities.

Result: Engineered features retain approximately 85% of raw gaze's action-recognition accuracy while reducing re-identification by about an order of magnitude (to roughly four times the chance rate across 206 identities). Representation choice substantially changes the privacy-utility tradeoff.

Conclusion: Abstraction alone does not guarantee privacy; engineered features provide a transparent privacy lever that reduces (but does not eliminate) identity leakage while maintaining reasonable task utility. This offers designers an interpretable and auditable approach that complements mechanisms like differential privacy.

Abstract: Intelligent extended reality (XR) systems increasingly use eye and head tracking to infer user intent, task, and attention, but the same signals can also reveal biometric identity. We study whether gaze data representation choice can serve as a lightweight privacy control at feature extraction, before adding perturbation or formal privacy mechanisms. Using the egocentric HoloAssist dataset, we compare three gaze representations under matched model capacity: raw gaze, spatial attention heatmaps, and engineered eye-movement features. We evaluate each representation on action recognition as task utility and closed-set user re-identification as privacy leakage. Representation choice substantially changes the privacy-utility tradeoff. Engineered features retain roughly 85% of raw gaze's action-recognition accuracy while reducing re-identification by about an order of magnitude, to roughly four times the chance rate across 206 identities. This reduction attenuates rather than eliminates identity leakage, and the differences across representations show that abstraction alone does not guarantee privacy. Engineered features expose interpretable and auditable structure, giving designers a transparent privacy lever that complements mechanisms such as differential privacy.

</details>


### [20] [Sound-based Multi-Person 3D Pose Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04902)
*Yusuke Oumi,Yuto Shibata,Go Irie,Akisato Kimura,Yoshimitsu Aoki,Mariko Isogawa*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The first approach to estimate multi-person 3D human poses solely from acoustic signals, addressing challenges of signal superposition and inter-person reflections through a novel encoder-decoder framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-person pose estimation from sound is challenging due to: (1) superposition of motion-dependent signal variations causing overlapping acoustic signatures, and (2) inter-person reflections introducing propagation delays that obscure temporal motion-acoustic relationships.

Method: Proposed SoundMHPE framework with two components: (1) Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder capturing diverse temporal and fine-grained frequency features to isolate subtle acoustic signatures from complex overlapping signals; (2) Temporal Pose Decoder using attention mechanism to disentangle multi-person information across successive frames, accounting for temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies.

Result: Constructed a 6-hour Acoustic Multi-person Pose (AMP) dataset with 432K synchronized frames of multi-person pose and acoustic data. SoundMHPE outperforms baseline models.

Conclusion: First work to demonstrate feasibility of multi-person 3D pose estimation from acoustic signals alone, opening a new research direction in acoustic-based perception.

Abstract: Can we recover the 3D poses of multiple people using only sound? This paper presents the first attempt to estimate multi-person 3D poses solely from acoustic signals. Estimating the poses of multiple individuals using acoustic signals is inherently challenging due to the superposition of motion-dependent signal variations. Unlike single-person scenarios, the presence of multiple subjects leads to overlapping acoustic signatures, making it difficult to attribute specific signal changes to an individual's pose. Furthermore, the complexity is compounded by inter-person reflections, which introduce intricate propagation delays that obscure the temporal motion-acoustic relationship. To address these issues, we propose SoundMHPE (Sound-based Multi-person Human Pose Estimator), a novel encoder-decoder framework consisting of two key components. First, the Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder captures diverse temporal and fine-grained frequency features to isolate subtle acoustic signatures from complex, overlapping signals. Second, the Temporal Pose Decoder employs an attention mechanism to disentangle multi-person information across successive frames. By jointly accounting for temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies, this component precisely reconstructs frame-wise individual poses. To validate our approach, we constructed the 6-hour Acoustic Multi-person Pose (AMP) dataset consisting of 432K synchronized frames of multi-person pose and acoustic data, and demonstrated that our SoundMHPE outperforms baseline models. Project page: https://oumi03.github.io/sound-mhpe/

</details>


### [21] [An Evaluation Framework for Generating Multi-View Images of a Person in a Scene](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04603)
*Mahir Majid,Young Kyung Kim,Guillermo Sapiro*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of training Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) to perform free-form, promptable camera angle changes around human subjects. The main bottleneck is the lack of specialized training data featuring paired multi-view images of people in natural scenes. The authors propose the Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric to evaluate camera movements by decoupling camera movement from head pose, enabling the creation of high-quality synthetic multi-view datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative image-editing Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) struggle with spatially consistent camera angle changes. A primary bottleneck is the lack of specialized training data featuring human subjects at fixed locations with varying camera angles (frontal, side-profile views) in natural scenes. Capturing such data in unconstrained environments is logistically challenging. Existing multi-view datasets cover generic 3D environments/objects but not human subjects in natural scenes.

Method: The authors first experimented with multiple state-of-the-art image editing models to create training data synthetically, but found these outputs frequently suffered from hallucinations involving how much the subject's head turns relative to the background, producing inconsistent environments. To address this, they proposed the Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric, which operates by decoupling camera movement from localized head pose manipulation. This allows quantitative evaluation of camera movements around a person.

Result: The HSRD metric provides the necessary pipeline to evaluate 3D spatial parallax for a person in a scene. This enables the reliable construction of high-quality multi-view synthetic datasets, addressing the training data scarcity issue for DiTs to perform camera angle changes.

Conclusion: The proposed HSRD metric successfully decouples camera movement from head pose, enabling quantitative evaluation of camera movements around a person. This metric paves the way for reliably constructing high-quality multi-view synthetic datasets, which can then be used to train foundation models to execute free-form, promptable camera angle changes on human subjects in natural scenes.

Abstract: Recent generative image-editing Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) demonstrate impressive semantic editing capabilities but still struggle with spatially consistent camera angle changes. A primary bottleneck in training foundation models to execute free-form, promptable camera angle changes is the lack of specialized training data. While multi-view datasets exist for generic 3D environments and objects, there remains an absence of paired, multi-view datasets featuring human subjects at fixed locations in natural scenes, including frontal and side-profile views. Capturing such multi-camera data in unconstrained environments is logistically challenging and unscalable. In this paper, we first experiment with multiple state-of-the-art image editing models to create this data synthetically, but find that the outputs are frequently prone to hallucinations involving how much the subject's head turns relative to the background, often producing inconsistent environments. To address this issue, we propose the Head Scene Rotation Difference (HSRD) metric to quantitatively evaluate camera movements around a person. The proposed metric operates by decoupling camera movement from localized head pose manipulation. As demonstrated by the extensive experimentation, HSRD provides the pipeline necessary to evaluate 3D spatial parallax for a person in a scene, paving the way to reliably construct high-quality multi-view synthetic datasets.

</details>


### [22] [Importance-Aware Low-Rank Distillation of Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04646)
*Denis Zavadski,Sebastian Heid,Damjan Kalšan,Stefan Roth,Carsten Rother*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SVDtrunc is a two-step block-level compression method for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) that allocates ranks across blocks and compresses via truncated SVD, followed by fine-tuning with modular knowledge distillation. It achieves state-of-the-art results on FLUX.dev across 40-90% compression ratios while maintaining near-full performance at 68% parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While truncated SVD is a principled tool for parameter reduction, evidence from LLMs shows naive low-rank approximation causes catastrophic failure. However, the authors discover that DiTs exhibit smooth degradation under SVD compression, with redundancy distributed across projection matrices throughout the network, enabling effective compression.

Method: SVDtrunc uses a two-step approach: (1) Rank allocation across transformer blocks and compress the least important ones via truncated SVD under a global parameter budget; (2) Fine-tune all blocks with modular knowledge distillation and a rectified-flow objective. The method also complements step distillation.

Result: Applied to FLUX.dev across 40-90% compression, SVDtrunc outperforms all competing approaches on GenEval, HPSv2, and DPG benchmarks. Near-full performance is retained at 68% parameters, and competitive results remain at 57%.

Conclusion: SVDtrunc provides a practical compression method for large-scale DiTs, achieving smooth degradation even under substantial global compression. It complements step distillation and positions as an efficient continuation beyond diffusion step reduction for large generative models.

Abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged as a dominant architecture for high-quality text-to-image generation, yet their scale poses challenges for efficient deployment. While truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) is a principled tool for parameter reduction, evidence from large language models (LLMs) suggests that naive low-rank approximation can cause catastrophic failure. In contrast, we find that truncated SVD in DiTs produces smooth degradation even under substantial global compression, with redundancy distributed across projection matrices throughout the whole network rather than concentrated in a few transformer blocks. Building on these insights, we introduce SVDtrunc, a two-step block-level compression scheme, first allocating ranks across blocks and compressing the least important ones via truncated SVD under a global parameter budget, and then fine-tuning all blocks with modular knowledge distillation and a rectified-flow objective. We apply SVDtrunc to FLUX.dev across compression levels ranging from 40-90% of the original parameter count. Across three benchmarks, GenEval, HPSv2, and DPG, we outperform all competing approaches. Notably, and in contrast to prior work, we retain near-full performance at 68% and remain competitive even at 57% of the original parameter budget. Furthermore, we show that SVDtrunc complements step distillation and achieves strong results even without fine-tuning, positioning it as a practical continuation of efficiency improvements beyond diffusion step reduction for large-scale generative models.
  Project page: https://vislearn.github.io/SVDtrunc/

</details>


### [23] [ReaDiT Guidance: Control for Image and Video Generation using Diffusion Transformer Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04649)
*Jay Mahajan,Chang Liu,Rauf Makharov,Viraj Shah,Alexander Schwing,Svetlana Lazebnik*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReaDiT Guidance is a lightweight framework that controls Diffusion Transformer (DiT) generation by using internal feature representations from a single DiT block. It enables spatial control (depth, pose, edge maps) for images and camera/motion control for video generation, achieving competitive results with fewer parameters than existing approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
