Motivation: Modern text-to-video models are built on DiT backbones, but there lacks a lightweight method to control their generation using internal features. Existing approaches either require many parameters (adapter-based) or lack flexibility. The authors aimed to develop a parameter-efficient method to steer generation using spatial targets provided at test time.

Method: ReaDiT Guidance extracts features from a single DiT block and uses them to steer the generative process according to spatial targets (depth, pose, edge maps) provided at test time. The approach naturally extends to video generation for camera and motion control.

Result: Experimental results show ReaDiT Guidance achieves competitive or improved results compared to existing feature-based and off-the-shelf adapter-based approaches while requiring fewer parameters.

Conclusion: ReaDiT Guidance provides an effective and parameter-efficient solution for controlling DiT-based generation, applicable to both image and video generation tasks. Its lightweight nature makes it practical for real-world applications where computational resources are limited.

Abstract: We present DiT Readout (ReaDiT) Guidance, a lightweight framework for controlling generation with Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models via their internal feature representations. ReaDiT Guidance uses features from a single DiT block to steer the generative process according to spatial targets - like depth, pose, or edge maps - provided at test time. Furthermore, since modern text-to-video models are largely built on DiT backbones, ReaDiT Guidance naturally extends to video generation, enabling camera and motion control. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or improved results compared to existing feature-based and off-the-shelf adapter-based approaches while requiring fewer parameters.

</details>


### [24] [Retinal OCTA Phenotyping with LLM Reporting for Alzheimer's Disease](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04689)
*Progga Paromita Dutta,Jeba Maliha,Md Rafiul Kabir*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an explainable OCTA (optical coherence tomography angiography) pipeline for early Alzheimer's disease identification that combines annotation-aware vessel segmentation, layer-specific biomarker extraction, label-free phenotyping, and LLM-based reporting. The framework achieves high performance (ROC-AUC 0.916-0.970) on a dataset of 117 images from 39 subjects and identifies a distinct vascular phenotype in held-out subjects, while providing transparent, non-diagnostic interpretation for research purposes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains challenging because established assessment methods are costly, resource-intensive, or unsuitable for population-scale screening. OCTA provides non-invasive visualization of retinal microvasculature, but existing approaches require diagnostic labels and offer limited measurement-level interpretation.

Method: The pipeline integrates: (1) annotation-matched segmentation models for superficial vascular complex (SVC), deep vascular complex (DVC), and combined SVC+DVC representations; (2) extraction of six density and fractal-dimension biomarkers to form subject-level profiles; (3) exploratory clustering for label-free phenotyping; (4) LLM-based reporting (GPT, Gemini, Llama) evaluated for measurement grounding, citation faithfulness, and diagnostic caution.

Result: Using 117 ROSE-1 images from 39 subjects, the models achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.916-0.970 and Dice scores of 0.695-0.781. Analysis of nine held-out subjects identifies an internally consistent lower-density, lower-fractal-dimension phenotype, though the absence of diagnostic labels prevents clinical interpretation.

Conclusion: The framework provides a transparent, non-diagnostic connection between retinal vascular measurements, exploratory phenotyping, and evidence-linked interpretation for Alzheimer's research. It demonstrates the potential of OCTA-based biomarkers for AD screening while emphasizing the need for diagnostic labels for clinical interpretation.

Abstract: Early identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains challenging because established assessment methods can be costly, resource-intensive, or unsuitable for population-scale screening. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) provides non-invasive visualization of retinal microvasculature, but existing approaches often require diagnostic labels and provide limited measurement-level interpretation. We present an explainable OCTA pipeline that integrates annotation-aware vessel segmentation, layer-specific vascular biomarker extraction, label-free phenotyping, and measurement-grounded LLM reporting. Using 117 ROSE-1 images from 39 subjects, we apply annotation-matched segmentation models to superficial vascular complex (SVC), deep vascular complex (DVC), and combined SVC+DVC representations. The models achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.916-0.970 and Dice scores of 0.695-0.781. Six density and fractal-dimension biomarkers form subject-level profiles for exploratory clustering. Analysis of nine held-out subjects identifies an internally consistent lower-density, lower-fractal-dimension phenotype, although the absence of diagnostic labels prevents clinical interpretation. Reports generated using GPT, Gemini, and Llama are evaluated for measurement grounding, citation faithfulness, and diagnostic caution. Overall, the framework provides a transparent, non-diagnostic connection between retinal vascular measurements, exploratory phenotyping, and evidence-linked interpretation for Alzheimer's research.

</details>


### [25] [Enhancing Multimodal Emotion Recognition via Multi-Feature Encoding and Attention-Based Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04690)
*Xu Lin,Ke Wang,Hui Kang,Xinying Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multimodal emotion recognition framework combining audio (Wav2Vec2, MFCC, acoustic descriptors + BiLSTM) and video (ResNet50-BiLSTM) features with multi-head attention-based fusion. It outperforms baselines on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets, particularly in unbalanced data settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal emotion recognition is important for human-computer interaction, remote education, and healthcare. The motivation is to develop a framework that effectively captures diverse emotional cues from both speech and visual expressions with improved accuracy and robustness.

Method: The framework uses: (1) Audio features: Wav2Vec2 semantic embeddings, MFCC, and statistical acoustic descriptors (pitch, energy, rhythm) processed by BiLSTM for temporal modeling; (2) Video features: ResNet50-BiLSTM architecture for spatiotemporal feature extraction from facial sequences; (3) Fusion: Multi-head attention-based feature-level fusion for adaptive cross-modal weighting.

Result: Experiments on MELD and IEMOCAP datasets show significant performance improvement over baselines in accuracy and robustness. Ablation studies confirm that the attention-based fusion strategy particularly improves performance in unbalanced data settings.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively captures diverse emotional cues from speech and visual expressions. It offers a practical and generalizable approach for real-world multimodal emotion recognition tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition has attracted growing interest due to its importance in human-computer interaction, remote education, and healthcare. This paper proposes a novel multimodal emotion recognition framework that integrates rich audio and visual feature extraction with an attention-based fusion strategy. For audio, we extract three complementary feature types: semantic embeddings from Wav2Vec2, MFCC features, and statistical acoustic descriptors such as pitch, energy, and rhythm. These are aligned and fused via a BiLSTM to capture temporal dependencies. For video, we propose a ResNet50-BiLSTM architecture that combines deep residual learning and sequential modeling to extract expressive spatiotemporal features from facial sequences. To enhance multimodal synergy, we introduce a feature-level fusion mechanism based on multi-head attention, allowing the model to adaptively weigh contributions across modalities. Experiments conducted on the MELD and IEMOCAP datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms baselines in both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, ablation studies show that the attention-based fusion strategy significantly improves performance in unbalanced data settings. Our findings suggest that the proposed framework effectively captures diverse emotional cues from speech and visual expressions, and offers a practical and generalizable approach for real-world multimodal emotion recognition tasks.

</details>


### [26] [LookThere! Sparse Vision by Reinforced Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04698)
*Sreehari Rammohan,Yousef Yassin,Anthony Fuller,Junfeng Wen,Carl Vondrick,Evan Shelhamer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LookThere is an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework for adaptive computation in vision transformers that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor, achieving state-of-the-art performance-compute trade-offs by selecting only task-specific input tokens without relying on auxiliary signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision transformers treat every image token as equally important, yet most computer vision tasks only require a fraction of tokens. Existing adaptive computation methods struggle at extreme sparsity and rely on heuristics (token diversity, attention scores) that may not generalize well across tasks.

Method: LookThere uses an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains two components: (1) a shallow input selector that learns where to look, and (2) a deep representation extractor that learns what to see. The framework saves computation by selecting only task-relevant input tokens without relying on auxiliary signals.

Result: LookThere achieves remarkable sparsity, maintaining accuracy with as little as 0.2% of input. It excels at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards) and generalizes across diverse tasks including: ImageNet classification (global recognition), ADE20K segmentation (local recognition), zero-shot classification (by distillation), and regression (counting). It surpasses state-of-the-art selection methods across all settings.

Conclusion: LookThere provides a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation in vision transformers, establishing a new Pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs. Its ability to generalize across tasks and models makes it a promising approach for efficient vision inference.

Abstract: Vision transformers typically treat every image token as equally important, yet for most tasks in computer vision only a fraction are needed. Adaptive computation methods accelerate inference by choosing which tokens to process, but existing methods struggle at extreme sparsity and require heuristics that may not generalize like token diversity and attention scores. We address these limitations with LookThere, achieving a new pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs through an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor. The selector learns where to look and the extractor learns what to see, together saving computation by selecting only what is worth processing for a given task without relying on auxiliary signals. We show that LookThere only selects the task-specific input, excelling at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards), and maintaining accuracy with as little as 0.2% of the input. It generalizes across tasks and models, including global recognition (ImageNet classification), local recognition (ADE20K segmentation), zero-shot classification (by distillation), and regression (counting). Across all settings, LookThere surpasses state-of-the-art selection to provide a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation.

</details>


### [27] [AngelFingerprint: A Traceable, Explainable, and White-Box Stealthy Watermark for Text-Guided Image Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04709)
*Bo-Han Kung,Futa Waseda,Ching-Chun Chang,Isao Echizen,Shang-Tse Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: AngelFingerprint is a novel watermarking framework for text-guided diffusion models that embeds the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into model weights via a LoRA, enabling edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness. It uses a velocity-alignment anchor to preserve edit quality and a frequency filter for imperceptibility. The method achieves 86% top-1 accuracy in 200-way prompt retrieval on MagicBrush dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of text-guided diffusion editing has raised significant disinformation concerns, making reliable image provenance essential. Existing watermarking methods carry a fixed ID that cannot explain what was changed or which prompt produced the edit. Additionally, under open-source white-box access, attackers can easily locate and remove watermarks added as separate modules.

Method: The framework integrates a LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) into the diffusion model to embed the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the model's weights. An extractor recovers this embedding from the image pixels alone. Two key techniques enable this: (1) a velocity-alignment anchor that preserves edit quality, and (2) a specially designed frequency filter that keeps the watermark imperceptible yet recoverable and robust.

Result: On the MagicBrush dataset, the extractor achieves 86% top-1 accuracy in a 200-way prompt retrieval task, compared to only 20% for prompt inversion methods.

Conclusion: AngelFingerprint provides a promising solution for ensuring edit traceability and explainability in text-guided diffusion models. By embedding semantic information (the CLIP text embedding) directly into model weights, it achieves both explainability (knowing what was changed and which prompt produced it) and stealthiness (hard to detect and isolate even under full white-box access). The high retrieval accuracy demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in practical applications.

Abstract: Text-guided diffusion editing raises disinformation concerns, making reliable image provenance essential. While watermarks are commonly used for this purpose, most methods carry a fixed ID that cannot explain what was changed and which prompt produced it. Furthermore, under open-source white-box access, attackers can easily locate and remove watermarks added as separate modules. Targeting this setting, we propose AngelFingerprint, a novel watermarking framework ensuring edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness. It integrates a LoRA into the diffusion model to embed the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the model's weights. An extractor then recovers this embedding from the image pixels alone. This semantic payload explains the edit, while the weight-integrated design makes it hard to detect and isolate even under full white-box access. Two techniques make this possible: a velocity-alignment anchor that preserves edit quality, and a specially designed frequency filter that keeps the watermark imperceptible yet recoverable and robust. On the MagicBrush dataset, our extractor achieves $86\%$ top-1 accuracy in a 200-way prompt retrieval, versus $20\%$ for prompt inversion.

</details>


### [28] [Counting Beyond Instances: A Benchmark for Group-Individual Object Counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04716)
*Rui Wang,Junyi Huang,Jiahui Li,Qiao Yu,Yixue Hao,Long Hu,Baoru Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC), a new counting task that requires counting both individual objects and semantic groups (e.g., a bunch of grapes, a stack of plates) within a unified framework. The authors present BunchCount, a benchmark with 1,330 images and corresponding annotations, and propose a counting-unit guided relational counting framework that leverages group-individual containment relations to improve group-level counting while preserving individual-level performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual counting formulations focus on instance-level counting (counting individual objects), but real-world scenarios often require counting semantic groups (higher-level semantic units formed by multiple instances). This semantic granularity conflict has been largely overlooked in prior work.

Method: 1) BunchCount benchmark: 1,330 images with 89,254 individual annotations and 11,065 group annotations, including containment relations between groups and their constituent individuals.

2) Counting-unit guided relational counting framework: Exploits group-individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training.

Result: Current advanced counting models perform well on individual instances but fail to count semantic groups accurately. The proposed method substantially improves group-level counting while better preserving individual-level counting ability.

Conclusion: The GIC setting and BunchCount benchmark establish a new research direction for counting beyond instances. The proposed method serves as a strong baseline that addresses the semantic granularity conflict in visual counting.

Abstract: Visual counting is commonly formulated at the instance level, aiming to estimate how many objects of a queried category appear in an image. However, real-world counting often involves higher-level semantic units formed by multiple instances, such as a bunch of grapes, a stack of plates, or a pair of shoes. This exposes a key limitation of existing counting formulations, which mainly focus on what to count, while largely overlooking at which semantic unit to count. We introduce Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC), a new setting that requires models to count both individual objects and semantic groups within a unified framework. To support this new task, we present BunchCount, a real-world benchmark with 1,330 images, 89,254 individual annotations, and 11,065 group annotations. BunchCount provides paired individual-group annotations within the same image and explicitly records containment relations between each group and its constituent individuals. Experiments on BunchCount show that current advanced counting models perform well on individual instances but fail to count semantic groups more accurately. To mitigate semantic granularity conflict, we propose a counting-unit guided relational counting framework, which exploits group-individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training. Our method substantially improves group-level counting while better preserving individual-level counting ability, establishing a strong baseline for counting beyond instances.

</details>


### [29] [HiSfM: Disambiguating Structure-from-Motion via Scaffold-Anchored Hierarchical Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04718)
*Ziding Zhao,Hainan Cui,Peilin Tao,Shuhan Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HiSfM is a hierarchical coarse-to-fine Structure-from-Motion framework that improves robustness against visual ambiguity (repeated/symmetric structures) and reduces computational cost through scaffold construction. It forms local communities, builds a compact skeleton using edge-disjoint spanning trees, verifies edges with a two-view disambiguator, and then absorbs remaining images for refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional SfM pipelines fail under hard visual ambiguity caused by repeated or symmetric structures, and incur heavy computational cost due to redundant cameras and constraints. There is a need for a more robust and efficient approach.

Method: The proposed HiSfM framework uses a hierarchical coarse-to-fine approach: (1) Form strong local communities using geometrical induced heuristics; (2) Connect communities with a compact skeleton by packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST); (3) Verify skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator; (4) Reconstruct a stable scaffold on the verified skeleton as an anchor; (5) Absorb remaining images via efficient registration and triangulation for further refinements.

Result: Experiments on ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets show that HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods.

Conclusion: HiSfM successfully addresses both robustness (against visual ambiguity) and efficiency (computational cost) challenges in SfM, providing a practical solution for sparse 3D reconstruction in robotics and vision applications.

Abstract: Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a fundamental tool for sparse 3D reconstruction with broad impact in robotics and vision, supporting mapping, localization, and large-scale scene modeling. However, conventional pipelines often fail under hard visual ambiguity caused by repeated or symmetric structures, and incur heavy computational cost due to redundant cameras and constraints. We present HiSfM, a hierarchical coarse-to-fine SfM framework that improves robustness and efficiency through scaffold construction. HiSfM first forms strong local communities using geometrical induced heuristics, then connects communities with a compact yet strong skeleton by packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST) while verifying skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator. We reconstruct a stable scaffold on this verified skeleton, serving as an anchor to capture the essence of the scene, and subsequently absorb remaining images via efficient registration and triangulation for further refinements. Experiments on ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets show that HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods. Code is available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/HiSfM.

</details>


### [30] [Bridging Modalities and Tasks: A Unified Hierarchical ViT for SAR-to-Optical Translation and Semantic Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04726)
*Siyuan Liu,Xuze Zhang,Yongshun Wang,Licong Pan,Hang Liu,Huihui Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes BMT (Bridging Modalities and Tasks), a unified dual-task learning framework that jointly optimizes SAR-to-optical image translation and semantic segmentation using a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer. The framework addresses the interpretability limitations of SAR images by combining image translation with semantic understanding through innovative architectural components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SAR images have all-weather capabilities but suffer from speckle noise and non-intuitive scattering mechanisms, limiting their interpretability. Existing SAR-to-optical (S2O) conversion methods focus on visual quality but ignore semantic structure constraints needed for downstream tasks.

Method: The framework uses a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer with four key components: (1) LocalViTBlock fusing global self-attention with spatial depthwise convolution via learnable gating; (2) Enhanced output module with multi-scale refinement, color correction, and anti-aliasing; (3) ControlNet-style conditional injection encoding SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid injected at each encoder layer through zero-initialized convolution; (4) Bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting scheme to balance task contributions.

Result: The method achieves competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance on the WHU-OPT-SAR paired dataset and a self-constructed unpaired ship dataset (from HRSID and DIOR).

Conclusion: The proposed BMT framework successfully integrates SAR-to-optical translation and semantic segmentation in a unified model, balancing visual quality with semantic structure constraints for downstream tasks.

Abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images have all-weather, day-and-night observation capabilities. However, compared with optical images, their speckle noise and non-intuitive scattering mechanism limit the interpretability of the images. Generative models for SAR-to-optical (S2O) conversion can improve visual interpretability, but existing methods often ignore the constraints on semantic structure, which are necessary for downstream tasks, for the sake of visual effects. We propose a unified collaborative dual-task learning framework, termed BMT (Bridging Modalities and Tasks), that jointly optimizes S2O image translation and semantic segmentation through a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer. The framework integrates: (1) a LocalViTBlock that fuses global self-attention with spatial depthwise convolution through a learnable gating mechanism; (2) an enhanced output module combining multi-scale refinement processing, color correction and anti-aliasing, which calibrates channel-level color statistics through feature fusion; (3) a ControlNet-style conditional injection mechanism that encodes SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid and injects them at each encoder layer through zero-initialized convolution; (4) a bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting scheme that prevents either task from dominating the shared representation. We evaluate the framework under both paired and unpaired translation settings, on the public WHU-OPT-SAR paired dataset and a self-constructed unpaired ship dataset built from HRSID and DIOR, respectively. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance. The dataset and source code have been publicly released at https://github.com/Lewisyuaner/BMT-S2O-main.

</details>


### [31] [Where to Look Matters: Learning Influential Views for VLM-based 3D Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04741)
*Tsung-Chih Chiang,Hsuan-Kung Yang,Jou-Min Liu,Ting-Ru Liu,Chun-Wei Huang,Quan Kong,Chun-Yi Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IVSGround is a framework that learns to select influential camera views for VLM-based 3D visual grounding, replacing heuristic view selection with a trained view selector that identifies discriminative evidence for grounding objects from natural language queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing zero-shot 3D visual grounding methods rely on heuristic rules to select camera views, which prioritize object visibility rather than grounding relevance. This leads to suboptimal view selection that doesn't necessarily provide the most discriminative information for accurate grounding.

Method: IVSGround uses a lightweight view selector trained to identify query-conditioned influential views for each candidate object. Training signals are generated using feedback from a reasoning VLM through a two-stage rejection sampling process. During inference, the learned selector predicts influential views, which are then evaluated by a frozen reasoning VLM through comparative grounding.

Result: Experiments on ScanRefer and NR3D datasets show that IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines, demonstrating the importance of selecting discriminative views for effective 3D visual grounding.

Conclusion: Selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding. Learning to choose influential views based on grounding relevance significantly outperforms heuristic approaches that prioritize object visibility.

Abstract: Recent zero-shot 3D visual grounding methods leverage vision-language models (VLMs) to localize objects in 3D scenes from natural language queries. However, these methods typically rely on heuristic rules to select which camera views are provided to the VLM, often prioritizing object visibility rather than grounding relevance. We present IVSGround, a framework that learns Influential View Selection for VLM-based 3D visual grounding. Instead of using fixed heuristics, a lightweight view selector is trained to identify views that provide discriminative evidence for grounding. To obtain supervision signals, we generate training signals using feedback from a reasoning VLM through a two-stage rejection sampling process. During inference, the learned selector predicts query-conditioned influential views for each candidate object, which are then evaluated by a frozen reasoning VLM through comparative grounding. Experiments on ScanRefer and NR3D show that IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines, demonstrating that selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding. Project page: https://ivsground.github.io/

</details>


### [32] [SeamFlow: Structure-Aware Flow Matching on Edge Probabilities for Artist-Like UV Unwrapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04751)
*Yuming Zhao,Zangyueyang Xian,Qijian Zhang,Rendong Liang,Qin Jia,Ying He,Junhui Hou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SeamFlow is a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping that reformulates the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in edge-probability space, addressing limitations of traditional geometric optimization and autoregressive generative methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional geometric optimization methods focus on reducing parameterization distortion but overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence but limited perception of mesh topology often causes inaccurate local cuts. This work aims to address both limitations simultaneously.

Method: The method reformulates discrete mesh-cutting as continuous flow matching in high-dimensional edge-probability space. Through continuous relaxation, SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides smooth probability flow through Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) solving.

Result: SeamFlow improves topology awareness through edge tokenization while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion.

Conclusion: SeamFlow presents a promising approach that combines the strengths of geometric optimization and generative models, achieving superior semantic coherence in seam layouts while maintaining low parameterization distortion.

Abstract: 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping are fundamental problems in computer graphics. Traditional geometric optimization methods mainly focus on reducing parameterization distortion, but they often overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Recent autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence, yet limited perception of mesh topology often causes inaccurate local cuts. To address these limitations, we introduce SeamFlow, a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting. We reformulate the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in a high-dimensional edge-probability space. Through continuous relaxation, SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides smooth probability flow through Ordinary Differential Equation solving. Compared with existing autoregressive generative frameworks, SeamFlow improves topology awareness through edge tokenization while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion. The project page is https://meshy-dev.github.io/seamflow.

</details>


### [33] [LUMIN: Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04775)
*Pengfei Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses two critical bottlenecks in industrial anomaly detection: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. It proposes PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline), a four-stage adaptive sampling method using 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five visual plugins that requires zero backbone forward passes, achieving 341× speedup over FPS. Additionally, two engineering optimizations (parallel similarity computation and stratified pixel sampling) reduce evaluation time by 20× with minimal accuracy loss. LUMIN is introduced as a lightweight validation backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial anomaly detection systems face two fundamental engineering bottlenecks: (1) Memory bank construction latency - traditional sampling algorithms like Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) and K-Means require numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, resulting in construction times ranging from minutes to hours; (2) Inference efficiency - heavy computation components like multi-scale feature extraction cannot meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. These limitations prevent practical deployment in time-sensitive manufacturing environments.

Method: The paper proposes two core technical contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline) - a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline comprising: metadata extraction (18-dimensional pixel features), coarse filtering (sub-second numerical sorting), plugin-based refinement (five complementary visual plugins), and sampling output. PSP achieves zero backbone forward passes during sampling, with metadata extraction as a one-time offline cost. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies: parallel memory bank similarity computation for inference acceleration (reducing memory and latency by over 95%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (20× computation reduction). The validation backbone LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) features extreme segmentation-head compression to explore the accuracy-efficiency frontier.

Result: Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate: (1) PSP achieves state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost, with 341× speedup compared to FPS; (2) Inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20× while maintaining stable metrics with negligible accuracy loss; (3) The parallel similarity computation reduces inference memory and latency by over 95%.

Conclusion: The paper successfully addresses the two engineering bottlenecks in industrial anomaly detection through PSP's zero-forward-pass sampling pipeline and optimization strategies. PSP achieves comparable sampling accuracy to state-of-the-art methods with dramatically reduced construction cost (341× faster than FPS), while the inference optimizations deliver 20× speedup with minimal accuracy degradation. The proposed LUMIN backbone with extreme segmentation compression systematically explores the accuracy-efficiency frontier, making real-time industrial deployment more feasible. The approach supports progressive deployment and incremental updates, further enhancing practical utility.

Abstract: Industrial anomaly detection faces two engineering bottlenecks: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. Traditional sampling algorithms (Farthest Point Sampling, K-Means, etc.) rely on numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; heavy computation components such as multi-scale feature extraction struggle to meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. This paper focuses on sampling efficiency and inference optimization for industrial deployment with two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline)---a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. PSP completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering is sub-second numerical sorting, and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies---parallel memory bank similarity computation (reducing inference memory and latency by over 95\%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reducing computation time by 20$\times$ while keeping metrics stable). As a vehicle for validation, we introduce LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression, systematically exploring the accuracy-efficiency frontier against strong baselines. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341$\times$ faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20$\times$ with negligible accuracy loss.

</details>


### [34] [CoMLP: Cooperatively-Gated MLPs for Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Information Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04781)
*Mingyuan Meng,Shuchang Ye,Mingjian Li,Zhenyu Zhao,Jinman Kim,Lei Bi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoMLP proposes a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal fusion in medical image segmentation, avoiding the computational burden of cross-attention by using cooperative cross-gating with regional and dilated MLP interactions to capture local and global dependencies across imaging modalities and clinical reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cross-attention-based fusion approaches suffer from high computational complexity that scales quadratically with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction impractical for high-resolution feature maps, particularly in volumetric medical images. There is a need for an efficient alternative that can preserve subtle spatial details while capturing semantic dependencies across modalities.

Method: CoMLP employs cooperative cross-gating built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions. Regional MLPs capture local cross-modal dependencies while dilated MLPs capture global dependencies. The module enables both inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual clinical reports, achieving heterogeneous information integration without dense cross-attention.

Result: Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods. Ablation studies confirm that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to performance gains.

Conclusion: MLP-based interaction represents an effective and efficient alternative to attention-based mechanisms for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation, offering a promising direction for heterogeneous multi-modal medical image analysis.

Abstract: Multi-modal medical images and clinical reports provide complementary anatomical, functional, and semantic information for medical image segmentation. Effectively exploiting these heterogeneous sources requires fine-grained cross-modal information fusion that preserves subtle spatial details while capturing semantic dependencies across modalities. Existing fusion approaches frequently rely on cross-attention, whose computational burden increases rapidly with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction difficult on high-resolution feature maps, particularly for volumetric medical images. In this work, we propose CoMLP, a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation. CoMLP models cross-modal dependencies through cooperative cross-gating, built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions, to capture local and global cross-modal dependencies. We further develop a multi-source fusion architecture in which CoMLP performs both inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual reports, enabling heterogeneous information to be integrated without relying on dense cross-attention. Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks, covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods. Ablation studies further show that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to the performance gains. These results demonstrate the potential of MLP-based interaction as an effective alternative for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation.

</details>


### [35] [CLON: Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding for Zero-Shot 6D Pose Front-Ends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04784)
*Seojin Ji,Yoojin Kwon,Hyung-Sin Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CLON is a novel front-end for zero-shot 6D pose estimation that requires no task-specific training for new objects. It uses linguistic semantic memory to guide SAM 3 for high-recall proposals and cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring, improving detection AP by 8.1 pp, segmentation AP by 6.2 pp, and 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 pp over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipelines rely on strong downstream pose solvers, but their performance is limited by the front-end. The front-end must preserve partially visible true positives while rejecting semantically plausible distractors. Existing methods like CNOS and SAM-6D have limitations in proposal generation and scoring.

Method: CLON uses rendered templates of the onboarded object set to construct: (1) a linguistic semantic memory for top-down proposal generation that guides SAM 3 toward high-recall proposals for onboarded objects, and (2) object-set cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring computed once from the onboarded object set before scene inference and kept fixed during online scoring.

Result: On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points, segmentation AP by 6.2 percentage points, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 percentage points over CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.

Conclusion: CLON provides an effective front-end for zero-shot 6D pose estimation that achieves significant improvements in detection, segmentation, and downstream pose estimation without requiring task-specific training for new objects.

Abstract: Zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipelines increasingly rely on strong downstream pose solvers, but their performance is often limited by the front-end: object proposals must preserve partially visible true positives while rejecting semantically plausible distractors. We introduce Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding (CLON), a front-end requiring no task-specific training for new objects. Given rendered templates of the onboarded object set, CLON constructs a linguistic semantic memory for top-down proposal generation and object-set cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring. The linguistic memory guides SAM 3 toward high-recall proposals for onboarded objects, while cue weights are computed once from the onboarded object set before scene inference and kept fixed during online scoring. On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points (pp), segmentation AP by 6.2 pp, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 pp over CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.

</details>


### [36] [An Attention-Guided Global and Local Fusion Framework for Lesion-Focused Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04791)
*Mst Shafia Tasnima,Md Samaun Elaheea,Tanjim Taharat Aurpab,Md Musfique Anwar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A three-branch attention-guided deep learning framework using DenseNet-121 that adaptively fuses global contextual information and lesion-focused local information to improve image classification performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lesion-focused image classification faces challenges where discriminative signals are sparse, spatially dispersed, and easily obscured by background noise. Conventional CNNs process entire images uniformly, potentially diluting signal relevance.

Method: Three-branch framework built on DenseNet-121: (1) Global branch learns full-image representations with Grad-CAM to generate attention maps; (2) Local branch uses CBAM to extract refined features from masked inputs; (3) Adaptive fusion branch learns instance-specific weights to dynamically prioritize contextual and localized information.

Result: Evaluated on synthetic SSPD and three benchmark datasets (skin lesion, guava leaf, grape leaf). Fusion branch outperformed individual global and local branches, achieving 97.75% accuracy on skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on guava leaf dataset.

Conclusion: Attention-guided architectures improve model transparency, strengthen feature relevance, and support more reliable data-driven decision-making in medical image analysis.

Abstract: Lesion-focused image classification presents a core analytical challenge, as discriminative signals are often sparse, spatially dispersed, and easily obscured by background noise, while conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process entire images uniformly and may dilute signal relevance. This study hypothesizes that adaptive fusion of global contextual information and lesion-focused local information can improve classification performance compared with using either representation independently. We propose a three-branch, attention-guided deep learning framework built on Densely Connected Convolutional Network-121 (DenseNet-121) to improve feature attribution, interpretability, and classification reliability. The architecture consists of a global branch that learns representations from full images, followed by Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to generate attention maps that highlight prediction-relevant regions and produce masked inputs, and a local branch enhanced with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to extract refined spatial and channel-wise features from these focused regions. An adaptive fusion branch integrates global and local representations by learning instance-specific weights, allowing dynamic prioritization between contextual and localized information. The framework is evaluated on a synthetic Spot Pattern Dataset (SSPD) and three benchmark datasets, including skin lesion, guava leaf, and grape leaf image datasets, where the fusion branch outperformed the individual global and local branches, reaching 97.75% accuracy on the skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on the guava leaf dataset. The results highlight the value of attention-guided architectures in healthcare analytics by improving model transparency, strengthening feature relevance, and supporting more reliable data-driven decision-making in medical image analysis.

</details>


### [37] [Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation of CLIP for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04800)
*Hyun Seok Seong,Woojin Jun,SuBeen Lee,Jae-Pil Heo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A new Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) that enables temporally-aware frame embeddings from frozen CLIP models through two novel mechanisms: Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation (allowing visual transformer layers to attend over neighboring frames) and Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation (softly aggregating top-k frames based on text-frame affinities for weakly supervised learning).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PRVR methods rely on frozen CLIP frame features lacking temporal understanding, and video-level predictions can be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence. The field needs approaches that enable fine-grained temporal understanding while maintaining parameter efficiency.

Method: Two main components: (1) Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation - modifies the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames, providing temporally-aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters; (2) Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation - addresses weakly supervised PRVR by softly aggregating top-k frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments.

Conclusion: The ITA framework effectively addresses temporal understanding limitations in PRVR while maintaining parameter efficiency through frozen CLIP backbone, enabling precise frame-level retrieval in partially relevant video scenarios.

Abstract: Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) aims to retrieve untrimmed videos that contain moments relevant to a text query. Since the target moment occupies only a portion of the video, PRVR requires retrieval based on fine-grained understanding beyond coarse video-level matching. However, existing methods often rely on frozen CLIP frame features, which lack temporal understanding. Even with recent progress in parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation, video-level predictions can still be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence. In this paper, we propose an Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for PRVR. First, our Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation allows the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames. This provides temporally aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters. Second, we introduce Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation to address the weakly supervised nature of PRVR, softly aggregating top-$k$ frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments. Our code is available at github.com/hynnsk/ITA.

</details>


### [38] [Linguistic Trajectory Encoding for Efficient Long-Horizon Spatial Memory in Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04802)
*Tianyidan Xie,Shenyi Wang,Qiang Tang,Mingjie Wang,Zhicheng Qiu,Xuanfu Li,Zhan Xu,Jian Yang,Lanjun Wang,Zili Yi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LTE (Linguistic Trajectory Encoding) is a novel memory representation for embodied agents that compresses dynamic object motion histories into a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. It enables queryable per-object timelines across long observation horizons (hours-to-days), addressing limitations in existing systems that either drop fine-grained motion, keep only raw coordinates, or organize memory around immediate task context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing embodied agent memory systems fail to maintain queryable state transitions of dynamic objects in natural language across extended time horizons. Current approaches either lose fine-grained motion (video-language embeddings), retain only raw coordinates (geometric SLAM), or organize around immediate task context (agent working memories). There was no system providing per-object timelines with linguistically queryable state transitions.

Method: LTE uses a hybrid representation that adapts compression to motion complexity: (1) periods without reliable observations are anchored to the last seen location, (2) motion is represented with geometric waypoints for accuracy, and (3) natural language descriptions preserve semantic information. The approach was evaluated on the Spatial Memory Benchmark (SMB) constructed from EgoLife multi-day recordings, testing semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval capabilities.

Result: LTE achieves 45.3% success in semantic trajectory retrieval and 48.7% in long-horizon object retrieval on SMB, outperforming structured-memory and VLM baselines (best prior: 31.9% and 34.4%). Trajectory compression achieves 8.7× to 26.1× factor with sub-second query latency on 24-hour video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, the system reaches 28.75% R@1 and 55.10% R@5, representing improvements of +15.80 and +31.30 percentage points over EgoVLPv2.

Conclusion: LTE successfully provides a per-object timeline representation where state transitions are queryable in natural language across extended time horizons. The hybrid representation balancing language, spatial anchors, and visual anchors enables effective long-horizon memory retrieval while maintaining compression efficiency and low query latency, outperforming existing baselines on multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: Embodied agents performing long-horizon tasks require a memory representation in which the state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across hours-to-days observation horizons. Existing systems either drop fine-grained motion (clip-level video-language embeddings), keep it only as raw coordinates (geometric SLAM), or organise it around immediate task context (agent working memories). None of them gives the agent a per-object timeline whose state transitions are themselves queryable in language. Our key contribution is \textbf{Linguistic Trajectory Encoding} (LTE), which compresses dynamic object motion histories via a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. LTE adapts compression to motion complexity by anchoring periods without reliable observations to the last seen location, while representing motion with geometric waypoints and linguistic descriptions to preserve accuracy. To evaluate these capabilities across extended time horizons, we construct the \textbf{Spatial Memory Benchmark} (SMB) from EgoLife multi-day recordings, targeting capabilities absent in existing benchmarks: semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval. On SMB, the LTE-based system achieves $45.3\%$ success in semantic trajectory retrieval and $48.7\%$ in long-horizon object retrieval, outperforming structured-memory and VLM baselines (best prior: $31.9\%$ and $34.4\%$). LTE achieves trajectory compression by factors of $8.7\times$ to $26.1\times$ with sub-second query latency on $24$\,h video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, the system reaches $28.75\%$ / $55.10\%$ R@1/R@5, $+15.80$ / $+31.30$ pts over EgoVLPv2.

</details>


### [39] [Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04827)
*Zhaoming Xu,Chan-Wei Hu,Kuan-Ru Huang,Zihao Zhu,Renjie Li,Yang Zhou,Zhengzhong Tu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything (DA-W) is a framework that improves monocular depth estimation under adverse weather conditions (fog, rain, snow, low-light) by disentangling style from content using a Style Filter and zero-initialized adapter, achieving 3.7% average improvement in AbsRel while maintaining performance on clean benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monocular depth estimation foundation models like Depth Anything suffer from critical failures under adverse weather conditions (fog, rain, snow, night), limiting their real-world applicability. The core challenge is maintaining robustness across diverse conditions while preserving generalization on normal conditions.

Method: The paper proposes: (1) A Style Filter trained on real and synthetic degradation datasets to extract content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings; (2) A parameter-efficient, zero-initialized adapter injected into the Depth Anything backbone for lightweight modulation; (3) A pseudo-label distillation and alignment strategy for training the adapter; (4) A unified model that adapts to diverse weather conditions without catastrophic forgetting.

Result: DA-W achieves state-of-the-art robust depth estimation, improving AbsRel by an average of 3.7% on curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming performance on standard clean benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed DA-W framework successfully enables a single unified model to robustly estimate depth across diverse adverse weather conditions while preserving core generalization abilities on normal conditions, representing a significant advancement for depth estimation in real-world applications.

Abstract: Monocular depth estimation foundation models, such as the Depth Anything series, have achieved remarkable performance across diverse domains. However, they still suffer from critical failures under adverse weather conditions, such as fog, rain, snow, or at night. To address this, we present Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything (DA-W), a framework that explicitly disentangles style from content for weather-robust depth estimation. Specifically, we introduce a Style Filter trained on a curated mix of real and synthetic degradation datasets to extract content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings. This style embedding is then injected into the Depth Anything backbone using a parameter-efficient, zero-initialized adapter. Such a lightweight modulation allows a single unified model to robustly adapt to diverse conditions, including fog, rain, snow, and low-light, while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of its core generalization abilities in normal conditions. We train the adapter using a pseudo-label distillation and alignment strategy. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DA-W achieves state-of-the-art robust depth estimation, improving AbsRel by an average of 3.7% on our curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming performance on standard clean benchmarks. Our project page is available at https://zhaoming-tamu.github.io/WCDA/.

</details>


### [40] [PAPT++: Risk-Aware Adversarial Tuning and Generation for Single Domain Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04837)
*Zhipeng Xu,De Cheng,Xinyang Jiang,Lingfeng He,Huaijie Wang,Dongsheng Li,Nannan Wang,Xinbo Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PAPT++ is a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for single domain generalization (SDG) that uses text-to-image diffusion models to generate challenging yet semantically consistent samples. It iteratively refines both the generated samples and the classifier to progressively expose the model to difficult variations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While text-to-image diffusion models can enrich source distributions for SDG, diversity alone is insufficient - useful generated samples must capture variations that the current classifier finds difficult. The goal is to combine distributionally robust optimization (DRO) principles with generative models to create effective training samples.

Method: PAPT++ works in three stages: (1) Learn diverse semantic reference images for each class through image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization; (2) Use these references as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis to reduce semantic drift while targeting challenging variations; (3) Combine generated samples with source data to update the classifier, which then guides the next synthesis round in an iterative adversarial manner.

Result: Extensive experiments on standard SDG benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of PAPT++ and the effectiveness of its main components.

Conclusion: PAPT++ successfully bridges the gap between generative diversity and classifier-targeted difficulty by iteratively exposing the classifier to challenging yet semantically consistent variations, achieving robust generalization to unseen target domains.

Abstract: Single domain generalization (SDG) aims to learn a model from one labeled source domain that generalizes to unseen target domains. A common strategy is to enrich the source distribution with augmented or generated samples, and recent text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models provide a strong generative prior for this purpose. However, diversity alone is insufficient for robust generalization, because useful generated samples should also capture variations that the current classifier finds difficult. Motivated by distributionally robust optimization (DRO), we define a semantic ambiguity set in the class-conditional generative space of a pretrained T2I model and search it for samples with high classification loss under the current classifier. To this end, we introduce PAPT++, a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for SDG. PAPT++ first learns diverse semantic reference images for each class through image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization. These references then serve as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis, reducing semantic drift while guiding generation toward challenging variations. The generated samples are combined with the source data to update the classifier, and the updated classifier guides the next synthesis round in return. In this way, PAPT++ progressively exposes the classifier to challenging yet semantically consistent variations. Extensive experiments on standard SDG benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed PAPT++ method and the effectiveness of its main components.

</details>


### [41] [LetOccVote: Learning Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy through Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04846)
*Chi Zhang,Qi Song,Feifei Li,Jie Li,Rui Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LetOccVote is a weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve pseudo-label quality. It uses two key mechanisms: Depth Vote for geometric refinement and Semantic Vote for semantic supervision filtering, achieving state-of-the-art performance (53.27 IoU, 20.39 mIoU) on Occ3D-nuScenes without requiring 3D annotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction learning from 2D pseudo-labels is vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets because existing methods use these imperfect pseudo-labels directly as supervision. The authors observe that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability.

Method: The proposed LetOccVote framework uses two voting mechanisms: (1) Depth Vote exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision; (2) Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations.

Result: On Occ3D-nuScenes, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.

Conclusion: The cross-frame voting approach effectively addresses the noise problem in pseudo-labels for weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction, demonstrating that leveraging agreement across repeated observations is a reliable way to assess and improve pseudo-label quality.

Abstract: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction reduces the reliance on costly 3D annotations by learning from 2D pseudo-labels generated by vision foundation models. However, existing methods typically use these imperfect pseudo-labels directly as supervision, making occupancy learning vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets. We observe that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{LetOccVote}, a weakly supervised Gaussian-based occupancy framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve both geometric and semantic supervision. For geometry, Depth Vote exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision. For semantics, Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations. On Occ3D-nuScenes, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.

</details>


### [42] [Mitigating Performance Discrepancy in Cross-Domain 3D Class-Incremental Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04860)
*Jinge Ma,Gautham Vinod,Bruce Coburn,Jui-Feng Chi,Siddeshwar Raghavan,Fengqing Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses class-incremental learning (CIL) for 3D point clouds, identifying a new challenge called "performance discrepancy" where model degradation varies across heterogeneous domains (CAD, RGB-D scans, video reconstructions, corrupted data). The authors propose PolyMem, an exemplar-free method using high-order statistics to enhance cross-domain robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D perception is crucial for autonomous driving, robotics, and AR/VR. These models must adapt to new object categories (class-incremental learning). Unlike 2D images, 3D point clouds are heterogeneous—objects from the same class can come from various sources (CAD models, RGB-D scans, video reconstructions, corrupted observations). This heterogeneity introduces a previously overlooked challenge: performance degradation varies substantially across domains, termed "performance discrepancy."

Method: The authors established Domain3D-CIL, a training and evaluation protocol containing point cloud categories from heterogeneous domains. They adapted mainstream CIL methods to the 3D modality as baselines. To address performance discrepancy, they introduced PolyMem, an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models rich high-order statistics of the feature distribution to enhance cross-domain robustness.

Result: The performance discrepancy consistently appeared across all baseline methods. The proposed PolyMem effectively alleviates performance discrepancy while improving the model's performance across domains.

Conclusion: The paper identifies a novel problem (performance discrepancy) in 3D point cloud CIL due to domain heterogeneity. PolyMem demonstrates that modeling high-order statistics of feature distributions can enhance cross-domain robustness in class-incremental learning scenarios.

Abstract: 3D perception plays a crucial role in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and AR/VR. In practical scenarios, 3D perception models need to continually adapt to newly emerging 3D object categories, making class-incremental learning (CIL) particularly important. However, unlike 2D images, 3D point clouds are inherently heterogeneous: objects from the same class may not only come from the clean CAD domain, but also from RGB-D camera scans of varying quality, video reconstructions, or even corrupted observations. We discover that such heterogeneity introduces a new challenge beyond catastrophic forgetting: the degree of performance degradation can vary substantially across domains, a phenomenon we term performance discrepancy. To investigate this problem, we establish the Domain3D-CIL training and evaluation protocol, which contains point cloud categories from heterogeneous domains. We further adapt a wide range of mainstream CIL methods to the 3D modality. The results demonstrate that this performance discrepancy consistently appears across these baselines. To mitigate this issue, we introduce PolyMem, an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models rich high-order statistics of the feature distribution to enhance cross-domain robustness. Experiments demonstrate that our method effectively alleviates the performance discrepancy while improving the model's performance across domains. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

</details>


### [43] [SimFuse3D: Source-Guided Target Simulation and Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting for Cross-Platform 3D Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04886)
*Yongchun Lin,Xinliang Zhang,Yun Zou,Zhixuan Xiao,Liang Lei,Jianya Guo,Yuqiang Zhai,Xiaofeng Wang,HaiKuo Xu,Haoang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SimFuse3D addresses cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation by resolving box-point inconsistency between predicted boxes and actual point cloud observations. It combines object memory retrieval, target simulation, and confidence-guided reweighting to improve detection accuracy across different sensor platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation is challenging because changes in sensor height and viewpoint alter object-level point distributions. Existing self-training methods suffer from box-point inconsistency, where retained predictions provide target locations but contain sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box.

Method: SimFuse3D comprises three key components: (1) Object Memory retrieves compatible labeled source instances for target pseudo-objects; (2) Target Simulation places ground-truth boxes at target locations, aligns points with target viewing geometry, and filters aligned crops to approximate target observations; (3) Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps pseudo-object confidence scores to bounded weights shared by RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving the detector architecture and inference graph unchanged.

Result: Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D exceeds Pi3DET-Net on every reported AP metric and ranks first among compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among compared adaptation methods with both evaluated detectors.

Conclusion: SimFuse3D effectively addresses the box-point inconsistency problem in LiDAR UDA through novel target simulation and confidence-guided reweighting mechanisms, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple cross-platform transfers while maintaining inference-time architecture compatibility.

Abstract: Changes in sensor height and viewpoint alter object-level point distributions, making cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) difficult. Self-training uses labeled source scans and unlabeled target scans, yet a retained prediction may provide a useful target location while enclosing sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box. We refer to this mismatch as box-point inconsistency. We introduce SimFuse3D, which preserves the target placement and repairs the associated pseudo-object using measured geometry from labeled source scans. Object Memory retrieves a compatible labeled source instance. Target Simulation places its ground-truth box at the target location, aligns its points with the target viewing geometry, and filters the aligned crop to approximate the target observation. Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps each target pseudo-object confidence score to a bounded weight shared by RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving the detector architecture and inference graph unchanged. Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D exceeds Pi3DET-Net on every reported AP metric and ranks first among the compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among the compared adaptation methods with both evaluated detectors.

</details>


### [44] [InterSing: Explicit Interaction Dynamics for 3D Duet Singing Animation and Beyond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04903)
*Yihan Zhou,Zikai Huang,Yuyang Yu,Xuemiao Xu,Cheng Xu,Shengfeng He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: InterSing is a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances. It introduces "interaction logits" - a latent representation modeling cross-performer engagement - to condition an interaction-aware diffusion model driven by audio features and interaction dynamics, enabling unified multi-mode generation of independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions between them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models fail to capture duet singing structure, where performers balance individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments (phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, call-and-response). These interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent, requiring a new representation approach.

Method: 1) Represent duet coordination as a time-varying signal reflecting cross-performer engagement strength; 2) Introduce interaction logits - an interpretable latent representation learned using weak supervision; 3) Condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction logits; 4) Enable unified multi-mode generation spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and transitions.

Result: InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. The formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over when and how performers engage.

Conclusion: The interaction logits approach successfully captures the sparse, rhythm-dependent nature of duet coordination, enabling controllable and realistic 3D head animations for singing performances with applications in multi-singer scenarios.

Abstract: We present InterSing, a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances. Unlike solo singing, duet performance requires each singer to balance individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments, such as phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, and call-and-response passages. Because these interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent, existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models do not adequately capture their structure. Our key insight is that duet coordination can be represented as a time-varying signal that reflects how strongly performers engage with one another throughout a song. Based on this observation, we introduce interaction logits, an interpretable latent representation that models the degree of cross-performer engagement at each time step. We learn these logits using weak supervision and use them to condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction dynamics. This formulation enables unified multi-mode generation, spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions between them. Experiments show that InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. We further demonstrate that the same formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over when and how performers engage.

</details>


### [45] [Methane Detection On Board Satellites from Unorthorectified Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04906)
*Luca Marini,Maggie Chen,Hala Lamdouar,Laura Martínez-Ferrer,Dr C. P. Bridges,Giacomo Acciarini*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: UnorthoDOS introduces a dataset and approach for training machine learning models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery for methane plume detection, bypassing traditional orthorectification and matched-filter steps. The approach achieves comparable performance to orthorectified models while enabling onboard deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional methane detection methods require orthorectification and matched filters, which are designed for ground processing and poorly suited to onboard execution. This limits timely methane detection from satellites.

Method: The researchers developed U-Net models trained on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery from the EMIT sensor, and tested FP16 compression for onboard deployment. They compared performance against orthorectified models and the mag1c matched-filter baseline.

Result: U-Net models trained on unorthorectified data achieved IoU of 16.91%, approaching the performance of orthorectified models (18.47% IoU). Both substantially outperformed the mag1c matched-filter baseline (4.76% IoU). FP16 compression halved model size with under 0.3% output deviation.

Conclusion: The approach enables onboard methane detection directly from unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery, with minimal performance loss compared to orthorectified processing. The trained models and datasets are publicly available.

Abstract: As a potent greenhouse gas, methane is a major driver of climate change. Its effective mitigation relies on timely detection. Conventional detection methods rely on orthorectification to correct geometric distortions and matched filters to enhance plume signals, which are steps designed for ground processing and poorly suited to onboard execution. We introduce UnorthoDOS, a dataset and approach for training machine learning models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery, bypassing both orthorectification and matched-filter products. Our U-Net models trained on unorthorectified data approach the performance of models trained on orthorectified data (IoU 16.91% vs. 18.47% on all plumes), while both substantially outperform the mag1c matched-filter baseline (IoU 4.76%). We further demonstrate the feasibility of onboard deployment: FP16 compression halves model size with under 0.3% output deviation. The trained ML models and two ML-ready datasets -- orthorectified and unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery from the EMIT sensor -- are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SpaceML/UnorthoDOS, with code at https://github.com/spaceml-org/plume-hunter.

</details>
