### [46] [TourPhysics: Bringing Physics to World Models for Exploration and Manipulation from a Single Image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04911)
*Xin Zhang,Yabo Chen,Zixuan Duan,Haibin Huang,Chi Zhang,Feng Xu,Xuelong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TourPhysics is an online visual world model framework that distinguishes camera motion (observation) from physical intervention (object manipulation) by combining deterministic physics simulation with video generation. It initializes from a single image and declarative physical configuration, separating simulator state, geometric evidence, generator controls, and appearance memory to maintain physical/spatial consistency over long horizons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video world models are largely driven by appearance priors and often lose physical or spatial consistency over long horizons. They cannot distinguish observation (camera motion revealing new surfaces) from physical intervention (which changes object motion, contact, and deformation).

Method: TourPhysics combines deterministic simulation with video generation by assigning separate roles to: (1) simulator state, (2) geometric evidence, (3) generator controls, and (4) appearance memory. For each action, the simulator computes a finite physical and camera trajectory before generating the corresponding observation. Accepted observations publish terminal state and update appearance memory and generator controls. The framework separates simulator geometry (for projection/visibility) from relative depth (for generator conditioning). A reference-anchored memory retrieves accepted static appearance through geometric cross-view correspondence and incorporates it through a bounded residual.

Result: TourPhysics follows prescribed camera and object trajectories more closely than evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.

Conclusion: TourPhysics extends PhysOmni from finite physics-grounded video synthesis to persistent exploration and manipulation, maintaining physical consistency and reducing appearance drift over extended video generation horizons.

Abstract: Interactive visual world models must distinguish observation from physical intervention. Camera motion reveals new surfaces, whereas intervention changes object motion, contact, and deformation. Current video world models are largely driven by appearance priors and often lose physical or spatial consistency over long horizons. We present TourPhysics, an online framework initialized from a single image and a declarative physical configuration. TourPhysics extends PhysOmni, our ACM Multimedia 2026 work, from finite physics-grounded video synthesis to persistent exploration and manipulation. TourPhysics combines deterministic simulation with video generation while assigning separate roles to simulator state, geometric evidence, generator controls, and appearance memory. For each action, the simulator computes a finite physical and camera trajectory before the corresponding observation is generated. Accepted observations publish the terminal state and update the appearance memory and subsequent generator controls, while the committed state and simulator geometry remain fixed throughout synthesis and retry. We further separate the simulator geometry used for projection and visibility from the relative depth used to condition the generator. A reference-anchored memory retrieves accepted static appearance through geometric cross-view correspondence and incorporates it through a bounded residual that reverts to the native path when no valid correspondence exists. On simulator-defined camera tours and object manipulations, TourPhysics follows prescribed camera and object trajectories more closely than the evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.

</details>


### [47] [One Diffusion Model, Two Roles: Guided Trajectory Planning and Safety-Critical Scenario Generation in Closed-Loop Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04921)
*Arka Pal,Rajesh Kumar,Hannes Eriksson,Rémi Lacombe,Arvid Laveno Ling,Ankit Gupta,Maciej Wozniak*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a unified framework using a single pretrained diffusion probabilistic model for both ego motion planning and safety-critical scenario generation in autonomous driving. The approach combines an SSDS diffusion-transformer decoder with a training-free guidance scheme called DAPSE, demonstrating that one learned traffic prior can simultaneously improve motion planning and enable systematic robustness evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address two key challenges in autonomous driving: (1) improving motion planning performance by better capturing multi-modal, interaction-rich trajectory distributions, and (2) creating realistic safety-critical scenarios for stress-testing planners. The core insight is that a single diffusion model can serve dual complementary roles in the autonomous driving development loop.

Method: Three key technical contributions: (1) SSDS (Single-Stream Dual-Stream) diffusion-transformer decoder that fuses scene context via joint attention rather than late cross-attention; (2) DAPSE (Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy), a training-free guidance scheme that injects arbitrary energy functions at the clean-sample level without requiring first-order approximations or auxiliary networks; (3) Inference-time guidance to steer selected agents toward safety-critical behaviors (aggressive cut-ins, lead-vehicle braking, combined longitudinal-lateral interactions) while preserving realistic traffic behaviors.

Result: The SSDS-based planner achieves stronger nominal performance on nuPlan benchmark. However, when evaluated under the generated safety-critical scenarios, it experiences larger performance degradation than other planners. The generated scenarios successfully expose failure modes that remain hidden under standard benchmarks, demonstrating that benchmark superiority does not necessarily translate to robustness.

Conclusion: A single learned traffic prior can simultaneously improve motion planning performance and provide a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation. The work demonstrates the dual utility of diffusion models in autonomous driving development: enhancing planning capabilities while enabling comprehensive stress-testing through controllable scenario generation.

Abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models can capture the multi-modal, interaction-rich distribution of joint future trajectories in driving scenes. We show that a single pretrained diffusion traffic model can serve two complementary roles in the autonomous driving development loop: as an ego motion planner, and as a controllable generator of safety-critical scenarios for stress-testing the planners. On the planning side, we introduce a Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) diffusion-transformer decoder that fuses scene context via joint attention rather than late cross-attention, improving closed-loop performance on nuPlan. We further propose Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy (DAPSE), a training-free guidance scheme that injects arbitrary energy functions at the clean-sample level, avoiding the first-order approximation errors while requiring no auxiliary networks. Beyond planning, we leverage the same diffusion model as a controllable scenario generator to create realistic long-tail driving interactions for closed-loop evaluation. Through inference-time guidance, selected agents are steered toward safety-critical behaviors, including aggressive cut-ins, lead-vehicle braking, and combined longitudinal-lateral interactions, while preserving realistic traffic behaviors. Evaluated in closed-loop nuPlan simulations with independent black-box planners, the generated scenarios expose failure modes that remain hidden under standard benchmarks. Although the SSDS-based planner achieves stronger nominal performance, it experiences larger degradation under these challenging scenarios, demonstrating that benchmark superiority does not necessarily translate to robustness. These results demonstrate that a single learned traffic prior can simultaneously improve motion planning and provide a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation.

</details>


### [48] [LensStyle: Learning the Optical Aesthetics for Controllable Stylized Lens Effect Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04939)
*Yachuan Huang,Liwen Xiao,Liao Shen,Qiwen Wang,Huiqiang Sun,Zhiyu Pan,Zhiguo Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LensStyle is a unified framework for controllable stylized lens effect rendering that models lens aesthetics through joint continuous-discrete control, separating continuous optical parameters (focus distance, blur strength) from discrete lens-style conditioning (circular, polygonal, donut, cat-eye, starburst effects).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing lens effect rendering methods focus on simulating blur transitions but overlook stylistic aspects - they fail to produce diverse bokeh effects under large apertures or capture distinctive photographic phenomena like starbursts under small apertures.

Method: Dual-Path Controller that disentangles continuous optical parameter modulation from discrete lens-style conditioning, trained on a curated MultiLens dataset containing multi-lens image pairs synthesized under real optical constraints.

Result: Achieves superior realism, controllability, and aesthetic quality compared with existing lens effect rendering approaches and diffusion-based image editing models.

Conclusion: Advances computational photography toward multiple-lens-style simulation through a unified, physically grounded framework.

Abstract: The visual aesthetics of photographs are deeply influenced by lens characteristics such as aperture shape, optical vignetting and optical diffraction, which together define a camera's unique optical style. Existing lens effect rendering methods primarily focus on accurately simulating the blur transition from small to large apertures but overlook the stylistic aspects of lens effects. As a result, they fail to produce diverse bokeh effects under large apertures or capture distinctive photographic phenomena such as starbursts that emerge under small apertures. In this work, we introduce LensStyle, a unified framework for controllable stylized lens effect rendering that explicitly models lens aesthetics through joint continuous-discrete control. Our model incorporates a Dual-Path Controller that disentangles continuous optical parameter modulation (e.g., focus distance and blur strength) from discrete lens-style conditioning (e.g., circular, polygonal, donut, cat-eye, and starburst effects), enabling fine-grained, interpretable, and physically grounded lens manipulation within a single unified framework. To support model training, we curate a comprehensive MultiLens dataset containing multi-lens image pairs synthesized under real optical constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LensStyle achieves superior realism, controllability, and aesthetic quality compared with existing lens effect rendering approaches and diffusion-based image editing models, advancing computational photography toward multiple-lens-style simulation.

</details>


### [49] [Learning 3D Editing without Paired Supervision via Generative Prior Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04942)
*Hao Wen,Weibin Yun,Hongxing Fan,Haotian Lu,Rui Chen,Zehuan Huang,Lu Sheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes PriorEdit3D, a novel framework that learns feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision by distilling knowledge from foundation models (image editing model and VLM) into a 3D editing model via differentiable rendering, supplemented by a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization to prevent geometric collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction-guided 3D editing lacks high-quality paired training data. Existing approaches rely on slow test-time optimization or pseudo-pairs with complex pipelines, causing structural drift and geometric artifacts. The authors seek a method to learn feed-forward 3D editing without ground-truth 3D pairs.

Method: The framework uses Generative Prior Distillation with three components: (1) 2D visual prior from an image editing model at the main editing view, (2) semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model at novel views for instruction following and identity preservation, and (3) 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization in the 3D latent space using a pretrained image-to-3D teacher model to constrain outputs within realistic 3D asset manifold.

Result: The method achieves superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in extensive experiments.

Conclusion: The proposed Generative Prior Distillation approach successfully enables feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision, effectively addressing geometric collapse and multi-view inconsistency issues through the integration of visual, semantic, and geometric priors from foundation models.

Abstract: Instruction-guided 3D editing is essential for interactive content creation, yet it faces a significant bottleneck: the severe scarcity of high-quality paired training data. Existing approaches attempt to bypass this by either relying on slow test-time optimization or training on pseudo-pairs constructed via complex pipelines, which often introduce structural drift and geometric artifacts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that learns feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision via Generative Prior Distillation. Instead of relying on ground-truth 3D pairs, our core idea is to distill visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from powerful foundation models directly into a 3D editing model. Specifically, through a differentiable rendering pipeline, we supervise the 3D representation using two complementary signals: a 2D visual prior from an image editing model at the main editing view, and a semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model at novel views to ensure strict instruction following and source identity preservation. Crucially, to address the geometric collapse and multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 2D projection supervision, we introduce a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization. Acting as a geometric prior, this term operates in the 3D latent space, constraining the edited output to remain within the manifold of realistic 3D assets defined by a pretrained image to 3D teacher model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Our project is available at: https://github.com/thiamine128/PriorEdit3D.

</details>


### [50] [MCPO: Modality-Contrastive Preference Optimization for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04947)
*Guangheng Yang,Zhenliang Ni,Zhenkai Wu,Han Shu,Juan Feng,Wenming Yang,Jie Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MCPO is a two-stage method for compressing multimodal Chain-of-Thought reasoning in vision-language models. It uses step-level NCMI pruning to remove visual-independent reasoning steps, followed by asymmetric multimodal preference alignment. The method achieves 69.5% length reduction and 3.34x speedup with only 900 training samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal reasoning models with long Chains-of-Thought incur high computational costs and KV-cache pressure. Existing CoT compression methods lack fine-grained cross-modal constraints, leading to visual laziness and hallucinatory reasoning.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) Compression stage using step-level Normalized Cross-Modal Mutual Information (NCMI) pruning to identify and remove visual-independent reasoning steps by comparing with-image vs no-image contexts; (2) Alignment stage with supervised fine-tuning followed by asymmetric multimodal length-controlled preference loss using nonlinear odds-ratio formulation.

Result: Reduces CoT length by up to 69.5%, achieves 3.34x end-to-end inference speedup while preserving original accuracy, using fewer than 900 training samples.

Conclusion: MCPO provides an effective solution for compressing multimodal reasoning chains with minimal training data, addressing computational efficiency while maintaining reasoning quality through cross-modal constraint enforcement.

Abstract: Recently, multimodal large-scale reasoning models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks through long Chains-of-Thought (M-CoT). However, excessively long reasoning trajectories incur substantial computational costs and significant KV-cache pressure. Existing CoT compression and alignment paradigms mainly rely on static rules or single-dimensional preferences, lacking fine-grained cross-modal constraints; as a result, they are prone to inducing visual laziness and hallucinatory reasoning. To address these issues, we propose Modality-Contrastive Preference Optimization (MCPO), a highly sample-efficient two-stage length-compression method that requires fewer than 900 training samples. In the compression stage, we introduce a step-level Normalized Cross-Modal Mutual Information (NCMI) pruning algorithm, which automatically identifies and removes visual-independent reasoning steps by comparing the reasoning discrepancies between with-image and no-image contexts. This significantly reduces redundancy and hallucinatory content in the reasoning chains. In the alignment stage, the model first undergoes supervised fine-tuning to achieve domain-adaptive initialization, followed by optimization using an asymmetric multimodal length-controlled preference loss. This objective adopts a highly nonlinear odds-ratio formulation that provides steep gradients in the with-image context to reinforce length constraints for preferred trajectories, while applying a scaled, flat-gradient linear difference in the no-image context to maintain modality consistency, thereby achieving stable cross-modal preference alignment. Extensive experiments on mainstream base models such as Qwen3-VL-Thinking show that our method can reduce CoT length by up to 69.5% and achieve up to 3.34x end-to-end inference speedup while preserving original accuracy.

</details>


### [51] [VICAL: Vicinal Consistency Alignment for Long-Tailed Visual Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04948)
*Jiangang Zhu,Zheng Wang,Bin Zhu,Yi-Ping Phoebe Chen,Jingjing Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper challenges the common assumption that expert diversity is the key benefit of multi-expert models for long-tailed learning, and instead proposes that variance reduction is more important. The authors introduce VICAL, a framework with two components: Self-Consistency Learning and Deep Ensemble Distillation, which achieves state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors question the central assumption in multi-expert models for long-tailed learning—that diversity induced by logit adjustment or regularizers improves ensemble accuracy. They reveal through investigation that this assumption does not hold, and instead hypothesize that variance reduction is the actual benefit.

Method: The proposed VICAL framework has two key components: (1) Self-Consistency Learning, which discourages reliance on unstable high-frequency information by smoothing the local loss landscape to mitigate overfitting, especially for tail classes; (2) Deep Ensemble Distillation, which promotes cross-expert low-frequency semantic agreement using a low-resolution view, avoiding optimization conflicts with established knowledge.

Result: VICAL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018, validating the effectiveness of the consistency-driven design.

Conclusion: Multi-expert models benefit more from variance reduction than diversity maximization. The VICAL framework successfully improves long-tailed recognition by reducing prediction variance through self-consistency learning and deep ensemble distillation, rather than enforcing expert diversity.

Abstract: Multi-expert models have become the dominant paradigm for long-tailed learning, largely attributed to their presumed ability to benefit from expert diversity. However, we revisit this central assumption and reveal that diversity induced by logit adjustment or explicit regularizers does not guarantee better ensemble accuracy. Our work suggests that multi-expert models benefit more from variance reduction than diversity maximization. We introduce \textbf{VICAL}, a \textbf{VI}cinal \textbf{C}onsistency \textbf{AL}ignment framework that improves long-tailed recognition not by enforcing expert diversity, but by reducing prediction variance. Specifically, our approach comprises two key components: Self-Consistency Learning and Deep Ensemble Distillation. Self-Consistency Learning discourages reliance on unstable high-frequency information, smoothing the local loss landscape and mitigating overfitting, especially for tail classes. Deep Ensemble Distillation promotes cross-expert low-frequency semantic agreement using a low-resolution view, thereby sidestepping optimization conflicts with established knowledge. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 show that VICAL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of our consistency-driven design. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/FlamieZhu/Vicinal-Consistency-Alignment}{VICAL}.

</details>


### [52] [MINT: A Unified Model for World-Space Camera and Hand Motion Estimation from Scalable Egocentric Pipeline Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04958)
*Zijie Zhu,Weiren Cai,Yizhou Wang,Zhenjie Yang,Yide Liu,Jiahao Chen,Guanqi He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MINT is the first foundation model that directly produces complete world-space two-hand trajectories from egocentric RGB video, jointly predicting camera trajectory, hand states, and hand presence from a single shared spatiotemporal representation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing systems decompose camera and hand motion recovery into separate stages (camera motion, depth, hand reconstruction, trajectory refinement), causing computational overhead and preventing joint modeling. The scarcity of paired world-space camera and hand annotations also limits training.

Method: MINT uses a single shared spatiotemporal video representation to jointly predict camera trajectory, camera-frame hand states, and per-frame hand presence, then produces world-space hand motion via explicit coordinate transformations. Training involves pre-training on large-scale pseudo-labels generated by the EGOPIPELINE, followed by fine-tuning on high-quality annotations.

Result: MINT achieves significant improvements in world-space hand trajectory accuracy, camera trajectory estimation, and end-to-end trajectory generation speed over existing methods, while generalizing zero-shot to unseen egocentric datasets.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates that a unified foundation model can effectively solve the egocentric camera and hand motion recovery problem at scale, enabled by the EGOPIPELINE for pseudo-label generation and a curated 1,021-hour dataset.

Abstract: Recovering camera and hand motion in world coordinates from egocentric video is a key capability for activity understanding, robot learning, and augmented reality. Existing systems typically decompose this problem into separate stages for camera motion, depth, hand reconstruction, and trajectory refinement, resulting in substantial computational overhead and preventing the joint modeling of camera and hand motion. We introduce MINT (Minting IN-the-Wild Trajectories), the first foundation model that directly produces complete world-space two-hand trajectories from ego-centric RGB video. From a single shared spatiotemporal video representation, MINT jointly predicts the camera trajectory, camera-frame hand states, and per-frame hand presence, and then produces world-space hand motion via explicit coordinate transformations. Training such a model at scale is challenging, since paired world-space camera and hand annotations are scarce. We therefore develop an open-source labeling EGOPIPELINE that converts large collections of public egocentric videos into structured camera-and-hand trajectory supervision. MINT is first pretrained on these large-scale pseudo-labels and then fine-tuned on a small set of high-quality joint annotations. Across public benchmarks, MINT achieves [xxx] improvement in world-space hand trajectory accuracy, [xxx] improvement in camera trajectory estimation, and [xxx] faster end-to-end trajectory generation than the labeling pipeline, while generalizing zero-shot to unseen egocentric datasets. We release the model, training and inference code, labeling pipeline, and a curated 1,021-hour egocentric trajectory dataset.

</details>


### [53] [ARC-Loc: Leveraging Azimuthal Ray Convergence as a Geometric Cue for Direct Cross-View Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04965)
*Hyeongsik Kim,Mincheol Kim,Heejoon Moon,Je Hyeong Hong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes ARC-Loc, a novel cross-view localization method that matches ground images to satellite images using azimuthal ray convergence, eliminating the need for computationally heavy BEV transformations or external depth models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CVL methods rely on BEV transformations or 2D-to-3D lifting, which are fundamentally ill-posed from single ground images, causing geometric distortions and high computational costs. Using external depth foundation models introduces latency and noise susceptibility.

Method: The method introduces two key components: (i) A minimal Azimuthal Ray Convergence (ARC) solver that identifies intersection point of azimuthal rays translated from ground keypoints, and (ii) An ARC loss for optimizing the matching network. The approach uses direct line-to-point correspondences without external depth models.

Result: ARC-Loc achieves competitive localization accuracy on VIGOR and KITTI datasets while offering faster, memory-efficient inference due to elimination of BEV transformations and depth model dependencies.

Conclusion: The proposed ARC-Loc demonstrates that direct ground-to-satellite matching via azimuthal ray convergence is a viable alternative to complex 3D lifting approaches, achieving practical localization performance with improved efficiency and compatibility with existing frameworks.

Abstract: Cross-view localization (CVL) estimates the pose of a ground image by matching it to a geo-referenced satellite image. To bridge the extreme viewpoint gap, mainstream pipelines rely on Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) transformations or 2D-to-3D lifting. However, deriving 3D structures from a single ground image is fundamentally ill-posed, causing these methods to endure geometric distortions and computational costs during 3D lifting or BEV projection. Furthermore, relying on external depth foundation models to resolve this introduces latency and remains susceptible to noisy predictions. In this work, we present a different approach inspired by a human navigation technique called resection, that can perform direct ground to satellite image matching and localization without relying on external depth foundation models. The key insights of our method are that (i) ground keypoints can be translated into azimuthal rays on the satellite map, and (ii) these rays ideally converge at the user location. Exploiting this geometric constraint through direct line-to-point correspondences, we introduce a minimal Azimuthal Ray Convergence (ARC) solver to identify the intersection, alongside an ARC loss to optimize the matching network. By eliminating dependencies on computationally heavy BEV transformations and external depth foundation models, our approach achieves faster, memory-efficient inference, while its explicit feature matching ensures straightforward compatibility with existing frameworks. Experiments on VIGOR and KITTI demonstrate that ARC-Loc maintains competitive localization accuracy compared to recent approaches, highlighting its practicality.

</details>


### [54] [RefDiT: Local Attribute Guidance in Reference-Based Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04976)
*Rameshwar Mishra,Srikrishna Karanam,A V Subramanyam*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefDiT is a novel reference-guided image generation framework that addresses limitations in existing personalization and style transfer methods by using local region guidance instead of global-level guidance. It employs attribute-level decomposition of identifier tokens and trains LoRA blocks in a DiT-based generative model to enable more effective local guidance for complex real-world scenes with multiple objects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalization models and style transfer methods perform well on single-object reference images but fail when applied to complex scenes with multiple objects. These methods rely on global-level guidance, which cannot localize relevant elements in the reference image. Additionally, using a single identifier token results in lack of individual, attribute-level control. This work aims to enable precise local attribute control in reference-guided image generation.

Method: RefDiT uses local region guidance by decomposing identifier tokens at the attribute level. It constructs an attribute-aware conditioning signal from the reference image through attribute-level decomposition. The method performs context adjustment in the inference prompt and trains low-rank adapter (LoRA) blocks in a diffusion transformer (DiT)-based generative model to learn the correspondence between identifier tokens and local regions in the reference image.

Result: The method enables more effective local guidance by learning the correspondence between identifier tokens and local regions, allowing generation of new images based on local attributes in the reference image rather than relying on global style guidance.

Conclusion: RefDiT provides a solution for reference-guided image generation in complex scenes by introducing local region guidance through attribute-level decomposition and LoRA-based fine-tuning of DiT models. This approach enables attribute-level control over generated images, addressing the limitations of previous global-level guidance methods.

Abstract: Personalization models generate new images guided by a few subject references, while style transfer methods aim to produce images aligned with a global style derived from a reference image. Recent approaches perform well when the reference image contains a single object, effectively capturing a global style that encompasses all implicit attributes. However, when applied to complex real-world scenes containing multiple objects with distinct attribute characteristics, these methods, due to their global-level guidance, fail to localize relevant elements in the reference image. The global guidance restricts their ability to generate new images based on the local attributes in the reference image. Moreover, existing methods typically employ a single identifier token to capture all details from the reference, resulting in a lack of individual, attribute-level control. Motivated by these limitations, we propose RefDiT, a novel framework for reference-guided image generation. RefDiT takes as input a reference image, a text prompt, and an optional user-provided guidance context. RefDiT employs local region guidance using the attributes of local elements. It constructs an attribute-aware conditioning signal from the reference image by performing attribute-level decomposition of the identifier token and performs context adjustment in the inference prompt to train low-rank adapter (LoRA) blocks of a diffusion transformer (DiT)-based generative model. RefDiT learns the correspondence between identifier tokens and local regions in the reference image, enabling more effective local guidance.

</details>


### [55] [Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular Video Dynamic Human Body Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04984)
*Tianle Du,Jie Wang,Xiaolong Xie,Wei Li,Pengxiang Su,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields (TR-NeRF) for efficient dynamic human body 3D reconstruction from video sequences. The method addresses MLP limitations in capacity, training time, and computational resources by introducing a temporal residual field, parameter reduction techniques, and a multi-dimensional loss function, achieving significant improvements in PSNR and SSIM while maintaining similar accuracy to state-of-the-art methods with 780x faster rendering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLPs for human body reconstruction in static scenes face capacity limitations, requiring substantial training time and computational resources. These constraints become more significant when reconstructing dynamic scenes, where the quality of reconstruction is severely limited. There is a need for a method that can effectively process complex spatiotemporal signals in dynamic human 3D modeling while maintaining computational efficiency.

Method: The proposed method consists of three key components: 1) A temporal residual field that is independent of the MLP architecture to represent temporal signals in video sequences; 2) An integrated approach that reduces trainable parameters and accelerates rendering to improve reconstruction efficiency and enhance feature representation capability; 3) A multi-dimensional loss function to accurately measure the loss between predicted and actual spatial pixel values.

Result: The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) and SSIM (Structural Similarity Index) accuracy metrics compared to the latest representative methods. It maintains similar accuracy to Anim-NeRF and Neural Body while achieving a nearly 780-fold increase in time efficiency.

Conclusion: The Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields method successfully addresses the limitations of MLPs in dynamic scene human 3D reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art quality metrics with dramatically improved computational efficiency. The 780-fold speedup makes it practical for real-world applications while maintaining competitive accuracy with existing methods.

Abstract: In the field of computer vision and graphics, high-quality reconstruction of the human body in static scenes has been achieved in recent years by a single multilayer perceptron (MLP) in a number of approaches. However, MLPs have capacity limitations, requiring substantial training time and computational resources for dynamic scene reconstruction. And the quality of reconstruction is significantly constrained. This paper proposes a method for effectively processing complex spatiotemporal signals in dynamic scene human 3D modeling. The proposed method uses Temporal Residual Neural Radiance Fields to achieve novel view rendering and new pose synthesis of human bodies.To address the problem of representing temporal signals in video sequences, we construct a temporal residual field which is not related to the MLP architecture. Secondly, to improve reconstruction efficiency, we propose an integrated approach that reduces trainable parameters and accelerates rendering, thereby enhancing the network's feature representation capability. Finally, we design a multi-dimensional loss function to accurately measure the loss between predicted and actual spatial pixel values. The experimental results show that our proposed approach improves the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM) accuracy metrics compared to the latest representative methods. It maintains similar accuracy to Anim-NeRF and Neural Body while achieving a nearly 780-fold increase in time efficiency.

</details>


### [56] [Compositional Reward Models for Conditional Medical Image Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05028)
*Aayush Kumar Tyagi,Prathosh A. P.,Mausam*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PRISM is a novel framework for conditional medical image generation that uses a compositional reward model with hierarchical constrained propagation to decompose image quality evaluation into multiple stages (low-level attributes, structural alignment, semantic fidelity), addressing limitations of single-reward approaches in reinforcement learning fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key motivation is to overcome two major limitations in medical image generation: (1) existing conditional diffusion models fail to capture fine-grained properties (intensity, texture) and semantic consistency, and (2) prior reinforcement learning fine-tuning approaches rely on a single scalar reward that conflates diverse failure modes and provides weak corrective signals.

Method: The proposed method PRISM consists of two core components: (1) Compositional Reward Model (CRM) that decomposes image quality into verifier-grounded stages evaluating distinct aspects (low-level intensity/texture, structural alignment with conditioning inputs, high-level semantic fidelity); (2) Hierarchical Constrained Propagation (HCP) mechanism that enforces fine-to-coarse correctness, ensuring lower-level deficiencies are resolved before higher-level rewards are accrued.

Result: PRISM was evaluated on three medical imaging datasets: PanNuke (multi-class cell segmentation), CeDeM (villi/crypt detection and measurement), and ISIC (skin lesion classification). Results show: 2.3% increase in mDice on PanNuke, 8.5% reduction in Mean Relative Error (MRE) on CeDeM, and 5.9% increase in F1 score on ISIC, compared to closest baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed PRISM framework successfully improves conditional medical image generation by using a multi-stage compositional reward model with hierarchical constraint propagation. This approach prevents easier objectives from masking critical failures and provides stronger corrective signals for training downstream models, demonstrating consistent improvements across diverse medical imaging tasks.

Abstract: Acquiring high quality annotated medical image data is critical for training deep learning models; however, annotation is expensive, time consuming, and requires domain expertise. Conditional diffusion models, such as ControlNet, offer an alternative by generating images conditioned on semantic masks and text. However, existing approaches fail to capture fine grained properties (e.g., intensity and texture), as well as semantic consistency expected by domain experts, limiting their effectiveness for downstream tasks. Recent attempts to address these issues using reinforcement learning fine-tuning remain limited due to the reliance on a single scalar reward, which conflates diverse failure modes and provides weak corrective signals. We propose PRISM, a Compositional Reward Model (CRM) framework for conditional medical image generation. Instead of assigning a single reward, we decompose image quality into verifier grounded stages, each evaluating a distinct aspect of correctness from fine to coarse properties, including low level attributes (intensity and texture), structural alignment with conditioning inputs, and high level semantic fidelity. These stage wise rewards are composed through a Hierarchical Constrained Propagation (HCP) mechanism that enforces a fine to coarse notion of correctness, ensuring that lower level deficiencies are resolved before higher level rewards are accrued, preventing easier objectives from masking critical failures.
  We evaluate PRISM across three datasets spanning diverse medical imaging tasks: PanNuke (multi-class cell segmentation), CeDeM (villi/crypt detection and measurement), and ISIC (skin lesion classification). Training downstream models with data generated by PRISM yields improvements over closest baselines, including a 2.3% increase in mDice on PanNuke, a 8.5% reduction in Mean Relative Error (MRE) on CeDeM, and increases ISIC F1 by 5.9%.

</details>


### [57] [PuTR-CouT: Counting-by-Tracking in Camera-Trap Image Sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05038)
*Fagner Cunha,Juan G. Colonna,Eulanda M. dos Santos*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PuTR-CouT is a transformer-based counting-by-tracking framework for animal counting in camera trap images, using weakly supervised pseudo-tracking labels generated from structural priors (static backgrounds, short temporal bursts) to address the scarcity of annotated tracking data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Species identification in camera trap images has been widely studied, but species abundance or density estimation requires counting individual animals. The lack of counting labels and low frame rates (~1 frame per second) make sequence-level tracking and count estimation particularly challenging.

Method: 1) Generate synthetic training data by exploiting structural priors (static backgrounds, short temporal bursts) to heuristically create pseudo-tracking labels in a weakly supervised manner. 2) Build a transformer-based learned association mechanism for sequence-level animal counting. 3) Associate detections across frames using the resulting tracks to estimate per-species counts. 4) Refine the MaxBoxCount heuristic used by top solutions of iWildCam 2021 challenge.

Result: The framework delivers competitive counting results compared to the improved MaxBoxCount on the iWildCam 2021 benchmark, achieving the highest score reported to date for MaxBoxCount. It also provides multi-species predictions and track-level verification capabilities.

Conclusion: PuTR-CouT successfully addresses the challenge of individual animal counting in camera trap images through a transformer-based tracking approach with weakly supervised learning. It achieves competitive performance while offering additional capabilities like multi-species predictions and track-level verification, making it a promising solution for ecological monitoring applications.

Abstract: Species identification in camera trap images has been widely studied, but key ecological modeling tasks such as species abundance or density estimation also require counting individual animals. However, the lack of counting labels in most datasets and low frame rates (typically ~1 frame per second) make sequence-level tracking and count estimation particularly challenging. In this work, we present PuTR-CouT, a counting-by-tracking framework built on a transformer-based learned association mechanism for sequence-level animal counting in camera trap images. To address the scarcity of annotated tracking data, we generate synthetic training data by exploiting structural priors, such as static backgrounds and short temporal bursts, to heuristically create pseudo-tracking labels in a weakly supervised manner. The resulting tracker associates detections across frames, using these tracks to estimate per-species counts. We also refine the MaxBoxCount heuristic used by the top solutions of the iWildCam 2021 challenge as a strong baseline, setting the highest score reported to date. When evaluated on the iWildCam 2021 benchmark, our framework PuTR-CouT delivers competitive counting results compared to the improved MaxBoxCount, with the added capability of multi-species predictions and track-level verification.

</details>


### [58] [Efficient Multi-Timescale Event Representations for Feed-Forward Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05049)
*Fredrik Lundell,Per-Erik Forssen,Mårten Wadenbäck,Astrid Lundmark*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a confidence-normalized continuous multi-timescale representation for event cameras that encodes temporal information directly within the event representation, using logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding and a geometry-aware local confidence mechanism. When combined with a fixed feed-forward EventCenterNet detector, this approach outperforms the compact CSTR representation on PEDRo and Gen1 datasets while maintaining computational efficiency through recursive exponential-polynomial approximation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems require robust low-latency perception under rapidly changing scene dynamics and challenging illumination. Existing event camera object detection methods rely on recurrent architectures to accumulate sparse temporal information over time, which introduces latency. This work aims to encode temporal information directly within the event representation to enable efficient feed-forward detection without recurrent temporal modeling.

Method: The proposed method includes: (1) A confidence-normalized continuous multi-timescale representation using logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding; (2) A geometry-aware local confidence mechanism that exploits the spatial structure of event generation; (3) A recursive exponential-polynomial approximation for efficient event-by-event updates. The approach is evaluated using a fixed feed-forward EventCenterNet detector on PEDRo and Gen1 datasets, comparing against the compact CSTR representation.

Result: The proposed representations consistently outperform the compact CSTR representation on both PEDRo and Gen1 datasets. The recursive exponential-polynomial approximation enables efficient event-by-event updates while largely preserving detection performance. The results demonstrate that carefully designed event representations can capture a substantial portion of the temporal information typically learned through recurrent temporal modeling.

Conclusion: Carefully designed event representations can effectively capture temporal information without requiring recurrent temporal modeling. This provides a promising foundation for efficient feed-forward, event-driven, and future neuromorphic object detection systems, achieving performance comparable to recurrent approaches while maintaining the advantages of feed-forward processing.

Abstract: Autonomous systems require robust low-latency perception under rapidly changing scene dynamics and challenging illumination. In event cameras object detection commonly relies on recurrent architectures to accumulate sparse temporal information over time. This work investigates how temporal information can be encoded directly within the event representation. We propose a confidence-normalized continuous multi-timescale representation based on logarithmic B-spline temporal encoding together with a geometry-aware local confidence mechanism that exploits the spatial structure of event generation. Using a fixed feed-forward EventCenterNet detector, we show that the proposed representations consistently outperform the compact CSTR representation on PEDRo and Gen1 datasets. We further introduce a recursive exponential-polynomial approximation that enables efficient event-by-event updates while largely preserving detection performance. These results demonstrate that carefully designed event representations can capture a substantial portion of the temporal information learned through recurrent temporal modeling, providing a promising foundation for efficient feed-forward, event-driven, and future neuromorphic object detection.

</details>


### [59] [Adaptive Multi-Granularity Temporal Modeling for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05066)
*Changyi Li,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive temporal modeling framework for weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WSVAD) that addresses limitations of traditional Multiple Instance Learning approaches with rigid temporal priors. The framework consists of three key components: a Temporal Refinement Module for long-range dependency modeling, an adaptive Event Segmentation Module for boundary detection, and a similarity-based fusion strategy for multi-level predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing WSVAD methods using MIL frameworks rely on rigid, hand-crafted temporal priors to supervise anomaly scoring, which fail to adapt to the wide variation in anomaly durations and temporal dynamics in real-world videos. This leads to unstable or unreliable snippet-level predictions.

Method: The proposed framework includes three novel components: (1) Temporal Refinement Module (TRM) using dynamic positional encoding and learnable class token for long-range temporal dependencies and global representation distillation; (2) Adaptive Event Segmentation Module (ESM) that identifies event boundaries through temporal discontinuity analysis and aggregates snippet features into event-level representations; (3) Adaptive similarity-based fusion strategy that dynamically integrates anomaly scores using global semantic relevance instead of fixed top-k aggregation.

Result: The proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on two benchmark datasets for video anomaly detection.

Conclusion: The adaptive temporal modeling framework effectively addresses the limitations of traditional MIL-based WSVAD methods by explicitly accounting for variations in video dynamics across multiple temporal granularities, leading to more stable and reliable anomaly predictions.

Abstract: As the scale of video surveillance data outpaces manual annotation capacities, weakly supervised video anomaly detection (WSVAD) has emerged as a critical research frontier. Most existing approaches formulate WSVAD within a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that relies on rigid, hand-crafted temporal priors to supervise anomaly scoring. However, such formulations exhibit limited adaptability to the wide variation in anomaly durations and temporal dynamics observed in real-world videos, often leading to unstable or unreliable snippet-level predictions. To address this limitation, we propose an adaptive temporal modeling framework for WSVAD that explicitly accounts for variations in video dynamics across multiple temporal granularities. First, we introduce a Temporal Refinement Module (TRM) that leverages dynamic positional encoding and a learnable class token to model long-range temporal dependencies while distilling a stable global video-level representation. Second, to capture anomalous events with varying frequency and duration, we develop an adaptive Event Segmentation Module (ESM) that identifies event boundaries through temporal discontinuity analysis and aggregates snippet features into discriminative event-level representations. Finally, for snippet-level and event-level predictions, we propose an adaptive similarity-based fusion strategy that dynamically integrates anomaly scores into video-level predictions, replacing fixed top-k aggregation heuristics with global semantic relevance. Extensive experiments on two benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [60] [MultiAttenGastro: Multi-Dimensional Attention Augmentation for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05070)
*Sadhana Devarajan,Praveen Kumar Chandaliya,Dhruvin Jashvant Kumar Shah,Kishor Upla,Kiran Raja*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MultiAttenGastro is a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual heads for GI endoscopy classification. The first systematic cross-dataset evaluation across 8 CNN/transformer backbones on 5 public datasets (80 runs) reveals that attention effectiveness is not universal but depends on the representational gap between ImageNet pretraining and target distribution—improving 6/8 backbones on large-gap Kvasir-Capsule (98.33% macro F1), failing on small-gap Kvasir-v2 (0/8), with mixed intermediate results. Ablation shows combined heads yield positive mean effect but not statistically significant (p=0.47-0.63). CKA analysis links gains to low inter-head representational redundancy under large domain gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated GI endoscopy classification requires models that generalize across diverse modalities and class distributions, often far from natural-image (ImageNet) pretraining. The representational gap between ImageNet features and target distributions varies significantly across GI datasets, making it crucial to understand when attention mechanisms help versus hurt generalization.

Method: MultiAttenGastro: a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual attention heads. Systematic cross-dataset evaluation across 8 CNN and transformer backbones on 5 public GI datasets (80 backbone-dataset runs). Five-seed ablation on ConvNeXt-Tiny + Kvasir-Capsule. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) analysis to measure inter-head representational redundancy.

Result: MultiAttenGastro improves 6/8 backbones on Kvasir-Capsule (large gap; best macro F1 98.33%), shows 0/8 improvement on Kvasir-v2 (small gap), and mixed results on intermediate-gap datasets. Ablation shows directionally consistent but non-significant improvement (paired t: p=0.47; Wilcoxon: p=0.63). Individual heads not uniformly beneficial; only their combination yields positive mean effect. CKA reveals low inter-head redundancy under large domain gaps coincides with consistent gains, while high redundancy under small gaps coincides with losses.

Conclusion: Multi-dimensional attention helps GI endoscopy classification only when there is a large representational gap between ImageNet pretraining and target distribution, as low inter-head redundancy allows complementary attention heads to provide meaningful improvements. The framework is not a strictly superior architectural choice—its effectiveness is conditional on domain gap magnitude. The study provides evidence for when and why attention mechanisms help, rather than claiming universal superiority.

Abstract: Automated gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy classification requires models that generalize across diverse modalities and class distributions, often far from natural-image pretraining. We propose MultiAttenGastro, a plug-and-play attention framework with parallel 1-D channel, 2-D spatial, and 3-D contextual heads, and present the first systematic cross-dataset evaluation across eight CNN and transformer backbones on five public GI datasets (80 backbone--dataset runs). We find that attention effectiveness is not universal but tracks the representational gap between ImageNet features and the target distribution: MultiAttenGastro improves 6 of 8 backbones on Kvasir-Capsule (14-class WCE, large gap; best macro F1 98.33\%), is uniformly negative on the small-gap Kvasir-v2 benchmark (0/8), and shows mixed outcomes on datasets with intermediate gap. Five-seed ablation on the strongest case (Kvasir-Capsule, ConvNeXt-Tiny) shows this improvement is directionally consistent, but not statistically decisive (paired $t$: $p=0.47$; Wilcoxon: $p=0.63$), and that individual attention heads are not uniformly beneficial in isolation only their combination yields a positive mean effect. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) analysis links this pattern to representational redundancy: low inter-head CKA under large domain gaps coincides with the framework's only consistent gains, while high redundancy under small gaps coincides with its losses. We report these results, including the non-significant margins, as evidence for when and why multi-dimensional attention helps GI endoscopy classification, rather than as a claim that MultiAttenGastro is a strictly superior architectural choice.

</details>


### [61] [Training-Free Logical and Structural Anomaly Detection via Calibrated Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05091)
*Changyi Li,Miao Yu,Kai Dong,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a training-free anomaly detection method that addresses both structural (local texture) and logical (global rule violations like object count) anomalies in industrial settings. The key innovation is a "normal-set calibration" that aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues using statistics from normal images, enabling their fusion without additional training or part-level supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing anomaly detectors favor either structural or logical anomalies but not both. Training-free methods effectively use frozen representations but lack object count reasoning, while counting-based methods require category-specific component modeling. The authors aim to introduce counting ability into training-free anomaly detection without additional training or part-level supervision.

Method: The proposed method uses a normal-set calibration technique that aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues using statistics from normal images, enabling their direct fusion within a unified training-free framework. This allows combining complementary frozen cues to address both logical and structural anomalies.

Result: On MVTec-LOCO, the method achieves image-level AUROCs of 89.0 (logical) and 95.9 (structural), averaging 92.5—best among training-free detectors. It remains competitive with methods requiring network training or part annotations. On MVTec-AD, its structural variant matches PatchCore with 99.1 image-AUROC.

Conclusion: The normal-set calibration successfully introduces counting ability into training-free anomaly detection without additional training or part-level supervision. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free detectors on MVTec-LOCO and generalizes well to MVTec-AD, demonstrating that the proposed calibration approach is effective beyond logical anomaly detection.

Abstract: Industrial anomaly detection must handle two distinct defect families: structural anomalies, which manifest as local texture corruptions, and logical anomalies, which violate global rules on object count, composition, or arrangement. Existing detectors typically favor one family at the expense of the other. In particular, training-free methods effectively exploit frozen representations but lack an explicit notion of object count, while methods that reason about counts usually rely on category-specific component modeling. We show that counting ability can be introduced into training-free anomaly detection without additional training or part-level supervision. Our key idea is a normal-set calibration that aligns heterogeneous anomaly cues using statistics from normal images, enabling their direct fusion within a unified training-free framework. Built upon this calibration, our detector combines complementary frozen cues to address both logical and structural anomalies. On MVTec-LOCO, our method achieves image-level AUROCs of 89.0 and 95.9 on logical and structural anomalies, respectively, yielding a 92.5 average---the best among training-free detectors in our comparison. It remains competitive with methods requiring network training or part annotations, while its structural variant matches PatchCore on MVTec-AD (99.1 image-AUROC), suggesting that the proposed calibration generalizes beyond logical anomaly detection.

</details>


### [62] [VoxelFix: Post-Hoc Semantic Correction of Completed 3D Voxel Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05114)
*Sunesh Praveen Raja Sundarasami,Taehyoung Kim,Johannes Scherer,Tomaž Cotič,Sivasubiramaniam Subbiah,Andreas Greiner,Paul Spannaus,Sebastian Houben*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper presents a graph-based method for post-hoc correction of semantic 3D maps in aerial robotics. Instead of relying on original observations or retraining perception pipelines, the method corrects voxel labels directly from the completed map using local geometry and neighboring semantic information. Training is done on corrupted OccuFly maps simulating class confusions. The method achieves consistent mIoU improvements of 4.23-5.00 percentage points across four different 2D segmentation models, with strongest gains for tree, roof, and wall classes, and shows transferability to out-of-distribution scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semantic 3D maps are increasingly constructed automatically for aerial robotics, but errors in the perception and mapping pipeline can persist in the resulting maps, reducing reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing refinement methods have limitations (relying on original observations, treating occupancy as part of prediction, or using non-learned local regularization). This work explores whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping geometry and occupancy fixed.

Method: The authors introduce a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To generate training pairs, they corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. The method is evaluated on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models.

Result: The method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23-5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across evaluated semantic classes. Particularly strong improvements are observed for tree, roof, and wall classes. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond environments seen during training.

Conclusion: The proposed graph-based correction method can effectively recover semantic accuracy directly from completed 3D maps without modifying geometry or occupancy. The approach shows consistent improvements across different segmentation models and classes, with notable transferability to out-of-distribution aerial scenes, demonstrating practical value for improving reliability of semantic 3D maps in aerial robotics applications.

Abstract: Semantic 3D maps are increasingly constructed automatically for aerial robotics by integrating learned semantic predictions into 3D representations. While this avoids costly manual 3D annotation, errors in the perception and mapping pipeline can persist in the resulting map, reducing its reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing 3D semantic map refinement methods either rely on the original observations, treat occupancy as part of the prediction problem, or apply non-learned local regularization to completed maps. Instead, we study post-hoc semantic correction, asking whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping its geometry and occupancy fixed. We introduce \method, a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To obtain training pairs, we corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. We evaluate \method on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models. \method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23--5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across the evaluated semantic classes and particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond the environments seen during training.

</details>


### [63] [WeAgent-MMGenEdit: A Full-Stack Recipe for Multimodal Agentic Image Generation and Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05171)
*Hui Zhang,Zongkai Liu,Liqiang Niu,Juntao Liu,Han Li,Zhen Cao,Wenchao Chen,Chengduo Zhao,Fandong Meng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WeAgent-MMGenEdit is a full-stack agentic system for knowledge-intensive image generation and editing, addressing limitations in existing methods by combining retrieval tools with visual verification, persistent evidence management, and post-training on a large-scale dataset of 23K supervised trajectories and 14.7K RL tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current image generation and editing models fail when prompts require external world knowledge because they rely on bounded and long-tail parametric knowledge. Existing agentic methods have limitations including insufficient visual verification, overloaded policy models, and weak integration of retrieved textual and visual evidence.

Method: The system includes: (1) WeAgent-Harness - a multimodal runtime with persistent evidence management and dedicated verification/integration tools; (2) A scalable pipeline for prompt synthesis and agentic trajectory collection producing 23K supervised trajectories and 14.7K RL tasks with three-layer verifiable checklists; (3) WeBench-MMGenEdit - a bilingual benchmark for knowledge-intensive image generation and multi-image editing; (4) Two-sided post-training recipe using SFT and RL to improve both agent policy and image backend.

Result: WeAgent-MMGenEdit enables a 30B-total/3B-active policy to outperform similarly sized policy models and approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.

Conclusion: The full-stack approach combining multimodal harness, scalable data construction, comprehensive benchmarking, and post-training methods successfully enables smaller models to achieve performance comparable to much larger agents in knowledge-intensive image generation and editing tasks.

Abstract: Image generation and editing models have advanced rapidly, yet remain unreliable when prompts require external world knowledge. Bounded and long-tail parametric knowledge prevents direct or reason-then-generate approaches from recovering the required facts and visual appearances. Existing agentic generation and editing methods mitigate this limitation with retrieval tools, yet remain constrained by insufficient visual verification, overloaded policy models, and weak integration of retrieved textual and visual evidence. To address these limitations, we present WeAgent-MMGenEdit, a full-stack recipe including a multimodal harness, a scalable data construction pipeline, a comprehensive benchmark, and post-training methods for the agent policy and image backend. We first introduce WeAgent-Harness, a multimodal runtime with persistent evidence management and dedicated verification and integration tools that organize retrieved multimodal evidence into a dense carrier. Upon this, we develop a scalable pipeline for prompt synthesis and agentic trajectory collection, yielding 23K supervised trajectories and 14.7K RL tasks with three-layer verifiable checklists. We further introduce WeBench-MMGenEdit, a bilingual benchmark covering both knowledge-intensive image generation and multi-image editing. Finally, a two-sided post-training recipe based on SFT and RL improves the agent policy and image backend. Together, WeAgent-MMGenEdit enables a 30B-total/3B-active policy to outperform similarly sized policy models and approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.

</details>


### [64] [SMILE: Self-Explainable Multimodal Information Bottleneck for Medical Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05174)
*Yuqing Yang,Alexander Schmatz,Zhaozhao Ma,Changkyu Choi,Robert Jenssen,Shujian Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a self-explainable multimodal diagnosis method using the information bottleneck (IB) framework. The approach jointly optimizes predictive performance and modality-specific explainability by identifying the most informative elements within each modality. It uses matrix-based Renyi's α-order entropy functional for tractable optimization, and demonstrates strong performance on medical datasets, including a 9.1 percentage point accuracy improvement on the iCTCF dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current explainability methods in healthcare are mostly post-hoc and designed for unimodal data, which limits their applicability in multimodal diagnostic settings that are increasingly prevalent in clinical practice.

Method: The paper formulates self-explainable multimodal diagnosis within the information bottleneck (IB) framework. It proposes a unified learning paradigm that jointly optimizes predictive performance and modality-specific explainability. The method identifies the most informative elements inside each modality that contribute to diagnostic decisions. To enable tractable and stable optimization, a matrix-based Renyi's α-order entropy functional is employed under the assumption of sufficiently expressive encoders.

Result: The proposed method consistently achieves strong diagnostic performance across representative medical datasets spanning heterogeneous modalities. Notably, it achieves an absolute accuracy improvement of 9.1 percentage points on the iCTCF dataset. The learned explanations provide transparent and modality-aware insights into feature relevance, improving both explainability and generalization.

Conclusion: The proposed IB-based framework enables effective self-explainable multimodal diagnosis, achieving superior accuracy while providing modality-aware explanations that improve transparency and generalization in medical AI systems.

Abstract: Explainability is increasingly seen as a crucial requirement in AI-based medical diagnosis, particularly in safety-critical clinical decision-making. Most existing explainability methods in healthcare operate in a post-hoc manner and are predominantly designed for unimodal data, which limits their applicability in increasingly prevalent multimodal diagnostic settings. This paper addresses the problem of self-explainable multimodal diagnosis by formulating it within the information bottleneck (IB) framework. We propose a unified learning paradigm that jointly optimizes predictive performance and modality-specific explainability by identifying the most informative elements inside each modality that contribute to diagnostic decisions. To enable tractable and stable optimization, we employ a matrix-based Renyi's $α$-order entropy functional under the assumption of sufficiently expressive encoders. Extensive experiments on representative medical datasets spanning heterogeneous modalities demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves strong diagnostic performance, including an absolute accuracy improvement of 9.1 percentage points on the iCTCF dataset. Moreover, the learned explanations provide transparent and modality-aware insights into feature relevance, thereby improving both the explainability and generalization.

</details>


### [65] [Conserved Immune Topology Improves Pathology Foundation Model Generalization for Cross-Cancer MSI-H Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05182)
*Dasari Naga Raju*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CIT proposes a lightweight spatial representation called Conserved Immune Topology that augments pathology foundation model embeddings with biologically motivated immune descriptors to enable cross-cancer MSI-H prediction without requiring annotations or target-domain data. The method identifies immune-associated tiles via unsupervised clustering and encodes immune-related structures (tertiary lymphoid structures, peritumoral immune reactions, TIL density, immune-tumor mixing) from frozen embeddings and tile coordinates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pathology foundation models with MIL achieve good accuracy within single-cancer cohorts but fail to generalize across cancers due to organ-specific histological and architectural differences. There is a need for organ-invariant representations that can transfer across different cancer types.

Method: CIT uses unsupervised clustering to identify immune-associated tiles from foundation-model embeddings, then encodes four biologically motivated immune descriptors: (1) tertiary lymphoid structures, (2) peritumoral immune reactions, (3) multi-scale tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, and (4) immune-tumor mixing. These are computed from frozen foundation-model embeddings and tile coordinates without requiring annotations or target-domain data. Evaluated under zero-shot cross-cancer transfer settings.

Result: Zero-shot cross-cancer transfer with CIT increased TransMIL AUC from 0.6627 to 0.7161, an absolute gain of 0.0534 (p=0.003). Consistent improvements were observed across all three MIL aggregators tested. The method was evaluated on CPTAC-COAD and TCGA-STAD cohorts, which introduce scanner variability, distribution shifts, and organ-specific architectural variations.

Conclusion: Spatial immune topology provides a potentially organ-invariant representation for MSI-H prediction, enabling cross-cancer generalization of pathology foundation models. This suggests immune-related spatial features are conserved across different cancer types and can serve as domain-invariant biomarkers.

Abstract: Pathology foundation models integrated with multiple instance learning achieve competitive accuracy within single-cancer cohorts, yet cross-cancer generalization remains unresolved due to organ-specific histological and architectural differences. In this paper, we propose Conserved Immune Topology (CIT), a lightweight spatial representation for cross-cancer MSI-H prediction that augments foundation-model embeddings with biologically motivated immune descriptors. CIT uses unsupervised clustering to identify immune-associated tiles, then encodes tertiary lymphoid structures, peritumoral immune reactions, multi-scale tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, and immune-tumor mixing from frozen foundation-model embeddings and tile coordinates without requiring annotations or target-domain data. The proposed method was evaluated under cross-site and cross-cancer settings using CPTAC-COAD and TCGA-STAD cohorts, which introduce scanner variability, distribution shifts, and organ-specific architectural variations. Zero-shot cross-cancer transfer with CIT increased TransMIL AUC from 0.6627 to 0.7161, an absolute gain of 0.0534 (p=0.003), with consistent improvements across all three MIL aggregators. These results suggest that spatial immune topology provides potentially an organ-invariant representation for MSI-H prediction, supporting cross-cancer generalization of pathology foundation models.

</details>


### [66] [BLASt3R: Bundle Adjustment of Any Image Set with Multi-View Matching and Monocular Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05210)
*Vincent Leroy,Philippe Weinzaepfel,Lojze Zust,Yohann Cabon,Jérome Revaud*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a regularized Bundle Adjustment (BA) framework that combines a fast multi-view matcher with monocular priors to support both online Visual SLAM (VSLAM) and offline reconstruction from unordered image collections within a unified optimization framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hybrid SfM systems, while accurate, suffer from high computational costs due to dense correspondence estimation, making them impractical for time-critical online applications like VSLAM. There is a need for a more scalable and efficient approach that maintains accuracy while enabling real-time performance.

Method: The authors introduce a regularized BA framework that leverages: (1) a fast multi-view matcher for correspondence estimation, and (2) monocular priors for initialization and regularization. This unified approach supports both online VSLAM and offline reconstruction tasks with shared hyperparameters.

Result: Extensive experiments across both VSLAM and offline reconstruction domains demonstrate improved performance and speed tradeoffs over traditional, feed-forward, and hybrid baselines. Notably, the uncalibrated VSLAM method outperforms all previous calibrated approaches.

Conclusion: The proposed regularized BA framework successfully bridges the gap between online VSLAM and offline reconstruction, achieving superior performance with better speed/accuracy tradeoffs. The ability to use uncalibrated methods in VSLAM while surpassing calibrated approaches represents a significant advancement in practical 3D reconstruction systems.

Abstract: Recent hybrid Structure-from-Motion (SfM) systems combine the robustness of feed-forward 3D reconstruction with the accuracy of traditional bundle adjustment (BA) with pixel matching. They are usually the best performing methods however their scalability and usability remains limited since estimating dense correspondences between views is prohibitively costly, especially considering time constraints inherent to online applications like Visual SLAM (VSLAM). In this paper, we introduce a regularized BA framework that leverages a fast multi-view matcher and monocular priors for initialization and regularization. In contrast to existing systems, our unified approach seamlessly supports both online VSLAM and offline reconstruction from unordered image collections within the same optimization framework and sharing common hyperparameters for all tasks. Extensive experiments across both domains demonstrate improved performance and speed tradeoffs over traditional, feed-forward, and hybrid baselines. Notably for VSLAM, our uncalibrated method outperforms all previous calibrated approaches.

</details>


### [67] [First Things First: Teaching LLM-Based Agents to Prioritize Must-Haves before Nice-to-Haves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05224)
*Tianjie Ju,Xinyue Xu,Wanxuan Sun,Lingxiao Diao,Gongshen Liu,Zhuosheng Zhang,Cheng Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses a critical gap in MLLM agents: their inability to handle complex, structured user requirements with multiple priority levels. It proposes FTF-rl, a reinforcement learning approach that explicitly optimizes reasoning over multi-priority requirements, achieving substantial improvements across real-world service scenarios and reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs excel at general tasks but fail when asked to fulfill complex, structured requirements - a common real-world scenario. The authors identify three distinct requirement scenarios that reflect realistic service applications, revealing catastrophic failures in existing models when dealing with must-have vs. nice-to-have requirements and appropriate abstention.

Method: The authors evaluate state-of-the-art MLLMs on 3,649 carefully constructed problems across e-commerce, booking, and map-based/ride-hailing scenarios. They then propose First Things First Reinforcement Learning (FTF-rl), which explicitly optimizes reasoning over multi-priority user requirements by prioritizing must-have constraints before considering nice-to-have preferences.

Result: Existing MLLMs exhibit catastrophic failures: they misinterpret task requirements, violate must-have requirements, and produce invalid solutions across all three scenarios. FTF-rl substantially improves task success rate compared to strong baselines, and demonstrates general effectiveness on logical and mathematical reasoning tasks including LogicVista, MathVision, and InfoQA.

Conclusion: Enhancing requirement-aware reasoning capability provides a simple yet effective pathway to improve generalization of MLLM agents. The work suggests that explicitly modeling requirement priorities is crucial for deploying MLLMs as autonomous agents in real-world service applications.
