TL;DR: A systematic review of 66 peer-reviewed studies (2023-March 2026) on LLMs for HVAC operations finds the field is still nascent, with no studies ready for industry adoption. LLMs show promise as semantic/workflow layers rather than autonomous controllers, with near-term potential in point-name normalization, document-grounded operator support, and BEM workflow assistance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building automation systems generate rich sensor data but remain insight-poor due to heterogeneous point naming, missing metadata, and fragmented documentation. This review addresses the need to understand LLMs' current capabilities and readiness for HVAC operations.

Method: Systematic review analyzing 66 peer-reviewed studies, classified across five application families and three LLM method families. Assessed evidence realism, deployment readiness, and responsibility boundaries between LLMs and physical HVAC decisions.

Result: Corpus concentrated in building energy modelling (BEM, 32/66 papers). Only 4 studies reached pilot-level evidence; none reported sustained operational deployment. 63 studies classified as research-only, 3 near-term, 0 ready-now. Conventional ML, MPC, RL, and ontology-based tools remain more adopted for high-frequency control and numerical forecasting.

Conclusion: LLMs should primarily serve as semantic and workflow layers rather than autonomous HVAC controllers. Near-term potential exists in bounded human-in-the-loop applications: point-name normalization, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance, and advisory interfaces around physics-based controllers. Future work should prioritize field-validated benchmarks, orchestration evaluation under operational constraints, and LLM-MPC/RL architectures with bounded latency and verifiable safety properties.

Abstract: Building automation systems generate rich sensor data yet remain insight-poor because heterogeneous point naming, missing metadata, and fragmented documentation obstruct their operational use. This systematic review analyses and codes 66 peer-reviewed studies on large language models (LLMs) for HVAC operations published between 2023 and March 2026. Each study is classified across five application families and three LLM method families and assessed for evidence realism, deployment readiness, and the responsibility boundary between the LLM and physical HVAC decisions. The corpus is concentrated in building energy modelling (BEM, 32 of 66 papers), while load forecasting remains too sparse for subfield-level conclusions. Only four studies reach pilot-level evidence, and none reports sustained operational deployment. No study was classified as ready-now for industry adoption; three were near-term and 63 research-only. Nevertheless, several bounded, human-in-the-loop uses merit near-term trials, including point-name normalisation, document-grounded operator support, BEM workflow assistance, and advisory interfaces around physics-based controllers. Conventional machine learning (ML), model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning (RL) and ontology-based tools remain more adopted for high-frequency control, short-horizon numerical forecasting, and well-posed ontology mapping, while autonomous agentic operation and unvalidated occupant proxies remain research-stage. Current evidence therefore supports LLMs primarily as semantic and workflow layers rather than autonomous HVAC controllers. Future work should prioritise field-validated benchmarks, orchestration evaluation under operational constraints, and LLM-MPC/RL architectures with bounded latency and verifiable safety properties.

</details>


### [180] [LLM-Driven Algorithm Design for Quantum Circuit Synthesis based on Binary Decision Diagrams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05327)
*Yoonju Sim,Federico Berto,Chuanbo Hua,Jinkyoo Park,Changhyun Kwon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents QuantumEvo, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to generate QCC-aware BDD variable ordering heuristics for reversible quantum circuit synthesis. The discovered heuristic HGA-QE achieves 70.9% tie-or-win rate against baselines and is strictly best on 13.5% of benchmark functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current BDD-based reversible circuit synthesis relies on variable ordering heuristics that minimize BDD size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). There is a need for ordering heuristics that directly optimize for QCC rather than BDD size.

Method: The proposed QuantumEvo framework uses an LLM as a heuristic generator that searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic HGA-QE modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm to better align with QCC.

Result: HGA-QE achieves a 70.9% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline across the benchmark set, and is strictly best on 13.5% of the functions. The heuristic shows clearer relative advantage in strict wins on benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

Conclusion: The evolutionary approach with LLM-generated heuristics successfully discovers QCC-aware ordering heuristics that outperform traditional BDD-size-based methods. The results demonstrate that directly optimizing for quantum cost yields better synthesis outcomes, with the approach showing particularly strong performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

Abstract: Quantum circuits are central to implementing quantum algorithms on quantum devices, where quantum gates must be reversible. Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Existing ordering heuristics commonly minimize BDD size because it is closely tied to the circuit size. However, BDD size is an imperfect proxy for the quantum cost of the synthesized circuit (QCC). We propose \texttt{QuantumEvo}, an evolutionary framework that uses an LLM as a heuristic generator for QCC-aware BDD variable ordering. Instead of predicting orderings directly, \texttt{QuantumEvo} searches over ordering heuristics initialized from multiple heuristic families. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. The discovered heuristic, HGA-QE, modifies the sifting step inside a genetic algorithm so that the procedure is better aligned with QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

</details>


### [181] [Technical Manual for a Toolkit for Measuring Contextual Individuation in Transformer Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05333)
*José Luciano Verçosa Marques,Frederico Jorge Heitmann,Daniel Omar Perez,Marcelo Vinicius de Paula,Tárcio André dos Santos Barros*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper documents an open-source toolkit for testing whether transformer language models distinguish word senses based on context. The core innovation is the "bridge form" construct - a single word that appears unchanged across different subject domains with different meanings. The toolkit provides a complete pipeline for corpus acquisition, representation extraction, and analysis, while explicitly addressing methodological failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The belief that transformer models individuate word occurrences by context in later layers (despite using context-independent embeddings at the input layer) had not been cleanly tested. Existing approaches lacked a controlled way to hold word form fixed while varying context and intended sense. This work addresses the need for a rigorous methodological framework to test contextual word sense representation in transformers.

Method: The paper describes a complete pipeline: (1) Declarative specification of bridge forms and source domains, (2) Corpus acquisition from Wikipedia, (3) Occurrence localization, (4) Layer-wise representation extraction from transformer models, (5) Domain-pairwise silhouette measurement for assessing separation in representation space, and (6) Paired visualization protocol. Each stage is designed to avoid specific methodological pitfalls including sense contamination, multi-group bias, subword-tokenization misalignment, and axis-comparability artifacts.

Result: This is a methodological reference paper - no empirical results are reported. The toolkit, source code, and corpora are archived separately with persistent identifiers for use by other researchers.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous methodological framework for investigating how transformer models represent word senses across different contexts. By providing a well-documented toolkit with explicit attention to methodological failure modes, the authors enable future studies to produce and interpret empirical results about contextual word sense representation in a controlled, reproducible manner.

Abstract: A transformer language model assigns a single, context-independent vector to a word type at its embedding layer, yet is widely believed to individuate that word's occurrences by context in its later layers. Testing this belief cleanly requires a construct that holds the word form fixed while its context and intended sense vary in a controlled, labeled way. This manual documents an open toolkit built around such a construct, which we call a bridge form: a single written word that recurs, unchanged, across two or more subject domains with a different sense in each. We describe, and justify, every stage of the pipeline: the declarative specification of bridge forms and their source domains, corpus acquisition from Wikipedia, occurrence localization, layer-wise representation extraction, a domain-pairwise silhouette measurement of separation in the model's representation space, and a paired visualization protocol. Each design choice is presented together with the methodological failure mode it is meant to avoid (sense contamination from overly broad category labels, the multi-group bias of the silhouette coefficient, subword-tokenization misalignment, and axis-comparability artifacts in dimensionality-reduced plots, among others). This manuscript is a methodological and implementation reference: it does not report or interpret empirical outcomes of running the toolkit on any particular model or bridge-form set. The toolkit, its full source, and the corpora used to exercise it are archived separately (Section 9) under a persistent identifier, and are intended to be cited as an instrument by studies that use it to produce and interpret empirical results.

</details>


### [182] [Does Your Agent's Memory Survive a Model Upgrade? A Controlled Study of Memory Portability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05339)
*Ankit Goyal,Jaideep Ray*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates memory migration failures when AI agents upgrade to new models. It compares four memory preservation approaches (long-context reading, RAG, compressed notes, and knowledge graphs) across 48 synthetic test cases using two open-weight models. The study finds that fixed-schema knowledge graphs are most robust to model changes, while compressed notes show severe model coupling. The research emphasizes the need for direction-specific migration testing, embedding space isolation, and retention of raw source histories for successful memory repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical but overlooked problem: AI agents can "forget" even when their memory store is preserved intact during model upgrades. This occurs because new models may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions break retrieval, and repair may fail without original evidence. The authors aim to systematically compare different memory storage approaches to understand which can reliably transfer knowledge across model changes.

Method: The study uses 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes and exact scoring. Two open-weight models with sub-10 billion parameters were tested. Four memory approaches were compared: (1) LC-RAW - preserving history verbatim for long-context reading; (2) RAG - dividing history into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation; (3) NOTES - compressing history into natural-language notes via a model; and (4) KG-fixed - normalizing history into a fixed-schema knowledge graph. The authors measured accuracy changes after "writer swaps" (migrating from one model to another) and performed diagnostic decomposition to attribute deficits to specific failure modes.

Result: Key findings include: (1) KG-fixed is most robust, with accuracy changing only +0.0004 ± 0.0020 after writer swap; (2) NOTES shows high model coupling, with accuracy shifting asymmetrically by +9.91 or -13.28 percentage points depending on migration direction; (3) RAG partial migration (50/50 mixed index) captures only 4.96-point improvement vs. 11.90-point gain from full re-embedding; (4) Diagnostic decomposition shows 80% (0.467 ± 0.014) of NOTES deficit stems from information lost during initial construction, while 81% (0.364 ± 0.012) of RAG deficit is due to retrieval failures; (5) Store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach 90% performance recovery in all 48 cases, but retaining raw source history enables recovery in 34/48 cases.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate that memory migration is fundamentally different from model upgrades and requires specialized treatment. The research establishes three practical requirements: (1) direction-specific migration testing must be conducted in both migration directions; (2) strict embedding space isolation should be enforced, avoiding mixed embedding versions; and (3) source histories must be retained to enable memory repair. Fixed-schema structures like knowledge graphs transfer most reliably across model changes, while compressed notes are highly vulnerable to model-specific degradation. The study provides empirical guidance for building robust memory systems that can survive model upgrades.

Abstract: Model upgrades are routine; memory migrations are not. An agent can keep the same memory store and still forget: a new model may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions may break retrieval, and repair may fail without the original evidence. We compare memory as the same history is preserved verbatim for long-context reading (LC-RAW), divided into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), compressed by a model into natural-language notes (NOTES), or normalized into a fixed-schema knowledge graph (KG-fixed). The study uses 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes, exact scoring, and two open-weight models with sub 10 billion parameters.
  Our measurements show that fixed-schema structures transfer reliably, with KG-fixed accuracy changing by only $+0.0004 \pm 0.0020$ following a writer swap. Conversely, compressed NOTES exhibit high model coupling, with accuracy shifting asymmetrically by $+9.91$ or $-13.28$ percentage points depending on the specific migration direction. In RAG systems, partial embedding migrations using a 50/50 mixed index capture only a 4.96-point accuracy improvement, forfeiting the majority of the 11.90-point gain achieved through full re-embedding. Diagnostic decomposition attributes 80% ($0.467 \pm 0.014$) of the NOTES accuracy deficit to information lost during initial construction, whereas retrieval failures drive 81% ($0.364 \pm 0.012$) of the RAG deficit. Finally, store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach a 90% performance recovery target in all 48 test cases, whereas retaining the raw source history enables successful recovery in 34 of 48 cases for one tested direction. These findings highlight the necessity of direction-specific migration testing, strict embedding space isolation, and the retention of source histories for memory repair.

</details>


### [183] [Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05346)
*Rayed AlGhamdi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study investigates how students interpret and respond to AI-generated feedback when explicitly told that ChatGPT (rather than a human instructor) produced the evaluation and score. Through qualitative analysis of reflections from 13 male computing students in a Saudi Arabian university, the research identifies four themes: feedback usefulness, awareness of AI limitations, conditional trust distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority, and reflection on the instructor's institutional role. The key finding reveals students view AI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but maintain that human instructors should hold evaluative authority for grading decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and student perceptions of its usefulness, there is limited understanding of how students interpret AI-mediated evaluation when explicitly informed that an AI system (rather than a human instructor) produced the feedback and score. This gap is significant as instructors increasingly adopt AI tools for assessment feedback.

Method: Qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task. Submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with task objectives. Students were explicitly informed that ChatGPT generated the score and feedback, then invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Data was analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.

Result: Four themes emerged: (1) perceived usefulness of feedback; (2) awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; (3) conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and (4) reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions.

Conclusion: The study identifies a distinction between "feedback utility" and "evaluative authority" - two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale. Students find AI feedback useful for certain tasks (surface-level revision) but believe human instructors should retain authority over grading decisions, highlighting the importance of maintaining human oversight in AI-mediated assessment contexts.

Abstract: The integration of GenAI tools into higher education assessment raises important questions about how students understand, interpret, and respond to AI-mediated evaluation. As instructors increasingly explore AI tools for providing feedback, prior research has examined whether GenAI-generated feedback improves writing performance and how students perceive its usefulness; comparatively little is known, however, about how students interpret such evaluation when they are explicitly informed that an AI system, rather than a human instructor, produced the feedback and the score. This study reports findings from a qualitative pedagogical inquiry conducted in an undergraduate technical communication course for computing students at a Saudi public university. Thirteen male undergraduate computing students completed an in-class handwritten writing task; the scanned submissions were evaluated by ChatGPT using a rubric-based prompt aligned with the task objectives. Students were then explicitly informed that ChatGPT had generated the score and feedback and were invited to reflect on the evaluation in writing. Inductive thematic analysis of these reflections identified four themes: perceived usefulness of feedback; awareness of AI's contextual and pedagogical limitations; conditional trust, distinguishing feedback utility from evaluative authority; and reflection on the institutional and pedagogical role of the human instructor. Participants accepted GenAI feedback as useful for surface-level revision but consistently positioned the human instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions. The study identifies this as a distinction between feedback utility and evaluative authority, two judgments that students treat as analytically separate rather than as opposite ends of a single approval scale...

</details>


### [184] [CUA-Universe: A Scalable and Dynamic Environment for Hybrid GUI+CLI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05374)
*Haoting Shi,Wenhao Wang,Weicheng Fang,Yaozhong Liang,Tian Jin,Pengxiang Zhao,Guangyi Liu,Siheng Chen,Yanfeng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CUA-Universe is a scalable pipeline that transforms real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments for training computer-use agents. It includes App-Forge (application adaptation), Task-Weave (task synthesis), and Path-Steer (trajectory optimization). Training on harvested data improves both success rate and efficiency across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents rely mostly on GUI interactions, producing inefficient trajectories. Real-world work requires both GUI (visual-state inspection) and CLI (precise, high-throughput commands). Existing agents struggle to use both modalities complementarily, and scalable hybrid environments are scarce due to manual engineering requirements.

Method: CUA-Universe comprises three components: (1) App-Forge adapts real applications into reproducible VMs with discovered/wrapped/generated CLI surfaces, scaling to 16 applications; (2) Task-Weave synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty from reusable operations over seed files; (3) Path-Steer steers rollouts along efficient hybrid paths and harvests verified trajectories for post-training.

Result: 9B model trained on this data shows significant improvements: CUA-Verse (Score +39.3 pts; -37% steps, -60% tokens), OSWorld (SR +16.8 pts; -57% steps, -44% tokens), OSWorld-MCP (Score +7.84 pts; -27% steps, -30% tokens). Behavior shifts from inefficient GUI interaction and brittle CLI scripting toward effective GUI+CLI orchestration.

Conclusion: CUA-Universe provides a scalable path toward more capable and efficient computer-use agents by enabling hybrid GUI+CLI training data generation across multiple real applications.

Abstract: Computer-use agents have advanced on benchmarks like OSWorld and AndroidWorld, but still act mostly through the GUI, often producing inefficient trajectories. Real-world computer work is hybrid, combining visual-state inspection with precise, high-throughput command-line operations, so capable agents must coordinate both modalities over shared application state. Yet scalable hybrid environments remain scarce because supporting both GUI and CLI over real applications typically requires substantial manual engineering for each application. Existing agents also struggle to use the two interfaces complementarily: CLI-native agents lack visual perception for tasks involving interface state or layout, while GUI-native agents are inefficient for operations better executed through commands. We introduce CUA-Universe, a scalable environment-to-data pipeline that turns real desktop software into hybrid GUI+CLI environments. App-Forge adapts applications into reproducible VMs and command-line surfaces it discovers, wraps, or generates, scaling to 16 applications; Task-Weave synthesizes diverse hybrid tasks of controllable difficulty from reusable operations over seed files; and Path-Steer steers rollouts along efficient hybrid paths and harvests verified trajectories for post-training. Training on this data shifts behavior from inefficient GUI interaction and brittle CLI scripting toward effective GUI+CLI orchestration. Our 9B model improves both success and efficiency on CUA-Verse (Score +39.3 pts; -37% steps, -60% tokens), OSWorld (SR +16.8 pts; -57% steps, -44% tokens), and OSWorld-MCP (Score +7.84 pts; -27% steps, -30% tokens). CUA-Universe provides a scalable path toward more capable and efficient computer-use agents.

</details>


### [185] [Molecular Déjà Vu: Digit-Level Retrieval of Published Values in Frontier Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05381)
*Matthias Busch,Marius Tacke,Sviatlana V. Lamaka,Mikhail L. Zheludkevich,Christian J. Cyron,Roland C. Aydin,Christian Feiler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers audited 22 frontier LLMs on 12 molecular property regression benchmarks for verbatim retrieval (memorization of published values). They found retrieval is widespread but benchmark-specific, with reasoning level significantly affecting retrieval behavior (89% more flags at higher reasoning levels). Suppressing retrieval changes the relative error distribution between models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM accuracy metrics on molecular property benchmarks cannot distinguish between genuine property prediction and verbatim retrieval of published values, making it difficult to assess true model capabilities.

Method: Audited 22 frontier LLMs on 12 regression benchmarks at two reasoning levels, tested methods to interrupt retrieval in contaminated cases, and analyzed how retrieval suppression affects prediction error distributions across models.

Result: Verbatim retrieval is widespread but benchmark-specific: >50% of LLMs show retrieval on five datasets, but only isolated cells in others. Higher reasoning levels flag 89% more retrieval than lower levels. Strongest models still recognize transformed SMILES with original labels. Suppressing retrieval moves models closer together in relative error terms.

Conclusion: General predictive capability of LLMs is not determined solely by memorized values. The work provides the first comprehensive overview of verbatim retrieval depth in molecular regression benchmarks, highlighting the need to distinguish between retrieval and genuine prediction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on molecular property benchmarks, but accuracy cannot distinguish a model that predicts a property from one that retrieves a published number. We audit 22 frontier models on 12 regression benchmarks for verbatim retrieval and find that it is widespread but relatively benchmark-specific: on five datasets more than $50\%$ of the LLMs show verbatim retrieval, while on the remaining datasets it appears only in isolated cells. We run our experiments at two reasoning levels and find that reasoning changes retrieval. The same experiments, on the same molecules and with the same prompt, are flagged $89\%$ more often at the higher reasoning level than at the lowest one. Finally, we test a way to interrupt retrieval in our most contaminated cases, and find that the strongest models in some cases still recognise a combination of transformed SMILES strings and original labels. Furthermore, suppressing retrieval moves the prediction errors of the different models closer together in relative terms, while their differing use of verbatim retrieval spreads them apart. This indicates that the general predictive capability of an LLM is not determined solely by the amount of memorised values. This work provides an overview of the amount and depth of verbatim retrieval in molecular regression benchmarks using LLMs.

</details>


### [186] [Necessary or Sufficient? Evaluating LLM Explanations With Behavioural Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05385)
*Urja Pawar,Rajitha Ramanayake,Nabeel Kemal,Ashwin Kandath,Owen O'Neill,Guillaume Bourgeon,Houssem Chatbri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether LLM-provided explanations for their decisions actually reflect the model's decision behavior. The authors test two interpretations of factors cited by LLMs (necessity and sufficiency) through black-box interventions across eight models. They find moderate correlations but significant unreliability: cited factors often don't correspond to the most influential ones in practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM decision components in agent workflows provide explanations alongside their recommendations. Operators rely on these explanations for monitoring, diagnostics, and escalation decisions. However, there's no guarantee that the cited factors actually correspond to the model's real decision-making behavior. This creates a potential oversight risk where human operators may make incorrect assumptions about why the LLM made a particular decision.

Method: The authors use black-box interventions across two synthetic use cases (advisor recommendation and prompt harmfulness judgment). They evaluate necessity (how often changing a factor changes the output) and sufficiency (how often retaining a factor preserves the output) by measuring output changes under controlled interventions. They compare these measured scores against the LLM's own cited rankings of the top three influential factors.

Result: Across eight models (Claude, GPT, Gemini families), mean Spearman correlations between cited rankings and measured scores were 0.349 (necessity) and 0.354 (sufficiency) for advisor recommendation, and 0.431 (necessity) and 0.580 (sufficiency) for prompt monitoring. An uncited factor exceeded the lowest-scoring cited factor in 57.6% of advisor responses under necessity and 58.1% under sufficiency; corresponding rates for prompt monitoring were 25.8% and 8.9%.

Conclusion: The cited top three factors contain useful information but do not reliably identify the three factors with the strongest measured influence under necessity or sufficiency. The framework provides a black-box reliability check for explanations used in agent oversight, though it remains scoped to individual LLM decisions. This highlights a significant limitation in relying on LLM-provided explanations for operational oversight.

Abstract: LLM decision components that can operate within agent workflows often produce action-relevant recommendations or judgements together with explanations. Operators may use the named factors to monitor a system, diagnose errors, or decide when to escalate an output. Such use assumes that the explanations agree with the component's observable decision behaviour. We test two interpretations of the named factors: necessity, meaning that changing a factor would change the output, and sufficiency, meaning that retaining it while removing other changeable information would preserve the output. We evaluate these interpretations in two synthetic use cases: recommending advisors to clients and judging prompts for harmfulness or risk. Models return an output and the top three factors that most influenced it. Controlled black-box interventions estimate a necessity score for each factor by measuring how often changing it changes the output, and a sufficiency score by measuring how often retaining it preserves the output. Across eight models from the Claude, GPT, and Gemini families, the mean Spearman correlations between the cited ranking and the necessity and sufficiency scores are 0.349 and 0.354 for advisor recommendation, and 0.431 and 0.580 for prompt monitoring. Furthermore, an uncited factor scores above the lowest-scoring cited factor in 57.6% of advisor responses under necessity and 58.1% under sufficiency; the corresponding prompt-monitoring rates are 25.8% and 8.9%. The cited top three contain useful information but do not reliably identify the three factors with the strongest measured influence under necessity or sufficiency. The framework provides a black-box reliability check for explanations used in agent oversight while remaining scoped to individual LLM decisions.

</details>


### [187] [Multi-Step Tool-Calling over Korean Open Public APIs: A Benchmark and a Data-Synthesis Recipe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05395)
*Dain Kim,Eungi Cho,Kyumin Kim,Shinyeong Noh,Kyuseong Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of deploying open-source LLM agents for multi-step tool-calling across government APIs under data-sovereignty constraints. The authors introduce KOPA-Bench (145 Korean public API tasks) and EDGE (a method to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories by building and traversing verified tool-output graphs). Fine-tuning a 9B model with GRPO on EDGE-generated data nearly matches a 27B model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data-sovereignty regulations require public institutions to use open-source, on-premise LLM agents that chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in multi-step settings, and no existing benchmark measures this performance gap.

Method: The authors propose two contributions: (1) KOPA-Bench, a benchmark with 145 real-world Korean public API tasks; (2) EDGE (Execution-grounded Dynamic Graph for tool-calling data synthEsis), which builds a graph of tool output-to-input connections, validates links through actual API calls, and traverses verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. The model is fine-tuned using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) on the synthesized dataset.

Result: The 9B model fine-tuned on EDGE-generated data nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, achieving substantial improvements on both KOPA-Bench and the BFCL benchmark.

Conclusion: EDGE effectively bridges the performance gap between small and large open-source models in multi-step tool-calling scenarios. The combination of a realistic benchmark (KOPA-Bench) and execution-grounded data synthesis enables practical deployment of compact LLM agents for government API orchestration under data-sovereignty requirements.

Abstract: Data-sovereignty regulations increasingly require public institutions to deploy open-source, on-premise LLM agents that chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in this multi-step setting, and no existing benchmark measures the gap. We introduce the Korean Open Public API Benchmark (KOPA-Bench), comprising 145 real-world tasks. To close this gap, we present EDGE, an Execution-grounded Dynamic Graph for tool-calling data synthEsis driven by live execution. EDGE builds a graph of how each tool's output can feed another's input, keeps only the links that succeed when actually called against the live APIs, and traverses these verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. Fine-tuned via GRPO on the resulting dataset, our 9B model nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, improving substantially not only on KOPA-Bench but also on the BFCL benchmark.

</details>


### [188] [A Deep Generative Model for Synthesizing Labeled Wireless Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05396)
*Yuxiao Li,Keke Hu,Santiago Mazuelas,Yuan Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes IIns-GAN, a deep learning-based method to generate realistic labeled wireless signals for wireless sensing applications, addressing the challenge of expensive real-world data acquisition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acquiring real-world wireless signal datasets with position labels is costly due to measurement and labeling expenses. Traditional synthesis methods rely on environmental models, requiring extensive hyper-parameter tuning and lacking realism for comprehensive model training.

Method: The authors propose Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN), a novel DL-based method that generates realistic labeled wireless signals adaptive to different environment scenarios. The approach is evaluated on public Ultra-Wideband (UWB) datasets for tasks including distance estimation and environment identification.

Result: The generated signals mirror the physical characteristics of real-world measurements and significantly improve model training performance in diverse wireless sensing tasks.

Conclusion: IIns-GAN effectively addresses the data acquisition challenge in wireless sensing by generating realistic labeled signals that can support various model training tasks, demonstrating potential for practical deployment in wireless sensing applications.

Abstract: Wireless signals with position-related labels are pivotal for both performance evaluation and model training in the realm of wireless sensing. However, acquiring real-world datasets is often challenged by significant measurement and labeling costs. Traditional methods for synthesizing labeled wireless signals typically rely on environmental models, leading to extensive hyper-parameter tuning and inadequate realism for comprehensive model training purposes. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel deep learning (DL)-based method, namely Inter-Instance Generative Adversarial Networks (IIns-GAN), to generate realistic labeled wireless signals. The generated signals are particularly adaptive to different environment scenarios and well-suited for various model training tasks, including distance estimation and environment identification. We have conducted extensive experiments on public Ultra-Wideband (UWB) datasets to evaluate the realism and utility of the generated signals. The results demonstrate that the signals generated by IIns-GAN mirror the physical characteristics of real-world measurements, and significantly contribute to the improvement of model training in diverse wireless sensing tasks.

</details>

# cs.MM [[Back]](#toc)

### [189] [Embodied Multimedia: A Tutorial](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04204)
*Yang Liu,Wei Zuo,Guanwei Zhao,Juncen Guo,Jiangchuan Liu,Abdulmotaleb Saddik,Liang Song*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This tutorial paper introduces "Embodied Multimedia" as a new cross-disciplinary research paradigm that extends traditional multimedia (designed for human observers) to support autonomous agents that perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. The paper proposes a four-layer architecture (Data, Communication, Cognitive, Evaluation) and identifies five frontier application directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional multimedia technology is built around human observers (perceptual compression, human-centric quality metrics). However, the rise of embodied intelligence creates a fundamental mismatch: autonomous agents need to perceive, reason, and act in real-time physical environments, which conventional multimedia infrastructure cannot support. This gap necessitates a new paradigm.

Method: The paper presents a four-layer unified architecture: (1) Data Layer - multimodal data as perceptual/communicative substrate, (2) Communication Layer - data transmission, (3) Cognitive Layer - perception-decision-action processing, (4) Evaluation Layer - assessing agent performance. It provides structured review of enabling technologies within each layer.

Result: Five frontier application directions are identified where Embodied Multimedia can serve a foundational role: (1) multimedia communication, (2) physical intelligence, (3) embodied anomaly perception, (4) the metaverse and interactive multimedia, and (5) AI-driven art creation.

Conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing open technical challenges and future research directions to guide the community in this emerging field of Embodied Multimedia.

Abstract: Traditional multimedia technology has been built around optimizing content delivery for human observers, from perceptually driven compression standards to human-centric quality metrics. With the rapid rise of embodied intelligence, autonomous agents must perceive, reason, and act within the physical world in real time, exposing fundamental mismatches between conventional multimedia infrastructure and the demands of embodied tasks. In this regard, this tutorial paper formally introduces Embodied Multimedia as a cross-disciplinary research paradigm that treats multimodal data as the perceptual and communicative substrate spanning the full perception-decision-action loop. To be specific, we present a four-layer unified architecture comprising Data, Communication, Cognitive, and Evaluation layers, and provide a structured review of key enabling technologies within each layer. Furthermore, we identify five frontier application directions where Embodied Multimedia is positioned to serve a foundational role: multimedia communication, physical intelligence, embodied anomaly perception, the metaverse and interactive multimedia, and AI-driven art creation. Open technical challenges and future research directions are discussed to guide the community in this emerging field.

</details>


### [190] [Encore: Infinite Audio-Video Generation with Adaptive Signal Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04249)
*Shaohua Pan,Junbao Chen,Shengyi He,Jingfeng Xue,Wen Tao,Haocheng Feng,Siming Fan,Dongwei Pan,Yi Yang,Wei He,Hang Zhou*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: Encore is a long-form synchronized audio-video generation method that uses a factorized design combining iterative generation with cross-chunk context propagation for local continuity and reference signals with shifted position embeddings for global consistency. It introduces Adaptive Signal Routing (ASR) to adaptively modulate conditioning signals, enabling infinite-length audio-to-video and video-to-audio synthesis at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing audio-video generation methods are limited to short durations, while long-video generation methods lack audio entirely. Generating long audio-video jointly is fundamentally harder because each chunk must maintain video temporal coherence, audio temporal coherence, and cross-modal synchronization simultaneously, with conditioning signals entering through different pathways.

Method: 1) Factorized design: (a) Iterative generation with cross-chunk context propagation for local continuity, (b) Reference audio-video signals with shifted position embedding for global consistency. 2) Adaptive Signal Routing (ASR): learnable attention biases within self-attention and learnable residual scales on cross-attention outputs to adaptively modulate conditioning signals. 3) End-to-end training for joint audio-video generation.

Result: Experiments on extended VerseBench demonstrate that Encore significantly outperforms existing methods in both generation quality and temporal coherence.

Conclusion: Encore significantly outperforms existing methods in both generation quality and temporal coherence for long-form synchronized audio-video generation. The method supports infinite-length audio-to-video and video-to-audio synthesis at inference by conditioning on ground-truth modality.

Abstract: Existing audio-video generation methods produce well-synchronized clips but are limited to short durations, while long-video generation methods extend duration through chunk-based iterative synthesis yet lack audio entirely. Generating long audio-video jointly is fundamentally harder than either task alone: each chunk must simultaneously maintain video temporal coherence, audio temporal coherence, and cross-modal synchronization, whose conditioning signals enter the model through different pathways. In this work, we present Encore for long-form synchronized audio-video generation. Our key insight is to factor this challenge into: (1) local continuity handled by iterative generation with explicit cross-chunk context propagation, and (2) global consistency enforced via reference audio-video signals with shifted position embedding. Building on this design, we propose Adaptive Signal Routing (ASR), which introduces learnable attention biases within self-attention and learnable residual scales on cross-attention outputs, enabling the model to adaptively modulate the influence of each conditioning signal. Trained end-to-end for joint audio-video generation, Encore also supports infinite-length audio-to-video and video-to-audio synthesis at inference by conditioning on the ground-truth modality throughout the denoising process. Experiments on our extended VerseBench for long audio-video evaluation demonstrate that Encore significantly outperforms existing methods in both generation quality and temporal coherence. Code and data for this paper are at https://github.com/shaohua-pan/Encore.

</details>


### [191] [AVENUE: Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04253)
*Hayeon Kim,Yoojin Jang,Jaejun Yoo*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: AVENUE introduces a benchmark and evaluation framework for audio-video editing, addressing the lack of modality-selective editing evaluation. The benchmark contains 1,291 source clips and 7,957 editing instructions across audio-targeted, video-targeted, and AV-coupled edit types, with a sample-specific, modality-aware evaluation framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AV editing benchmarks have limited coverage of edit types and modality combinations, and existing evaluation systems are modality-blind and sample-agnostic, making it difficult to assess whether models faithfully preserve unintended modalities when editing one modality.

Method: The authors created AVENUE with two components: (1) a benchmark of 1,291 source clips and 7,957 editing instructions curated from VGGSound, covering audio-targeted, video-targeted, and AV-coupled edit types; (2) a sample-specific, modality-aware evaluation framework that specifies intended changes and content to preserve for each sample. They evaluated representative AV editing models across three paradigms: joint, sequential, and separate.

Result: The study reveals a fundamental open challenge: when editing one modality, existing models frequently induce unintended changes in the other modality, regardless of the editing paradigm used (joint, sequential, or separate).

Conclusion: AVENUE provides a comprehensive benchmark and modality-aware evaluation framework to drive progress toward more controllable AV editing models. The dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face.

Abstract: Audio-video (AV) editing aims to modify audio and video content according to a target prompt. Unlike single-modality editing, AV editing requires models to infer a modality-selective edit scope from the prompt alone: determining not only what should change, but also which modality should be preserved. Faithfully evaluating such models therefore requires both (i) benchmarks that span diverse edit types and modality categories, and (ii) evaluation that is itself modality-aware and sample-specific. However, existing AV editing benchmarks provide limited coverage of edit types and modality combinations, while current evaluation systems are often modality-blind and sample-agnostic, making it difficult to assess whether models faithfully preserve the unintended modality. To address these gaps, we introduce AVENUE, Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation, comprising two contributions: (1) a benchmark of 1,291 source clips and 7,957 editing instructions across audio-targeted, video-targeted, and AV-coupled edit types, curated and human-verified from VGGSound; and (2) a sample-specific, modality-aware evaluation framework that specifies, for each sample, both the intended change and the content that must remain intact. We evaluate representative AV editing models spanning three editing paradigms : joint, sequential, and separate, providing the first systematic analysis of modality-selectivity across paradigms. Our findings reveal a fundamental open challenge: when editing one modality, existing models frequently induce unintended changes in the other, regardless of paradigm. AVENUE provides a benchmark and modality-aware evaluation framework to drive progress toward more controllable AV editing models. Our dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AVENUE-dataset/AVENUE.

</details>


### [192] [PRISM-Bench: An Audio-Centric Diagnostic Benchmark for Text-to-Audio-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04867)
*Yuchen Sun,Qian Yang,Jun Wang,Detai Xin,Guoqiao Yu,Guanglu Wan,Qi Jia*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: PRISM-Bench is the first audio-centric diagnostic benchmark for text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation, featuring 900 human-verified samples that evaluate audio along two axes (audio type and sound-source visibility) across four perceptual dimensions with 35 fine-grained criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2AV evaluation benchmarks underestimate the audio modality—they either treat audio as auxiliary to video or assess it in isolation, making it difficult to diagnose where current systems succeed or fail in audio generation.

Method: PRISM-Bench uses a curated dataset of 900 human-verified samples, factorizing audio evaluation along audio type (Speech, Music, Sound) and sound-source visibility (On-screen vs. Off-screen). It employs an enhanced MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol with blind, side-by-side comparison against ground truth, achieving over 70% mean agreement with human raters.

Result: Evaluation of recent T2AV systems reveals a significant performance gap between frontier and open-source models. Current generation paradigms overfit to perceptual fidelity but struggle with complex grounding and control tasks, particularly in music and synchronized On-screen audio generation.

Conclusion: PRISM-Bench provides a rigorous diagnostic tool for T2AV audio generation, identifying key limitations in existing systems and offering a foundation for future improvement in audio-centric evaluation.

Abstract: Text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation has advanced rapidly, but its evaluation still underestimates the audio modality. Existing benchmarks either treat audio as an auxiliary component of video quality or assess it in isolation from audiovisual grounding, making it difficult to diagnose where current systems truly succeed or fail in audio generation. We present PRISM-Bench, the first audio-centric diagnostic benchmark for T2AV generation. Built from a rigorously curated dataset of 900 human-verified samples, PRISM-Bench factorizes audio evaluation along two orthogonal axes: audio type (Speech, Music, and Sound) and sound-source visibility (On-screen vs. Off-screen). It evaluates generated content across four perceptual dimensions (Audio-Visual Coherence, Audio Quality, Audio Expressiveness, and Prompt Following) with 35 fine-grained criteria. To ensure reliable assessment, we adopt an enhanced MLLM-as-a-Judge protocol based on blind, side-by-side comparison against ground-truth references, demonstrating strong alignment (over 70% mean agreement) with human raters. Our evaluation of recent T2AV systems highlights a significant performance gap between frontier and open-source models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that current generation paradigms overfit to perceptual fidelity while struggling with complex grounding and control tasks, particularly in generating music and synchronized On-screen audio.

</details>

### [193] [DTM: Deterministic Approaches for Black-box Test Suite Minimization with Tree-based Similarity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04205)
*Md Siam,Shartaz Sajid Nahid,Md Arif Hasan,Nurul Ahad Tawhid,Kazi Sakib*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: DTM is a deterministic framework for black-box test suite minimization that converts test cases into ASTs and uses tree-based similarity measures with three deterministic algorithms (Modified MST, Spectral Clustering, Dynamic Programming) to achieve consistent, effective test reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evolutionary search-based TSM approaches produce non-deterministic results across runs, undermining reliability in automated testing pipelines. There's a need for deterministic approaches that maintain effectiveness and efficiency.

Method: 1) Convert test cases into Abstract Syntax Trees; 2) Compute pairwise similarities using four tree-based measures; 3) Apply three deterministic subset selection algorithms: Modified Minimum Spanning Tree, Spectral Clustering, and Dynamic Programming

Result: Achieved average accuracy of 0.74 with execution time of 0.98 minutes on 16 Java projects (661 buggy versions from Defects4J), outperforming all state-of-the-art approaches while producing identical results across multiple runs.

Conclusion: DTM provides a fully deterministic solution for black-box test suite minimization that maintains high effectiveness and efficiency, making it suitable for reliable automated testing pipelines.

Abstract: Black-box Test Suite Minimization (TSM) techniques reduce testing costs without requiring access to production code. However, existing effective approaches rely on evolutionary search algorithms, introducing non-determinism that produces inconsistent results across runs, undermining reliability in automated testing pipelines. We propose DTM (Deterministic approaches for black-box Test suite Minimization), a framework that ensures deterministic test suite reduction while preserving effectiveness and efficiency. DTM converts test cases into Abstract Syntax Trees and computes pairwise similarities using four tree-based measures. For subset selection, it employs three deterministic algorithms: Modified Minimum Spanning Tree, Spectral Clustering, and Dynamic Programming. We evaluated DTM on 16 Java projects from Defects4J with 661 buggy versions. Experimental results show that DTM achieved an average accuracy of 0.74 with an execution time of just 0.98 minutes, outperforming all state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, it consistently produced identical results across multiple runs, ensuring full determinism.

</details>


### [194] [Breaking the Alphabet: Rethinking File Ordering in Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04207)
*Md Shamimur Rahman,Zadia Codabux,Chanchal K. Roy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates how file ordering in Pull Requests affects code review effectiveness through a large-scale survey of 1,355 developers across 182 open-source projects. The research reveals that alphabetical ordering (the default in most tools) is considered optimal by only 10.2% of reviewers, with majority reporting increased cognitive load, context switching, and concerns about missing bugs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While code review is central to software quality, there is limited research on how the ordering of changed files in Pull Requests influences review effectiveness. Most tools default to alphabetical ordering, which prioritizes predictability over contextual relevance, despite unclear impact on cognitive load and review thoroughness.

Method: Large-scale survey of 1,355 professional developers across 182 widely used open-source projects using mixed-methods analysis.

Result: Only 10.2% of reviewers consider alphabetical ordering optimal. More than half (57.6%) report that it increases context switching, disrupts logical reasoning, and contributes to review fatigue. 63.9% expressed concern that default ordering may cause them to miss bugs. 66% of reviewers requested dependency-aware grouping and customizable file ordering.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the need for reviewer-centric interface designs that better align tool behavior with human cognition. Developers want customizable, dependency-aware file ordering rather than alphabetical default.

Abstract: Effective code review is central to maintaining software quality, yet there is limited research about how the ordering of changed files in Pull Requests (PRs) influences review effectiveness. Most popular code review tools default to alphabetical ordering, favoring predictability over contextual relevance. While prior studies examined how file position shapes reviewer attention, it remains unclear how such ordering influences cognitive load and perceived review thoroughness. This study presents the first large-scale survey of 1,355 professional developers across 182 widely used open-source projects to investigate how file ordering impacts review behavior, comprehension, and perceived effectiveness. Our mixed-methods analysis reveals that only 10.2% of reviewers consider alphabetical ordering optimal, underscoring a cognitive misalignment in their interpretation of code changes. Although some developers appreciate its predictability, more than half (57.6%) report that it increases context switching, disrupts logical reasoning, and contributes to review fatigue, and 63.9% expressed concern that the default ordering may cause them to miss bugs. We further identify key challenges in multi-file reviews and elicit developers' expectations for improved tooling, including dependency-aware grouping and customizable file ordering (requested by 66% of reviewers). These findings highlight the need for reviewer-centric interface designs that better align tool behavior with human cognition.

</details>


### [195] [AI Writes Code, Humans Pay the Debt. An Empirical Study on the Sustainability and Evolution of Agent-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04208)
*Antonino Coppola,Matteo Esposito,Rick Kazman,Valentina Lenarduzzi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the long-term impact of Generative AI coding agents on software quality, focusing on issue localization accuracy, technical debt introduction, and evolution over time using a large-scale dataset of 628k issue tickets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Generative AI coding agents provide short-term productivity benefits, their long-term impact on software quality and technical debt remains unclear, necessitating empirical investigation to inform responsible adoption.

Method: Large-scale mining software repositories study using SQuaD dataset (628k issue tickets), generating agent-based implementations and comparing with actual developer commits using static analysis metrics across multiple LLM-based agents and release versions.

Result: Expected to provide empirical evidence on trade-offs including localization accuracy differences, technical debt variations, and long-term evolution divergence across different LLMs.

Conclusion: Results will highlight variability across LLMs, enrich understanding of software evolution with agents, and inform responsible adoption of AI coding agents in software development.

Abstract: Context. The increasing adoption of Generative AI coding agents in software engineering is transforming how developers implement and maintain code. While these systems provide short-term productivity benefits, their long-term impact on software quality and technical debt remains unclear. Aim. We aim to investigate how agent-generated code affects software quality, focusing on issue localization accuracy, the introduction of technical debt, and its evolution over time. Method. We will conduct a large-scale mining software repositories study using the SQuaD dataset, employing a candidate set of 628k issue tickets. We will generate agent-based implementations for these issues, and compare them with the actual commits done by developers using static analysis metrics and tools. We will analyze differences at the commit level and across releases, and we will consider multiple LLM-based Agents selected through a systematic benchmarking strategy. Expected Results. We expect to provide empirical evidence on the trade-offs introduced by agent-based development, including differences in localization accuracy, variations in technical debt introduction, and potential divergence in long-term evolution. We expect the results to highlight variability across LLMs, to enrich our understanding of software evolution with Agents, and to inform more responsible adoption of Agents in software development.

</details>


### [196] [The Prompt Triangle: A Registered Report on Prompts as Hybrid Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04209)
*Shalini Chakraborty,Jan-Philipp Steghöfer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This registered report presents a Stage 1 protocol for a confirmatory study examining how AI-based coding assistant prompts evolve and how their alignment with requirements engineering (RE) activities predicts development outcomes. The study uses the Prompt Triangle model (Functionality/Quality, General Solutions, Specific Solutions) and tests four hypotheses through controlled experiment (n=30), community uploads, and mined data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-based coding assistants are transforming software development from writing code to crafting prompts, yet there is little empirical evidence on how prompts function as software engineering artifacts. The researchers aim to understand prompt evolution and its relationship with development outcomes.

Method: Controlled experiment (n=30), community uploads analysis, and mined data using dual-coding. The study tests four hypotheses examining: 1) prompt evolution, 2) developer characteristics, 3) RE activity alignment, and 4) temporal patterns. Uses the Prompt Triangle conceptual model with three components: Functionality and Quality (requirements), General Solutions (architectural guidance), and Specific Solutions (implementation constraints).

Result: Results pending - this is a Stage 1 protocol registration, not actual results.

Conclusion: This study aims to provide empirical evidence on prompting patterns as software engineering artifacts and their predictive relationship with development success, filling a gap in understanding how prompts function in practice.

Abstract: AI-based coding assistants are transforming software development by shifting effort from writing code to crafting prompts that guide code generation. Despite their growing importance, little empirical evidence exists on how prompts function as software engineering artifacts. Building on prior work framing prompts as mixed artifacts combining requirement intent and solution guidance, we build on the Prompt Triangle, a conceptual model describing prompts along three components: Functionality and Quality (requirements), General Solutions (architectural guidance), and Specific Solutions (implementation constraints). This registered report presents the Stage 1 protocol for a confirmatory study investigating how prompts evolve and how their alignment with requirements engineering (RE) activities predicts development outcomes. We preregister four hypotheses examining prompt evolution, developer characteristics, RE activity alignment, and temporal patterns. We employ a controlled experiment (n=30), community uploads, and mined data using dual-coding to test whether prompting patterns predict development success.

</details>

### [198] [Data-Related Challenges and Requirements for Event Log Generation in Process Mining: A Systematic Literature Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04211)
*Ghita El Alaoui Talibi,Oleksandr Kosenkov,Anastasija Nikiforova*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This systematic literature review addresses the overlooked issue of event log generation as the initial phase of process mining, bridging the gap between event log generation and data/requirements engineering. The study identifies 29 data-related challenges and categorizes them into 5 basic requirement categories, highlighting existing solutions that incorporate data engineering and domain knowledge engineering techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Process mining is crucial for business process improvement and digital economy software technologies, but data quality is a pressing challenge. The research gap identified is the insufficient attention to event log generation (the first phase of process mining) and its relationship with data engineering and requirements engineering.

Method: Systematic literature review (SLR) examining data-related challenges, requirements, and solutions in event log generation.

Result: Identified 29 challenges that can be addressed with 5 basic categories of requirements. Found that existing solutions embed data engineering and domain knowledge engineering techniques for event log generation.

Conclusion: The review provides guidance for researchers and practitioners to understand current trends in event log generation for process mining and leverage data and requirements engineering techniques to improve log generation and process mining outcomes.

Abstract: Process mining is becoming an essential technology that not only supports the improvement of business processes but also enables the software technologies underlying the future digital economy. Among the multiple challenges discussed by the process mining community, data quality is emerging as the most pressing one. However, insufficient attention has been paid to event log generation as the very first phase of process mining and to its relationship with data engineering and requirements engineering. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review of data-related challenges, requirements, and solutions in event log generation. Our results show that a wide range of 29 challenges can be addressed with 5 basic categories of requirements. Existing solutions already embed some form of data engineering and domain knowledge engineering techniques for event log generation. This review can support researchers and practitioners in understanding current trends in event log generation for process mining and in leveraging data and requirements engineering techniques to improve log generation and, ultimately, process mining outcomes.

</details>

### [200] [Toward Model-Driven Digital Twin Configuration: Separating Structure Semantics and Runtime with SysML SAREF and Ditto](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04213)
*Andrey Sadovykh,Matthew Rusakov,Kirill Korikov*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This position paper proposes a three-tool approach for creating digital twins in energy communities: SysML for system structure modeling, SAREF4ENER as a standard energy vocabulary, and Eclipse Ditto (via W3C Web-of-Things Thing Description) for the running representation. The goal is to replace manual configuration of digital twins with a systematic derivation process from annotated SysML models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current digital twin setup for energy communities is manual, leading to issues: arbitrary field names, implicit units, and lack of machine-readable descriptions of device relationships. This prevents reliable interpretation by other systems and hinders interoperability.

Method: The paper proposes conceptual rules (not executable) for deriving a Ditto configuration from a SysML model annotated with SAREF4ENER vocabulary. This is illustrated using a greenhouse energy-community node modeled in Modelio.

Result: The proposed split approach improves traceability and configuration consistency, and establishes semantic hooks needed for interoperability compared to hand-written alternatives.

Conclusion: The contribution is scoped to design-time configuration. The approach offers a systematic way to generate digital twin configurations automatically, though the generator is not yet implemented. Limitations are acknowledged but not detailed.

Abstract: Energy communities, neighbourhoods that jointly produce, store, and consume electricity, increasingly rely on \emph{digital twins}: live software copies of physical devices such as a solar panel, a battery, or a heater, kept in sync for monitoring and control. Setting up such a twin is today mostly manual: an engineer hand-writes a configuration whose field names are arbitrary, whose units are implicit, and which carries no machine-readable description of how devices relate, so other systems cannot reliably interpret it. This position paper argues that the task should be split across three complementary tools, each doing what it does best: a modelling language for the system's structure (SysML), a standard energy vocabulary for its meaning (SAREF4ENER), and a digital-twin platform for the running representation (Eclipse Ditto, via the W3C Web-of-Things Thing Description). We give conceptual rules (not yet an executable generator) for deriving a Ditto configuration from a SysML model annotated with that vocabulary, illustrate them on a greenhouse energy-community node modelled in Modelio, and argue that the split improves traceability and configuration consistency, and establishes the semantic hooks needed for interoperability, over hand-written alternatives. We scope the contribution to design-time configuration and discuss its limits.

</details>


### [201] [A Mixed-Method Empirical Study of LLM Assistance in Software Engineering Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04214)
*Pamali D. Weerasinghe,Roshan N. Rajapakse,Isuru Dharmadasa,Chamath Keppitiyagama*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how Large Language Models affect software development workflows by comparing first-year and fourth-year undergraduates. Through a survey (n=157) and quasi-experiment (n=20), researchers found that LLM benefits are task-dependent and mediated by developer expertise and verification practices, not just generation speed. AI-assisted workflows show different patterns (AI-first entry, copy-transfer integration) than non-AI workflows (documentation, templates, trial-error).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a gap in understanding how LLMs affect software development, specifically that their effects are often discussed without distinguishing between task types, developer seniority, and verification demands. The study aims to provide empirical evidence on these nuanced impacts.

Method: Mixed-method empirical study with two phases: (1) Preliminary survey (n=157) assessing LLM exposure, reliance, and trust calibration among first-year and fourth-year undergraduates; (2) Task-based quasi-experiment with purposive sample (n=20) comparing AI-assisted vs non-AI conditions across implementation, constraint-driven algorithm selection, and architectural reasoning tasks. Data collection included screen recordings and qualitative coding of behavioral traces.

Result: Survey results show widespread LLM adoption and substantial verification effort, with cohort differences in perceived LLM capability for constraint-heavy scenarios. The quasi-experiment reveals that AI assistance fundamentally changes workflow structure: AI-assisted participants use AI-first task entry, copy-transfer integration, and AI-mediated debugging, while non-AI participants rely more on documentation, prior templates, and iterative trial-error refinement. Benefits are task-dependent and mediated by expertise and verification practices.

Conclusion: The benefits of LLM assistance in software engineering are not universal but depend on task type, developer expertise level, and verification practices. Simply measuring generation speed is insufficient to capture LLM impact; future research and tool design must consider these mediating factors.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software development workflows, yet their effects are often discussed without distinguishing between task types, developer seniority, and verification demands. This paper presents a mixed-method empirical study of LLM-assisted software engineering with first-year and fourth-year undergraduates. Phase 1 is a preliminary survey (n=157) that characterizes LLM exposure, reliance, and trust calibration among the two groups. Phase 2 is a task-based quasi-experiment with a purposive sample from both cohorts (n=20). Here, we compare AI-assisted and non-AI conditions on a structured set of software engineering tasks spanning implementation, constraint-driven algorithm selection, and architectural reasoning. We then analyze performance outcomes alongside behavioral traces captured via screen recording and a qualitative coding process. Survey results indicate widespread LLM adoption and substantial verification effort, alongside cohort differences in perceived LLM capability for constraint-heavy scenarios. The quasi-experiment further shows that AI assistance changes workflow structure. For example, participants frequently adopt AI-first task entry, copy-transfer integration, and AI-mediated debugging, whereas non-AI workflows rely more on documentation, prior templates, and iterative trial-error refinement. Overall, our findings suggest that the benefits of LLM assistance are task-dependent and mediated by expertise and verification practices, rather than by generation speed alone.

</details>


### [202] [A systematic literature review on logging smell detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04215)
*Nora Madi,Manal Binkhonain*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This systematic literature review (SLR) examines 21 studies on detecting logging smells—defects that reduce log usefulness. The review finds that current research is fragmented, lacks standardized benchmarks, and shows inconsistencies in smell types and detection approaches. Future directions include better tools, LLM adoption, and standardized datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logging is crucial for software development but poor logging practices introduce "logging smells" that compromise system monitoring and debugging. Despite growing research on automatic detection, there was no comprehensive understanding of existing techniques, datasets, and evaluation methods. The study aims to fill this gap through a systematic review.

Method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) of 21 primary studies focused on logging smell detection. They defined key logging-related terms, mapped smell types to an existing taxonomy, and analyzed detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation strategies across the studies.

Result: Research on logging smell detection is scattered and inconsistent across studies. Key issues include: (1) No common benchmark or standardized evaluation approach exists, making cross-study comparison difficult. (2) Studies differ in the types and number of smells they target, leading to inconsistent treatment of log smells. (3) The field lacks unified terminology and methodology.

Conclusion: The field needs improvement in both research practice and detection capabilities. The authors recommend: developing better detection tools, leveraging large language models (LLMs) for improved detection, and building standardized datasets for evaluation. These directions could help establish consistency and advance the state of logging smell detection research.

Abstract: Context:Logging is an important part of software development that helps developers monitor systems, understand behavior, and fix problems. But when logging is done poorly, it can introduce logging smells, which are defects that reduce the usefulness of logs or even make them problematic. Objective:This study looks at how logging smells are currently detected. The goal is to better understand the existing research on automatic detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation methods. Method:We conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) of 21 studies focused on detecting logging smells. In this review, we define key logging-related terms, identify and map the types of smells to an existing taxonomy, and examine the detection techniques, datasets, and evaluation strategies used across the studies. Results:We found that the research is still scattered and inconsistent. For example, there is no common benchmark or standardized approach for evaluating results, making it difficult to compare studies. In addition, we observe inconsistencies in the way log smells are addressed, as studies differ in the types and number of smells they target. Conclusion:There is still room for improvement in how logging smells are studied and detected. We point out several challenges and suggest future directions, such as developing better tools, using large language models (LLMs), and building more standardized datasets for evaluation.

</details>


### [203] [Engineering as Code: Bringing Software Engineering Methodology to Engineering Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04216)
*Song Difei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes "Engineering as Code" (EaC) paradigm to address limitations of large language models in engineering design fields (architecture, mechanical engineering, HVAC). The core problem is the absence of computable design representations ("Design as Code"). The solution includes ADL (Assembly Definition Language) with three sub-languages and ESA (Engineering Static Analysis) for compliance checking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models excel in verifiable domains (code, chip design) but struggle with engineering design tasks. The root cause is identified as the lack of "Design as Code" computable foundations - design representations that can be consumed, verified, and versioned by machines. Current CAD/BIM systems couple design logic with geometry, causing quality assurance to drift downstream and Automated Compliance Checking (ACC) to suffer from geometric false positives and naming-dependent overhead.

Method: The paper proposes the Engineering as Code (EaC) paradigm: expressing engineering design as text-native declarative language with automated rule engines, version control, and package management as quality gates. Key technical contributions: (1) Information Representation Hypothesis - engineering AI bottleneck stems from missing computable design representations; (2) ADL (Assembly Definition Language) with Part as atom, organized into PDL (Part Definition), PML (Part Mating), and PLL (Part Layout); (3) ESA (Engineering Static Analysis) - shifting compliance checking from downstream to design-time, operating on semantic categories (Family types, Mate relations) rather than geometry.

Result: A prototype validates ADL expressiveness and ESA detection across three cross-domain samples (telecom rack expansion, modular datacenter, mechanical keyboard). The system checks 69 rules in under 200ms. A controlled violation injection experiment achieves 100% detection rate with zero false positives. The SD-HWE-Bench benchmark is designed as an empirical testbed.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the engineering AI bottleneck is due to missing computable design representations rather than model capability limitations. The EaC paradigm with ADL and ESA provides a solution that enables design-time compliance checking with zero false positives, validating the Information Representation Hypothesis.

Abstract: Large language models have made significant progress in verifiable domains such as code generation and chip design, yet remain limited on engineering design tasks in fields like architecture, mechanical engineering, and HVAC.
