This paper argues the root cause is not model capability but the absence of a "Design as Code" computable foundation: design representations that can be consumed, verified, and versioned by machines. Existing CAD/BIM systems couple design logic with geometry, causing quality assurance to drift downstream; Automated Compliance Checking (ACC) suffers from geometric false positives and naming-dependent model reconstruction overhead. We propose the Engineering as Code (EaC) paradigm: expressing engineering design as text-native declarative language with automated rule engines, version control, and package management as quality gates. Core contributions: (1) the Information Representation Hypothesis, arguing the engineering AI bottleneck stems from missing computable design representations rather than model capability; (2) ADL (Assembly Definition Language) with Part as atom, organized into three orthogonal sub-languages -- PDL (Part Definition), PML (Part Mating), and PLL (Part Layout); (3) ESA (Engineering Static Analysis), shifting compliance checking from downstream review to design-time, operating on semantic categories (Family types, Mate relations) rather than geometry, eliminating false positives and naming dependencies. A prototype validates ADL expressiveness and ESA detection across three cross-domain samples (telecom rack expansion, modular datacenter, mechanical keyboard), checking 69 rules in under 200ms. A controlled violation injection experiment achieves 100% detection rate with zero false positives. The SD-HWE-Bench benchmark design is complete as an empirical testbed for the hypothesis.

</details>


### [204] [A Governance Methodology Layer for AI-Assisted Software Development: Defect Taxonomy, Controlled Ablation, and Process-Over-Capability Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04218)
*Sungjin Kwon*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses the gap between syntactic correctness and semantic correctness in AI-generated code. It proposes a defect taxonomy, a portable governance gate, a methodology-as-code framework, and presents an ablation study showing structured review outperforms unstructured review (62% vs 50% lenient recall, 25% vs 0% strict recall).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous coding agents produce syntactically correct code but miss semantic aspects like design boundaries, security invariants, and maintainability contracts. Current automated pipelines cannot detect these semantic defects, creating a gap between what passes automated checks and what actually meets quality standards.

Method: The paper presents: (1) a defect-class taxonomy grounded in five AI agent permission/governance modules; (2) a runtime-decoupled governance gate using a file-based protocol; (3) methodology-as-code with a two-layer architecture (portable methodology + host-specific automation); (4) a controlled ablation experiment (E-ablation, N=5 artifacts, 8-item independent ground truth) comparing harness-structured review vs token-matched unstructured review.

Result: The structured review condition achieved 62% lenient ground-truth recall vs 50% for unstructured, 25% strict recall vs 0%, and applied more consistent severity grades. Both conditions missed document-quality defects identified by human QA, indicating complementarity between AI and human review.

Conclusion: Within the sample bounds, review-process design (rather than reviewer-model capability) is the dominant factor in critical-defect coverage for AI-assisted software development. Structured review processes significantly outperform unstructured approaches.

Abstract: Autonomous coding agents produce output that passes syntactic checks -- compilation, type safety, CI -- at high velocity. Yet syntactic correctness does not imply semantic correctness: design boundaries, security invariants, and maintainability contracts remain structurally invisible to automated pipelines. This paper makes four contributions toward closing this gap. First, we present a defect-class taxonomy grounded in five AI agent permission and governance modules, distinguishing defects structurally detectable by static analysis from those requiring semantic review. Second, we describe a runtime-decoupled governance gate -- a file-based protocol that reads generator output and emits a structured verdict without API coupling, making it portable across code-generation tools. Third, we formalize methodology-as-code: expressing a verification protocol as a version-controlled, executable, cross-platform artifact with a two-layer architecture separating portable methodology from host-specific automation. Fourth, we report a controlled ablation experiment (E-ablation, N=5 artifacts, 8-item independent ground truth) comparing harness-structured review against a token-matched unstructured review prompt on the same artifacts. The structured condition records 62% lenient ground-truth recall against 50% for the unstructured condition, with 25% strict recall against 0%, and applies more consistent severity grades where the unstructured condition inflates severity. Both conditions miss document-quality defects identified by a human QA reviewer, indicating a complementarity between structured AI review and human process inspection. Within the bounds of this sample, the results are consistent with the thesis that review-process design, rather than reviewer-model capability, is the dominant factor in critical-defect coverage for AI-assisted software development.

</details>


### [205] [Large Language Models for Fuzz Testing in Microservices: A Systematic Literature Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04219)
*Ying Song,Ke Ping,Yuqing Wang,Xiaozhou Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A systematic literature review analyzing 20 primary studies (2024-2026) on LLM-assisted fuzz testing for microservices. The review finds LLMs are primarily used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with emerging agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures. While evaluation shows improvements in valid input generation, coverage, and vulnerability detection, significant challenges remain in benchmark standardization, cost reporting, and scalability to multi-service systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microservice systems increasingly rely on heterogeneous APIs with combinatorial input spaces and stateful dependencies, challenging traditional fuzz testing. LLMs have emerged to enhance fuzzing with semantic reasoning, but there was no consolidated understanding of how LLMs are applied, evaluated, and what challenges persist in this domain.

Method: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following established guidelines, analyzing 20 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026 on LLM-assisted fuzz testing for microservices.

Result: LLMs are mainly used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with growing shift toward agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures. This improves valid input generation and modestly increases coverage and vulnerability detection. However, evaluation remains heterogeneous with limited benchmark standardization, scarce cost reporting, and bias toward single-service experiments (real-world multi-service systems underrepresented).

Conclusion: The review provides: (1) a taxonomy of LLM roles and integrations in fuzzing, (2) a consolidated view of evaluation practices, and (3) a mapping of open challenges to research directions. This supports the design and deployment of LLM-driven fuzzing in microservices, highlighting the need for standardized benchmarks, cost analysis, and multi-service evaluation approaches.

Abstract: Microservice systems (MSS) increasingly rely on heterogeneous APIs whose combinatorial input space and stateful dependencies challenge traditional fuzz testing. Meanwhile, Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been introduced to enhance fuzzing with semantic reasoning over specifications, inputs, and runtime feedback. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of LLM-assisted fuzz testing for microservices to synthesise how LLMs are applied, evaluated, and what challenges remain. Following established SLR guidelines, we analyze 20 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026. Results show LLMs are mainly used as semantic input generators in black-box fuzzing, with a growing shift towards agent-based and retrieval-augmented architectures, improving valid input generation and modestly increasing coverage and vulnerability detection. However, evaluation remains heterogeneous, with limited benchmark standardization, scarce cost reporting, and a bias toward single-service experiments, highlighting a gap with real-world multi-service systems. This review provides a taxonomy of LLM roles and integrations, a consolidated view of evaluation practices, and a mapping of open challenges to research directions, supporting the design and deployment of LLM-driven fuzzing in microservices.

</details>


### [206] [Robustness and Trade-offs for Code LLMs on Protected Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04220)
*Jin Wen,Yuejun Guo,Yujie Ma,Qiang Hu,Maxime Cordy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether deobfuscation is necessary before using code LLMs on obfuscated software. The study tests 7 code LLMs across 4 languages, 5 obfuscation methods, and 3 inference protocols. Surprisingly, direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds inference on deobfuscated code, with high-capability models like GPT-4.1 retaining ~90% Pass@1 on obfuscated inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deobfuscation is commonly used as preprocessing before code LLM analysis, but this practice had not been systematically validated. The authors wanted to determine if explicit deobfuscation is actually necessary for code LLM pipelines.

Method: Execution-based study with 7 code LLMs, spanning C++, Go, Java, and JavaScript, testing 5 obfuscation methods across 3 inference protocols: plain, obfuscated, and deobfuscated.

Result: Direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds inference on restored code. Higher-capability models (GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Coder-30B) retain ~90% Pass@1 on obfuscated translation. Same-model restoration recovers some failures but degrades many already-successful cases. Model capability is the primary factor; language and obfuscation method have secondary effects.

Conclusion: Protected-code workflows should use execution-based metrics rather than static similarity. Model-aware pipeline design is recommended, and explicit deobfuscation is often unnecessary, especially for high-capability models.

Abstract: Code large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used on software artifacts that may be intentionally obfuscated for intellectual-property protection, reverse-engineering resistance, or controlled access. In reverse engineering and security analysis, deobfuscation is commonly treated as the preprocessing step before downstream analysis or inference, yet its utility for code LLM pipelines has not been systematically validated across models and protection methods. We present an execution-based study of seven code LLMs on protected-code translation and completion, spanning source programs from C++, Go, Java, and JavaScript, five obfuscation methods, and three inference protocols: plain, obfuscated, and deobfuscated. Our results show that direct inference on obfuscated code often matches or exceeds inference on restored code. In this controlled benchmark, higher-capability models such as GPT-4.1 and Qwen3-Coder-30B retain about 90% Pass@1 on obfuscated translation inputs, indicating that explicit restoration is often unnecessary. Same-model restoration does recover some obfuscation-induced failures, but it also degrades many cases that already succeed, with lower-capability models showing the largest net losses. Across settings, model capability is the primary factor, while source language and obfuscation method have secondary but consistent effects. Overall, our findings support model-aware pipeline design and indicate that protected-code workflows should be evaluated primarily with execution-based metrics rather than static similarity alone.

</details>


### [207] [Automated Deployment of Real-Time Tasks for Phased Execution on Scratchpad-Based Multicore Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04221)
*Konstantin Dudzik,Maximilian Kirschner,Jürgen Becker*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A model-based deployment methodology that automates adaptation of real-time applications to phased execution on multicore systems, addressing shared memory contention with minimal application changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multicore real-time systems face interference from shared memory contention; phased execution restricts shared memory access to mutually exclusive phases but introduces complexity in management and scheduling, hindering adoption.

Method: Integrated tool-based deployment process that: (1) extracts required information directly from generated application binaries, (2) extends applications with necessary memory phases, (3) provides runtime environment to orchestrate execution on target hardware.

Result: Validated through an avionics case study on a RISC-V multicore system, demonstrating key components and principles of operation.

Conclusion: The proposed methodology enables adoption of phased execution in real-time applications with minimal changes to application implementation, while addressing shared memory contention challenges in multicore systems.

Abstract: The increasing throughput demands in real-time systems and the consolidation of functionality on few, high-performance platforms are driving a shift towards parallel architectures. A key challenge for multicore real-time systems is the interference from contention for access to shared memory. Phased execution approaches address this challenge by restricting shared memory access to mutually exclusive memory phases, while computation is limited to memories local to each core. However, the complexity of managing and scheduling said memory phases hinders the adoption of phased execution in real-time applications. To address this challenge, we propose a model-based deployment methodology that automates the process of adapting applications to phased execution. We present an integrated tool-based deployment process that extends the application through the necessary memory phases and provides a runtime environment to orchestrate execution on the target hardware platform. Our approach requires minimal changes to the application implementation since the deployment tool directly extracts the required information from the generated application binaries. We validate our methodology using an avionics case study on a RISC-V multicore system, showcasing its key components and principles of operation.

</details>


### [208] [Physics-Direct FPGA Tooth-Contact Computation for Deterministic Gear Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04248)
*Jiacheng Miao*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a "physics-direct" approach to gear tooth contact analysis, compressing closed-form contact physics (contact-point localization, principal-curvature extraction, elliptical Hertz solution) into a branch-free fixed-point FPGA datapath. The solution achieves real-time, deterministic performance with zero jitter, outperforming both traditional LTCA (seconds → constant latency) and neural network surrogates (18.9% vs 20.3% extrapolation error) without requiring any training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional loaded tooth contact analysis (LTCA) is too slow for real-time applications (seconds per mesh phase in fp64), while neural network surrogates require extensive training data and offer no guarantees beyond their training envelope. There's a need for a real-time, deterministic, and embeddable solver for gear digital twins, hardware-in-the-loop rigs, and active vibration control systems.

Method: The authors compress the closed-form contact physics directly into a branch-free fixed-point FPGA datapath using the fully open-source openXC7 flow (no vendor tools, no floating-point IP). This is validated on retired XC7K480T silicon. Four System-on-Chips (SoCs) are implemented: geometry kernel, Hertz solution, and two fused paths. Results are validated against a golden model using bit-exact JTAG readback.

Result: The on-chip preview tracks LCP body pressure to within -22% and loaded transmission error (LTE) peak-to-peak to within -19%, preserving the exact W^1/3 law. With zero training, it extrapolates in load more accurately than a trained neural network (18.9% vs 20.3% error). Latency is a compile-time constant with zero jitter (σ=0). The DSP-bound geometry kernel saturates the fabric near 63 lanes.

Conclusion: Physics-direct is an interpretable, deterministic alternative to neural surrogacy for embedded tooth-contact estimation. It achieves real-time performance with guaranteed behavior, requires no training, and outperforms neural networks in extrapolation tasks while maintaining interpretability and deterministic properties essential for embedded systems.

Abstract: Gear digital twins, hardware-in-the-loop rigs, and active vibration control close a loop around the instantaneous tooth-contact state, demanding a solver that is real-time, deterministic, and embeddable -- properties that loaded tooth contact analysis (LTCA), a data-dependent linear complementarity problem (LCP) costing seconds per mesh phase in fp64, structurally lacks; learned surrogates infer fast but spend one full LTCA solve per training sample and offer no guarantee beyond their training envelope. We instead compress the closed-form contact physics -- contact-point localization, principal-curvature extraction, and the elliptical Hertz solution -- directly into a branch-free fixed-point FPGA datapath, termed physics-direct, realized through the fully open-source openXC7 flow (no vendor tools, no floating-point IP) and validated on retired XC7K480T silicon. Four SoCs -- geometry, Hertz, and two fused paths -- pass bit-exact JTAG readback against a golden model. The on-chip preview tracks LCP body pressure to within -22% and loaded transmission error (LTE) peak-to-peak to -19%, preserving the exact $W^{1/3}$ law; with zero training it extrapolates in load more accurately than a trained network (18.9% versus 20.3%). Latency is a compile-time constant ($σ= 0$ jitter), and the DSP-bound geometry kernel saturates the fabric near 63 lanes. Physics-direct is an interpretable, deterministic alternative to neural surrogacy for embedded tooth-contact estimation.

</details>


### [209] [Reviewer Capability Governs Rejection Targeting, Not Repair Skill: Evidence from LLM Execute-Review-Revise Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04270)
*Faizan Tanveer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how reviewer capability affects multi-agent LLM pipelines for math problem-solving. Testing across 100 olympiad problems, they find a mid-tier cross-family reviewer improves accuracy by 12pp (52→64%) with zero damaged answers, while same-model self-review achieves highest error detection but provides no net benefit due to excessive false rejections. The weakest reviewer is inert—doubling cost while changing nothing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous literature assumed reviewer capability is fixed relative to the executor. This paper challenges that assumption by varying reviewer capability across a wide range—from a flagship model down to one that cannot solve the problems at all—to determine when and how verification stages actually help.

Method: Controlled experiment on a constant set of 100 olympiad mathematics problems. The executor remains fixed while reviewers of varying capability levels (cross-family mid-tier, same-model self-review, and weakest model) are substituted. Every individual rejection outcome is measured.

Result: Cross-family mid-tier reviewer boosted final accuracy from 52% to 64% (p=0.0005) with zero damaged answers. Same-model self-review achieved highest error-detection recall (0.85) but rejected 2.1× more often for only 15% repair rate vs 43% for cross-family reviewer, and falsely rejected 35% of its own correct answers vs 2% for cross-family (paired p=0.000015). The low damage rate of self-review stems from revision inertia: of 18 falsely rejected correct answers, all 3 where the executor complied became wrong, while the 15 ignored survived. The weakest reviewer changed zero answers while doubling token cost.

Conclusion: Verification is only beneficial within a capability window—too weak and it's inert; too strong (same-model) and revision inertia causes harm. The optimal is a mid-tier cross-family reviewer. Findings are limited to a single executor-reviewer configuration on 100 problems and should be treated as a controlled pilot rather than general claims.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM pipelines increasingly assign roles, including execution and verification, to models of different capability tiers. This is done because running a flagship model at every stage is expensive. Previous literature has established that verification stages are not always beneficial, but holds reviewer capability roughly fixed relative to the executor. We vary it. We replace the reviewer with models spanning a capability range down to one that cannot solve the problems at all, and measure the outcome of every individual rejection. This is done across a constant set of 100 olympiad mathematics problems.
  A cross-family mid-tier reviewer improves final accuracy by 12 percentage points, from 52 to 64 percent (p = 0.0005), with zero damaged answers. Same-model self-review attains the highest error-detection rate of any condition (0.85 recall) yet yields no significant gain: it rejects 2.1 times as often for a third the repair rate (15 against 43 percent, p = 0.0074) and falsely rejects 35 percent of its own correct answers against 2 percent for the cross-family reviewer (paired p = 0.000015). The low damage rate of self-review proves to be an artifact of revision inertia rather than reviewer quality: of 18 falsely rejected correct answers, the three where the executor complied all became wrong, while the fifteen it ignored survived unchanged. Below a capability floor the role becomes inert: our weakest reviewer changed zero of 100 final answers while doubling token cost. These findings describe a single executor-reviewer configuration on 100 problems and should be read as a controlled pilot rather than a general claim about verification stages.

</details>


### [210] [Integrating Crash Report Mining and LLMs for Bug Localization and Repair: An Industrial Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04483)
*Marcos Medeiros,Uirá Kulesza,Christoph Treude,Daniel Lucena,Rafael Gomes,Roberta Coelho,Eiji Adachi,Rodrigo Bonifacio*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the integration of crash report mining techniques (stack trace clustering, suspicious file/method ranking) with LLMs to support crash localization and repair in industrial Java enterprise systems. Evaluation on 38 crash bugs shows 71% localization accuracy and 52% repair accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analyzing crash-report bugs in large-scale industrial software systems requires substantial maintenance effort in production environments with large volumes of crash reports and source code artifacts. While LLMs have shown promise in maintenance tasks, their effectiveness in crash localization and repair in industrial settings remains unexplored.

Method: The researchers conducted a retrospective evaluation of five LLMs under four prompt configurations, then selected the best model to test on 38 crash bugs from two large Java enterprise systems. They analyzed structural characteristics and explanatory patterns of LLM-generated responses, assessing localization and repair effectiveness through manual validation.

Result: The best-performing configuration achieved up to 71% localization accuracy and correctly repaired 52% of crash bugs on the full dataset. The study provides empirical evidence that combining crash report mining with LLM-based repair can effectively support debugging activities in industrial maintenance workflows.

Conclusion: Integrating crash report mining techniques with LLMs can effectively support crash localization and repair in industrial maintenance workflows, with potential for practical application in production environments.

Abstract: Analyzing crash-report bugs in large-scale industrial software systems requires substantial maintenance effort, particularly in production environments where developers must handle large volumes of crash reports and source code artifacts to localize and fix their root causes. While recent studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) can assist with maintenance tasks, little is known about their effectiveness in supporting developers in analyzing crash-report bugs and repairing bugs associated with groups of crash reports in industrial settings. To address this gap, we investigate whether integrating crash report mining techniques---specifically stack trace clustering and suspicious file and method ranking---with LLMs can support crash localization and repair in production environments. We conduct a retrospective evaluation of five LLMs under four prompt configurations. After that, we chose the best model to run on 38 crash bugs collected from two large Java enterprise systems. We further analyze the structural characteristics and explanatory patterns of LLM-generated responses and assess localization and repair effectiveness through manual validation. Our results show that the best-performing configuration localizes up to 71% and correctly repairs 52% of crash bugs on the full dataset. These findings provide empirical evidence that combining crash report mining with LLM-based repair can effectively support debugging activities in industrial maintenance workflows.

</details>


### [211] [An Empirical Analysis of CodeQL False Positives and Query Refinements for Java Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04535)
*Amirali Sajadi,Saikat Dutta,Preetha Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates recurring patterns in CodeQL false positives for Java security analysis and proposes query-level refinements to reduce them. The study analyzes 167 CVE instances across 110 projects, identifying five categories of false positives. Refinements remove 81.8% of reviewed false positives while retaining most true positives. The paper also explores using agentic coding tools to adapt refinements to new projects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static application security testing (SAST) tools like CodeQL help developers find vulnerabilities before deployment, but false positives create substantial triage effort. The motivation is to understand whether these false positives form recurring, explainable patterns that can be reduced through analysis refinements.

Method: The researchers ran CodeQL's Java security query suite on 167 CVE instances from 110 projects, focusing on the ten queries with the highest false positive rates. They manually reviewed 500 sampled false positive paths and locations to construct a source-level taxonomy. Based on these findings, they implemented CodeQL refinements to detect and filter recurring false positive patterns at the query level. They also evaluated whether agentic coding tools could adapt refinement patterns to new projects.

Result: The five categories of false positives identified are: Missed Path Constraint or Sanitization (36.6%), Benign Execution Context (29.4%), Missing Trust Boundary Modeling (27.6%), Imprecise Concurrency Modeling (5%), and Imprecise Sink Modeling (1.4%). The refinements remove 81.8% of reviewed false positives. Across the full selected-query dataset, they remove 15.8% of reported paths and locations while retaining 7 of 8 true positives. Agentic coding tools succeed on 56% and 62% of tasks with templates (90%+ compile rates) vs. 28% without templates (30-36% compile rates).

Conclusion: Many false positives can be reduced through analysis refinements, although fixed refinements often depend on project-specific context. The paper proposes a refinement-oriented SAST workflow where recurring false positives are modeled in CodeQL queries and automatically adapted to different project contexts using agentic tools, reducing repeated triage effort.

Abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help developers find vulnerabilities before deployment, but false positives create substantial triage effort. We study whether CodeQL false positives in Java security analysis form recurring, explainable patterns that can be reduced by refining the analysis. We run CodeQL's Java security query suite on 167 CVE instances from 110 projects, focusing on the ten queries with the highest false positive rates. We manually review 500 sampled false positive paths and locations and construct a source-level taxonomy. The five categories are Missed Path Constraint or Sanitization (36.6%), Benign Execution Context (29.4%), Missing Trust Boundary Modeling (27.6%), Imprecise Concurrency Modeling (5%), and Imprecise Sink Modeling (1.4%).
  Guided by these findings, we implement CodeQL refinements that detect and filter recurring false positive patterns at the query level. The refinements remove 81.8% of reviewed false positives. Across the full selected-query dataset, they remove 15.8% of reported paths and locations while retaining 7 of 8 true positives. This shows that many false positives can be reduced in the analysis, although fixed refinements often depend on project-specific context. To address this generalization gap, we evaluate whether agentic coding tools can adapt refinement patterns to new projects. Given our patterns as templates, the two tools succeed on 56% and 62% of tasks, with query compile-pass rates above 90%. Without this guidance, both succeed on only 28%, while compile rates fall to 30-36%. These results support a refinement-oriented SAST workflow in which recurring false positives are modeled in CodeQL queries and automatically adapted to different project contexts, reducing repeated triage.

</details>


### [212] [Dynamic Adaptation of the LLM Context for Generating Routines with Coupled Semantics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04570)
*Gnaneswar Villuri,Hashmath Shaik,Alex Doboli*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses a key limitation in LLM-based code generation: static binding, where correctness depends on execution-dependent coupling between components that cannot be resolved from textual descriptions alone. The authors propose dynamic context adaptation, a validation-generation loop that uses a validation agent to extract structured diagnostic information from execution traces, a generation agent to propose candidates, a knowledge graph for semantic constraints, and simulated annealing for candidate selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based code generation fails when correctness depends on execution-dependent coupling (static binding) - where the meaning of one routine is defined by the runtime behavior of another. This limitation appears in various scenarios from cross-coupled optimizers to packing, routing, and symbolic search problems where correctness depends on joint execution behavior across components.

Method: The proposed method "dynamic context adaptation" consists of: (1) A validation agent that extracts structured diagnostic information from execution traces, providing gradient-like guidance to a generation agent; (2) A generation agent that proposes multiple candidates per iteration; (3) A knowledge graph derived from problem descriptions supplying semantic constraints; (4) Simulated annealing for candidate selection to avoid greedy collapse.

Result: The method outperforms zero-shot, Reflexion, and OpenEvolve on seven of eight problems at both 300 and 600 evaluations (p < 0.01). It also achieves the best score at 1000 evaluations on the primary motivating problem (cross-coupled optimization). Ablation results confirm that structured execution feedback is the primary driver of performance.

Conclusion: Structured execution feedback is most beneficial when correctness depends on runtime coupling. The dynamic context adaptation approach provides a sample-efficient solution for LLM-based code generation in scenarios where traditional static approaches fail due to execution-dependent dependencies between components.

Abstract: LLM-based code generation fails when correctness depends on execution-dependent coupling: the meaning of one routine is defined by the runtime behavior of another, a relationship that cannot be resolved from textual descriptions alone. This limitation, which we call static binding, is not confined to explicitly coupled problems; it appears to varying degrees whenever correctness depends on joint execution behavior across components, from explicit cross-coupled optimizers to subtler joint constraints in packing, routing, and symbolic search. This paper proposes dynamic context adaptation, a sample-efficient validation-generation loop designed for this setting. A validation agent extracts structured diagnostic information from execution traces, providing gradient-like guidance to a generation agent that proposes multiple candidates per iteration. A knowledge graph derived from the problem description supplies semantic constraints to the generation agent. Simulated annealing selects among candidates to avoid greedy collapse. Our method outperforms zero-shot, Reflexion, and OpenEvolve on seven of eight problems at both 300 and 600 evaluations (p < 0.01), a regime where population-based search has not yet accumulated sufficient diversity to compete. Notably, on the primary motivating problem (cross-coupled optimization), our method also achieves the best score at 1000 evaluations, consistent with the hypothesis that structured execution feedback is most beneficial when correctness depends on runtime coupling. Ablation results confirm that structured execution feedback is the primary driver.

</details>


### [213] [Software Engineering in the Agent Era From Trustworthy Change to Human Agent Software Organizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04630)
*Zhongjie Wang,Mingyi Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a governance framework for software agents that enable elastic digital execution. It introduces Trustworthy Change (TC) as the engineering object, Responsibility Topology to classify organizations by residual-risk acceptance authority distribution, and Human-Agent Cell (HAC) as the execution abstraction. The framework addresses how to govern scalable execution while maintaining human oversight and acceptance authority.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software agents enable parallelized digital execution without proportional human headcount, but human cognition, organizational authority, and economic capacity remain bottlenecks. The question is how scalable execution should be governed so organizations can accept and sustain its changes.

Method: Theoretical framework construction with three constructs: Trustworthy Change (TC), Responsibility Topology, and Human-Agent Cell (HAC). The framework makes authority an explicit classification axis and derives consequences for change state, shared engineering facts, verification, and flow control.

Result: A testable framework with two constructs (TC and Responsibility Topology) and one execution abstraction (HAC). Responsibility Topology classifies organizations into single-center (one final baseline responsibility anchor) or multi-anchor (requires joint acceptance across independently governed domains) topologies. HAC produces candidates, proposals, and evidence but grants no acceptance authority.

Conclusion: The paper contributes theory construction and operationalization for agent-scaled execution governance. Progressive Specification and bounded-capacity analysis remain hypotheses to test. Empirical validity remains open to controlled, longitudinal, and field studies.

Abstract: Software agents make digital execution elastic: repository analysis, code generation, testing, migration, tool use, and operations can be replicated and parallelized without proportional human headcount. Problem framing, semantic commitment, verification, integration, attention, and residual-risk acceptance remain bounded by human cognition, organizational authority, and economic capacity. How should scalable execution be governed so organizations can accept and sustain its changes?
  Our testable framework has two constructs and one execution abstraction. Trustworthy Change (TC) is the engineering object moving from intent through delegated execution, verification, integration, acceptance, and operation. Responsibility Topology classifies organizations by the distribution of independent residual-risk acceptance authority. A single-center topology has one final baseline responsibility anchor; a multi-anchor topology requires joint acceptance across independently governed domains. The Human-Agent Cell (HAC) produces candidates, proposals, and evidence; execution grants no acceptance authority. As execution and authority scale differently, distributed HACs create context-coherence and invalidation pressures, while multi-anchor governance adds joint acceptance and explicit responsibility closure.
  Responsibility, accountability, change management, specification, verification, and human oversight predate this work; our claim is only that agent-scaled execution changes how they fit together. We make that authority an explicit classification axis and derive consequences for change state, shared engineering facts, verification, and flow control. Progressive Specification and bounded-capacity analysis remain hypotheses to test, not laws. We contribute theory construction and operationalization; empirical validity remains open to controlled, longitudinal, and field studies.

</details>


### [214] [How Developers Discuss Generative AI: A Longitudinal Study of the Visual Studio Code Community](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04680)
*Panida Rumriankit,Akito Monden,Hiroki Inayoshi,Pattara Leelaprute,Bundit Manaskasemsak,Kundjanasith Thonglek,Arnon Rungsawang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper analyzes 25,227 AI-related issues from the VS Code GitHub repository (2021-2026) to understand how developers discuss generative AI tools in practice. It finds that discussions focus on operational concerns (agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, billing) rather than risks like hallucination and licensing that dominate survey-based studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI tools (GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, coding agents) have become widespread in software development, yet there is limited understanding of how mainstream open source communities discuss these tools in practice. Existing research relies heavily on surveys, leaving a gap in understanding real-world, workflow-oriented perspectives.

Method: Longitudinal analysis of 43,806 candidate issues from the VS Code GitHub repository (January 2021 - June 2026). The corpus was refined using keyword retrieval combined with semantic relevance filtering, yielding 25,227 AI-related issues. BERTopic was applied for topic identification, with the filtered corpus used for theme validation and robustness re-clustering. Temporal evolution was analyzed using monthly prevalence and Mann-Kendall trend tests.

Result: Developer discussions are dominated by practical operational concerns: agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, and billing. In contrast, risks frequently emphasized in survey-based studies (hallucination, licensing) rarely appear. Discussions evolved from AI-assisted code completion toward conversational and agent-based development over time.

Conclusion: GitHub Issues provide a practical, workflow-oriented perspective on generative AI that complements survey-based studies of developer perceptions. The findings suggest that real-world discussions in open source communities focus on operational aspects of AI-assisted software development rather than theoretical risks.

Abstract: Generative AI tools such as GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and coding agents have rapidly become part of everyday software development, yet little is known about how mainstream open source communities discuss them in practice. This paper presents a longitudinal analysis of generative-AI-related discussions in the Visual Studio Code (VS Code) GitHub repository, using 43,806 candidate issues created between January 2021 and June 2026. To improve corpus quality, we combined keyword retrieval with semantic relevance filtering, yielding a filtered corpus of 25,227 AI-related issues. We applied BERTopic to the retrieved corpus to identify discussion topics, using the filtered corpus for theme validation and a robustness re-clustering, and analyzed their evolution over time using monthly prevalence and Mann-Kendall trend tests. The results show that developer discussions are dominated by practical concerns regarding the operation of AI-assisted development environments, including agent management, configuration, reliability, authentication, and billing, whereas risks frequently emphasized in survey-based studies, such as hallucination and licensing, rarely surface in this venue. This suggests that discussions of generative AI in the VS Code issue tracker primarily focus on operational aspects of AI-assisted software development. Furthermore, discussions evolved from AI-assisted code completion toward conversational and agent-based development, reflecting the increasing integration of generative AI into software development workflows. These findings suggest that GitHub Issues provide a practical, workflow-oriented perspective on generative AI that complements survey-based studies of developer perceptions.

</details>


### [215] [Beyond Code Generation: Reliability, Verification, and Cost Economics in the Agentic Software Development Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04681)
*Happy Bhati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper examines the shift of AI coding systems from simple autocomplete to autonomous agents capable of complex software development tasks. It synthesizes evidence from 2024-2026 showing that while coding activity gains are meaningful, they attenuate sharply before shipping reliable software due to bottlenecks in review, integration, testing, security, and deployment stages. The authors propose four new engineering concepts to frame this challenge and shift the research question from code generation volume to production-qualified value delivery per dollar, reviewer-hour, and operational risk unit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in understanding AI coding agents' real impact on software delivery. While early studies show productivity gains in coding, newer evidence reveals these gains don't translate proportionally to shipped software. The authors seek to move beyond "how much code can agents generate" to "how much production-qualified value can systems deliver" - a more holistic measure accounting for costs, human review time, and operational risk.

Method: The paper employs a synthesis approach, aggregating evidence from multiple sources: peer-reviewed software engineering research, university studies, benchmark audits, production reports from major technology companies, developer telemetry, and cost-management evidence. The timeframe covers primarily 2024 through September 2026. No new model experiments are conducted; numerical findings are attributed to their original studies.

Result: The paper proposes four key engineering concepts: (1) Agentic SDLC Throughput Paradox - the observation that increased coding throughput doesn't proportionally increase shipped software; (2) Production-Qualified Change (PQC) - a metric for changes that are truly ready for production; (3) Verification Tax - the cost overhead of validating agent-generated code; (4) Agentic SDLC Control Plane - a framework for allocating autonomy subject to cost, reliability, and human-attention budgets. The evidence maps today's supervised agents toward future policy-bounded software factories.

Conclusion: The conclusion shifts the central research question from measuring agent code generation capacity to measuring production-qualified value delivery per dollar, per reviewer-hour, and per unit of operational risk. This represents a fundamental reframing of how we evaluate AI coding systems - from pure productivity metrics to comprehensive value delivery metrics that account for the full software development lifecycle and its associated costs and risks.

Abstract: AI coding systems are moving from autocomplete and chat toward agents that can inspect repositories, edit multiple files, run tools, write tests, open pull requests, and work for long periods with limited supervision. This capability changes the bottleneck in software delivery. Recent field studies show meaningful gains in coding activity, but newer evidence also shows that those gains attenuate sharply between writing code and shipping reliable software. Review, integration, testing, security, deployment, and production operations remain constraining stages, while the economics are shifting from predictable per-seat licensing toward variable token, tool, sandbox, CI, and rework costs.
  This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed software-engineering research, university studies, benchmark audits, production reports from major technology companies, developer telemetry, and cost-management evidence released primarily from 2024 through September 2026. No new model experiment is claimed; numerical findings remain attributed to their original studies. The synthesis proposes four engineering concepts: the Agentic SDLC Throughput Paradox, Production-Qualified Change (PQC), the Verification Tax, and an Agentic SDLC Control Plane that allocates autonomy subject to cost, reliability, and human-attention budgets. An evidence-based horizon then maps today's supervised agents to future policy-bounded software factories. The central research question shifts from how much code an agent can generate to how much production-qualified value an engineering system can deliver per dollar, per reviewer-hour, and per unit of operational risk.

</details>


### [216] [Building a research-software catalog with a coding agent: from hackathon prototype to public deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04711)
*Kazuyoshi Yoshimi,Satoshi Terasaki,Gotai Yamada*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper discusses the development of AI-assisted software portals for research software discovery, comparing a rapid prototype built during a 3-day hackathon with a larger, ongoing project (MateriApps retrieval agent). The key finding is that while coding agents enable rapid implementation, achieving reliable operation requires substantial additional engineering due to silent failures that produce plausible but incorrect outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accelerate research software development using generative AI and coding agents while addressing the increased need for efficient software discovery and maintenance in the research software ecosystem.

Method: The authors developed a repository catalog during a three-day hackathon and examined engineering requirements for public deployment, including adversarial review, data-quality checks, browser-level validation, and publication safeguards. They also explored transferring lessons to a larger human-curated portal (MateriApps) through a retrieval agent combining curated metadata, external documentation, vector search, and local language-model generation.

Result: Implementation with coding agents was rapid, but reliable operation required substantial additional engineering. The most consequential problems were not crashes but silent failures producing plausible yet incomplete or incorrect outputs, arising from incomplete data acquisition, misleading assessments, and retrieval or preprocessing failures.

Conclusion: AI-assisted software portals require explicit validation, monitoring, and repeated review. Curated metadata and maintained documentation remain essential. The MateriApps work is exploratory and preliminary, but the combination of curated metadata, automatically collected documentation, and retrieval-based assistance may be useful for extending other research-software portals.

Abstract: Generative AI and coding agents can accelerate research software development, but they also increase the need for efficient software discovery and maintenance. We developed a repository catalog during a three-day hackathon and subsequently examined the engineering required to make it suitable for public deployment, including adversarial review, data-quality checks, browser-level validation, and publication safeguards. We then explored whether the lessons learned from this prototype could be transferred to a much larger, human-curated portal, through a retrieval agent under development for MateriApps that combines curated portal metadata, external documentation, vector search, and local language-model generation. Implementation with coding agents was rapid, but achieving reliable operation required substantial additional engineering: the most consequential problems were not crashes but silent failures that produced plausible yet incomplete or incorrect outputs, arising from incomplete data acquisition, misleading assessments, and retrieval or preprocessing failures. These observations suggest that AI-assisted software portals require explicit validation, monitoring, and repeated review, and that curated metadata and maintained documentation remain essential. The MateriApps work is exploratory and remains under active development, so the observations reported for it are preliminary; a comparable combination of curated metadata, automatically collected documentation, and retrieval-based assistance may nevertheless be useful for extending other research-software portals.

</details>


### [217] [Same Request, Different Answer: Quantization Amplifies Cache-Induced Divergence in LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04748)
*Aditi Patodiya*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Prefix caching, a transparent optimization in LLM serving engines, introduces severe reproducibility issues that worsen with weight quantization. At 16-bit precision, 36.2% of agentic episodes diverge; at 4-bit, 75.0% diverge. Without caching, reproducibility is perfect (0/800 episodes). The root cause is that cache state is not included in requests or reset by default.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prefix caching is enabled by default in major open-source LLM serving stacks and treated as a transparent optimization. This paper investigates whether this optimization has hidden costs, particularly regarding reproducibility of LLM outputs.

Method: Controlled experiment: 80-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload, fixed model/decoding parameters/seed/request order, serial execution at batch size=1. Tested caching enabled vs. disabled across 2 engines and 4 weight formats. Three follow-up experiments to locate the cause of divergence.

Result: With caching: 36.2% trajectory change at 16-bit, 75.0% at 4-bit. Without caching: 0% divergence (0/800 episodes). A single server-level prompt-cache setting shifts divergence by 37.5 percentage points. Execution order matters only when that setting is active. Restoring cache state makes each path reproduce (40/40) but they still differ from each other (14/40). Divergence reaches task outcomes without changing aggregate accuracy.

Conclusion: Cached serving is deterministic given cache state, but irreproducible in practice because cache state is absent from requests and never reset by default. This represents a significant hidden cost of prefix caching that affects real-world deployments, especially with aggressive quantization.

Abstract: Prefix caching, in which a serving engine reuses the key and value tensors of a shared prompt prefix across requests, is enabled by default in the major open-source stacks and treated as a transparent optimization. We measure what it costs in reproducibility, and find that the cost rises sharply with weight quantization. Holding the model, decoding parameters, seed, and request order fixed, and issuing every request serially at batch size one, we ran an eighty-episode multi-turn agentic tool-use workload with caching enabled and disabled across two engines and four weight formats. Enabling the cache changed the agent's trajectory on 36.2 percent of episodes at 16-bit precision and on 75.0 percent at four-bit, a gradient that survives re-measurement under a controlled cache configuration. With caching disabled, repeated execution was bit-identical in every configuration, 0 of 800 episodes, which bounds other sources of nondeterminism at 0.5 percent. Repeated cache-enabled runs did diverge, and three experiments locate the cause: a single server-level prompt-cache setting moves run-to-run divergence by 37.5 percentage points, execution order acts only while that setting is active, and restoring cache state makes the cached and recompute paths each reproduce on 40 of 40 items while still differing from each other on 14. Cached serving is deterministic given cache state, and irreproducible in practice because that state is absent from the request and never reset by default. A single-turn bridge shows the divergence reaching task outcomes without shifting aggregate accuracy. We release the harness, logs, and analysis pipeline.

</details>


### [218] [Better Understanding, Better Fixes? A Study of Hallucination in LLM-based Automated Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04909)
*Xuemeng Cai,Jiakun Liu,Linhan Yang,Wei Ma,Lingxiao Jiang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates hallucination in LLM-based automated program repair (APR) through a multi-layered analysis examining both final patches and intermediate artifacts. The study evaluates three LLMs on 832 Defects4J bugs across three tasks: triggering testcase identification, line coverage prediction, and additional testcase generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing APR evaluations are result-centric and provide limited insight into hallucination during repair. Hallucination can occur not only in final patches but also in intermediate artifacts that guide patch generation, which has not been adequately studied.

Method: The researchers characterize hallucination as producing patches or intermediate artifacts not faithfully grounded in available repair evidence. They examine repair hallucination in final patches and understanding hallucination in intermediate artifacts through three tasks. Three representative LLMs were evaluated on 832 Defects4J bugs through both automatic evaluation and manual analysis of 812 sampled repairs.

Result: Only 21.0%-55.9% of generated patches pass the developer-written test suite. Manual analysis revealed repair hallucinations in 72.7% of cases, including patches passing all available tests. Incorrect causal localization accounts for 45.9% and incorrect repair strategies for 18.5% of hallucinations. Models frequently misidentify triggering testcases, mispredict line coverage involving branching control flow, and generate additional testcases with missing bug-triggering conditions or incorrect expected behavior. While more accurate intermediate artifacts are generally associated with successful repairs, this relationship does not always hold.

Conclusion: Both repair hallucination (in final patches) and understanding hallucination (in intermediate artifacts) remain prevalent in LLM-based automated program repair, highlighting the need for better evaluation metrics that go beyond result-centric assessment.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced automated program repair (APR), yet existing evaluations remain largely result-centric and provide limited insight into hallucination during repair. In APR, hallucination may arise not only in final patches but also in the intermediate artifacts that guide patch generation. To address this gap, we perform a multi-layered analysis of hallucination throughout the APR process. Specifically, we characterize hallucination as the production of patches or intermediate artifacts that are not faithfully grounded in the available repair evidence. We examine repair hallucination in final patches and understanding hallucination in intermediate artifacts through three tasks, namely triggering testcase identification, line coverage prediction, and additional testcase generation.We then evaluate three representative LLMs on 832 Defects4J bugs through automatic evaluation and manual analysis. Our results show that both repair and understanding hallucinations remain prevalent. Across models and settings, only 21.0%-55.9% of generated patches pass the developer-written test suite. Moreover, although more accurate intermediate artifacts are generally associated with successful repairs, this relationship does not always hold. Manual analysis of 812 sampled repairs identifies repair hallucinations in 72.7% of cases, including patches that pass all available tests; incorrect causal localization and incorrect repair strategies account for 45.9% and 18.5% of these hallucinations, respectively. Meanwhile, models frequently misidentify triggering testcases, mispredict line coverage involving branching control flow, and generate additional testcases with missing bug-triggering conditions or incorrect expected behavior.

</details>


### [219] [ARIA - An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Testing of Infotainment Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04913)
*António Azevedo,Bruno Lima,João Pascoal Faria*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ARIA is a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously tests Android automotive infotainment systems via visual interaction, using a closed-loop pipeline of four specialized agents plus a report stage. Evaluated on 30 scenarios, it achieved 93.3% completion rate with 71.4% ground truth match, caught all 5 known defects, and outperformed a single-agent baseline (52.6% vs 72.0% false positive rate).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automotive infotainment validation relies on slow, costly manual testing incompatible with agile releases and OTA updates. Scripted automation is brittle and high-maintenance. Existing LLM-driven frameworks target web/mobile apps using single/dual-agent setups that overload models with multiple tasks, leading to hallucinations and unproductive exploration loops given infotainment complexity.

Method: ARIA uses a closed-loop pipeline of four specialized agents per step (perception, planning, action selection, validation) plus a report stage. From single-sentence scenarios (path, action, expected outcome), it runs interactions and produces reports, reproducible scripts, and visual evidence. Evaluated on a manufacturer's physical Android infotainment system across 30 scenarios. A single-agent baseline was used for comparison.

Result: ARIA completed 28 of 30 scenarios (93.3%) with a verdict (2 errored). 20 of 28 (71.4%) matched ground truth. It caught all 5 known defects, with no fault passing as working. 8 false positives stemmed from navigation/image limits and unsupported gestures. Single-agent baseline showed 72.0% false positive rate vs ARIA's 52.6% (post-revisitation). Fault detection was perfectly consistent across repeated runs, with stability tracking complexity.

Conclusion: Multi-agent LLMs can run infotainment tests industrially while exposing the cost of low false-positive tolerance. The multi-agent design provides significant value over single-agent approaches, with lower false positive rates and better navigation vs. failure differentiation. The approach enables CI integration of visual testing with consistent fault detection.

Abstract: Automotive infotainment validation still relies on manual testing, slow, costly, and incompatible with agile releases and OTA updates. Scripted automation only partly helps: it couples test logic to implementation, yielding brittle, high-maintenance suites. Existing LLM-driven frameworks mostly target web/mobile apps, using single- or dual-agent setups that overload one or two models with perception, planning, action selection, and validation at once, prone to hallucinations and unproductive exploration loops given infotainment complexity. We present ARIA (Autonomous Real-time Infotainment Assessment), a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously runs end-to-end tests on Android infotainment systems via visual interaction, using a closed-loop pipeline of four specialized agents per step plus a report stage. From single-sentence scenarios (path, action, expected outcome), ARIA runs the interactions and produces reports, reproducible scripts, and visual evidence per step. Evaluated on a manufacturer's physical Android infotainment system across 30 scenarios, ARIA completed 28 (93.3%) with a verdict (2 errored), 20 of which (71.4%) matched ground truth. It caught all 5 known defects, no fault passed as working; its 8 false positives stem from navigation/image limits and unsupported gestures, showing multi-agent LLMs can run infotainment tests industrially while exposing the cost of a low false-positive tolerance. A single-agent baseline confirms the multi-agent design's value: on the first pass, before stronger-model revisitation narrows the gap, it shows a far higher false-positive rate (72.0% vs. 52.6%), conflating navigational difficulty with system failure. We report first-pass/post-revisitation results, token/call/cost per scenario, and show via repeated runs that stability tracks complexity, with fault detection perfectly consistent, pointing to CI integration of visual testing.

</details>


### [220] [An Empirical Study on Learning Paths and Gender Dynamics in Scrum Master Roles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05186)
*Manuela Petrescu,Paul Razvan Petrescu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the Scrum Master role in multicultural software companies, focusing on learning paths, team size requirements, and soft skills development monitoring. The study used two qualitative interview surveys with mixed analysis methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the widespread adoption of Agile development methodology and the persistent high demand for experienced Agile professionals, specifically Scrum Masters. The study aims to understand the learning path and career development for this role in multicultural contexts.

Method: Two-phase qualitative approach consisting of interview studies, with both qualitative and quantitative data analysis of the results.

Result: Three key findings: (1) The need for a Scrum Master depends on team size, with a six-member limit identified; (2) No standardized process exists for soft skills learning or metrics to measure progress; (3) Companies measure soft skills through client or team feedback, with some considering both. Many learning initiatives were employee-driven.

Conclusion: The study concludes that Scrum Master necessity correlates with team size, and soft skills development lacks standardization across companies, with learning often driven by individual employee initiative rather than formal company programs.

Abstract: Context: Agile development methodology has been widely adopted by industry and the demand for experienced professionals in Agile-related roles is persistently high. Objectives: We focus on the learning path for a Scrum Master role in multicultural software companies and investigate the role in relation to team size, together with the learning process for a career path, and how companies monitor soft skills development. Method: We conducted our study in two phases, two qualitative surveys (interview studies) and performed a qualitative and quantitative data analysis of the results. Conclusions: Our results identified that the need for a Scrum Master (SM) depends on the size of the team, with our study indicating a six-member limit. There is no overall standardized process for soft skills learning or metrics to measure progress. Some companies measure soft skills based on feedback received from the client or from the team, and other companies are taking both types of feedback into consideration. Many learning initiatives, especially on soft skills for an SM role, were based on actions of the employees.
  The version of Record of this contribution is published in Software Engineering and Advanced Applications. SEAA 2025. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 16083. Springer, Cham. and available online at: check DOI.

</details>


### [221] [T(r)opical Islands: Visualizing & Understanding Socio-Technical Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05254)
*Adam Štěpánek,Marco Raglianti,Vít Rusňák,Jan Byška,Barbora Kozlíková,Michele Lanza*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Projects hosted on collaborative software development platforms, such as GitHub, include many non-code artifacts documenting the project's lifecycle, with its challenges, plans, design, and even community. These socio-technical artifacts include, for example, bug reports, feature requests, and forum posts, offering a useful prospect on the project's evolution. However, these artifacts are dispersed over multiple communication channels and written in natural language, making their analysis difficult, as they are fragmented and with considerable noise.
  We present a 3D visualization approach mapping topics found across a project's socio-technical artifacts onto vegetation-covered islands, where the individual artifacts are depicted as trees of various types. The topic islands rise out of the ocean as they become discussed, to sink again when they are no longer so. We built a prototype implementing the entire visualization pipeline, from data mining to interactive rendering, leveraging machine learning techniques to cluster the artifacts and extract their topics. We present, through several case studies, the insights that our approach elicits about discussions of development topics throughout a project's history. The user study we conducted (N=34) further strengthens our conclusions about its suitability for understanding socio-technical artifacts and their evolution.

</details>


### [222] [Ritgard: T(r)opical Islands of Socio-Technical Artifacts on GitHub](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05278)
*Adam Štěpánek,Marco Raglianti,Jan Byška,Barbora Kozlíková,Michele Lanza*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Ritgard is a tool that mines GitHub repositories for socio-technical artifacts (Issues, Pull Requests, Discussions) and visualizes them as 3D islands with trees, where each tree represents an artifact and each island represents a topic. The terrain rises and falls based on topic activity over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Socio-technical artifacts (STAs) contain valuable information about project architecture and evolution that code alone cannot provide, but this information is fragmented across different communication channels and written in natural language, making it difficult to extract and explore.

Method: The tool mines GitHub repositories for STAs (Issues, PRs, Discussions), then uses text embedding and text summarization to extract topics from the artifacts. These are visualized as 3D islands where each tree represents a single artifact and each island represents a topic, with terrain elevation indicating topic activity over time.

Result: A functional visualization tool that depicts the evolution of features and concerns throughout a project's lifetime, showing when topics become active (island rises) or stale (island sinks).

Conclusion: The paper describes the usage and implementation of Ritgard, highlighting the technical challenges involved in creating this 3D visualization of socio-technical artifacts.

Abstract: A software project is more than just code. Non-code artifacts often document the human processes and decisions behind source code. The rationale behind a library change, an architectural decision, a problem encountered by a user are all examples of information typically present in socio-technical artifacts (STAs), created and persisted in channels separate from the repository itself (yet sometimes very close---e.g., GitHub Issues with GitHub repositories). These STAs are a trove of information about the project's architecture and its evolution, containing details and insights that code alone cannot provide. Unfortunately, this information is not easily extracted and explored as STAs are frequently fragmented over different communication channels, and are written in natural language.
  We present Ritgard, a tool that mines GitHub repositories for their STAs, namely Issues, Pull Requests, and Discussions, and visualizes them as 3D islands covered with trees. Each tree represents a single artifact and each island is a topic extracted from the artifacts through a combination of text embedding and text summarization. The terrain of the islands rises out of the ocean as the topic becomes active and sinks back in when it becomes stale, thus depicting the evolution of features and concerns throughout the project's lifetime. We describe the tool's usage and implementation, showing the numerous technical challenges behind Ritgard's visualization.

</details>

### [223] [Spectral-Target Physical Latent Structuring for JEPA-Style World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04264)
*Penghao Zhu,Salvatore Penachio,Kaustav Mukherjee,Aneesh Jonelagadda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies a new failure mode in latent world models called "physical representation laziness," where learned latent states fail to represent key physical properties despite not collapsing. The authors propose a "Fourier auxiliary head" method that provides training-time supervision to enforce physically-informed latent space structuring, improving planning success rates especially in dynamic environments and low-data regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models (like LeWorldModel) predict and plan in latent space rather than pixel space. While regularization techniques like SIGReg prevent representation collapse, the authors discovered a new failure mode called "physical representation laziness" - particularly in highly dynamic environments. In this case, latent states don't collapse but fail to represent key physical properties, leading to ubiquitous downstream planning failure.

Method: The proposed solution is a lightweight "Fourier auxiliary head" that provides training-time auxiliary supervision. This method enforces physically-informed structuring of the latent space with no additional inference-time cost and can be generalized to any environment. The Fourier auxiliary head incorporates physical knowledge into the learning process.

Result: Experiments show: (1) Substantially improved planning success rates in dynamic environments where baseline LeWM exhibits physical representation laziness; (2) Modest improvements in other environments even when baseline doesn't show laziness; (3) Higher latent space correlations with key physical properties; (4) Particularly impactful in low-data regimes for increasing success rate.

Conclusion: The Fourier auxiliary head method improves both overall success rate and data efficiency while avoiding representation laziness in latent world models. The superior planning performance is accompanied by physically-structured latent states, demonstrating the potential benefit of physically-informed representations for downstream planning tasks.

Abstract: Latent world models have become increasingly popular as a method to predict and plan in latent space rather than pixel space. Recent architectures, such as LeWorldModel (LeWM), jointly train the encoder and predictor using regularization techniques like SIGReg to prevent representation collapse. Even with such regularization preventing representation collapse, we identify a new world model failure mode of \textit{physical representation laziness}, particularly noted in highly dynamic environments. For these lazy cases, the learned latent states do not collapse but nonetheless fail to represent key physical properties, causing ubiquitous downstream planning failure. To resolve this issue, we propose training-time auxiliary supervision with a lightweight "Fourier auxiliary head", which enforces physically-informed structuring of the latent space with no additional inference-time cost and can be generalized to any environment. Experimentally, we show that the auxiliary head substantially improves planning success rates in dynamic environments where the baseline LeWM exhibits physical representation laziness. It also leads to modest improvements in other environments, even when the baseline does not exhibit physical representation laziness. We further observe superior planning performance being accompanied by higher latent space correlations with key physical properties, indicating both the ability of our method to physically structure latent states and the potential planning-side benefit to the learned representation being physically structured. We also see in low-data regimes, auxiliary supervision is particularly impactful in increasing success rate. These findings support the use of our Fourier auxiliary head method to improve both overall success rate and data efficiency, while avoiding representation laziness in latent world models.

</details>


### [224] [ProToMEx: Rapid, Interpretable Explanations via Structured Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04265)
*Athina Georgara,Adarsh Valoor,Sarvapali D. Ramchurn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProToMEx is a model-agnostic post-hoc explainer that uses Probabilistic Topic Models to learn latent "topics" representing high-level semantic reasons for classification decisions, providing both global and local explanations while being 30-40x faster than SHAP and LIME.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-hoc explainers focus on feature attribution, assigning importance scores to individual features. This approach fails to capture complex, combinatorial patterns that drive model decisions. There is a need for explainability methods that reveal underlying semantic structures rather than just feature-level importance.

Method: ProToMEx leverages Probabilistic Topic Models (PTMs) to learn latent "topics" representing distinct high-level reasons for classification. It is model-agnostic and provides both global explanations (model's overall behavior) and local explanations (disentangling multiple co-existing reasons for specific predictions).

Result: ProToMEx produces explanations of comparable fidelity to SHAP and LIME while being ~30-40x faster over standardized tabular datasets and synthetic datasets. It drastically reduces amortized computational cost for generating local explanations.

Conclusion: ProToMEx successfully bridges the gap between feature-level attribution and semantic explanation by using topic models. It achieves comparable fidelity to popular methods with significant computational advantages, making it highly suitable for real-time applications.

Abstract: Existing post-hoc explainers for machine learning classifiers primarily focus on feature attribution, assigning importance scores to individual features. While valuable, this approach struggles to articulate the complex, combinatorial patterns that often drive a model's decision-making process. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProToMEx, a new paradigm for explainability that leverages Probabilistic Topic Models (PTMs). Our model-agnostic framework learns latent ''topics'' that represent distinct, high-level reasons for a classification, moving beyond simple feature importance to reveal underlying semantic structures. ProToMEx naturally provides both global explanations of a model's overall behaviour and local explanations that can disentangle multiple co-existing reasons for a specific prediction. We demonstrate empirically that ProToMEx not only produces explanations of comparable fidelity to popular methods like SHAP and LIME but also drastically reduces the amortised computational cost of generating local explanations, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Specifically, we show that ProToMEx is ~30-40x faster than SHAP and LIME over standardised tabular datasets and synthetic datasets.

</details>


### [225] [A Data Fusion Framework for Grounding Aerospace Surrogate Model via Experimental Wind-Tunnel Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04267)
*Nitin Nagesh Kulkarni,Dheeraj Vemula,Yin Yu,Peter Lyu,Juan J. Alonso*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an experimentally grounded correction framework that adapts a CFD-trained deep learning surrogate (Geotransolver) using wind-tunnel Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP) measurements. The framework learns systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies without retraining the original surrogate, improving predictive accuracy at the wing suction peak, shock location, and pressure recovery regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While aerodynamic surrogate models trained on high-fidelity CFD data can accurately reproduce numerical predictions, they suffer from systematic discrepancies between CFD and experimental observations. The goal is to incorporate experimental information to improve predictive fidelity without losing the generalization capability and computational efficiency of the CFD-trained surrogate.

Method: 1) Train a Geotransolver surrogate on 2,300 high-fidelity CFD simulations of NASA CRM wing-body configuration (geometric variation, Mach 0.70-0.85, AoA 0-4°). 2) Train a separate correction network on spatially registered PSP measurements at two freestream Mach numbers (0.70 and 0.85) across the same AoA range. 3) The correction network learns the discrepancy between surrogate-predicted and experimentally measured surface-pressure distributions without modifying the pretrained surrogate parameters.

Result: At Mach 0.85, the correction substantially improves agreement with PSP, particularly at the wing suction peak, shock location, and subsequent pressure recovery. The method reduces both the magnitude of prediction error and the fraction of wetted surface where error exceeds 0.05 in Cp. On held-out angles of attack, the grounded surrogate agrees with measurement to within 2.3-2.7% of the measured Cp range, outperforming direct interpolation between measured conditions at every state tested.

Conclusion: Experimental measurements can successfully ground a large-scale simulation-trained surrogate by learning systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies while preserving its generalization capability and computational efficiency. This framework enables improved predictive accuracy using limited experimental data without modifying the original surrogate parameters.
