Abstract: Aerodynamic surrogate models trained on high-fidelity CFD data reproduce numerical predictions of both scalar outputs and entire fields accurately, yet their predictive fidelity is limited by systematic discrepancies between CFD and experimental observations. We present an experimentally grounded correction framework that adapts a CFD-trained deep learning surrogate using wind-tunnel PSP measurements. A Geotransolver surrogate trained on 2,300 high-fidelity CFD simulations of the NASA CRM wing-body configuration, spanning geometric variation, Mach 0.70-0.85, and angles of attack 0 to 4 degrees, reproduces the CFD integrated aerodynamic forces and pitching moment to R2 > 0.99 but does not match the experimental data. To incorporate experimental information without retraining the surrogate, a correction network is trained on spatially registered PSP measurements at two freestream Mach numbers (0.70 and 0.85) across the same angle-of-attack range, learning the discrepancy between the surrogate-predicted and experimentally measured surface-pressure distributions. At Mach 0.85 the correction substantially improves agreement with PSP, particularly at the wing suction peak, shock location, and subsequent pressure recovery, reducing both the magnitude of the prediction error and the fraction of wetted surface on which it exceeds 0.05 in Cp, and it does so from a limited experimental dataset without modifying the pretrained surrogate parameters. On held-out angles of attack the grounded surrogate agrees with measurement to within 2.3-2.7% of the measured Cp range, and outperforms direct interpolation between the measured conditions at every state tested. Experimental measurements can therefore ground a large-scale simulation-trained surrogate by learning systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies while preserving its generalization capability and computational efficiency.

</details>


### [226] [Quantum-Assisted Memory-Efficient Training for Parameter-Intensive Wi-Fi-Based Human Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04271)
*To Truong An,Jie Zhang,Guolin Yin,Junqing Zhang,Yanjiao Li,Trung Q. Duong,Simon L. Cotton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Q-MET, a quantum-assisted memory-efficient training framework for Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition (HAR). It uses hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to reduce trainable parameters by 90-95% while maintaining or improving classification accuracy, and integrates structured pruning for lightweight inference achieving 75-85% sparsity with less than 2% accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Wi-Fi-based HAR systems rely on deep learning models that are computationally and memory intensive in both training and inference, posing significant challenges for real-world deployment. Conventional training requires simultaneous updates of millions of parameters, leading to prohibitive memory consumption.

Method: The proposed Q-MET framework utilizes a hybrid quantum-classical neural network to indirectly generate parameters for HAR models, significantly reducing trainable parameter count compared to direct optimization. Structured pruning is integrated during the training phase to support deployment on resource-constrained devices.

Result: Q-MET achieves 90% to 95% reduction in trainable parameters compared with conventional backpropagation-based DL training while maintaining or even exceeding classical classification accuracy. Additionally, it supports lightweight inference through structured pruning, achieving 75% to 85% model sparsity with less than 2% loss in classification accuracy.

Conclusion: This work represents the first quantum-assisted approach to simultaneously tackle memory inefficiencies in both the training and inference stages of HAR systems, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices.

Abstract: Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition (HAR) has become an important part of integrated sensing and communications, paving the way for a range of context-aware services. However, most existing Wi-Fi-based HAR systems rely on deep learning (DL) models that are computationally and memory intensive in both training and inference, which poses significant challenges for real-world deployment. Conventional training requires simultaneous updates of millions of parameters, leading to prohibitive memory consumption. In this paper, we propose a novel quantum-assisted memory-efficient training framework (Q-MET) designed to improve efficiency in both training and inference. Q-MET utilizes a hybrid quantum classical neural network to indirectly generate parameters for HAR models, significantly reducing the trainable parameter count compared to direct optimization. To further support the deployment on resource-constrained devices, we integrate structured pruning during the training phase. Experimental results demonstrate that Q-MET achieves a 90% to 95% reduction in trainable parameters compared with conventional backpropagation-based DL training while maintaining or even exceeding classical classification accuracy. Additionally, Q-MET supports lightweight inference through structured pruning, achieving 75% to 85% model sparsity with less than 2% loss in classification accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first quantum-assisted approach to simultaneously tackle memory inefficiencies in both the training and inference stages of HAR systems.

</details>


### [227] [Evaluating Large Language Models for Forced Outage Risk Prediction: Benefits and Comparison to Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04272)
*Christos Petridis,Zoran Obradovic,Mladen Kezunovic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study evaluates large language models (LLMs) in a zero-shot setting for predicting weather-related forced outages in distribution grids, comparing them against supervised classifiers using six years of outage and weather data from central Texas.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore whether LLMs can predict weather-related grid outages without labeled training data, leveraging their reasoning capabilities and potential for geographic scalability.

Method: Binary severity classification across three forecast horizons (3h, 6h, 12h). Four zero-shot LLMs were benchmarked against two supervised classifiers under two input configurations: current weather observations and weather forecast data.

Result: Supervised models outperform LLMs on macro-F1 and precision, though newer LLM generations achieve competitive performance. LLMs provide complementary strengths in actionable reasoning and geographic scalability.

Conclusion: Combining LLMs with supervised models represents the best practice, leveraging the strengths of both approaches for outage prediction.

Abstract: This study examines the ability of large language models (LLMs) to predict the risk of weather-related forced outages in the distribution grid in a zero-shot framework, without labeled training data. The problem is formulated as a binary severity classification task across three forecast horizons (3h, 6h, 12h), using six years of outage records and high-resolution weather data for a utility service area in central Texas. Four zero-shot LLMs are benchmarked against two supervised classifiers across two input configurations: one using current weather observations and the other using weather forecast data. Results show that supervised models outperform LLMs on macro-F1 and precision, while newer LLM generations achieve competitive scores. Beyond accuracy, LLMs offer complementary strengths in actionable reasoning and geographic scalability, suggesting that combining them with supervised models may be the best practice.

</details>


### [228] [BER-PEF: Unified Human Mobility Predictability Evaluation via Bayes Error Rate Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04292)
*En Xu,Jingtao Ding,Zhiwen Yu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BER-PEF is a Bayes-error-rate-based framework for evaluating human mobility predictability estimators when ground truth is not directly observable. It maps different data types (symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, learned representations) into a common feature-label space and evaluates estimator outputs against controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human mobility predictability concerns the best prediction performance attainable, but its ground truth is not directly observable on real mobility data. This creates a challenge for comparing and evaluating different predictability estimators.

Method: The framework converts BER (Bayes Error Rate) estimation into mobility predictability estimation by mapping symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, and learned representations into a common feature-label space. It then evaluates estimator outputs along controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval, measuring deviations below, above, and across the full interval.

Result: Experiments on Foursquare NYC and TKY, GeoLife, and T-Drive datasets show that several BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing predictability methods on symbolic sequences and numeric trajectories. The estimates track changes in empirical prediction performance under perturbation. Additional analyses show that contextual inputs and multiple structured representations can be evaluated under the same protocol, and aggregating evidence across multiple perturbation levels provides more reliable estimator selection.

Conclusion: BER-PEF offers a unified and verifiable path for evaluating predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth predictability is unavailable, enabling fair comparison between different estimator approaches.

Abstract: Human mobility predictability concerns the best prediction performance attainable from a given target and input information, but its ground truth is not directly observable on real mobility data. We present BER-PEF, a Bayes-error-rate-based framework that converts BER estimation into mobility predictability estimation and provides a unified protocol for comparing estimators without observable ground truth. The framework maps symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, and learned representations into a common feature--label space, then evaluates estimator outputs along controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval by measuring deviations below the interval, above the interval, and across the full interval. Experiments on Foursquare NYC and TKY, GeoLife, and T-Drive show that several BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing predictability methods on symbolic sequences and numeric trajectories, while their estimates track changes in empirical prediction performance under perturbation. Additional analyses show that contextual inputs and multiple structured representations can be evaluated under the same protocol, and that aggregating evidence across multiple perturbation levels provides a more reliable basis for estimator selection than relying on a single unperturbed observation. BER-PEF therefore offers a unified and verifiable path for evaluating predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth predictability is unavailable.

</details>


### [229] [Data-Driven Learning of Unknown Nonlinear Differential Equations Using Functional Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04329)
*Seyyed Shaho Alaviani,Yongzhi Qu,Gregory W. Vogl*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new interpretable machine learning method for data-driven discovery of nonlinear ODEs from single trajectory data, using Functional Analysis and Operator Theory with a function-space-based cost function, capable of handling both autonomous and non-autonomous systems while simultaneously discovering external forces and underlying dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations of existing ML approaches for discovering nonlinear ODEs by proposing a method that does not require prior physics knowledge and can learn from only one single state trajectory.

Method: The method uses Functional Analysis and Operator Theory to formulate the problem, with a cost function constructed as an integral (distance between functions in function space) rather than discrete-sum of errors. An incremental learning algorithm enables online learning with new samples.

Result: The method can discover unknown vector fields from forced and unforced autonomous and non-autonomous (time-varying) dynamical systems, and can simultaneously discover unknown external forces as functions of time and unknown underlying dynamics.

Conclusion: Numerical examples demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method over existing approaches.

Abstract: In this paper, the problem of data-driven discovery of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is recast, and a new interpretable machine learning (ML) method is proposed. The proposed method aims to learn the unknown vector field of nonlinear dynamics without prior knowledge of the system's physics from only one single state trajectory's data. The proposed method has two fundamental differences with existing methods: 1) the formulation presented in this method is derived based on Functional Analysis and Operator Theory, and 2) the cost function is constructed in the function space as a distance between two functions as an integral, instead of the discrete-sum of errors used in existing ML approaches. An incremental learning algorithm is proposed to learn the unknown vector field to handle new training samples in an online manner. The proposed method can discover the unknown vector field from both forced and unforced autonomous and non-autonomous (or time-varying) dynamical systems. The proposed method is able to simultaneously discover unknown external forces as a function of time and unknown underlying dynamics. Finally, numerical examples are given to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method.

</details>


### [230] [Modular Deep Recurrent Neural Network: Application to Quadrotors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04339)
*Nima Mohajerin,Steven L. Waslander*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A modular deep RNN framework is proposed to enable easy deployment of various RNN architectures with automatic derivative computation. The key innovation is adding feedforward inter-layer connections, which improves learning of high-order dynamics and addresses vanishing/exploding gradient issues. Validated on quadrotor altitude dynamics modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses two main challenges: (1) difficulty in deploying various RNN architectures and computing derivatives for gradient-based learning, and (2) the vanishing/exploding gradient problem in multi-layer RNNs.

Method: A modular deep RNN framework is introduced that allows flexible deployment of RNN architectures and automatic derivative computation. The method adds feedforward inter-layer connections to the multi-layer RNN structure.

Result: Feedforward inter-layer connections significantly improve the RNN's ability to learn and model high-order dynamics and nonlinearities. The approach also alleviates vanishing/exploding gradient problems. In quadrotor altitude dynamics modeling, the proposed network achieves better generalization compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: The modular RNN with feedforward inter-layer connections provides an effective solution for learning complex dynamics, outperforming existing methods in generalization capability for the quadrotor case study.

Abstract: A modular deep Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is introduced to facilitate the process of deploying various architectures of RNNs, and to automatically compute derivatives for gradient-based learning methods. The modularity leads to a set of new architectures, one of which includes feedforward inter-layer connections. By adding feedforward inter-layer connections in a multi-layer RNN, it is observed that the capability of the RNN to learn and model high-order dynamics and nonlinearities is significantly improved. The problem of vanishing/exploding gradient in space for a multilayer RNN is also alleviated using feedforward connections. These results are demonstrated using a quadrotor case study, for which a model of the altitude dynamics is learned with our particular network structure, while existing methods are unable to generalize as quickly or at all.

</details>


### [231] [SharedSAE: One Feature Dictionary Across Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04344)
*Daniil Ognev,Célian Vasson,Lijie Hu,Kentaro Inui,Benjamin Heinzerling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SharedSAE is a method that uses a single shared sparse autoencoder across multiple language models instead of training separate SAEs for each model, combining a shared dictionary with model-specific encoder-decoder pairs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SAE training and latent labeling are typically repeated for every model, which is inefficient. The goal is to create a shared SAE that can interpret multiple language models while preserving reconstruction quality and enabling cross-model interpretability.

Method: SharedSAE combines a shared dictionary with model-specific encoder-decoder pairs. Unlike prior methods that discard activation magnitudes and require all models at inference, SharedSAE normalizes only selection scores (preserving magnitudes) and uses model dropout for single-model inference. Trained on four 1B-scale base language models spanning distinct families and tokenizers.

Result: SharedSAE retains 96.6% of dedicated SAEs' mean explained variance; its latent activations exhibit cross-model correlations 1.8 times as high as separate SAEs aligned post-hoc; its latent descriptions transfer across models. After the dictionary is frozen, new models can be efficiently adapted to it, achieving near-dedicated-SAE reconstruction quality.

Conclusion: A single shared SAE can replace a collection of dedicated per-model SAEs while maintaining high reconstruction quality, enabling cross-model latent descriptions transfer, and allowing efficient adaptation of new models to the shared dictionary.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret language model activations, but SAE training and latent labelling are typically repeated for every model. Here, we show that a single shared SAE can replace a collection of dedicated per-model SAEs. Our method, SharedSAE, combines a shared dictionary with model-specific encoder-decoder pairs. Unlike the closest prior method, which discards activation magnitudes and requires all models at inference, SharedSAE instead normalizes only selection scores, preserving magnitudes, and uses model dropout for single-model inference. We train SharedSAE on four 1B-scale base language models spanning distinct families and tokenizers. Despite sharing its latents across models, SharedSAE retains 96.6% of dedicated SAEs' mean explained variance; its latent activations exhibit cross-model correlations 1.8 times as high as separate SAEs aligned post-hoc, and its latent descriptions transfer across models. After the dictionary is frozen, new models can be efficiently adapted to it, achieving near-dedicated-SAE reconstruction quality while reusing the shared latent descriptions.

</details>


### [232] [A Quantum Variational Approach to Prototypical Recurrent Unit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04354)
*Mahyar Sadeghi Garjan,Tommaso Cesari,Michel Barbeau*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A lightweight Quantum Prototypical Recurrent Unit (QPRU) is proposed, requiring fewer parameters than classical (LSTM, GRU) and quantum (QLSTM, QGRU) baselines while achieving competitive forecasting performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the parameter efficiency and scalability issues in existing quantum recurrent neural networks for time series forecasting.

Method: Design of a compact quantum recurrent architecture (QPRU) that reduces trainable parameters while maintaining forecasting capability.

Result: QPRU achieves competitive forecasting performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines with significantly fewer parameters.

Conclusion: QPRU offers a more scalable and parameter-efficient alternative to existing quantum and classical recurrent architectures for forecasting tasks.

Abstract: We introduce a lightweight Quantum Prototypical Recurrent Unit (QPRU) that requires significantly fewer parameters than both classical recurrent architectures, such as Long Short- Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and quantum variants, including Quantum LSTM (QLSTM) and Quantum GRU (QGRU). Despite its compact design, the QPRU achieves competitive forecasting performance, matching state-of-the-art baselines while offering important structural and practical advantages, including enhanced scalability and a reduced number of trainable parameters.

</details>


### [233] [On the Abundance of Critical Points of the t-SNE Energy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04379)
*Nakul Haridas,Ryan Murray*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of the energy landscape of t-SNE, a popular dimensionality reduction algorithm. The authors investigate why t-SNE often produces spurious local minima that fail to preserve the topological and clustering structure of the original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: t-SNE has been widely adopted for visualization and clustering, but its non-convex energy function makes it difficult to understand what the algorithm actually captures. Empirical observations show that t-SNE can produce local minimizers that break topology and create spurious clusters, but there has been no rigorous explanation for these phenomena.

Method: The authors analyze a general family of energies that include both the original t-SNE and large data limits. For densities in feature space that obey a continuous symmetry, they construct infinite families of distinct critical points by identifying pairs of discrete symmetries—one in the original feature space and one in the target embedding space—that are preserved under gradient dynamics.

Result: The constructed critical points exhibit characteristics commonly observed empirically: topology breaking and spurious clustering. These critical configurations demonstrate how the algorithm can fail to preserve the underlying data structure, providing a theoretical explanation for observed numerical phenomena.

Conclusion: This work provides first steps toward a rigorous understanding of t-SNE's energy landscape. By revealing the mechanisms behind spurious local minima, this research offers insights that could guide the development of more reliable dimensionality reduction methods or better initialization strategies.

Abstract: This paper considers the energy landscape of the t-SNE algorithm. While this algorithm has enjoyed broad adoption, the non-convexity of the associated energy has made it difficult to rigorously understand what the algorithm captures in many settings. In particular, a number of well-known numerical examples, several of which are reproduced in this article, suggest a complicated energy landscape with many local minimizers that do not respect the topology or clustering structure of the underlying data. This work seeks to provide first steps towards a rigorous explanation of these phenomena. Specifically, for a general family of energies, which include both the original t-SNE algorithm and recently identified large data limits, and for densities in feature space which obey a continuous symmetry, we construct infinite families of distinct critical points. These critical points are based upon identifying pairs of discrete symmetries, one in the original feature space and the other in the target embedding space, which are preserved under gradient dynamics. These critical configurations exhibit many characteristics, such as topology breaking and spurious clustering, which are often observed empirically. Finally, numerical and analytical examples are given throughout as a means of illustrating the approach.

</details>


### [234] [Disentangling Attention in Deep Operator Learning: A Controlled Study of Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04407)
*Amar Alem Koric,Qibang Liu,Seid Koric*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a controlled study of five DeepONet variants with different attention mechanisms (cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, attention depth) under both data-driven and physics-informed training regimes, evaluated on three benchmark PDE problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Attention mechanisms have been introduced into neural operators but prior studies change multiple components simultaneously, making it difficult to identify what actually improves accuracy. This work aims to isolate the effects of different attention mechanisms.

Method: Systematic study of 5 DeepONet variants with distinct attention mechanisms. Evaluated on: (1) 1D nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation, (2) 1D viscous Burgers equation, (3) 2D Poisson heat-conduction with heterogeneous source fields. Training under both data-driven and physics-informed regimes.

Result: Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces mean relative L_2 error by factors of 2.4-28.0x vs classical DeepONet. Best attention configurations achieve 3.5-32.3x improvement. Branch self-attention with dot-product fusion is inconsistent for 1D but helps 2D. Adding self-attention on top of cross-attention improves all six cases. Increasing cross-attention depth improves accuracy with diminishing returns and higher cost under physics-informed training.

Conclusion: Query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable mechanism for improving neural operator accuracy. Branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex functional inputs. Global pre-mixing provides no consistent benefit.

Abstract: Deep neural operators learn mappings between input functions and complete PDE solution fields, enabling forward evaluations of new problem instances orders of magnitude faster than conventional numerical solvers. Attention mechanisms have recently been introduced into neural operators, but most studies change several architectural components at once, making it difficult to identify what actually improves accuracy. This work presents a controlled and systematic study of five deep operator network (DeepONet) variants with distinct attention mechanisms, trained under both data-driven and physics-informed regimes, to isolate the effects of cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, and attention depth. We evaluate them on a source-driven transient one-dimensional nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation, a transient one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation with variable initial conditions, and a two-dimensional Poisson heat-conduction problem with heterogeneous source fields. Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces the mean relative L_2 error of the classical DeepONet in all benchmark-training combinations by factors of 2.4-28.0, while the best attention configurations reach 3.5-32.3. Branch self-attention paired only with dot-product fusion is inconsistent, degrading the one-dimensional problems while helping the more complex two-dimensional source field; added on top of cross-attention it improves all six cases, though by less than cross-attention fusion alone. Global pre-mixing provides no consistent benefit. Increasing cross-attention depth further improves accuracy, but with diminishing returns and a substantially higher cost under physics-informed training. Overall, query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable mechanism, whereas branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex functional inputs.

</details>


### [235] [REFINE: LLM Refinement over Budgeted Text-Attributed Graphs for Personalized Medical Concept Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04415)
*Mohsen Nayebi Kerdabadi,Arya Hadizadeh Moghaddam,Dongjie Wang,Zijun Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REFINE is a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework that personalizes medical concept representations from text-attributed knowledge graphs using reinforcement learning and heterogeneous GNNs, improving EHR prediction across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning rich medical concept representations is essential for EHR prediction. Existing encoders process concepts uniformly across patients, but a code's meaning depends on patient-specific clinical context. Two key challenges: (1) deciding how much KG context to incorporate for each code, and (2) aligning semantic information with patient-specific relational structure.

Method: REFINE constructs patient-specific temporal graphs from a global TKG. A sequential reinforcement learning policy selects a personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code. The resulting patient graph is processed by a heterogeneous GNN to capture relation-aware structural dependencies, while a frozen LLM uses graph-aware soft prompts to semantically refine concept representations.

Result: REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones, outperforms strong baselines, and demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed REFINE framework effectively addresses patient-personalized medical concept encoding by combining KG-aware budgeted expansion with heterogeneous GNN processing and LLM-based semantic refinement, showing significant improvements in EHR prediction tasks.

Abstract: Learning rich medical concept representations is essential for EHR prediction. Text-attributed knowledge graphs (TKGs) provide a natural foundation by organizing heterogeneous medical relations together with textual semantics. However, most existing encoders process concepts uniformly across patients, despite the fact that a code's meaning and predictive value depend on patient-specific clinical context and trajectory. Learning patient-personalized concept representations from TKGs introduces two key challenges: (1) deciding how much KG context to incorporate for each observed code, and (2) aligning semantic information with the patient-specific relational structure. We propose REFINE, a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework for patient-personalized medical concept encoding. Starting from a global TKG, REFINE constructs patient-specific temporal graphs. A sequential reinforcement learning policy selects a personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code. The resulting patient graph is processed by a heterogeneous GNN to capture relation-aware structural dependencies, while a frozen LLM uses graph-aware soft prompts to semantically refine concept representations. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones, outperforms strong baselines, and demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency.

</details>


### [236] [Beyond a Universal Forecasting Selector: Demand-Conditioned Model Selection across Demand Patterns and Horizons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04425)
*Adolfo González*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study investigates whether forecasting-model selection should be context-dependent rather than universal. Five selection mechanisms are compared across various demand patterns, datasets, and horizons. The key finding is that no single selector performs best under all conditions, supporting a context-dependent approach to forecasting-model selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Forecasting-model selection remains challenging in heterogeneous demand environments because the optimal decision rule may vary depending on demand structure, data availability, and forecasting horizon. There is a need to determine whether selector performance itself should be treated as context-dependent.

Method: Five selection mechanisms (RMSSE, ERA, OWA, CCG-AHSC, and CCG-AHSCD) were compared across 24 optimized forecasting models, nine datasets, three training-testing partitions, and horizons from 1 to 12 cycles. Performance was evaluated ex post using Global Relative Accuracy (GRA), statistical tests, and a best-attainable-model reference.

Result: No selector dominates across all conditions. CCG-AHSC and CCG-AHSCD perform better for Smooth demand and several Erratic configurations, while OWA and ERA perform better in Intermittent and Lumpy settings. Selector suitability also changes with historical data availability and forecasting horizon.

Conclusion: The findings support a context-dependent rather than universal approach to forecasting-model selection. The optimal selector depends on demand pattern, data availability, and horizon, suggesting practitioners should adapt their selection strategy based on specific conditions.

Abstract: Forecasting-model selection remains difficult in heterogeneous demand because the most suitable decision rule may vary with demand structure, data availability, and forecasting horizon. This study examines whether the selector itself should be treated as a context-dependent component of the forecasting process. Five selection mechanisms - RMSSE, ERA, OWA, CCG-AHSC, and CCG-AHSCD - are compared across 24 optimized forecasting models, nine datasets, three training-testing partitions, and horizons from 1 to 12 cycles. Selector performance is evaluated ex post using Global Relative Accuracy (GRA), statistical tests, and a best-attainable-model reference. No selector dominates across all conditions. CCG-AHSC and CCG-AHSCD are more competitive for Smooth demand and several Erratic configurations, whereas OWA and ERA perform better in Intermittent and Lumpy settings. Selector suitability also changes with historical data availability and horizon, supporting a context-dependent rather than universal approach to forecasting-model selection.

</details>


### [237] [A Repeated-Measurement Study for Cultural Analytics of English Song Lyrics Using Five Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04428)
*E. Cho Smith,Samuel Ho,Dawn Laux*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study evaluates whether Large Language Models can reliably measure social constructs (self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, seeking recognition) in song lyrics. Using 5 LLMs as zero-shot annotators, the researchers found that reliability varies by construct—self-esteem is most reliable, while seeking recognition is least stable. They recommend reporting stability metrics before treating LLM outputs as valid measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical gap in cultural analytics: LLM outputs are increasingly used to measure latent social constructs, but their reliability has not been systematically validated. The researchers aim to establish whether LLM annotations can be treated as trustworthy measurements rather than just qualitative text outputs.

Method: The study employs a multi-faceted methodology: (1) Five LLMs were used as zero-shot annotators on a large corpus of English song lyrics; (2) Four social constructs were measured: self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, and seeking recognition; (3) Three reliability properties were examined: test-retest consistency (repeated runs), inter-model convergence, and transferability to supervised classification using consensus labels.

Result: The key findings reveal construct-dependent reliability: self-esteem showed the strongest repeated-measurement reliability across models; seeking recognition was generally less stable; self-control and seeking belonging exhibited intermediate but model-dependent reliability. Downstream classification confirmed that consensus LLM labels contain learnable signal, though this alone does not establish construct validity.

Conclusion: The study concludes that LLM-based measurement is not uniformly reliable across constructs. Researchers should report repeated-measurement stability and cross-model convergence before treating LLM annotations as scalable measurements in cultural analytics. The findings caution against uncritical adoption of LLMs as measurement tools without proper validation.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate cultural texts at scales that are impractical for human coders. However, before their outputs are treated as measurements of latent social constructs, it is necessary to establish whether those measurements are reliable. This study evaluates five LLMs as zero-shot annotators of four social constructs expressed in English song lyrics: self-esteem, self-control, seeking belonging, and seeking recognition. Using repeated annotations of a large lyric corpus, we examine three properties of LLM-based measurement: consistency across repeated runs, convergence across models, and transferability of consensus labels to supervised classification. The findings show that LLM-based measurement is not uniformly reliable across constructs. Self-esteem exhibits the strongest repeated-measurement reliability across models, while seeking recognition is generally less stable; self-control and seeking belonging show intermediate but model-dependent reliability. Downstream classification further indicates that consensus LLM labels contain learnable signal, although transferability does not itself establish construct validity. Repeated-measurement stability and cross-model convergence should therefore be reported before LLM annotations are treated as scalable measurements in cultural analytics.

</details>


### [238] [Conformity Breaks Conformal Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04445)
*Yibo Hu,Hanyu Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Conformal prediction certificates for LLM calibration become invalid when the LLM sees peer responses that unanimously assert wrong answers. This "score-mechanism shift" causes coverage to drop from 90% to 74% at alpha=0.10, with even worse degradation (87% to 47%) on low-confidence items. Standard conformal fixes fail because the underlying issue is a change in the model's scoring behavior, not the question distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers identified a critical vulnerability in conformal prediction for multi-agent LLM systems: when an LLM sees peer agents unanimously asserting wrong answers, the model's confidence scores for the correct answer change, invalidating previously valid calibration certificates. This undermines reliability guarantees in systems that depend on conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.

Method: The authors conducted experiments across open-weight models and multiple-choice QA tasks, systematically testing how LLM confidence scores change when the model observes peer responses, particularly unanimous-wrong peer answers. They measured coverage rates under standard conformal prediction operating points (alpha=0.10) and analyzed subgroup performance on low-confidence items.

Result: Coverage drops from a calibrated 90% to 74% when the LLM sees unanimous-wrong peers. More severely, targeting low-confidence items reveals an attacker can nearly halve coverage on that subgroup (from 87% to 47%) while the monitored average remains much higher. The failure extends to decision systems: a system that should escalate when uncertain can become confident enough to act on wrong answers. Standard conformal fixes fail because the question distribution remains unchanged—the model's scoring behavior itself has shifted.

Conclusion: Conformal prediction certificates are not robust to multi-agent LLM interactions. The "score-mechanism shift" phenomenon demonstrates that clean calibration in isolation does not guarantee reliable uncertainty quantification when LLMs observe peer responses. This reveals a fundamental limitation in applying conformal prediction to multi-agent LLM systems and requires new approaches that account for social influence on model scoring behavior.

Abstract: A conformal certificate can be valid when an LLM answers alone and invalid when the same LLM sees peers that unanimously assert a wrong answer. The question is unchanged; the model's score for the correct answer changes. We call this a score-mechanism shift: clean calibration certifies how the model scores answers alone, but not how it scores them under peer pressure. We show that this shift silently breaks conformal prediction in multi-agent LLM systems. Across open-weight models and multiple-choice QA tasks, coverage falls from a calibrated 90% to 74% under unanimous-wrong peers at the standard alpha = 0.10 operating point. The average hides a sharper failure: by targeting the low-confidence items the certificate still covers, an attacker nearly halves coverage on that subgroup, from 87% to 47%, while the monitored average remains much higher. The failure also reaches the decision layer: a system that should escalate when uncertain can instead become confident enough to act on the attacker's wrong answer. Standard conformal fixes do not solve the problem, because the question distribution has not changed; the model's scoring behavior has.

</details>


### [239] [When Load-Balancing Goes Too Far: Expert Pruning in Over-Dispersed Mixture-of-Experts Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04453)
*Berkcan Kapusuzoglu,Connor Pryor,Sangwoo Cho,Supriyo Chakraborty,Shi-Xiong Zhang,Sambit Sahu,Milind Naphade*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper identifies a critical failure mode in expert pruning for MoE models under over-dispersed routing (aggressive load-balancing). Standard assumptions about using router probabilities as importance signals break down, causing perplexity to fail as a predictor of task accuracy. The authors propose MESA, a domain-aware pruning method that minimizes worst-case domain degradation, achieving better performance across multiple benchmarks at 25% expert pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expert pruning assumes router probabilities indicate expert importance, but this assumption fails under over-dispersed routing (aggressive load-balancing). The authors aim to understand this failure mode and develop a principled pruning approach for load-balanced MoE models.

Method: The authors (1) identified over-dispersed routing as a distinct regime where importance signals collapse; (2) discovered that perplexity does not predict task accuracy in this regime; (3) found capability trade-offs where different scoring metrics favor different domains; (4) proposed MESA (Minimax Expert Score Allocation) which iteratively boosts importance scores for the worst-affected domain to minimize worst-case degradation.

Result: At 25% expert pruning, MESA achieves the smallest worst-case degradation across domains, outperforming activation-aware baselines on 7 of 11 benchmarks while reducing memory footprint. The method generalizes across multiple model architectures (gpt-oss-20B, gpt-oss-120B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, OLMoE-1B-7B).

Conclusion: Over-dispersed routing is a qualitatively distinct pruning regime where standard assumptions fail. Recognizing this regime is essential for principled expert pruning of load-balanced MoE models. MESA provides a practical solution by balancing domain-specific performance rather than optimizing average accuracy.

Abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory and serving cost of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by removing low-importance experts identified by the router, assuming router probabilities provide a reliable importance signal. We observe that this assumption breaks down under over-dispersed routing, a regime associated with aggressive load-balancing during training, in which tokens are distributed nearly uniformly across experts and importance signals collapse. In this regime, perplexity does not predict downstream task accuracy: on gpt-oss-20B, the lowest-perplexity pruning configuration yields the worst mathematical reasoning, while the highest-perplexity configuration preserves it. This does not occur under standard routing (e.g., Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct), where perplexity and accuracy degrade together. Pruning under over-dispersed routing also exposes a capability trade-off in which no single scoring metric dominates: activation-aware scoring preserves mathematical reasoning but severely degrades knowledge-intensive science (an 18-point gap on GPQA), whereas frequency-based scoring exhibits the reverse. We propose Minimax Expert Score Allocation (MESA), a domain-aware method that iteratively boosts importance scores for experts serving whichever domain is currently worst-affected, minimizing worst-case domain degradation rather than average accuracy. At 25% expert pruning MESA achieves the smallest worst-case degradation across domains, outperforming activation-aware baselines on 7 of 11 benchmarks at a correspondingly reduced memory footprint, and it generalizes to gpt-oss-120B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and OLMoE-1B-7B. Our results indicate that over-dispersed routing is a qualitatively distinct pruning regime in which standard assumptions fail, and that recognizing it is a prerequisite for principled expert pruning of load-balanced MoE models.

</details>


### [240] [On-board ML for Trace Gas detection in Imaging Spectroscopy data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04458)
*Vít Růžička,Adam Chlus,Andrew Thorpe,David R. Thompson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First demonstration of on-board methane point source detection using Imaging Spectroscopy with Edge ML, enabling real-time event detection during aerial campaigns rather than slow post-flight processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current aerial imaging spectroscopy pipelines rely on slow on-the-ground processing, delaying event detection and preventing immediate follow-up actions. Communication bottlenecks also limit immediate transmission of full datacubes during flight.

Method: Tokyo Field Campaign (March 2026) with AVIRIS-5 sensor. Efficient small machine learning model runs on-board to detect potential events; only predicted events (not full datacubes) are downlinked due to bandwidth limitations.

Result: Successfully demonstrated the first on-board detection of methane point source emission using Imaging Spectroscopy data with Edge ML, enabling real-time event detection during flight.

Conclusion: Edge ML enables practical on-board processing for transient event detection in aerial spectroscopy, overcoming communication bottlenecks and enabling immediate follow-up actions for detected events like methane emissions.

Abstract: Data collected during aerial and spaceborne imaging spectroscopy campaigns enables the detection of transient events such as trace gas emissions. However, current processing pipelines depend on slow, on-the-ground processing, which delays the time to information of each detected event and prohibits immediate follow-up actions. During the Tokyo Field Campaign of March 2026, we explored on-board processing of Imaging Spectroscopy data from the equipped AVIRIS-5 sensor. Due to communication bottlenecks, full datacubes cannot be downlinked immediately during the flight. Instead we downlink the potential events predicted by our efficient and small machine learning model. We show the first on-board detection of methane point source emission with Imaging Spectroscopy data using Edge ML.

</details>


### [241] [Nested Inductive Bias Framework for SPD Manifold Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04466)
*Tushar Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses representation learning on Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) manifolds in Geometric Deep Learning. It proposes a Nested Inductive Bias framework that uses two-stage diffeomorphic composition to pull non-Euclidean geometries (like Poincaré metric) onto SPD manifolds, enabling curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers. Additionally, it introduces the Rational Conformal Metric (RCM) for standard vectorized architectures to achieve geometric robustness against outliers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SPD manifold representation learning relies on pullback Euclidean metrics (e.g., Log-Euclidean Metric) which, while computationally efficient, induce flat geometry that fails to capture intrinsic relational priors of datasets. The Poincaré metric is widely used for domain-aligned relational priors in standard vector representations, but generalizing it to SPD manifolds has remained challenging.

Method: The authors propose: 1) A Nested Inductive Bias framework using two-stage diffeomorphic composition to formally pull back non-Euclidean target geometries onto the SPD manifold, enabling curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers that respect both matrix constraints and latent relational geometry; 2) Rational Conformal Metric (RCM) for standard vectorized architectures to establish geometric robustness against outliers by bounding the representation space.

Result: Empirical evaluations on kinematic and signal processing benchmarks, together with synthetic experiments, demonstrate that deep manifold networks experience degradation in class separability unless the metric curvature aligns with the intrinsic data distribution. RCM achieves state-of-the-art geometric robustness against outliers.

Conclusion: The paper successfully bridges the gap between non-Euclidean geometries and SPD manifolds through the Nested Inductive Bias framework, enabling curvature-aligned classifiers. The findings confirm that metric curvature must align with intrinsic data distribution for optimal performance. RCM provides effective geometric robustness for outlier scenarios in standard architectures.

Abstract: In Geometric Deep Learning, inductive biases serve two primary functions: enforcing manifold constraints and embedding relational priors. Currently, representation learning on SPD manifolds frequently relies on pullback Euclidean metrics, such as the Log-Euclidean Metric, to satisfy the former. While computationally efficient in avoiding domain boundary violations, these metrics induce a flat geometry that may fail to capture the intrinsic relational priors of datasets. While metrics such as the Poincaré metric are widely utilized to induce domain-aligned relational priors, generalizing them from standard vector representations to the SPD manifold has remained a challenge. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Nested Inductive Bias framework that utilizes a two-stage diffeomorphic composition to formally pull back non-Euclidean target geometries onto the SPD manifold. This framework enables the construction of curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers that simultaneously respect matrix constraints and the latent relational geometry of the data. Empirical evaluations on kinematic and signal processing benchmarks, together with synthetic experiments, demonstrate that deep manifold networks experience degradation in class separability unless the metric curvature aligns with the intrinsic data distribution. Furthermore, for standard vectorized architectures, we propose the Rational Conformal Metric (RCM), designed to establish state-of-the-art geometric robustness against outliers by bounding the representation space.

</details>


### [242] [Hakken: Predicting future discoveries to fill the gaps in today's knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04494)
*Tarek R. Besold,Uchenna Akujuobi,Pablo Sanchez,Alessandra Toniato,Kana Maruyama,Jihun Choi,Samy Badreddine,Frederick Gifford,Daniel Evans-Yamamoto,Sucheendra K. Palaniappan,Miquel Ferrer,Kae Nagano,Iris Rossell,Tom Joy,Hatem ElShazly,Chrysa Iliopoulou,Christoph Wehner,Thiviyan Thanapalasingam,Susana Nunes,Pedro G. Cotovio,Peter Wurman,Peter Stone,Hiroaki Kitano,Michael Spranger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hakken is a domain-agnostic system that predicts novel scientific relationships by combining transformer-based models on temporal knowledge graphs with LLM semantic knowledge. It includes an explanation framework for evaluating predictions and was demonstrated in biomedical domain, where it identified two previously undocumented interactions (TP53-BAMBI and RAF1-TNF) with implications for drug discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Growing scientific knowledge requires establishing novel relationships beyond deductive inference from existing knowledge. Current methods struggle with predicting relationships that are not contained within the logical deduction of prior knowledge.

Method: Transformer-based prediction model built on temporal sequences of knowledge graphs extracted from research publications, fused with LLM's semantic knowledge. Uses model-agnostic explanation framework to provide accompanying information for each prediction.

Result: Established new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction in biomedical domain. Generated 1.5 million above-confidence-threshold hypotheses related to aging. Two predictions (TP53-BAMBI and RAF1-TNF interactions) were empirically confirmed, with potential significance for drug discovery and repurposing.

Conclusion: Hakken successfully demonstrates the ability to predict novel scientific relationships with high accuracy. The confirmed TP53-BAMBI and RAF1-TNF interactions represent previously undocumented relationships in biomedical science, validating the system's practical utility for accelerating scientific discovery.

Abstract: We present Hakken, a domain-agnostic prediction and explanation system performing knowledge prediction, i.e., growing scientific knowledge by establishing novel relationships, ones that are not limited to the deductive hull of previous knowledge. Hakken uses a transformer-based prediction model built on temporal sequences of knowledge graphs extracted from vast bodies of research publications, fused with an LLM's semantic knowledge, to predict the presence and define the type of as-yet undocumented relationships between scientific concepts. It then calls a model-agnostic explanation framework to provide accompanying information for each prediction that allows scientists to evaluate the suggested new relationship. While general purpose, we demonstrate Hakken's practical capabilities by applying it to the biomedical domain. There, Hakken's prediction model establishes a new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction, and we show that the model's output stays coherent and informative over extended time spans in historic data. In addition, we scored 1.5 million above-confidence-threshold hypotheses related to aging, qualitatively validated batches of these predictions with biologists and progressed three of them for empirical validation in wet-lab. Two predictions with potentially significant impact in the context of drug discovery and repurposing were confirmed, introducing previously undocumented interactions between TP53 and BAMBI, and between RAF1 and TNF, to biomedical science.

</details>


### [243] [An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04530)
*Sebastian Schaffer,Lukas Exl*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic simulations by combining a convolutional autoencoder with a physics-informed latent neural ODE. The model preserves the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation in latent space, using a learned scalar potential with antisymmetric and dissipative operators. Training uses only trajectory data without physical supervision. The deep-quadratic latent energy achieves the best accuracy for long-term trajectory predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduced-order models for micromagnetics are computationally expensive when using full micromagnetic solvers. The authors aim to create a cheaper surrogate model that captures the essential physics while being computationally efficient for trajectory prediction, while preserving the physically meaningful structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation.

Method: The method combines: (1) A convolutional autoencoder for dimensionality reduction; (2) A structured latent neural ODE with an antisymmetric operator (precessional) and symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator derived from the gradient of a learned scalar potential. Models are trained on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses without time-derivative supervision, physical energy labels, or dissipation penalties. Three latent energy architectures are compared: quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic.

Result: Antisymmetric-dissipative models significantly outperform dissipative-only models on uninterrupted rollouts, though they achieve comparable accuracy on short training-style windows. The deep-quadratic energy provides the best overall accuracy for both field directions in the NIST μMAG Standard Problem 4 and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts extend to twice the training horizon.

Conclusion: The physics-informed latent ODE structure, particularly with antisymmetric-dissipative components and deep-quadratic energy, enables accurate long-term trajectory prediction at a fraction of the computational cost of full micromagnetic solvers. The approach demonstrates that preserving the mathematical structure of the underlying physical equation in the reduced-order model is crucial for long-term prediction accuracy.

Abstract: We develop an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. Motivated by the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, the latent vector field is generated from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator and a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. This potential is learned in nonunique latent coordinates and is not identified with the Gibbs free energy, but decreases monotonically along autonomous continuous-time solutions, while the antisymmetric component permits motion along its level sets. The encoder, decoder, latent energy, and operators are trained jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses alone, without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, an initial state is encoded once, evolved in latent space, and decoded only at the requested output times, enabling substantially cheaper trajectory prediction than the micromagnetic solver used to generate the training data. We compare quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic latent energies on two datasets parameterized by field amplitude and generated for the two applied-field directions of the NIST $μ$MAG Standard Problem 4. Dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models achieve comparable accuracy on short training-style windows but differ substantially on uninterrupted rollouts, for which the antisymmetric-dissipative models provide markedly more accurate trajectory predictions. The deep-quadratic energy gives the best overall accuracy for both field directions and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.

</details>


### [244] [Distilled Continuous Diffusion Language Models Can Write Code in Few Steps---or One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04531)
*Fred Zhangzhi Peng,Kaiwen Zheng,Anru R. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PlaidQ is a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code generation that can be distilled into few-step (16 steps) or one-step generation, achieving competitive or superior results compared to longer autoregressive generation while requiring far fewer sampling steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language generation is traditionally sequential (autoregressive) or uses discrete diffusion with long iterative refinement trajectories. The authors aim to leverage continuous diffusion to enable efficient code generation through aggressive trajectory distillation.

Method: PlaidQ repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings. Two distillation techniques are used: (1) distribution matching for few-step generation, and (2) paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation.

Result: At matched model scale, PlaidQ is competitive with discrete diffusion models. A 16-step distilled student achieves 31.78 pass@1 on HumanEval and 40.49 pass@10 on MBPP+, outperforming the same teacher sampled for 512 steps. One-step generation achieves 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval.

Conclusion: Continuous diffusion is a viable path to few-step and one-step code generation, enabling language models to inherit acceleration and distillation machinery from continuous diffusion modeling.

Abstract: Language generation is almost universally treated as a sequential process: autoregressive models emit one token at a time, while diffusion language models replace token-level seriality with a long trajectory of iterative refinement. In this work, we introduce PlaidQ, a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code generation, and show that its trajectory can be aggressively distilled into only a few denoising steps---or even one, enabling efficient code generation. PlaidQ repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings. We distill PlaidQ with distribution matching for few-step generation and paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation. At matched model scale, PlaidQ is competitive with discrete diffusion language models on code generation. Distillation then shifts the quality--compute frontier: a 16-step student reaches 31.78 and 40.49 pass@10 on HumanEval and MBPP+, surpassing the same PlaidQ teacher sampled for 512 steps. At the extreme, paired-trajectory distillation achieves 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval with a single denoising step, producing functionally correct programs. Together, these results establish continuous diffusion as a viable path to few-step and one-step code generation. Broadly, continuous diffusion is not merely another representation for language: it provides an interface through which language models can inherit the acceleration and distillation machinery of continuous diffusion modeling. Training and inference code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/pengzhangzhi/plaidq.

</details>


### [245] [Mitra-v2 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04540)
*Yefan Tao,Xiyuan Zhang,Xinyi Liu,Boran Han,Danielle Maddix,Haoyang Fang,Zhen Han,Jiading Gai,Xuanqing Liu,Michael Bohlke-Schneider,Yuyang,Wang,Gerald Friedland,Kevan Mah,Chris Lee,Chris Kong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mitra-v2 is a tabular foundation model trained on synthetic data that achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world classification and regression tasks, matching the 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 77M parameters (5% of its size).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a compact yet powerful tabular foundation model that can handle diverse real-world classification and regression problems (credit-risk scoring, clinical prediction, equipment-failure detection, house-price estimation) while being trained only on synthetic data.

Method: Built on a small 2D Transformer backbone (77M parameters) with improved optimization, supporting longer contexts and larger feature spaces. Pretrained on a larger and more diverse synthetic task distribution than its predecessor Mitra-v1.

Result: On TabArena benchmark: achieves state-of-the-art performance comparable to industry-scale TabFM and EXAONE Tabular models, significantly surpassing TabPFN-3 in both classification and regression. Matches 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 5% of its size. On TALENT: leads among top models, outperforming TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2. Ranks first on classification tasks with more than 10 classes despite being pretrained on tasks with at most 10 classes.

Conclusion: Mitra-v2 is one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models released to date, delivering frontier performance at a fraction of the cost. The model weights, inference and fine-tuning code, and evaluation results are released under Apache-2.0 license.

Abstract: We introduce Mitra-v2, a tabular foundation model that delivers state-of-the-art performance on real-world classification and regression problems, from credit-risk scoring and clinical prediction to equipment-failure detection and house-price estimation. Mitra-v2 is trained only on synthetic data, with a pretraining distribution that is much larger and more diverse than Mitra-v1's. Built on a small 2D Transformer backbone, Mitra-v2 supports longer contexts and larger feature spaces. Improved optimization lets it learn from this larger task distribution. We evaluate Mitra-v2 on the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, comprising more than 300 real-world datasets under two evaluation protocols. On the full TabArena benchmark, Mitra-v2 delivers state-of-the-art performance at the level of the industry-scale TabFM and EXAONE Tabular models, while surpassing TabPFN-3 by a wide margin in both classification and regression. Mitra-v2 matches the 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 5% of its size (77M parameters), delivering frontier performance at a fraction of the cost. On TALENT, Mitra-v2 remains among the leading models, clearly outperforming TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2. It also ranks first on classification tasks with more than ten classes, even though it was pretrained only on tasks with at most ten classes. These results make Mitra-v2 one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models released to date. We release the model weights, the inference and fine-tuning code, and our evaluation results under the Apache-2.0 license.

</details>


### [246] [Fast Surrogate Modeling of Excitable and Oscillatory FitzHugh-Nagumo Dynamics with Parametric Neural Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04549)
*Andrew Franck,Justin Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a machine learning approach using parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) with FiLM conditioning to surrogate the FitzHugh-Nagumo neuronal model, achieving sub-0.1% error and ~1000x speedup over traditional finite-difference solvers while capturing bifurcation dynamics in both oscillatory and excitable regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical finite-difference solvers are computationally expensive for rapid parameter sweeps in the 5D physiological parameter space of the FitzHugh-Nagumo system, which is important for neuromodulation and mapping voltage recordings back to biophysics.

Method: Train parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators as fast, differentiable surrogates for FHN voltage and recovery fields on a 1D domain, conditioning each Fourier layer via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) on the parameter vector λ = (Du, Dv, a, b, τ). Apply a single bifurcation analysis to delimit oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation) regimes, training one operator in each.

Result: In oscillatory regime: sub-0.1% relative L2 error on both fields, ~1000x speedup over finite-difference baseline, uniform generalization across parameter space, low single-digit percentage errors when extrapolating outside training bounds. In excitable regime: accurately reproduces firing threshold and c ∝ √Du conduction velocity law, replicates full traveling pulses, captures excitable bifurcation structure.

Conclusion: FNO surrogates with FiLM conditioning can effectively capture the full bifurcation structure of the FHN system across both oscillatory and excitable regimes, providing a fast, differentiable alternative to traditional numerical solvers for neuromodulation and biophysical mapping applications.

Abstract: The FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) system serves as a simplified model of neuronal voltage dynamics, capturing the activator-inhibitor structure behind both isolated action potentials and the rhythmic spiking seen across the brain. Exploring its 5D physiological parameter space is important for neuromodulation and mapping voltage recordings back to biophysics, yet classical finite-difference solvers make rapid parameter sweeps expensive. We train parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) as fast, differentiable surrogates for the FHN voltage and recovery fields on a one-dimensional spatial domain, conditioning each Fourier layer on the parameter vector $λ= (D_u, D_v, a, b, τ)$ via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). We apply a single bifurcation analysis that delimits the two distinct regimes the model spans, oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation), and we train one operator in each. In the oscillatory regime the surrogate attains sub-$0.1\%$ relative $L^2$ error on both fields, runs nearly three orders of magnitude faster than the finite-difference baseline, generalizes uniformly across the parameter space, and extrapolates to low single-digit percentage errors outside of the training bounds. In the excitable regime the same operator accurately reproduces the firing threshold and the $c \propto \sqrt{D_u}$ conduction-velocity law and replicates full traveling pulses, fully capturing the excitable bifurcation structure rather than just smoothly interpolating fields.

</details>


### [247] [Training-Free Halving of Activated Experts in Fine-Grained Mixture-of-Experts Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04575)
*Xing Chen,Hengshuai Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental issue in fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models where renormalizing router probabilities based on top-k experts causes both expert selection AND expert output strength to change when k is modified at inference. The authors propose a simple fix: normalize using the probability mass of top-k2 experts while activating only top-k1 experts, introducing one integer parameter with no overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard MoE routing, when the top-k is reduced at inference (to save compute), it not only changes which experts are used but also amplifies the output strength of the selected experts due to renormalization. This confounds the effect of expert pruning/compression, making it unclear whether performance drops come from using fewer experts or from the changed output calibration.

Method: The authors propose decoupling expert activation (k1) from renormalization reference (k2). Instead of normalizing by the sum of top-k1 probabilities, normalize by the sum of top-k2 probabilities (where k2 > k1). This preserves the output gain calibration from training while allowing fewer experts to be activated. They evaluate on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B models using MMLU and other benchmarks.

Result: On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, reducing from 8 to 4 experts causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop with standard renormalization but only 0.35 points with k2=16, while halving routed-expert compute. On the 11x larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, reducing from 10 to 5 experts loses only 0.55 points with appropriate k2. The paper also shows that: (1) removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic; (2) perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different k2 values; (3) expert identity matters more than expert weighting; (4) balanced/domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for pruning.

Conclusion: Preserving a suitable reference mass (k2 > k1) is crucial for MoE compression. Performance gains from expert pruning come primarily from reduced compute, not from eliminating "bad" experts. The method enables practical MoE compression without significant accuracy loss, though benchmark-specific tuning of k2 may be needed since perplexity and downstream accuracy optimize differently.

Abstract: Modern fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a small number of experts and renormalize their router probabilities. We show that this renormalization implicitly calibrates expert output gain to the training top-$k$: reducing $k$ at inference changes not only which experts are used but also the strength of the expert branch. We separate these effects by activating the top $k_1$ experts while normalizing by the probability mass of the top $k_2$ experts, introducing one integer with no parameters, training, or measurable compute overhead. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, reducing from 8 to 4 experts causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop under standard renormalization but only 0.35 points with $k_2=16$, while halving routed-expert compute. The result replicates on the $11\times$ larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, where reducing from 10 to 5 experts loses only 0.55 points with an appropriate reference set. Removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic, showing that preserving a suitable reference mass is crucial. We further find that perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different $k_2$, cautioning against selecting MoE compression settings using unlabeled text alone. Analyses also show that expert identity matters substantially more than expert weighting, while balanced and domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for expert pruning.

</details>


### [248] [Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04577)
*Katie Everett,Shikai Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how optimizer performance changes across different training horizons (overtraining factors from 1x to 256x), demonstrating that optimal hyperparameters and relative optimizer rankings shift substantially as training length increases. ADANA eventually outperforms AdamW with scaling advantages, while matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon and SOAP) provide constant token-efficiency gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in optimizer evaluation: most benchmarks only measure performance at a single training horizon, ignoring how optimizer rankings and optimal hyperparameters change with extended training. The authors hypothesize that training horizon is an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design.

Method: The authors compared four optimizers (AdamW, Muon, SOAP, and ADANA) across models ranging from 51M to 253M parameters, with overtraining factors from 1x to 256x. They swept the base learning rate at every setting and analyzed learning rate schedules, weight decay scaling, and memory allocation.

Result: Key findings: (1) Learning rate schedules can reverse across the overtraining axis; (2) Optimal weight decay scales approximately as sqrt(OT); (3) ADANA's scaling advantage over AdamW persists even after tuning AdamW's fixed memory at each horizon; (4) Log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown provide compounding gains for ADANA; (5) Muon and SOAP provide roughly constant token-efficiency advantages over AdamW, while ADANA starts behind but closes the gap at highest OT factors.

Conclusion: Training horizon is an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design. ADANA outscales AdamW with an exponent advantage close to DANA theory predictions, while matrix-preconditioned methods offer constant advantages that may increase at highest overtraining factors.

Abstract: We investigate how optimizers scale across the overtraining axis and show that relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon. In particular, we study how matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon and SOAP) and a momentum-scheduled method (ADANA) scale relative to AdamW. We compare these four optimizers across models from 51M to 253M parameters and overtraining (OT) factors from 1x to 256x, sweeping the base learning rate at every setting. The preferred learning rate schedule can reverse across the overtraining axis, the best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT), and longer horizons generally favor longer fixed memory. ADANA's scaling advantage over AdamW persists after tuning AdamW's fixed memory separately at each horizon. Log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown provide substantial gains for ADANA that compound as training increases. With this treatment, ADANA outscales AdamW with an exponent advantage close to that predicted by DANA theory on power-law random features. Muon and SOAP instead provide roughly constant token-efficiency advantages over AdamW across most of the measured range, although SOAP may gain further at the highest overtraining factors. ADANA begins behind both matrix-preconditioned optimizers but closes the gaps as training increases, surpassing Muon and becoming competitive with SOAP at our highest OT factors. These results establish training horizon as an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design.

</details>


### [249] [Representation Redundancy and Structural Complexity in Finite-Field Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04583)
*Zheng Zhang,Na Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how different coordinate representations of field inversion over F₂^n affect algebraic complexity and machine learning difficulty. The authors prove that inversion maps correspond to Galois orbits of ordered F₂-bases (n-to-1 mapping), and analyze three Boolean formulations with varying algebraic degrees and ANF leaps. Empirical tests with multilayer perceptrons confirm the theoretical findings on learning difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study is motivated by the observation that the representation chosen for a mathematical operation can affect both its algebraic form and its empirical learning difficulty. The authors specifically want to understand how different ordered F₂-bases for representing elements in F₂^n impact the inversion operation's structure and learnability.

Method: The authors use theoretical analysis to prove the relationship between Galois orbits and coordinate inversion maps, then analyze three Boolean formulations of inversion (reference, mixed representation, and complete raw). They validate results through exhaustive computations and controlled experiments with multilayer perceptrons.

Result: The key theoretical result is that two ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map if and only if they belong to the same Galois orbit, with each orbit having size n. The three Boolean formulations show distinct complexity: reference formulation has degree n-1 and joint ANF leap 1; mixed representation has degree 2(n-1) and joint ANF leap 2; complete raw has degree at most 3(n-1) and joint ANF leap at least n. Empirical tests with neural networks confirm the ordering in learning difficulty.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that exact redundancy among representations (Galois orbits) can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is exposed as part of the input. This demonstrates that representation choices have significant practical implications for both algebraic complexity and neural network learning.

Abstract: The representation chosen for a mathematical operation can affect both its algebraic form and its empirical learning difficulty.
