We study this phenomenon for inversion over \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), with field elements expressed in varying ordered \(\mathbb F_2\)-bases. We prove that two ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map if and only if they belong to the same Galois orbit. Since every orbit has size \(n\), the correspondence between ordered bases and distinct inversion maps is exactly \(n\)-to-one. We then analyze three Boolean formulations of inversion. The reference formulation has algebraic degree \(n-1\) and joint ANF leap \(1\), the mixed representation formulation has degree \(2(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap \(2\), and the complete raw formulation has degree at most \(3(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap at least \(n\). Exhaustive computations agree with the theoretical results and bounds in the cases considered. Controlled experiments with multilayer perceptrons show the same ordering in learning difficulty, while Galois orbit redundancy provides only a limited generalization benefit under the tested conditions. These results show that exact redundancy among representations can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is exposed as part of the input.

</details>


### [250] [GNN-Guided Graph Coarsening and Adaptive QUBO Penalties for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows on a Quantum Annealer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04593)
*Youssef Kamel Rezk,Paweł Gora*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses limitations in graph coarsening for solving Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW) via quantum annealing. The authors introduce adaptive penalty calibration to improve raw sample quality, replace hand-tuned merge heuristics with a graph neural network (GNN) for super-node generation, and validate findings on D-Wave Advantage2 hardware. The GNN achieves 100% feasibility across all Solomon benchmark families (vs. 80% for tuned heuristics on R-type), with the QUBO remaining 5-6 times smaller.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph coarsening heuristics for CVRPTW require family-specific tuning and remain unreliable on random instances, particularly for the Solomon benchmark. This limits the practical applicability of quantum annealing for vehicle routing problems.

Method: The study employed three approaches: (1) Adaptive penalty calibration involving constraint normalization and scaling to improve raw samples; (2) A graph neural network (GNN) trained to replace hand-tuned merge scores across all instance families; (3) Hardware experiments on D-Wave Advantage2 processor using simulated annealing as baseline. The Solomon benchmark was used for validation.

Result: Adaptive penalty calibration reduced mean raw constraint violations from 33.0 to 0.06 (p=3.7e-11, n=56). The GNN achieved 100% feasibility across all Solomon families at N=10 (vs. 80% for tuned heuristic on R-type), and 83% vs. 69% across N=10-100. The GNN was better or tied on 85/90 instance-size pairs, with significant difference at N=80,100 (p=0.002). Hardware experiments showed feasible samples increasing from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances. The QUBO remained approximately 5-6 times smaller.

Conclusion: Adaptive penalty calibration through constraint normalization and scaling is more effective than uniform penalty scaling. A GNN can replace family-specific hand-tuned heuristics with improved feasibility across all instance types. The conditioning effect (gains from better problem formulation rather than problem size reduction) was validated on quantum hardware, though classical repair with local search remains superior for end-to-end solution cost.

Abstract: Graph coarsening reduces the large Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations arising when vehicle-routing problems are solved by quantum annealing. Nearby customers with compatible time windows are merged into super-nodes, the reduced problem is solved, and the solution is expanded to the original graph. For the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW), existing coarsening heuristics require family-specific tuning and remain unreliable on random instances. We address these limitations on the Solomon benchmark using simulated annealing and a D-Wave Advantage2 processor.
  We first introduce adaptive penalty calibration. Uniform penalty scaling has little effect, whereas controlling the internal coefficient range substantially improves raw samples. Removing non-binding constraints, normalising binding ones, and scaling the remaining penalties reduces mean raw constraint violations from 33.0 to 0.06 at the same solver budget (p=3.7e-11, n=56). A variable-count-preserving control attributes this gain to conditioning rather than problem size.
  Second, we replace the hand-tuned merge score with a graph neural network (GNN) using one configuration across all families. At N=10, it achieves 100% feasibility across all Solomon families, including R-type (100% vs. 80% for the tuned heuristic). Across N=10,...,100, feasibility is 83% vs. 69%, with the GNN better or tied on 85/90 instance-size pairs. At N=80,100, the difference is significant (p=0.002; 25/25 pairs), while the QUBO remains approximately 5-6 times smaller.
  Finally, hardware experiments reproduce the conditioning effect at fixed logical variable count: feasible samples increase from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances. Classical repair with local search remains a reference bound for end-to-end solution cost.

</details>


### [251] [Too Rare to Learn: Prescribed Cyclone Tracks Degrade a Bay of Bengal Ocean Emulator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04635)
*Sumaiya Islam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether providing cyclone track information as input to neural ocean emulators improves regional forecasting in the Bay of Bengal. The surprising finding is that explicitly conditioning the model on cyclone tracks actually degrades forecast skill. The root cause is that cyclone events are too rare (only 7.9% of training days) relative to the model's training distribution, causing the model to learn incorrect responses to this rare signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural ocean emulators are being developed for regional forecasting in cyclone-prone coastal seas. A natural design choice is to provide the cyclone track as a prescribed input to the network. This paper challenges that assumption and investigates whether this design choice is actually beneficial or harmful.

Method: The authors withheld 15 whole cyclones (spanning 65 to 150 kt) from GLORYS12 reanalysis data. They compared two U-Net architectures that were identical except that one had four prescribed cyclone-track channels as input. Experiments were run across three random seeds. The ocean-only model was compared against the storm-conditioned model, with both compared against persistence baseline.

Result: The ocean-only model beats persistence in every run, while the storm-conditioned model loses to persistence in every run. The two skill ranges are statistically disjoint (p = 3.1e-5, paired across storms). The cause is exposure frequency rather than signal content: the cyclone channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days. The extra error from the storm-conditioned model falls inside the prescribed storm footprint. Notably, replacing the real cyclone map with a no-storm map at inference time improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5 to 16.4% in every seed.

Conclusion: Explicitly conditioning neural ocean emulators on cyclone tracks is harmful for forecasting. The model learns a confidently wrong response to a rare signal that is out of distribution during training. This highlights a critical design consideration: when rare events constitute only a small fraction of training data, explicitly providing them as input may cause the model to learn spurious correlations rather than meaningful physical relationships. The study suggests that for rare extreme events, implicit learning through the background state may be more effective than explicit conditioning.

Abstract: Neural ocean emulators are being proposed for regional forecasting in cyclone-exposed coastal seas, and a natural design choice is to hand the network the cyclone as a prescribed input. We test that choice in the Bay of Bengal and find it harmful. We withhold 15 whole cyclones spanning 65 to 150 kt from GLORYS12 reanalysis and compare two U-Nets that are identical except for four prescribed cyclone-track channels. Across three seeds the ocean-only model beats persistence in every run and the storm-conditioned model loses to it in every run, with the two skill ranges disjoint (p = 3.1e-5, paired across storms). The cause is exposure frequency rather than signal content: the channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days, so they are out of distribution the moment they activate. The extra error falls inside the prescribed storm footprint, and replacing the real cyclone map with a no-storm map at inference improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5 to 16.4% in every seed. The conditioned network has learned a response to a rare signal that is confidently wrong.

</details>


### [252] [SMILE: Bridging Continuous Optimization and Discrete Symbolic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04639)
*Mansooreh Montazerin,Antonio Ortega,Ajitesh Srivastava*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SMILE is a hybrid symbolic regression framework that combines continuous gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery through three stages: structural analysis, continuous optimization with interpretable activations, and symbolic recovery via pruning and rounding. It achieves superior performance on SRBench, particularly at high noise levels, while producing simpler expressions faster than competitors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing symbolic regression methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces, and (2) lack of mechanisms to exploit compositional structure in data. This work addresses both challenges by introducing a hybrid approach that bridges continuous optimization and discrete symbolic recovery.

Method: SMILE uses a three-stage approach: (1) Structural analysis of data to identify compositional hierarchy of the target expression; (2) Continuous optimization using a network with interpretable activations (Sine, Multiplication, Identity, Logarithm, Exponential) to learn parameters encoding the target expression; (3) Symbolic recovery through structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding to distill the network into a compact expression with exact symbolic constants.

Result: SMILE achieves the highest symbolic solution rate at the largest noise levels among competing methods, demonstrating strong robustness. It consistently lies on the Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity, recovering significantly simpler expressions in a fraction of the time required by competitors. Ablation studies validate each component's contribution.

Conclusion: SMILE represents a significant advance in symbolic regression by successfully combining gradient-based optimization with symbolic recovery. Its robustness to noise and ability to produce simpler, faster solutions make it a promising approach for interpretable machine learning. The three-stage architecture effectively bridges the gap between continuous deep learning and discrete symbolic computation.

Abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) discovers closed-form mathematical expressions from data, offering interpretability beyond black-box models. Existing methods suffer from slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces and lack mechanisms to exploit compositional structure in the data. We introduce SMILE (Sine, Multiplication, Identity, Logarithm, Exponential), a hybrid framework that unifies continuous gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery through three stages: structural analysis of the data to identify the compositional hierarchy of the target expression, continuous optimization to learn parameters of a network that encodes the target expression using interpretable activations, and symbolic recovery through structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding. This final stage distills the learned network into a compact expression with exact symbolic constants. We evaluate SMILE on SRBench across ground-truth and black-box datasets, with ablation studies validating each component. SMILE achieves the highest symbolic solution rate at the largest noise levels, demonstrating strong robustness where competing methods degrade substantially. It consistently lies on the Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity, recovering significantly simpler expressions in a fraction of the time required by the competing methods.

</details>


### [253] [Interpretability for Turing Machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04661)
*Billy Snikkers,Rumi Salazar,Daniel Murfet,Will Troiani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that susceptibilities, a neural network interpretability technique, can identify algorithmic structure in Turing machines by analyzing the local loss landscape of noisy Turing machines. The approach reveals that algorithmic symmetries induce specific patterns in susceptibility matrices, which can be extracted using PCA and clustering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research aims to bridge interpretability techniques from deep learning with formal methods in computation theory. Specifically, it investigates whether techniques developed for understanding neural networks can be applied to detect and analyze algorithmic structure in Turing machines and related computational models.

Method: The authors.probe the local loss landscape of a learning problem for noisy Turing machines (from prior work arXiv:2504.08075), analyze the susceptibility matrix structure, and prove that symmetries and path separation in algorithms induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in the matrix. Empirical validation is performed on DFAs using PCA and clustering.

Result: Theoretical proof that algorithmic symmetries and path separation in Turing machines correspond to specific structural patterns in susceptibility matrices. Empirical demonstration on DFAs shows that algorithmic features can be successfully recovered through PCA and clustering in susceptibility space.

Conclusion: Susceptibilities provide a bridge between neural network interpretability and formal algorithmic analysis, offering a novel method to detect and characterize algorithmic structure in computational models through loss landscape analysis.

Abstract: We show that susceptibilities, an interpretability technique developed for neural networks, can identify the presence of algorithmic structure in Turing machines by probing the local loss landscape of a learning problem for noisy Turing machines introduced by Murfet and Troiani (arXiv:2504.08075). We prove that symmetries and path separation in the algorithm implemented by a Turing machine induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in its susceptibility matrix. We study this empirically on a set of deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and demonstrate that algorithmic features can be recovered by principal component analysis and clustering methods in susceptibility space.

</details>


### [254] [WEECFP-SuRGE: Wide Embedded Extended Connectivity Fingerprint with Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04672)
*Robert Epps*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WEECFP is a parameter-free 1024-dimensional continuous molecular fingerprint that distributes Morgan substructures across ~32 signed positions. WEECFP-SuRGE is a transformer architecture using SuRGE (Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding) for positional encoding. This method achieves #1 on TDC ADMET leaderboard among non-pretrained methods and beats classical fingerprints on 3/4 MoleculeNet regression tasks. The tokenization enables near-lossless SMILES reconstruction (99.9% in-distribution, 98.93% cross-dataset).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Develop a parameter-free molecular fingerprint that achieves competitive or superior performance to pretrained models on ADMET prediction tasks, while using no external pretraining and maintaining interpretability through near-lossless tokenization.

Method: WEECFP: 1024-dimensional continuous fingerprint scattering Morgan substructures across ~32 signed positions. WEECFP-SuRGE: Transformer architecture with self-attention using SuRGE (RoPE-like rotation parameterized by molecular shortest-path graph distance). 7-model ensemble blend.

Result: Lowest average regression rank on TDC ADMET leaderboard; #2 overall (behind pretrained MapLight+GNN); #1 among non-pretrained methods. Leaderboard #1 on Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, LD50. WEECFP-NoSuRGE Blend #1 on HIA. Beats all classical-fingerprint baselines on 3/4 MoleculeNet regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). Near-lossless tokenization: 99.9% exact SMILES recovery in-distribution, 98.93% cross-dataset. Graph distance encoding achieves Pearson r = 0.901 correlation.

Conclusion: WEECFP-SuRGE achieves state-of-the-art performance among non-pretrained methods on ADMET prediction, competitive with pretrained approaches. The near-lossless tokenization enables molecular reconstruction, and the three-reference encoding provides efficient positional memory (O(S)) with high accuracy (r = 0.901).

Abstract: We introduce WEECFP, a parameter-free 1024-dimensional continuous molecular fingerprint that scatters each Morgan substructure across roughly thirty-two signed positions of a single vector, and WEECFP-SuRGE, a transformer architecture whose self-attention applies SuRGE (Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding) -- a RoPE-like rotation parameterized by molecular shortest-path graph distance -- to WEECFP substructure tokens. A 7-model blend of this architecture (the WEECFP-SuRGE Blend) achieves the lowest average regression rank on the TDC ADMET leaderboard; is #2 overall on the TDC ADMET leaderboard (behind only pretrained MapLight+GNN), and is #1 overall among methods that use no external pretraining; takes leaderboard #1 finishes on Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, and LD50 (with the WEECFP-NoSuRGE Blend separately reaching #1 on HIA) across the full 22-benchmark suite -- without any external pretraining. On MoleculeNet, WEECFP-SuRGE beats every classical-fingerprint baseline on 3 of 4 regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). We further show that WEECFP tokenization is near-lossless: a greedy overlap reconstruction recovers the exact canonical SMILES of 99.9% of in-distribution molecules across 9 MoleculeNet datasets and 98.93% of molecules in a cross-dataset holdout (HIV->Lipophilicity), and that a three-reference farthest-first encoding of graph distance correlates at Pearson r = 0.901 with the true pairwise distance, enabling O(S) positional memory at matching accuracy.

</details>


### [255] [Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04710)
*Junda Ying,Yuxuan Wang,Bowen Yang,Peijie Zhou,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SUDO is a simulation-free framework for Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport (UDOT) that enables efficient computation with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties, advancing single-cell cellular dynamics inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing UDOT solvers for inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots are limited: they either require computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or are restricted to quadratic penalties (Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao geodesics) due to dependence on analytical solutions. The choice of growth penalty is crucial for encoding biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis, but current methods cannot efficiently handle general growth penalties.

Method: The paper introduces SUDO (Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal transport), which: (1) learns conditional paths and transport costs, (2) solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and (3) leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve simulation-free solutions. The authors also proved that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated.

Result: On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient analytical solution-driven algorithms while significantly outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors, producing more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

Conclusion: SUDO provides an efficient, flexible framework for UDOT with general convex growth penalties, enabling more biologically plausible modeling of cellular dynamics. The work demonstrates that simulation-free approaches can achieve comparable or better accuracy than existing methods while offering greater computational efficiency and flexibility for encoding biological priors.

Abstract: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

</details>


### [256] [Locating and Steering Refusal Beyond Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04721)
*Preethi Carmel Bosco,Gopalakrishnan Srinivasan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether safety representations (refusal mechanisms) transfer across different neural network architectures—specifically from transformers to state-space models (SSMs). The authors discover that a single directional vector in the residual stream governs refusal across architectures, and this direction can be aligned via rotation. The key architectural difference is not where the direction is steered, but where it must be read (at the "write site" - the layer output before addition to residual stream). A detector-triggered gate using this direction reduces jailbreak success across four architecture families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand whether safety tooling developed for transformers can transfer to new architectures like SSMs that have fundamentally different token-mixing mechanisms (recurrent updates vs attention). The researchers ask: does the same safety representation survive this architectural shift, or must it be rediscovered for each architecture?

Method: The authors: (1) trained harm probes on transformers to identify refusal directions; (2) applied rotation-based alignment to map SSM representations to transformer space; (3) tested cross-architecture transfer by using transformer-trained probes on SSMs; (4) performed ablation experiments removing the aligned direction; (5) tested a detector-triggered gate intervention across four architecture families (SSM, transformer, recurrent, hybrid); (6) tested robustness against an attacker that tunes prompts against the defense.

Result: The safety representation survives across architectures. A single rigid rotation aligns representation spaces, allowing a harm probe trained on transformers to flag SSM harmful inputs. Removing this aligned direction makes models answer attacks they would otherwise refuse. The architecture-specific factor is where the direction must be read (the write site), not where it is steered. The detector-triggered gate lowers jailbreak success across all four architecture families and holds against adversarial prompt tuning on SSMs.

Conclusion: Safety tooling based on refusal directions ports to new architectures by re-estimating the direction at that architecture's write site, not by rebuilding from scratch. The key insight is that the "write site" (layer output before residual addition) is where harm is cleanly readable across architectures. This provides a pathway for transferring interpretability-based safety tools to emerging architectures.

Abstract: Where inside a language model does refusal live, and does that place change when the architecture does? In a transformer, refusal is governed by a single direction in the residual stream, a finding that safety and interpretability tooling now depend on. State-space models (SSMs) route information through a recurrent update instead of attention, sharing no token-mixing mechanism with a transformer. Does the same safety representation survive this shift, or must it be rediscovered per architecture? It survives. A single rigid rotation, which can only reorient a space and not reshape it, aligns one model's representation space with another's, so the two genuinely share the representation. A harm probe trained on a transformer then flags an SSM's harmful inputs, and removing the aligned direction makes a model answer attacks it would otherwise refuse, while a random direction of the same size does far less. What is architecture-specific is not where the direction is steered but where it must be read. Each layer computes a fresh output that is then added into the residual stream, and harm is cleanly readable at this output, the write site, before the addition. A control that holds the intervention's strength fixed shows that what matters is where the direction is estimated, not where it is applied. Applied through a detector-triggered gate, this direction lowers jailbreak success in all four architecture families we test (SSM, transformer, recurrent, hybrid), and on the SSM it holds against an attacker that tunes its prompt against the defense. The gate only matches a trivial rule that returns a fixed refusal whenever the same detector fires, so what transfers across architectures is the direction itself, not defense strength. Safety tooling built on refusal therefore ports to a new architecture by re-estimating the direction at that architecture's write site, not by rebuilding it.

</details>


### [257] [Training Large Language Models for Small-Molecule Design with Synthetic Task Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04735)
*Frank Hu,Shriram Chennakesavalu,Zichen Wang,Patricia Suriana,Bodhi Vani,Kirill Shmilovich,Kangway Chuang,Colin Grambow*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can learn molecular design strategies from cheaper synthetic tasks that generalize to expensive molecular lead optimization settings, finding that curriculum-based training surpasses larger frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing viable drug candidates requires searching a combinatorially large chemical space with multiple competing objectives. While RLVR can improve LLMs, chemically relevant scoring functions are prohibitively expensive (hours to days per evaluation), making direct online training infeasible.

Method: The authors investigate curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks, enabling LLMs to learn molecular design strategies from cheaper synthetic tasks that can generalize to expensive real-world lead optimization settings.

Result: Curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic tasks enable strong performance that surpasses that of much larger frontier models on structure-based lead optimization.

Conclusion: Scaling post-training using synthetic tasks is an effective strategy for adapting LLMs to high-cost experimental scenarios that are too expensive to directly train on.

Abstract: Designing viable drug candidates requires searching a combinatorially large and rugged chemical space for molecules that satisfy multiple, often competing, objectives. Large language models (LLMs) provide a useful generative prior for this problem because of their representational capacity, reasoning ability, and flexibility when incorporating information from the external environment. While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can be used to improve the capabilities of LLMs, many chemically relevant scoring functions require hours or even days per evaluation, making them prohibitively expensive to use directly during online training. Here, we investigate whether LLMs can learn molecular design strategies from cheaper synthetic tasks that generalize to expensive molecular lead optimization settings. We find that curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks enable strong performance that surpasses that of much larger frontier models on structure-based lead optimization. Our results suggest that scaling post-training using synthetic tasks is an effective strategy for adapting LLMs to high-cost experimental scenarios that are too expensive to directly train on.

</details>


### [258] [A Fairness Audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern Method: Format-Specific and Gender-Differential Bias, with an Interpretable Calibration Layer for Cricket Target Revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04754)
*Soumyadeep Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper conducts the first large-scale empirical audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method using 8,150 international cricket matches, revealing significant prediction biases including a previously unquantified gender differential bias in ODIs. The authors propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight calibration layer that reduces bias by 31% in ODIs and 19% in T20Is.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite over two decades of operational use of the DLS method as the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias had been published. The authors identified two key issues: 1) DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across different match states, and 2) a significant gender-differential bias exists in ODIs (women's matches over-predicted by +7.63 runs vs +1.51 for men's).

Method: The authors analyzed 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. They benchmarked DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble. They proposed DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer with 27K parameters that outputs a state-conditioned correction added to DLS.

Result: The study documented two structured biases in DLS: 1) prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets, and 2) a gender-differential bias on ODIs with mean over-prediction of +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women (gap of +6.13 runs, F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I. A gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged.

Conclusion: The DLS method exhibits significant structured biases that can be effectively corrected through a lightweight calibration layer (DLS-Cal). The discovered gender differential bias in ODIs is particularly important for women's cricket, as the gender-aware variant nearly eliminates this bias. The proposed solution is interpretable (27K parameters) and provides substantial improvements in target score accuracy for rain-affected matches.

Abstract: The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method has been the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket since 1999. Despite over two decades of operational use, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias has been published. We conduct such an audit on 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. We document two structured biases. First, DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets. Second, DLS exhibits a gender-differential bias on ODIs that has not previously been quantified: on the training split, mean over-prediction is +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women, a gap of +6.13 runs (F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). We benchmark DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble, and propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer (27K parameters) outputting a state-conditioned correction added to DLS. DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I, and a gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged. We release code, models, and data.

</details>


### [259] [Resilience Beyond Stationary Client Unavailability: Unlocking Efficient and Unbiased Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04763)
*Ming Xiang,Stratis Ioannidis,Edmund Yeh,Carlee Joe-Wong,Lili Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Due to resource constraints or external and internal uncertainties, clients in real-world federated learning systems are often intermittently available edge devices. In highly dynamic environments, the parameter server lacks prior real-time knowledge of clients' availability, making it challenging to adapt traditional federated learning algorithms to be resilient to uncertainties in client availability. If not carefully addressed, complex client availability can introduce significant bias, potentially harming the performance of the trained model. Most prior work either fails to account for non-stationary client availability dynamics or demands significant memory and computational overhead. This paper aims to develop efficient federated learning algorithms that are provably resilient to heterogeneous and non-stationary stochastic client availability. We propose FedSWE, which admits novel algorithmic structures to (i) compensate for missed computations, (ii) stabilize and diffuse the global updates over rounds, and (iii) evenly mix the local updates through implicit gossiping, despite being agnostic to non-stationary dynamics. Compared with the standard FedAvg, FedSWE introduces light additional memory and computation overhead. We show that FedSWE converges to a stationary point of non-convex objectives while achieving the desired linear speedup property in certain special cases. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments over diversified client unavailability dynamics on real-world data sets.

</details>


### [260] [A Robust Watermark-based Fingerprint Framework for GNNs Ownership Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04772)
*Han Zhang,Yan Wang,Guanfeng Liu,Pengfei Ding,Huaxiong Wang,Kwok-Yan Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: REMARK is a novel ownership verification framework for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that generates in-distribution watermark graphs to maximize output differences between models, enabling robust fingerprint extraction without relying on unrealistic assumptions about surrogate models or specific output levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The high training cost of GNNs raises concerns about model ownership infringement (model stealing, unauthorized misuse). Existing watermark-based and fingerprint-based verification methods suffer from three key limitations: performance degradation from out-of-distribution (OOD) watermark graphs, unrealistic assumptions about surrogate model training, and over-reliance on specific output levels for fingerprint extraction.

Method: REMARK proposes a two-stage approach: (1) Generate carefully crafted in-distribution watermark graphs that maximize output differences between GNN models, addressing OOD-induced performance degradation; (2) Extract robust fingerprints from these output differences to verify ownership, eliminating the need for surrogate models to be trained on watermark-containing datasets or expose specific output levels.

Result: Extensive experiments on real-world datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that REMARK achieves state-of-the-art ownership verification accuracy and robustness while preserving the utility of protected models.

Conclusion: REMARK successfully addresses the limitations of prior GNN ownership verification methods by using in-distribution watermarks and robust fingerprint extraction, providing a practical solution for protecting GNN model ownership against theft and unauthorized use.

Abstract: The high training cost of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has raised growing concerns regarding model ownership infringement, such as model stealing and unauthorized misuse. To verify model ownership and prevent significant economic losses, two groups of GNN Ownership Verification (OV) methods have been proposed: watermark-based methods and fingerprint-based methods. However, these methods typically face three limitations: (1) the performance degradation of protected models caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) watermark graphs with respect to the training set; (2) the unrealistic assumption that surrogate models have been trained on a watermark-containing training set; and (3) over-reliance on specific output levels for fingerprint extraction. In this paper, we propose a Robust watErMArk-based fingeRprint frameworK for GNNs, named REMARK. REMARK first generates carefully crafted in-distribution watermark graphs that maximize output differences between GNN models, thus mitigating OOD-induced performance degradation. REMARK then extracts robust fingerprints from these output differences to verify GNN ownership, thereby removing the assumptions that surrogate models must be trained on a watermark-containing dataset or expose specific output levels. Extensive experiments across widely used real-world datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that REMARK achieves state-of-the-art OV accuracy and robustness while preserving the utility of protected models.

</details>


### [261] [Persistent Teacher Anchoring for Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04773)
*Hyun Bin Park,Kyungho Song,Sangmin Lee,Du-Seong Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PTA (Persistent Teacher Anchoring) addresses distribution drift in LLM on-policy knowledge distillation for tool use by adding turn-level teacher commitment on top of chunk-level verification, plus persistent lookahead to improve throughput. Results show 2.5-2.8 point improvements in macro best@4 and 24% throughput gain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In LLM post-training, on-policy knowledge distillation (OPKD) suffers from teacher-student distribution gap accumulation, especially in tool use where student-written calls execute before supervision and shape later prefixes. Existing proposer-verifier generation only governs text but leaves tool execution outside scope.

Method: PTA retains chunk-level verification and adds turn-level commitment: a call reaches the environment only after teacher verifies the entire turn. Verified chunks are treated as atomic generation units. Persistent lookahead fills idle rollout capacity by advancing future samples and carrying unfinished ones across student updates under fixed verifier.

Result: Applying PTA before downstream RL improves macro best@4 by 2.5 and 2.8 points over OPKD under same downstream RL budget, while lookahead improves throughput by 24%. Tested on Search-R1-style retrieval and DeepEyes-style perception RL.

Conclusion: PTA effectively addresses distribution drift in tool-use distillation by combining turn-level commitment with chunk-level verification, and persistent lookahead significantly improves training throughput without accuracy loss.

Abstract: Distillation is common in LLM post-training, where on-policy knowledge distillation (OPKD) uses student-generated trajectories to prepare the student for downstream RL. At each state, the student matches a next-token distribution supplied by the teacher. As the rollout enters states the teacher would not visit, the teacher-student distribution gap can accumulate. In tool use, this gap becomes consequential because student-written calls execute before supervision and their observations shape later prefixes. Proposer-verifier generation addresses this drift by letting the teacher decide which student-proposed text is retained during generation. Existing formulations govern text but leave tool execution outside their scope. We propose Persistent Teacher Anchoring (PTA), a student-induced but teacher-committed rollout construction. PTA retains chunk-level verification and adds turn-level commitment, allowing a call to reach the environment only after the teacher has verified the entire turn. Treating verified chunks as atomic generation units, we introduce persistent lookahead, which fills idle rollout capacity by advancing future samples and carrying unfinished ones across student updates under the fixed verifier. Across Search-R1-style retrieval and DeepEyes-style perception RL, applying PTA before downstream RL improves macro best@4 by 2.5 and 2.8 points over OPKD under the same downstream RL budget, while lookahead improves throughput by 24%.

</details>


### [262] [Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04779)
*Huan Liu,Pengfei Jiao,Jie Yin,Hongjiang Chen,Zhidong Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This survey provides the first systematic review of Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph (DHG) representation learning methods, addressing challenges of modeling evolving AI systems with complex interactions. It proposes a unified formal definition for both discrete-time and continuous-time DHGs and introduces a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy categorizing methods into embedding-based, GNN-based, and Transformer-based approaches, while highlighting their modeling biases regarding dynamic granularity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world AI systems evolve as heterogeneous entities with complex interactions, posing challenges to static or homogeneous modeling approaches. There was a need for a systematic review to organize the fragmented research on DHG representation learning.

Method: The authors propose a unified formal definition for DHGs from temporal granularity perspective, and develop a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy to categorize existing literature, explicitly highlighting modeling biases with respect to dynamic granularity.

Result: The survey organizes existing DHG representation learning methods into three categories: early embedding-based approaches, GNN-based models, and Transformer-based methods. It also summarizes representative applications, commonly used datasets and benchmarks, and identifies promising future research directions.

Conclusion: This survey establishes a foundational framework for understanding DHG representation learning, providing researchers with a systematic organization of methods, benchmarks, and future research opportunities in this rapidly evolving field.

Abstract: Graph representation learning (GRL) serves as a canonical paradigm for modeling complex networks. However, real-world AI systems inherently manifest as evolving heterogeneous entities with complex interactions, posing significant challenges to static or homogeneous modeling. To address these complexities, representation learning for Dynamic Heterogeneous Graphs (DHGs) has emerged as a vital approach for learning low-dimensional representations that simultaneously preserve structural semantics and temporal dynamics. This survey presents the first systematic review of DHG representation learning methods. We first introduce a unified formal definition that encompasses both discrete-time and continuous-time DHGs from the perspective of temporal granularity. Building upon this formulation, we propose a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy that categorizes existing literature, including early embedding-based approaches, graph neural network (GNN)-based models, and relatively recent Transformer-based DHG methods, while explicitly highlighting their intrinsic modeling biases with respect to dynamic granularity. Furthermore, we summarize representative applications of DHG representation learning, along with commonly used datasets and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss promising research directions that guide future advances in this rapidly evolving field.

</details>


### [263] [Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04787)
*Hailiang Zhao,Peng Chen,Xueyan Tang,Jianwei Yin,Shuiguang Deng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This survey provides a comprehensive synthesis of learning-augmented algorithms, which integrate machine learning predictions into classical algorithms while maintaining formal performance guarantees. It covers prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency-robustness trade-offs, and five construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to consolidate the rapidly growing field of learning-augmented algorithms by systematically organizing the various approaches, theoretical guarantees, and practical considerations. The field has seen fragmented results across different problem domains, and this survey aims to provide a unified framework for understanding the trade-offs and design principles.

Method: The survey employs an orthogonal analysis along two axes: (1) a problem-level axis covering five representative construction mechanisms across different domains, and (2) a theorem-level axis distinguishing achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. It also explicitly separates formal theoretical guarantees from empirical systems evidence.

Result: The synthesis identifies sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning in learning-augmented algorithms and provides explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback mechanisms, and composition. The work establishes conditions under which predictions can be effectively integrated while maintaining robustness guarantees.

Conclusion: The survey concludes by delineating four key open problems: (1) cost-aware prediction, where the computational expense of generating predictions is explicitly considered; (2) endogenous error, addressing errors that arise from the prediction process itself; (3) semantic predictors, which move beyond traditional error models; and (4) benchmarking, establishing proper evaluation frameworks for comparing different approaches.

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

</details>


### [264] [How Faithful Is Attribution for Sales Forecasting? A Counterfactual Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04797)
*Glib Kechyn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper adds a post-hoc counterfactual interpretability layer to a WaveNet sales forecasting model trained on a large grocery dataset (174,685 series). The method decomposes forecasts into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding artifacts from additive SHAP-style methods. The key contribution is rigorous faithfulness evaluation and honest characterization of the method's limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep models for sales forecasting (like WaveNet) are accurate but opaque - they don't explain why a particular prediction was made. The authors wanted to add an interpretability layer to understand model behavior, particularly for understanding how the model uses promotion signals and captures weekly sales cycles.

Method: Post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer applied to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster. Uses deletion/insertion protocol for faithfulness evaluation. The method decomposes each forecast into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding allocation artifacts from additive SHAP-style attribution.

Result: Deletion gap 0.22 (p<0.001) and insertion gap 0.27 (p<0.01), robust across five background-sampling seeds. Promotion signal reliance is heterogeneous (median ratio ~1.0, ~20% with strong effect). Model captures day-of-week cycle shape (r=0.78) but systematically under-predicts amplitude.

Conclusion: The interpretability layer provides faithful attributions that reflect genuine model behavior. The authors honestly characterize where attribution is and isn't informative - the method is not about improving accuracy but providing interpretability with rigorous evaluation and candid acknowledgment of limits.

Abstract: Deep models for sales forecasting, such as WaveNet-style dilated convolutional networks, are accurate but opaque: when a single model predicts sales for one of many series, it offers no account of why. We add a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster trained on the full Corporacion Favorita grocery dataset (174,685 series over 1,688 days). The method decomposes each forecast into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding the allocation artifacts we observed with additive SHAP-style attribution. We evaluate faithfulness with a deletion/insertion protocol and find a statistically significant effect on both tests (deletion gap 0.22, p<0.001; insertion gap 0.27, p<0.01; robust across five background-sampling seeds), establishing that the attributions reflect genuine model behavior rather than plausible-looking artifacts. We then characterize, honestly, where attribution is and is not informative: reliance on the promotion signal is heterogeneous across series (median ratio approximately 1.0, with roughly 20% of series showing a strong effect), and the model captures the shape of the weekly sales cycle (day-of-week r=0.78) while systematically under-predicting its amplitude. Our contribution is not improved accuracy but an interpretability layer with a rigorous faithfulness evaluation and a candid account of its limits.

</details>


### [265] [Federated Attack Campaign Detection via Contrastive Encoding of Threat Indicators in Gradient Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04815)
*Manuel Röder,Bibin Babu,Frank-Michael Schleif*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedIoC is a federated learning framework that enables multiple organizations to collaboratively detect coordinated cyberattack campaigns without sharing sensitive threat indicators. It uses a supervised contrastive loss encoder that embeds IoC-matched network flows together, allowing the server to recover global campaign patterns by clustering aligned gradient updates from clients who share indicators for the same attack.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that detecting orchestrated cyberattack campaigns spanning multiple organizations requires sharing sensitive telemetry and threat intelligence across boundaries, which is often blocked by privacy concerns, regulatory barriers, and competitive dynamics. Existing approaches require direct sharing of Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), which organizations are reluctant to do.

Method: The proposed method involves: (1) A modular federated learning framework called FedIoC where clients encode locally available structured threat indicators into gradient updates; (2) A supervised contrastive loss client-side encoder that groups IoC-matched flows within each training batch (positive set) while pushing non-IoC embeddings apart; (3) Gradient clustering by cosine similarity at the server to recover global campaign patterns without any direct IoC transmission; (4) Evaluation on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients with disjoint indicator sets.

Result: The evaluation demonstrates that in a regime where each client observes only fragments of active campaigns and holds disjoint indicator sets, the FL server can recover cross-organizational campaign cohorts directly from gradient geometry. The paper identifies non-IID gradient structure as the main driver of successful recovery.

Conclusion: FedIoC successfully enables collaborative threat detection without sharing sensitive IoCs. The key insight is that gradient alignment naturally reveals when multiple clients are detecting the same campaign. The main limitation and open problem is designing encoders that improve upon the non-IID gradient structure for better detection accuracy.

Abstract: Detecting orchestrated cyberattack campaigns that span multiple organizations traditionally requires sharing sensitive telemetry and threat intelligence across institutional boundaries and country borders, a barrier that Federated Learning removes by training shared threat detectors directly on local data. We propose FedIoC, a modular framework in which clients fold locally available structured threat indicators into their gradient updates; we instantiate the client-side encoder with a supervised contrastive loss over IoC-matched flows. Within each training batch, flows that match any known indicator pattern form the positive set; the contrastive objective pulls their learned embeddings together and pushes non-IoC embeddings away, so that campaign-relevant structure is, by design, expressed in the gradient direction. Clients sharing indicators for the same attack campaign then produce aligned gradient components, which the server clusters by the cosine similarity of their updates to recover global campaign patterns without any direct IoC transmission. We evaluate FedIoC on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients that each observe only a fragment of every active campaign and hold disjoint indicator sets derived from their local telemetry. In this regime the FL server recovers cross-organizational campaign cohorts directly from gradient geometry. We contribute FedIoC as a modular framework for this setting, and use it to pinpoint the non-IID gradient structure as the main driver of recovery and to define the open problem of designing encoders that improve on it.

</details>


### [266] [Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning via Layer-Wise Multi-Threshold Random Sketching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04830)
*Xu Zhang,Xingyu Hou,Jiacheng Cheng,Kaiyuan Feng,Maoguo Gong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a communication-efficient personalized federated learning (PFL) framework using layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching to address high communication costs in bandwidth-constrained systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing one-bit compression methods for PFL use a single threshold for the entire model, which fails to capture layer-wise differences in parameter distributions and provides only coarse binary information.

Method: The proposed method assigns each layer its own set of quantization thresholds, enabling the compressed representation to adapt to layer-specific statistics. Multiple intervals are used to provide finer low-bit description of sketched parameters, supporting bidirectional communication with compact low-bit sketches.

Result: The method improves the communication-accuracy tradeoff compared with existing one-bit compression approaches.

Conclusion: The layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching approach effectively addresses the limitations of single-threshold methods by providing adaptive, fine-grained quantization that better handles heterogeneous parameter distributions across network layers.

Abstract: Personalized federated learning (PFL) is a promising paradigm for collaborative learning over distributed devices, where edge nodes collaboratively train personalized models without sharing raw data. Although PFL addresses data heterogeneity by learning client-specific models, it still suffers from substantial uplink and downlink communication costs when exchanging high-dimensional parameters in bandwidth-constrained systems. Recent one-bit methods achieve extreme compression, but they usually rely on a single thresholding rule applied to the whole model. This design has two limitations. First, it overlooks layer-wise differences in parameter distributions and quantization sensitivities. Second, a single threshold provides only coarse binary information and cannot capture fine-grained variations in parameter distributions. To address these issues, we propose a communication-efficient PFL framework via layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching. In the proposed method, each layer is assigned its own set of quantization thresholds, so that the compressed representation can adapt to layer-specific statistics while using multiple intervals to provide a finer low-bit description of sketched parameters. The proposed method supports bidirectional communication using compact low-bit sketches and improves the communication-accuracy tradeoff compared with existing one-bit compression approaches.

</details>


### [267] [PACE: Propagation-Aware Collaborative Correction for One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04832)
*Ruizhe Huang,Chengran Li,Xiaochuan Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PACE addresses client heterogeneity in one-shot personalized federated graph learning by treating collaborative knowledge as a compact correction to a complete Local predictor rather than a replacement. It uses rank-r update carriers and diagonal sketches, with CNLL calibration to select between Local and External logits using validation nodes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Client heterogeneity creates tension in personalized federated graph learning: knowledge from other clients may complement a receiver's local model, but incompatible transfer can override reliable predictions. One-shot communication intensifies this risk as unsuitable server returns cannot be corrected later.

Method: Each client uploads a rank-r update carrier and a diagonal sketch of propagated message moments. The server constructs a propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction while the receiver retains its full Local model. Convex negative-log-likelihood calibration (CNLL) then selects one coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes; model parameters remain fixed with no feedback sent.

Result: At Rank-6, personalized returns occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across six datasets. The correction improves Accuracy and weighted-F1 on five datasets; on ogbn-arxiv, CNLL assigns zero weight to correction and preserves Local predictions exactly. Applying CNLL to baselines on three citation datasets does not account for these gains.

Conclusion: A small transported correction can augment a complete Local model when receiver evidence supports it, while leaving Local predictions unchanged otherwise. This demonstrates that correction-based knowledge transfer outperforms replacement-based approaches in federated graph learning.

Abstract: Client heterogeneity creates both an opportunity and a risk in personalized federated graph learning. Knowledge held by other subgraphs may complement a receiver's Local model, but an incompatible transfer can override reliable predictions. One-shot communication sharpens this tension because an unsuitable server return cannot be corrected later. We introduce PACE, which treats collaborative knowledge as a compact correction to a complete Local predictor rather than as its replacement. Each client uploads a rank-r update carrier and a diagonal sketch of propagated message moments. The server uses them to construct a propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction, while the receiver retains its full Local model. Convex negative-log-likelihood calibration (CNLL) then selects one coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes; model parameters remain fixed and no feedback is sent. At Rank-6, personalized returns occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across the six evaluated datasets. The correction receives nonzero weight and improves both Accuracy and weighted-F1 over Local on five datasets; on ogbn-arxiv, CNLL assigns zero predictive weight to the correction and preserves Local predictions exactly. Applying the same CNLL rule to matched baselines on three citation datasets does not account for these gains. The central result is therefore that a small transported correction can augment a complete Local model when receiver evidence supports it while leaving the Local prediction unchanged otherwise.

</details>


### [268] [KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04852)
*Di Chai,Leye Wang,Zeshen Su,Zhiguo Xia,Zhihang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KVMem is a KV-context virtualization system that enables LLM agents to access workspace histories exceeding their native context window (up to 1M tokens) by storing overflowed KV state across GPU, host memory, and NVMe, using attention-space indexes for efficient retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent systems face context overflow when accumulated workspace history exceeds both GPU KV capacity and the model's native context window. Current solutions (compaction/summarization or text retrieval) either lose fine-grained execution evidence or require repeatedly prefilling already-processed content, leading to inefficiency and information loss.

Method: KVMem preserves overflowed workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe storage. It uses lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant historical blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model's native context window.

Result: On long-context agent benchmarks (LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, AgentLongBench) with histories up to 1M tokens, KVMem achieves higher task utility and inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches. In DeepSWE test with Qwen3.8-27B, task success improved from 43.8% (compaction-only) to 48.4%. Locally, KVMem runs Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP on a 24GB RTX 5090 laptop, virtualizing 1M-token workspaces at ~50 tokens/s.

Conclusion: KVMem decouples addressable workspace size from the LLM's native context window, providing a practical path toward long-running agents with workspaces growing beyond the context window while maintaining interactive responsiveness.

Abstract: Modern LLM agents operate in persistent workspaces whose accumulated history can exceed both GPU KV capacity and the model's native context window. Existing systems typically compact older context into summaries or retrieve it later as text, either losing fine-grained execution evidence or repeatedly prefilling content that the model has already processed. We present KVMem, a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. KVMem uses lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant historical blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model's native context window. Extensive evaluations on long-context agent benchmarks spanning histories up to one million tokens, including LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, show that KVMem generally achieves higher task utility and greater inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches, the de facto standard for handling context overflow. In the DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% with compaction-only context management to 48.4%.
  In our local-deployment evaluation, KVMem runs Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP on an off-the-shelf laptop equipped with a 24\,GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, virtualizing agent workspaces of up to 1M tokens-four times the model's native 256K-token context window. In a single-session setting, KVMem generates $\sim$50 tokens/s, providing interactive responsiveness for local agent execution. More broadly, by decoupling addressable workspace size from the LLM's native context window, KVMem provides a practical path toward long-running agents whose workspaces can grow beyond that window.

</details>


### [269] [When Genomic Masking Priors Fail to Transfer: Strong Variant Prediction, Weak Functional Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04861)
*Susu Hu,Preetam Gattogi,Jens Lehmann,Sahar Vahdati,Stefanie Speidel,Julien Vibert*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GenDA is a bidirectional discrete diffusion model for genomic sequence modeling that uses entropy-guided span placement. After supervised fine-tuning, it achieves ClinVar SNV AUROC of 0.774, outperforming an autoregressive model by 0.103. However, a random-span control achieves nearly identical performance (0.777), and the model fails zero-shot functional inpainting stress tests across various genomic regions, failing to outperform a simple 3-mer composition-preserving shuffle control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors hypothesized that entropy-guided span placement during training would concentrate reconstruction pressure on compositionally complex regions, thereby improving both variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation. They sought to validate whether this specific corruption prior provides meaningful improvement over random span placement.

Method: GenDA is a 202M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model trained with entropy-guided span placement. The model was supervised fine-tuned on genomic sequences. Performance was evaluated using ClinVar SNV AUROC for variant effect prediction, and a zero-shot functional inpainting stress test across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries. A matched random-span variant and a shuffle control (preserving 3-mer composition) served as controls.

Result: 1) ClinVar SNV AUROC: GenDA achieves 0.774 vs autoregressive model 0.671 (improvement of 0.103)
2) Random-span control achieves 0.777, providing no evidence that entropy guidance explains the ClinVar improvement
3) GenDA fails the zero-shot functional inpainting stress test - does not consistently outperform the 3-mer composition-preserving shuffle control across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries
4) Failure persists for 50-500bp gaps; enhancer degradation worsens at longer gaps
5) Diagnostics identify boundary conditions: entropy measures local complexity not functional importance; 1-mer tokenization limits context; training spans capped at 300bp; high AlphaGenome fidelity can coexist with negative control-normalized restoration

Conclusion: Strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional generation are distinct claims requiring separate validation. The entropy-guided span placement hypothesis is not supported - the improvement over autoregressive models appears to stem from the bidirectional diffusion architecture itself rather than the entropy guidance. The model fails to demonstrate genuine functional inpainting capability, as simple composition-preserving controls perform comparably or better.

Abstract: Bidirectional discrete diffusion model appears naturally suited to genomic modeling because it can reconstruct missing sequence from both flanks. We developed GenDA (Genomic Density-optimized Absorbing Diffusion) under the additional hypothesis that entropy-guided span placement would concentrate reconstruction pressure on compositionally complex regions, improving both downstream variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation. Our results only partially support this premise. After supervised fine-tuning, the 202M-parameter GenDA model reaches a pooled ClinVar SNV AUROC of 0.774, exceeding a similarly scaled autoregressive model by 0.103. However, a matched random-span variant reaches 0.777, providing no evidence that entropy guidance causes the ClinVar improvement. More unexpectedly, GenDA fails a zero-shot functional inpainting stress test: across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries, it does not consistently outperform a control that shuffles the native gap while exactly preserving 3-mer composition. Failure is already present for 50--500-bp gaps, although enhancer degradation worsens at longer gaps. Diagnostics identify several boundary conditions: entropy measures local sequence complexity rather than functional importance; 1-mer tokenization limits physical context; training spans are capped at 300 bp; and high absolute AlphaGenome fidelity can coexist with negative control-normalized restoration. These results show that strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional generation are distinct claims that require separate validation.

</details>


### [270] [From Deep to Shallow: Unconstrained and Efficient Layer Merging Strategy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04881)
*Petro Shulzhenko,Gabriele Spadaro,Enzo Tartaglione*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses computational demands of Deep Neural Networks by proposing an efficient depth compression strategy that enables merging of layers without analytical solutions (like convolutions with padding) without increasing kernel size, validating on multiple architectures and embedded platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Neural Networks have high computational demands that limit their application in resource-constrained environments. Existing depth compression methods face two key challenges: they cannot be applied to convolutions with padding due to lack of analytical solutions, and they increase kernel size limiting speed-up gains.

Method: The authors propose an efficient strategy that enables merging of layers without an existing analytical solution and without increasing kernel size. They validate this approach across multiple architectures and datasets, measuring inference speed-up gains on real embedded platforms.

Result: The abstract indicates successful validation across multiple architectures and datasets, with measured inference speed-up gains on real embedded platforms. The code is publicly released.

Conclusion: The proposed method overcomes limitations of existing depth compression methods by enabling layer merging for cases without analytical solutions while maintaining kernel size, achieving practical inference speed-ups on embedded hardware.

Abstract: Although Deep Neural Networks have become foundational in many areas of Machine Learning, high computational demands limit their application in resource-constrained environments. To address this issue, depth compression methods have been proposed to identify and linearize redundant activation functions, thereby allowing for the merging of layers without intermediate non-linearities. However, these methods face two key challenges: they cannot be directly applied to convolutions with padding due to the absence of an analytical solution for merging these layers, and they typically increase the kernel size of merged layers, thus limiting speed-up gains. To overcome these limitations, we propose an efficient strategy that enables merging of layers without an existing analytical solution, and also without increasing kernel size. We validate our approach across multiple architectures and datasets, and measure inference speed-up gains on real embedded platforms. We publicly released the code at https://github.com/ShulzhenkoPetr/deep-to-shallow.

</details>


### [271] [Adaptation Interfaces for In-Context Tabular Foundation Models in Time-to-Event Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04901)
*Minh-Khoi Pham,Luca Cotugno,Dan Cernei,Alina Sirbu,Stefano Masi,Giuseppe Prencipe,Alessandro Pingitore,Patrizia Landi,Working Group on Uric Acid,Cardiovascular Risk of the Italian Society of Hypertension,Tai Tan Mai,Martin Crane,Marija Bezbradica*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates tabular foundation models (TabFMs) for censored time-to-event prediction, comparing zero-shot inference, classification-based fine-tuning, and survival-head adaptation on 74 single-risk and 4 competing-risk datasets. CoxPH provides the most reliable performance, especially for Integrated Brier Score, while DeepHit shows strength in time-dependent Concordance Index. Effective transfer depends on data regime and adaptation interface choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend TabFMs from standard classification/regression to censored time-to-event prediction, which requires handling censoring and event-time dynamics - a challenging task that lacks established methods.

Method: Evaluate three adaptation approaches: (1) temporal zero-shot reformulation, (2) classification-based fine-tuning, and (3) survival-head adaptation using frozen TabFM backbones. Link TabFMs with CoxPH and DeepHit models, revise context-resampled training procedure. Test on 74 single-risk and 4 competing-risk datasets.

Result: Zero-shot inference works well on smaller datasets; supervised adaptation improves with larger datasets. CoxPH provides most reliable strong performance, especially for IBS on larger datasets. DeepHit stronger for time-dependent C-index than IBS. Cause-specific MTLR ranks highest in competing-risk analysis. Classification fine-tuning becomes more competitive with scale but remains weaker for probabilistic prediction.

Conclusion: Effective TabFM transfer for survival analysis depends on data regime (size) and the statistical structure of the chosen adaptation interface. No single approach dominates; optimal method depends on dataset characteristics and evaluation metric.

Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TabFMs) achieve strong performance on structured data, particularly for standard classification and regression problems. Yet, extending them to censored time-to-event prediction is challenging because it requires properly handling censoring and event-time dynamics. Building on our prior work, we further link TabFMs with CoxPH and DeepHit and revise the context-resampled training procedure. We evaluate temporal zero-shot reformulation, classification-based fine-tuning, and survival-head adaptation using frozen TabFM backbones on 74 single-risk data sets, and we additionally study 4 competing-risk data sets. Zero-shot inference is effective on smaller single-risk data sets, whereas supervised adaptation becomes increasingly advantageous as data sets scale. Cox provides the most reliably strong interface, especially for Integrated Brier Score (IBS) on larger data sets. DeepHit is relatively stronger for the time-dependent Concordance Index than for IBS, while cause-specific MTLR ranks highest among the TabFM survival heads in the four-data-set competing-risk analysis. Classification fine-tuning becomes more competitive with zero-shot inference as data sets grow but remains weaker for probabilistic prediction. Overall, our results indicate that effective TabFM transfer depends on the data regime and on the statistical structure represented by the chosen adaptation interface. The implementation scripts used for this work are available at https://github.com/kaylode/survival-fm.

</details>


### [272] [Fast Gauss Sums via Flash Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04910)
*Nicolaj Rux,Sebastian Neumayer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a method to compute Gaussian kernel sums using flash attention by augmenting inputs, achieving better performance than existing GPU implementations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gaussian kernel sums are fundamental to many kernel methods (MMDs, kernel gradient flows, SVGD), but current implementations are computationally expensive. The motivation is to leverage the highly optimized flash attention mechanism to accelerate these computations without custom GPU code.

Method: The authors show that Gauss kernel sums with arbitrary signed weights can be computed via flash attention through two small input augmentations that transform the normalized softmax reduction into an unnormalized Gauss sum.

Result: For feature dimension D>8 in fp16, this approach beats compiled PyTorch and PyKeOps kernels in speed, memory overhead, and accuracy, with linear memory scaling.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates that flash attention can be repurposed for Gaussian kernel computations, offering a simple yet efficient solution that outperforms dedicated kernel implementations without requiring custom GPU code.

Abstract: Gaussian kernel sums are the computational core of maximum mean discrepancies (MMDs), kernel gradient flows, Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD), and many other kernel methods. At the same time, softmax attention has received an extraordinary amount of hardware-aware code engineering, culminating in flash attention. We show that Gauss kernel sums with arbitrary, signed weights can be evaluated via flash attention: two small input augmentations turn the normalized softmax reduction into the unnormalized Gauss sum, without writing a single line of custom GPU code. For feature dimension D>8 in fp16, this approach beats compiled PyTorch code as well as PyKeOps kernels (often significantly) in speed, memory-overhead and accuracy. Indeed, its memory scaling remains linear.

</details>
