We also show that for any fixed distribution the excess error contracts geometrically along the path, ruling out any single instance that witnesses any polynomial lower bound at every depth.
  Finally, we prove the same optimal rate for logistic classification in the logit-passing model of Bateni et al., which considers the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss. The same improved upper bound of $O(M^2/D)$ holds, and we transfer all the regression lower bounds by showing that on those examples the logistic path follows the least-squares path up to rescaling.

</details>


### [298] [Embedded Graph Flows for Categorical Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05328)
*Ethan Ma,Zihan Wang,Chris Siu Yeung Chow,Xinguo Feng,Qingqing Li,Rui Jiang,Naipeng Dong,Guangdong Bai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EGF (Embedded Graph Flows) is a generative model for categorical graphs that learns continuous embeddings for node and edge categories, using a graph transformer to transport Gaussian noise to these embeddings, then maps back to discrete categories via terminal readout. It achieves state-of-the-art results on molecular benchmarks QM9 and ZINC250k.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional graph generators use one-hot vectors to encode categories, which artificially imposes equidistant geometry between categories. This creates a problematic structure where all categories are equally distant from each other, regardless of their actual relationships. The authors sought a more coherent approach that doesn't depend on node order and produces genuinely meaningful category representations.

Method: EGF consists of three main components: (1) Continuous embedding learning for node and unordered-edge categories, replacing one-hot vectors; (2) A permutation-equivariant graph transformer that transports Gaussian noise toward the learned embeddings; (3) A terminal readout that maps embeddings back to discrete graph categories. This flow-based approach maintains permutation invariance while learning meaningful continuous representations.

Result: On QM9, EGF achieved the best results across all four reported metrics among three methods, including a Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) of 0.150, significantly outperforming DiGress (0.717) and GruM (0.812). On ZINC250k (larger molecules), EGF retained the lowest maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) using the neighbourhood subgraph pairwise distance kernel (NSPDK), indicating close agreement with reference molecular substructures.

Conclusion: EGF successfully addresses the limitation of one-hot encoding in graph generation by learning continuous embeddings that capture meaningful category relationships. The flow-based approach with graph transformers enables effective noise transport to discrete categories, resulting in superior molecular generation quality as measured by FCD and MMD metrics. The code is available on GitHub.

Abstract: Generating categorical graphs requires choosing node and edge types that form a coherent structure without depending on node order. Many graph generators encode categories as fixed one-hot vectors, which can impose an artificial geometry in which categories are equidistant. We propose Embedded Graph Flows (EGF), a generative model that learns continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories and transports Gaussian noise towards these learnt endpoints using a permutation-equivariant graph transformer. A terminal readout maps the embeddings back to discrete graph categories. Across molecular benchmarks, EGF achieved competitive performance. On QM9, EGF gives the best result on all four reported metrics among the three methods, including a Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) of 0.150, compared with 0.717 for the categorical-diffusion baseline DiGress and 0.812 for the bridge-based baseline GruM. When applied to larger molecules in ZINC250k, EGF retains the lowest maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) using the neighbourhood subgraph pairwise distance kernel (NSPDK), indicating close agreement with the local substructures of the reference molecules. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trusted-System-Lab/EGF.

</details>


### [299] [Variational Continuation for Double Pendulum Periodic Orbits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05337)
*Leo Yao,Ziming Liu,Max Tegmark*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Hessian-based method using automatic differentiation to numerically continue periodic orbits in dynamical systems, demonstrated on double pendulum oscillations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for continuing periodic orbits require hand-derived Jacobians, which is labor-intensive and error-prone. The authors seek to automate this process using machine learning techniques.

Method: 1) Parameterize periodic orbit candidates as Fourier series; 2) Define loss function based on deviation from physical differential equations; 3) Leverage automatic differentiation to compute gradients/Hessians; 4) Use flat directions (zero eigenvalues) of loss landscape to determine continuation direction; 5) Integrator-free approach.

Result: Successfully performed full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations from fixed points, detected bifurcations along orbit families, categorized branches of periodic orbits, and discovered previously undocumented orbits where both masses are never simultaneously at rest.

Conclusion: The automatic differentiation approach enables efficient and automated periodic orbit continuation, with the ability to detect orbit family intersections and subharmonic bifurcations. The method reveals previously unknown periodic orbit types in the double pendulum system.

Abstract: We present a Hessian-based approach to numerically continue periodic orbits in dynamical systems. A loop (periodic orbit candidate) is parametrized as a Fourier series; a loss function is defined based on the deviation of the loop from the physical differential equations. Unlike previous work relying on hand-derived Jacobians, our method automates the process by leveraging automatic differentiation, a common machine learning technique. The continuation direction can be determined by the flat directions of the loss landscapes (directions with zero eigenvalues), making the search of periodic orbits efficient and guided. Our method is integrator-free, precisely initializes oscillations around unstable fixed points, and efficiently detects orbit family intersections and subharmonic bifurcations. As a demonstration, we present full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations from fixed points, showing bifurcations along orbit families and categorizing branches of periodic orbits. In particular, we find periodic orbits where both pendulum masses are never simultaneously at rest, which to our knowledge has been missing in the literature.

</details>


### [300] [Distill Globally, Adapt Locally: Reasoning Distillation and Product-Type Test-Time Training for Scalable Trade-Up Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05363)
*Siliang Liu,Mohammad Ghasemi,Sapan Patel,Amin Banitalebi-Dehkordi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-level framework for trade-up recommendation that distills LLM reasoning into an efficient student model. A retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher generates labels and rationales, which supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier. Product-type test-time training (PT-TTT) further adapts the model to specific categories. The 15.5M-parameter student achieves AUC 0.924, improving to 0.941 with PT-TTT, while being 5,000x faster and 10,000x cheaper than direct LLM inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly applying LLMs to hundreds of millions of product pairs for trade-up recommendation is operationally impractical due to computational cost and latency. There's a need to distill LLM reasoning capabilities into an efficient non-generative student model.

Method: Two-level framework: (1) Level 1 - Retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher generates structured relation labels and natural-language rationales, which supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier through alignment and contrastive objectives; (2) Level 2 - Product-type test-time training (PT-TTT) uses few-shot demonstrations to optimize lightweight category-specific adapters over the frozen student. The student uses only two precomputed 768-dimensional product embeddings at inference with no LLM calls.

Result: On 8,352 human-annotated pairs: 15.5M-parameter four-class reasoning-distilled student achieves AUC 0.924 (95% CI [0.918, 0.929]) vs 0.912 for label-only student. PT-TTT improves AUC from 0.924 to 0.941 and average precision from 0.920 to 0.940. On 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student is ~5,000x faster and ~10,000x lower in estimated cost than direct LLM inference.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully distills LLM reasoning into an efficient student model that achieves strong performance on trade-up recommendation while being operationally practical. The reasoning-distilled student significantly outperforms label-only distillation, and PT-TTT provides additional gains by adapting to product-type-specific criteria.

Abstract: Trade-up recommendation identifies higher-quality alternatives that preserve a customer's purchase intent while offering upgraded benefits. Large language models (LLMs) can reason about such distinctions, but applying them directly to hundreds of millions of product pairs is operationally impractical. We introduce a two-level framework that distills LLM reasoning into an efficient non-generative student and adapts its decision boundary to product-type-specific trade-up criteria. At Level 1, a retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher generates structured relation labels and natural-language rationales. These rationales supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier through alignment and contrastive objectives; at inference, the student uses only two precomputed 768-dimensional product embeddings, with no LLM calls or text generation. On a fixed human-annotated benchmark of 8,352 pairs, a 15.5M-parameter four-class reasoning-distilled student achieves AUC 0.924 (95% CI [0.918, 0.929]), compared with 0.912 for the four-class label-only student. At Level 2, product-type test-time training (PT-TTT) uses few-shot demonstrations to optimize lightweight category-specific adapters over the frozen student. PT-TTT improves AUC from 0.924 to 0.941 and average precision from 0.920 to 0.940. On a 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student on a single eight-GPU machine is approximately 5,000x faster and 10,000x lower in estimated cost than direct LLM inference.

</details>


### [301] [RegionFed: Federated Learning for Personalized Query Understanding in Heterogeneous Retail Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05403)
*Quoc H. Nguyen,Ali Lafzi,Abhijeet Phatak,Siddharth Pratap Singh,Rohit Upadhyay,Yogananda Domlur Seetharama,Chittaranjan Tripathy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RegionFed is an architecture-robust federated learning framework that operates at the gradient level to handle data heterogeneity in retail search systems across diverse geographic regions. It uses ℓ2 conflict between regional and global gradients to diagnose heterogeneity, route regions to appropriate personalization strategies, and adaptively control personalization strength. The method achieves 92.27% accuracy, closing the gap to centralized training (92.04%) while providing differential privacy (ε≈0.60) and works on T5, RoBERTa, and CNN architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail search systems serve diverse geographic regions with distinct query patterns, vocabularies, and product preferences, creating significant data heterogeneity. This challenges both privacy-preserving training and model personalization. Standard federated learning produces global models that sacrifice regional performance, while existing personalized FL approaches operate at the parameter level and catastrophically collapse on modern transformers (below 10% accuracy on T5) due to tied embeddings and LayerNorm interactions.

Method: RegionFed operates entirely at the gradient level, treating models as differentiable black boxes. It uses the ℓ2 conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal that (i) diagnoses heterogeneity, (ii) routes each region to the cheapest sufficient personalization strategy, and (iii) adaptively controls personalization strength. This architecture-robust approach deploys on T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, and CNN with zero code changes.

Result: Across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures, RegionFed-Meta achieves 92.27%, closing the gap to the privacy-violating centralized upper bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04%, Δ=0.23pp, within 1σ) while providing (ε≈0.60)-differential privacy and O(1/√T) convergence. Large gains on transformers where parameter-level methods collapse, and consistent improvements on CNNs.

Conclusion: RegionFed successfully addresses the challenge of federated learning for heterogeneous retail search data across regions. By operating at the gradient level rather than parameter level, it avoids the catastrophic collapse seen in existing personalized FL approaches on modern transformers. The framework provides strong privacy guarantees while achieving performance comparable to centralized training, demonstrating architecture-robustness across diverse model families.

Abstract: Retail search systems serve diverse geographic regions with distinct query patterns, vocabularies, and product preferences, creating significant data heterogeneity that challenges both privacy-preserving training and model personalization. Federated learning offers a natural solution for privacy, but standard FL methods produce global models that sacrifice regional performance, while existing personalized FL approaches operate at the parameter level and catastrophically collapse on modern transformers (below 10\% accuracy on T5) due to tied embeddings and LayerNorm interactions. We introduce RegionFed, an \textit{architecture-robust} federated learning framework that sidesteps this failure by operating entirely at the gradient level. RegionFed uses the $\ell_2$ conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal that (i) diagnoses heterogeneity, (ii) routes each region to the cheapest sufficient personalization strategy, and (iii) adaptively controls personalization strength. Because it treats models as differentiable black boxes, RegionFed deploys on T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, and CNN with zero code changes, providing large gains on transformers (where parameter-level methods collapse) and consistent improvements on CNNs. Across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures, RegionFed-Meta achieves 92.27\%, closing the gap to the privacy-violating centralized upper bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04\%, $Δ$=0.23pp, within 1$σ$) while providing $(ε{\approx}0.60)$-differential privacy and $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence.

</details>

# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [302] [Beyond SDR: How Music Source Separation Reshapes Rhythm-Relevant Signal Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04224)
*Chuxin Ding*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates how music source separation (MSS) algorithms affect rhythm-critical signal properties (onset timing, transient, dynamics) that are essential for musicology research but ignored by standard evaluation metrics like SDR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MSS is increasingly used in music research to analyze drum stems for microtiming, dynamics, and groove studies. However, the field evaluates separators using SDR (signal-to-distortion ratio), which was not designed to preserve the attack and envelope properties that determine a sound's perceived temporal location (p-centre). This mismatch could introduce systematic biases in rhythm research using separated stems.

Method: The authors evaluated four open-source separators spanning four architecture generations (Spleeter, HT-Demucs, BS-Roformer, SCNetXL) on the 50-track MUSDB18-HQ test set. They measured onset timing using onset F-measure, transient and dynamic shape distortion, and examined how input length affects these properties. Correlation analysis with SI-SDR was performed using Spearman's rho.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Onset timing is preserved - onset F-measure correlates with SI-SDR (rho = 0.62) and is invariant to input length. (2) Transient and dynamic shape are significantly distorted - correlation with SI-SDR is weak (|rho| ≤ 0.29), and model rankings invert; the SDR-best model distorts drum attacks twice as much as a capability-matched CNN, while the SDR-worst preserves dynamics better. Each model imposes systematic, model-specific bias on dynamics. (3) Input length marginally affects rendered attack (p = 0.044 for transformer) but leaves onset locations unchanged.

Conclusion: For rhythm-focused musicology studies, separator choice and input conditions are methodological variables that must be reported. SDR alone cannot stand in for rhythm-critical property evaluation. Researchers using MSS for rhythmic analysis should look beyond SDR metrics and consider the specific biases of each separator model.

Abstract: Music source separation (MSS) is increasingly used not to remix music but to measure it: separated drum stems feed studies of microtiming, dynamics, and groove. The field evaluates separators almost exclusively by signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR), yet microrhythm research shows that a sound's perceived temporal location (its p-centre) is co-determined by its attack and envelope, precisely the properties SDR was not designed to protect. We quantify what four open separators spanning four architecture generations (Spleeter, HT-Demucs, BS-Roformer, SCNetXL) do to rhythm-critical signal properties, using the 50-track MUSDB18-HQ test set, where true stems make every claim falsifiable. Three findings emerge. (1) Onset timing is safe: onset F-measure tracks SI-SDR (Spearman rho = 0.62) and is invariant to input length. (2) Transient and dynamic shape are not: their distortion correlates only weakly with SI-SDR (|rho| <= 0.29), and the model ranking inverts - the SDR leader distorts drum attacks twice as much as its capability-matched CNN counterpart, while the SDR-worst model preserves dynamics better than a mid-pack one. Each model imposes a systematic, model-specific bias on the dynamic profile. (3) Input length reshapes the rendered attack of a fixed passage (marginally more for the transformer; paired p = 0.044) while leaving onset locations untouched. For rhythmic studies, separator choice and input conditions are methodological variables to be reported, and SDR alone cannot stand in for them.

</details>


### [303] [VocalCoachBench: Benchmarking Audio-Language Models on Expert Feedback for Singing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04241)
*Hayeon Bang,Hounsu Kim,Wonil Kim,Juhan Nam*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VocalCoachBench is a benchmark for evaluating audio-language models on expert vocal coaching feedback for singing. It contains 515 recordings annotated by 18 professional vocal trainers, with 1,056 expert submissions and 12,051 atomic coaching claims. The benchmark includes same-song and diverse-song subsets, and uses claim-based evaluation for open-ended feedback. Experiments with 12 models reveal significant gaps in fine-grained issue identification and diagnosis alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current audio-language models are evaluated on recognition, description, and reasoning, but expert-facing applications require the capability to produce feedback that identifies problems and suggests corrective actions grounded in audio input.

Method: VocalCoachBench contains 515 recordings annotated by 18 professional vocal trainers (1,056 expert submissions, 12,051 atomic coaching claims). It comprises two subsets: same-song for controlled comparison and diverse-song for segment-grounded feedback. The benchmark separates deterministic structured targets from claim-based assessment of free-form diagnosis and corrective guidance.

Result: Experiments with 12 recent audio-language models reveal a consistent gap: while models can compare performances and identify broad issue domains in free-form feedback, Top-3 fine-grained issue-label identification remains below label-prior baselines and strict diagnosis alignment stays below 7%.

Conclusion: VocalCoachBench provides the first public testbed for evaluating audio-grounded expert feedback for singing, moving audio-language evaluation beyond description toward analytic feedback.

Abstract: Recent audio-language models are increasingly evaluated on recognizing, describing, and reasoning about audio, but expert-facing applications require a different capability: producing feedback that identifies problems and suggests corrective actions grounded in the input. We introduce VocalCoachBench, a benchmark for evaluating audio-language models on expert vocal coaching feedback for singing. VocalCoachBench contains 515 recordings annotated by 18 professional vocal trainers, yielding 1,056 expert submissions and 12,051 atomic coaching claims. It comprises a same-song subset for controlled comparison and a diverse-song subset for segment-grounded feedback across varied songs and recording conditions. To accommodate the open-ended nature of expert feedback, VocalCoachBench sep- arates deterministic structured targets from claim-based assessment of free-form diagnosis and corrective guidance. Human annotation analysis shows that expert agreement varies strongly with label granularity, motivating hierarchical structured metrics and claim-based evaluation of open-ended feedback. Experiments with 12 recent audio-language models reveal a consistent gap: while models can compare performances and identify broad issue domains in free-form feedback, Top-3 fine-grained issue-label identification remains below label-prior baselines and strict diagnosis alignment stays below 7%. To our knowledge, VocalCoachBench pro- vides the first public testbed for evaluating audio-grounded expert feedback for singing, moving audio-language evaluation beyond description toward analytic feedback.

</details>


### [304] [Grounded Decoding for Autoregressive Speech Enhancement via Adaptive Code-Space Grounding and Local LLM Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04245)
*Hao Shi,Yuan Gao,Zhaoheng Ni,Junyi Peng,Gongping Huang,Yu Tsao,Xugang Lu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes an evidence-grounded generative speech enhancement framework that combines deterministic and LLM-based approaches. It uses a Whisper-guided DPRNN to produce evidence, which conditions an autoregressive clean-speech token generator through Code-Space Grounding (CSG). Two novel techniques are introduced: SNR-CSG for adaptive grounding strength based on acoustic difficulty, and GNR-LLM for local neighborhood refinement using LLM ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the trade-off between LLM-based autoregressive speech enhancement (which may hallucinate content) and deterministic SE (which may retain residual noise). The goal is to leverage LLM capabilities while grounding outputs in observation-coupled evidence to improve content fidelity and perceptual quality.

Method: The framework uses: (1) Whisper-guided DPRNN to produce enhanced waveform as imperfect evidence; (2) Tokenization of blended evidence into discrete sequence; (3) Code-Space Grounding (CSG) penalizing candidates by Hamming distance in FSQ space; (4) SNR-Conditioned CSG (SNR-CSG) mapping residual-SNR to adaptive grounding strength; (5) Grounded Neighborhood Refinement with LLM ranking (GNR-LLM) intersecting LLM top-K candidates with local FSQ Hamming neighborhood.

Result: Experiments on in-domain, controlled-SNR, and DNS no-reverb conditions show: (1) SNR-CSG provides robust automatic grounding; (2) GNR-LLM substantially improves low-SNR perceptual quality without sacrificing content fidelity.

Conclusion: The proposed evidence-grounded generative SE framework successfully balances LLM generation quality with observation-based grounding. SNR-CSG enables adaptive grounding strength, while GNR-LLM effectively improves low-SNR perceptual quality through local neighborhood refinement, addressing the limitations of both pure LLM-based and deterministic SE approaches.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based autoregressive speech enhancement (SE) produces natural speech using learned clean-speech priors, but may hallucinate content unsupported by the input. Deterministic SE better preserves observation-coupled evidence, yet often retains residual noise or local distortion. We propose an evidence-grounded generative SE framework that uses a deterministic estimate as imperfect evidence. A Whisper-guided DPRNN produces an enhanced waveform, which is blended with the observation and tokenized into a discrete evidence sequence. The evidence conditions an autoregressive clean-speech token generator and is reused during decoding through Code-Space Grounding (CSG), which penalizes candidates according to their Hamming distance in the factorized finite-scalar-quantized (FSQ) space. Because the appropriate grounding strength depends on acoustic difficulty, we introduce SNR-Conditioned CSG (SNR-CSG), which maps a calibrated residual-SNR estimate to an utterance-level strength and constructs an adaptive grounded anchor. Although grounding improves content fidelity, the anchor may retain local acoustic defects inherited from the evidence. Since such defects are predominantly local in the FSQ space, nearby tokens may provide better acoustic realizations without large departures from the observation-supported trajectory. We therefore propose Grounded Neighborhood Refinement with LLM ranking (GNR-LLM). It performs one additional teacher-forced pass conditioned on the grounded-anchor history, intersects the LLM top-$K$ candidates with a local FSQ Hamming neighborhood. Experiments on in-domain, controlled-SNR, and DNS no-reverb conditions show that SNR-CSG provides robust automatic grounding, while GNR-LLM substantially improves low-SNR perceptual quality without sacrificing content fidelity.

</details>


### [305] [Motion-Omni: End-to-End Joint Speech and Full-Body Motion for Spoken Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04250)
*Chengqian Ma,Wei Tao,Haoyu Zhang,Yiwen Guo*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Motion-Omni is an end-to-end framework that enables spoken dialogue models to natively output facial expressions and full-body motion (hand, upper-body, lower-body) directly from the hidden states that produce speech, eliminating the need for separate cascade systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current systems use separate model families for speech and co-speech motion, requiring a cascade approach (generate speech first, then run motion model on audio). This is inefficient (requires two inference passes) and prevents joint optimization between speech and motion generation.

Method: Motion-Omni uses a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone where the LLM, Speech Generator, and Motion Generator are jointly trained under both objectives. Motion is generated directly from hidden states that produce speech. Training uses a scalable pipeline with pseudo-labeled consistent-voice speech responses (422,856 pairs, 1,402 hours). Released SwDA-500 dataset and a comprehensive evaluation protocol for stochastic open-ended full-body spoken dialogue.

Result: Motion-Omni-Q7 achieves: (1) Within 2% on reference-free motion metrics vs same-audio teacher cascade; (2) 5.4x faster inference (RTF=0.78, faster than real time); (3) Best beat correlation and diversity among non-teacher cascades; (4) 2.62% word error rate (lowest among omni-modal systems).

Conclusion: Joint training of speech and motion generation is essential - without it, motion misaligns with audio. The framework successfully enables end-to-end full-body spoken dialogue with fast inference and competitive quality, while being the first to provide a public evaluation protocol for this task.

Abstract: An avatar that holds a conversation should decide what to say and to move while saying it, yet these abilities live in separate model families: spoken dialogue models produce speech without motion, and co-speech motion models produce motion only from audio handed to them. The standard remedy is a cascade that first generates the spoken response and then runs a motion model over the finished audio, which requires a second full inference pass and precludes any joint optimisation between the two. We present Motion-Omni, an end-to-end framework in which a spoken dialogue model natively outputs explicit facial expression together with hand, upper-body and lower-body motion, generated directly from the hidden states that produce the speech. Joint training is not optional here: with the speech pathway frozen, motion remains misaligned with the audio, and co-adapting the LLM, Speech Generator and Motion Generator under both objectives is what recovers alignment while retaining spoken-dialogue ability. Supervision comes from a scalable, model-agnostic pipeline that pseudo-labels consistent-voice speech responses with a replaceable motion teacher, yielding 422,856 quality-ranked pairs (1,402 hours). We further release SwDA-500 and, to our knowledge, the first public evaluation protocol for stochastic open-ended full-body spoken dialogue, matching audio across motion systems while unifying rendering, automatic metrics, human evaluation, and latency measurement. Instantiated with a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone, Motion-Omni-Q7 matches the same-audio teacher cascade to within 2% on reference-free motion metrics while responding 5.4 x faster (RTF=0.78, faster than real time), surpasses all non-teacher cascades on beat correlation and diversity, and reaches a 2.62% word error rate, the lowest among the omni-modal systems compared.

</details>


### [306] [Low-Latency Spell Correction for Japanese Music Search Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04262)
*Anshul Garg,Pavni Tandon,Karan Bhukar,Tanmay Khandelwal,Ujjal Kumar Dutta*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a compact BART-based sequence-to-sequence model (3 encoder + 3 decoder layers) for low-latency spell correction of Japanese music search queries. The core contribution is a script-aware synthetic misspelling generation pipeline that produces realistic training data by combining keyboard-layout models, phonetic confusion priors, voiced/unvoiced consonant alternations, and kana case errors. The model uses a custom byte-level BPE tokenizer and normalizes mixed-script catalog titles to a canonical script before misspelling synthesis. Achieves 41.09% exact-match accuracy and 11.62% CER with sub-4ms inference latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Japanese spell correction presents unique challenges due to the co-existence of four writing scripts (romaji, hiragana, katakana, and kanji), each inducing distinct error patterns. There is a need for low-latency spell correction specifically for Japanese music search queries.

Method: 1) Compact BART-based seq2seq model (3 encoder + 3 decoder layers) for low-latency inference. 2) Script-aware synthetic misspelling generation pipeline combining: keyboard-layout models (QWERTY and flick input), phonetic confusion priors from real query logs, voiced/unvoiced consonant alternations, and kana case errors. 3) Normalizing mixed-script catalog titles to a single canonical script before misspelling synthesis to reduce hallucinations. 4) Custom byte-level BPE tokenizer on target music catalog for unified vocabulary across all four scripts.

Result: Exact-match accuracy: 41.09%; Character error rate (CER): 11.62%; Inference latency: sub-4ms on single GPU. Outperforms edit-distance baselines and achieves lowest CER among all evaluated systems. Analysis shows effectiveness across individual scripts and mixed-script queries through systematic ablation studies.

Conclusion: The script-aware data augmentation approach is critical for effective Japanese spell correction. Normalizing mixed-script catalog titles to a canonical script before misspelling synthesis is essential for reducing model hallucinations. The compact BART model achieves strong accuracy-latency trade-off suitable for production deployment.

Abstract: Spell correction for Japanese search queries presents unique challenges due to the co-existence of four writing scripts (Latin/romaji, hiragana, katakana, and kanji) and the distinct error patterns each script induces. We present a compact BART-based sequence-to-sequence model (3 encoder + 3 decoder layers) designed for low-latency spell correction of Japanese music search queries. The core contribution lies in a script-aware synthetic misspelling generation pipeline that produces realistic training data by combining keyboard-layout models (QWERTY and flick input), phonetic confusion priors mined from real query logs, voiced/unvoiced consonant alternations, and kana case errors. A key design decision is normalizing mixed-script catalog titles to a single canonical script before misspelling synthesis, which we show is critical for reducing model hallucinations. We train a custom byte-level BPE tokenizer on the target music catalog to handle all four scripts in a unified vocabulary. Experiments on a curated evaluation set show that our model achieves an exact-match accuracy of 41.09% and a character error rate (CER) of 11.62%, outperforming edit-distance baselines and achieving the lowest character error rate among all evaluated systems while maintaining sub-4ms inference latency on a single GPU. We further analyze performance across individual scripts and mixed-script queries, demonstrating the effectiveness of script-aware data augmentation through systematic ablation studies.

</details>


### [307] [Scalable Context Orchestration for Serving LLMs Over Voice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04288)
*Linyi Jiang,Silvery D. Fu,Yifei Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: llmovoice is a context-management middleware for voice AI applications that explicitly models voice-specific context (paralinguistic and environmental states) and uses an LLM to generate runtime directives for system responses. It addresses limitations in existing LLM systems that represent conversation context as flat message sequences, leading to poor alignment with user preferences, degraded interaction quality under adverse conditions, and high costs over long sessions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM systems represent conversation context as flat, growing sequences of messages, leaving voice-specific context (how users speak - speaking rate, and conditions - background noise, packet loss) implicit in the audio. This causes: 1) responses poorly aligned with user preferences, 2) degraded interaction quality under adverse environmental conditions, and 3) high costs over long voice sessions.

Method: llmovoice constructs a bounded voice context at each turn from: 1) current user input, 2) relevant interaction history, and 3) explicit paralinguistic and environmental states. It then uses the serving LLM to reason over this context and generate runtime directives that guide how the system responds.

Result: Evaluation on real-world voice applications and benchmarks shows: 1) Speaking-rate alignment error reduced by 52.4%, 2) False-interruption rate under packet loss reduced from 46.0% to 0.9%, 3) Model usage cost reduced by 79.2%, 4) Per-turn cost for long sessions reduced by up to 24.9x while retaining up to 98.7% of baseline answer quality.

Conclusion: llmovoice effectively addresses voice-specific context management in LLM-based voice applications by explicitly modeling paralinguistic and environmental states, significantly improving user preference alignment, robustness under adverse conditions, and cost efficiency while maintaining high answer quality.

Abstract: Voice AI applications are gaining popularity as advances in large language models (LLMs) enable more natural and accessible spoken interactions. Serving these applications requires accounting not only for what users say, but also for how they speak (e.g., speaking rate) and the conditions under which their audio is captured and transmitted (e.g., background noise and packet loss). However, existing LLM systems represent conversation context as a flat, growing sequence of messages, leaving voice-specific context implicit in the audio. As a result, they can generate responses that are poorly aligned with user preferences, degrade interaction quality under adverse environmental conditions, and incur high costs over long voice sessions.
  We present llmovoice, a context-management middleware that explicitly models voice context and orchestrates its use. At each turn, llmovoice constructs a bounded voice context from the current user input, relevant interaction history, and explicit paralinguistic and environmental states. It then uses the serving LLM to reason over this context and generate runtime directives that guide how the system responds. We evaluate llmovoice on real-world voice applications and benchmarks. It reduces speaking-rate alignment error by 52.4%, lowers the false-interruption rate from 46.0% to 0.9% under packet loss, and reduces model usage cost by 79.2%. For long sessions, llmovoice reduces per-turn cost by up to 24.9 times while retaining up to 98.7% of baseline answer quality.

</details>


### [308] [Knowing When Not to Answer: Pseudo-Ensembles for Abstention in Music Audio-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04362)
*Aanya Maheshwari,Vatsal Raina*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in evaluating music audio-language models: the inability to distinguish between genuine understanding and lucky guesses in multiple-choice settings. The authors propose creating pseudo-ensembles from a single pretrained model by perturbing inputs (shuffling answer orderings, corrupting audio, swapping labels) that cannot change the correct answer. This approach enables ensemble-based uncertainty measures without training multiple models. Evaluating TinyMU on MuChoMusic, the method improved accuracy from 55.7% to 59.2% and reduced the area under the error retention curve from 0.293 to 0.261, making abstention practical for compact models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of music audio-language models relies solely on multiple-choice accuracy, which cannot differentiate between true musical understanding and random guessing. There is no mechanism to detect when the model lacks genuine knowledge, preventing appropriate abstention. Traditional solutions like ensemble of independently trained models are prohibitively expensive, leaving only single-model entropy as the confidence signal—which is insufficient.

Method: The authors propose constructing pseudo-ensembles from a single pretrained model by introducing controlled perturbations to the input that cannot alter the correct answer: (1) shuffling the order of candidate answers, (2) corrupting audio inputs, and (3) swapping option labels. By averaging the resulting predictive distributions over these perturbations, the method generates multiple predictions per question. This supports the full family of ensemble-based uncertainty measures: entropy of the expected distribution, expected entropy, and their difference (mutual information).

Result: Averaging predictions over four option orderings improved accuracy from 55.7% to 59.2%. The resulting uncertainty measures rank model errors better than the single-pass entropy baseline, reducing the area under the error retention curve from 0.293 to 0.261. The approach requires only a few extra forward passes with no retraining, making it practical for compact music audio-language models.

Conclusion: Pseudo-ensembles created through input perturbations provide a cost-effective solution for uncertainty quantification in music audio-language models. This method enables both improved accuracy through prediction averaging and reliable detection of low-confidence predictions, allowing models to abstain when appropriate. The approach is computationally efficient and requires no additional training, offering a practical pathway for deploying trustworthy music understanding systems.

Abstract: Music audio-language models are evaluated almost entirely by accuracy on multiple-choice questions. This protocol forces the model to commit to an option, so a lucky guess looks the same as real musical understanding. What is missing is a way to tell when the model does not know the answer, so that it can abstain instead of guessing. The usual solution, an ensemble of independently trained models, is far too expensive here, which leaves the entropy of a single predictive distribution as the only available confidence signal. We instead build pseudo-ensembles from one pretrained model by perturbing its input in ways that cannot change the correct answer, then averaging the resulting distributions over the options. Our main construction simply shuffles the order in which the candidate answers are presented; we also study ensembles built from corrupted audio and from swapped option labels. A pseudo-ensemble gives several predictive distributions per question, so it supports the full family of ensemble-based uncertainty measures (entropy of the expected distribution, expected entropy, and their difference, the mutual information) rather than entropy alone. Evaluating TinyMU on MuChoMusic, we find that averaging over four option orderings raises accuracy from 55.7% to 59.2%, and that the resulting uncertainty measures rank the model's errors better than the single-pass entropy baseline, reducing the area under the error retention curve from 0.293 to 0.261. All of this costs a few extra forward passes and no retraining, which makes abstention practical for compact music audio-language models.

</details>


### [309] [Pitch-class Steering for Diffusion-based Music Generation via Latent-space Probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04516)
*Yushi Ye,Wilson Zheng,Yongyi Zang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a lightweight method to control pitch content in audio generated by Stable Audio Open (a latent diffusion model) using a small convolutional probe trained to decode pitch-class activations from the VAE latent space. The probe serves as a differentiable loss function at inference time, enabling gradient-based steering toward user-specified pitch sequences without modifying the base model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Controllable music generation has primarily focused on autoregressive models, leaving diffusion-based systems comparatively underexplored. The authors address this gap by developing a method to steer the pitch content of audio produced by Stable Audio Open, a latent diffusion model for music synthesis.

Method: A small convolutional probe (~125k parameters) is trained to decode frame-level pitch-class activations from the model's VAE latent space, using paired audio and MIDI data. At inference, the frozen probe acts as a differentiable loss function—its gradient with respect to the denoising latent is used to nudge generation toward a user-specified pitch-class sequence, requiring no retraining or architectural modification of the base model.

Result: Across 27 evaluation trials (9 text prompts × 3 target melodies), probe-guided generation increases melodic coherence by 2.4x over the unguided baseline, with statistically significant results (p < 1e-5, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

Conclusion: Musically meaningful structure is both recoverable and steerable in diffusion-based music latent spaces, demonstrating the effectiveness of the probe-based steering approach for controllable music generation.

Abstract: Recent work on controllable music generation has focused on autoregressive models, leaving diffusion-based systems comparatively underexplored. We present a lightweight method for steering the pitch content of audio produced by Stable Audio Open, a latent diffusion model for music synthesis. A small convolutional probe containing approximately 125k parameters is trained to decode frame-level pitch-class activations from the model's variational autoencoder latent space, using paired audio and MIDI data. At inference time, the frozen probe serves as a differentiable loss function: its gradient with respect to the denoising latent is used to nudge generation toward a user-specified pitch-class sequence, requiring no retraining or architectural modification of the base model. Across 27 evaluation trials spanning 9 text prompts and 3 target melodies, probe-guided generation increases melodic coherence by 2.4x over the unguided baseline (p < 1e-5, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), demonstrating that musically meaningful structure is both recoverable and steerable in diffusion-based music latent spaces.

</details>


### [310] [SCAPES: Semantically Conditioned Autoregressive Prior for Environmental Sounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04634)
*Esteban Gutiérrez,Lonce Wyse,Frederic Font,Xavier Serra*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SCAPES is a lightweight, resource-efficient generative model for synthesizing high-fidelity environmental sounds through semantic control. It uses a neural audio codec's continuous latent manifold with Continuous Normalizing Flow and Flow Matching, requiring only a consumer-grade GPU for training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the prohibitive computational and ecological costs of current generative audio models, which require industrial-scale resources and massive datasets to synthesize everyday sounds.

Method: SCAPES operates on the continuous latent manifold of a neural audio codec, bypassing discrete tokenization constraints. It uses a segmentation strategy decomposing audio into overlapping segments, enabling a Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) to model latent trajectory evolution via Flow Matching.

Result: A 36-million parameter model trained on limited, uncurated datasets using a single consumer-grade GPU achieves convergence after training approximately twice the source audio duration. The model produces high-fidelity outputs with robust long-term stability, semantic consistency, and smooth semantic interpolation.

Conclusion: SCAPES provides a flexible and accessible tool for open research and creative sound design, demonstrating that high-quality environmental sound synthesis is achievable with modest computational resources.

Abstract: As generative audio models grow in complexity, the computational and ecological costs of synthesizing everyday sounds have become increasingly prohibitive, often requiring industrial-scale resources and massive datasets. In this paper, we present SCAPES: a Semantically Conditioned Autoregressive Prior for Environmental Sounds. SCAPES is a lightweight, resource-efficient generative model designed to synthesize high-fidelity environmental textures through high-level semantic control. By operating on the continuous latent manifold of a neural audio codec, our approach bypasses the rigid structural constraints inherent to discrete tokenization. We propose a segmentation strategy that decomposes audio into overlapping segments, enabling a Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF) to model the evolution of latent trajectories using Flow Matching. Our experiments demonstrate that a 36-million parameter instance of SCAPES can be trained on limited, uncurated datasets using a single consumer-grade GPU. Notably, convergence is achieved after training for approximately twice the source audio duration, yielding high-fidelity outputs with robust long-term stability and semantic consistency. Furthermore, we showcase the model's capacity for smooth semantic interpolation, providing a flexible and accessible tool for open research and creative sound design. Code, pretrained weights, audio examples, and an interactive demo are publicly available on our project page https://cordutie.github.io/projects/scapes.html

</details>


### [311] [Harmonica: Accurate and Lightweight Instrument-Agnostic Music Transcription](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04640)
*Longshen Ou,Héctor Martel,Joe Hennessy-Priest,Taemin Cho*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Harmonica is a family of instrument-agnostic music transcription models built around multi-depth harmonic convolution. It includes x-large (state-of-the-art), medium (competitive with fast inference), and nano (only 26.3K parameters, 1,622.5x real-time speed) variants. The nano model achieves 0.796 frame F1, outperforming Basic Pitch by 14.6 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing music transcription models often struggle with computational efficiency and require instrument-specific designs. The paper aims to develop an instrument-agnostic model that achieves high accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency across different model scales.

Method: The core innovation is multi-depth harmonic convolution, which exploits harmonic information at multiple depths. The method is compared with existing harmonic aggregation approaches including harmonic stacking, harmonic attention, single-depth harmonic convolution, and HD-Conv layer.

Result: At each model scale, Harmonica achieves the best performance among evaluated models. The x-large model attains state-of-the-art performance. The nano variant with only 26.3K parameters achieves 0.796 frame F1 (14.6 percentage points higher than Basic Pitch) while running at 1,622.5 times real time.

Conclusion: Multi-depth harmonic convolution effectively exploits harmonic information and benefits transcription performance. The Harmonica family offers a strong trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency, from state-of-the-art accuracy (x-large) to extreme efficiency (nano).

Abstract: This paper introduces Harmonica, a family of instrument-agnostic music transcription models built around multi-depth harmonic convolution. At each model scale, Harmonica achieves the best performance among the evaluated models: the x-large model attains state-of-the-art performance in instrument-agnostic transcription, while the medium variant offers competitive accuracy with faster inference than all baselines. Pushing the limit of computational efficiency, the nano variant has only 26.3K parameters and runs at 1,622.5 times real time, yet achieves a frame F1 of 0.796 on the development set, 14.6 percentage points higher than Basic Pitch. We further demonstrate that multi-depth harmonic convolution effectively exploits harmonic information to benefit transcription performance through comparative experiments with existing harmonic aggregation methods, including harmonic stacking, harmonic attention, single-depth harmonic convolution, and the HD-Conv layer.

</details>


### [312] [ProLombard: Structured Multi-Scale Modeling for Normal-to-Lombard Speech Conversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04828)
*Hongyang Chen,Xinmeng Xu,Youqiang Zheng,Xingyu Liu,Yuhong Yang,Zhongyuan Wang,Weiping Tu,Song Lin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: ProLombard is a multi-scale normal-to-Lombard speech conversion framework that models the Lombard effect at utterance, phoneme, and frame levels. It addresses key limitations in existing methods by introducing an aligned speaker encoder to prevent Lombard leakage in speaker representations and a phoneme-aware disentanglement mechanism for better Lombard-content separation. The approach achieves improved speech intelligibility, Lombard similarity, and perceptual quality while preserving speaker identity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing N2L methods model the Lombard effect only at utterance or frame level, ignoring its hierarchical nature. This leads to two key problems: (1) Lombard leakage in speaker representations (where Lombard characteristics contaminate speaker identity), and (2) incomplete separation between Lombard characteristics and linguistic content. The goal is to improve speech intelligibility in noisy environments while preserving speaker identity and speech quality.

Method: The paper proposes ProLombard with three key components: (1) Multi-scale hierarchical modeling across utterance-, phoneme-, and frame-level representations; (2) Aligned Speaker Encoder (ASE) that suppresses Lombard leakage by aligning Lombard-speech speaker embeddings with normal-speech counterparts; (3) Phoneme-aware disentanglement and injection mechanism extending frame-level modeling to phoneme level; (4) VQ-median module using vector quantization for segmentation and median-frame aggregation to provide robust phoneme-level representations.

Result: Experiments on Mandarin and English Lombard datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in speech intelligibility, Lombard similarity, and perceptual quality over baseline methods, while maintaining speaker identity.

Conclusion: The structured multi-scale modeling approach is essential for effective N2L speech conversion. The hierarchical representation learning with proper speaker alignment and phoneme-level disentanglement successfully addresses the limitations of prior approaches.

Abstract: Normal-to-Lombard (N2L) speech conversion aims to improve speech intelligibility in noisy environments by transforming normal speech into Lombard-style speech while preserving linguistic content, speaker identity, and speech quality. Despite recent progress, existing methods typically model the Lombard effect at the utterance level or the frame level, overlooking its hierarchical nature and its entanglement with both speaker identity and phoneme-level content. This limitation leads to Lombard leakage in speaker representations and incomplete separation between Lombard characteristics and linguistic content. In this work, we propose ProLombard, a structured multi-scale N2L framework that explicitly models the Lombard effect across utterance-, phoneme-, and frame-level representations. To address Lombard-speaker entanglement, we introduce an aligned speaker encoder (ASE) that suppresses Lombard leakage by aligning Lombard-speech speaker embeddings with their normal-speech counterparts. To achieve more complete Lombard-content disentanglement, we develop a phoneme-aware disentanglement and injection mechanism that extends conventional frame-level modeling to the phoneme level. Furthermore, we design a vector quantization (VQ)-median module that provides robust phoneme-level representations through VQ-based segmentation and median-frame-based aggregation. Extensive experiments on Mandarin and English Lombard datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves speech intelligibility, Lombard similarity, and perceptual quality over baselines while maintaining speaker identity. These results highlight the importance of structured multi-scale modeling for effective N2L speech conversion.

</details>


### [313] [SwanWeave:One-Stage Multi-Task Instruction-Guided 3D Spatial Audio Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04975)
*Ke Lei,Chenyuhao Wen,Yu Zhang,Wenxiang Guo,Changhao Pan,Sashuai Zhou,Yongshi Li,Ruiqi Li,Ruofan Hu,Haorui Xu,Xiang Yin,Zhou Zhao*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SwanWeave is the first one-stage multi-task framework for instruction-guided 3D First-Order Ambisonic (FOA) spatial audio editing. It addresses the problem of editing spatial audio based on user instructions while preserving unrelated scene elements, using a Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing and Spatial Preference Optimization (DPO-based alignment) to handle complex compound editing tasks across multiple axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language-guided audio editors mainly target conventional audio or rely on sequential operations, failing to support one-stage editing for complex 3D spatial instructions. Spatial audio editing must jointly reason about audio events, spatial information, dynamic changes, and environmental information in FOA waveforms, requiring a dedicated solution.

Method: 1) Built paired FOA supervision from open-source speech and sound-effect corpora using controllable room simulation, covering 10+ single-operation and compound tasks across four editing axes. 2) Developed Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing: task-aware expert combinations for compound instructions and frame-level routed/null experts for local edit decisions. 3) Introduced Spatial Preference Optimization (SPO), a DPO-based alignment objective with edit-specific negative targets. 4) Adopted staged training to improve natural-language grounding.

Result: SwanWeave achieves better editing quality than existing general audio editors and spatial audio baselines across all tasks.

Conclusion: This work presents the first one-stage multi-task framework for 3D FOA spatial audio editing, demonstrating that the proposed SE-MoE architecture with dual-level routing and DPO-based alignment can effectively handle complex compound editing instructions while preserving spatial audio quality.

Abstract: Spatial audio editing modifies an existing soundfield according to a user's instruction while preserving the rest of the scene. Unlike conventional audio editing, it must reason jointly about audio events, spatial information, dynamic changes, and environmental information in first-order Ambisonic (FOA) waveforms. Existing language-guided editors mainly target conventional audio or rely on sequential operations, and therefore do not directly support one-stage editing for complex 3D spatial instructions. We present SwanWeave, the first one-stage multi-task framework for instruction-guided 3D FOA spatial audio editing. We build paired FOA supervision from open-source speech and sound-effect corpora using controllable room simulation, covering more than ten single-operation and compound tasks across the four editing axes. To handle this heterogeneous edit space, SwanWeave uses Spatial Edit Mixture-of-Experts (SE-MoE) with dual-level routing, selecting task-aware expert combinations for compound instructions and frame-level routed/null experts for local edit decisions. We further introduce Spatial Preference Optimization (SPO), a Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)-based alignment objective with edit-specific negative targets, and adopt staged training to improve natural-language grounding. Experiments show that SwanWeave achieves better editing quality than existing general audio editors and spatial audio baselines across all tasks. Spatial audio editing demos can be found at https://swanaigc.github.io/#swanweave, code can be found at: https://github.com/MM-Speech/SwanWeave.

</details>


### [314] [KanAdapter: A Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-based Plug-and-Play Module for Efficient Fine-tuning of Foundation Speech Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05281)
*Phuong Tuan Dat,Phuong Khai Minh,Tran Huy Dat*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: KanAdapter replaces traditional MLP adapters with Group-Rational Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GR-KAN) modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of self-supervised speech models, achieving 97.5% parameter reduction while maintaining competitive performance across speaker verification, speech emotion recognition, and deepfake detection tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fully fine-tuning SSL speech models is computationally prohibitive, and existing MLP-based adapters have limited representational expressiveness due to fixed activation functions under tight parameter budgets.

Method: KanAdapter uses a parallel bottleneck design with trainable GR-KAN branches alongside frozen Transformer encoder blocks, leveraging weight transfer from pre-trained MLP layers for stable initialization.

Result: Up to 97.5% trainable parameter reduction relative to full fine-tuning while remaining highly competitive; consistently outperforms AdaptFormer under comparable parameter budgets. In continual learning, yields up to 83.6% error reduction over full fine-tuning and MLP-based adapters.

Conclusion: First work exploring KAN-based modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of speech foundation models; the localized rational activations of GR-KAN mitigate catastrophic forgetting in continual learning scenarios.

Abstract: Fully fine-tuning self-supervised learning (SSL) speech models for downstream tasks is computationally prohibitive, and existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches predominantly rely on MLP-based adapters whose fixed activation functions limit their representational expressiveness under tight parameter budgets. We propose \textbf{KanAdapter}, a lightweight adapter framework that replaces conventional MLP bottlenecks with Group-Rational Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GR-KAN) modules for more expressive and parameter-efficient adaptation. Following a parallel bottleneck design, KanAdapter inserts trainable GR-KAN branches alongside frozen Transformer encoder blocks and leverages weight transfer from pre-trained MLP layers for stable initialization. Across speaker verification, speech emotion recognition, and deepfake detection, KanAdapter achieves up to 97.5\% reduction in trainable parameters relative to full fine-tuning while remaining highly competitive, and consistently outperforms AdaptFormer under comparable parameter budgets. In continual learning, it yields up to 83.6\% error reduction over full fine-tuning and MLP-based adapters, which we attribute to the localized nature of GR-KAN's rational activations that mitigates catastrophic forgetting. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explore KAN-based modules for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of speech foundation models.

</details>

### [315] [STyMo: Fast and Controllable Few-Shot Motion Style Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04500)
*Jose Luis Ponton,Alexander Winkler,Ladislav Kavan,Yuting Ye,Petr Kadlecek*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: STyMo is a few-shot motion style transfer method that learns from seconds of paired data in 1-2 minutes by decomposing style into static (posture) and temporal (dynamics) components, enabling runtime adjustments while maintaining robustness via a stylizability gate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current motion style transfer methods require either large stylized datasets or pre-trained models that cannot generalize beyond their training distribution. There is a need for a few-shot approach that can learn motion style from minimal data.

Method: STyMo decomposes motion style into two components: (1) static component capturing time-invariant posture, and (2) temporal component capturing frame-wise dynamics. This decomposition enables runtime adjustments. Additionally, a stylizability gate is introduced to prevent artifacts on out-of-distribution motions.

Result: STyMo can learn motion style from only seconds of paired data, trains in 1-2 minutes, and produces interpretable controls for posture intensity, temporal exaggeration, and per-body-region style adjustments. The stylizability gate ensures robustness on arbitrary inputs.

Conclusion: STyMo enables few-shot motion style learning with only seconds of paired data, training in 1-2 minutes. The decomposition approach provides interpretable runtime controls (posture intensity, temporal exaggeration, per-body-region style). The stylizability gate ensures robustness on out-of-distribution inputs. The method supports diverse styles from subtle emotional variations to exaggerated archetypes, with a released paired dataset for future research.

Abstract: Supporting a wide variety of motion styles is critical for creating diverse virtual characters, but current methods either require large stylized datasets or pre-trained models that cannot generalize beyond their training distribution. We present STyMo, a few-shot approach that learns motion style from only seconds of paired data and trains in one to two minutes. Our key insight is to decompose style into two components: a static component capturing time-invariant posture, and a temporal component capturing frame-wise dynamics. This decomposition yields an interpretable system where posture intensity, temporal exaggeration, and per-body-region style can be adjusted at runtime. Furthermore, the reduction in required training data and computation time structurally permits an iterative authoring workflow. To ensure robustness on arbitrary inputs, we further introduce a stylizability gate that automatically prevents artifacts on out-of-distribution motions. We demonstrate results across diverse motion styles, from subtle emotional variations to exaggerated character archetypes, and release our processed paired dataset to facilitate future research.

</details>


### [316] [LayoutShop: Content-Constrained Exploratory Design of Creative Article Layout](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05098)
*Jialuo Li,Pengfei Xu*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: LayoutShop is a computational framework for designing creative article layouts. It uses layout templates to construct a design space, extracts eligible layout structures, determines geometry via optimization, and employs two neural networks for assessment. User studies confirm its effectiveness in helping users create high-quality layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to automate and assist the article layout design process, which is traditionally manual and time-consuming. The paper aims to help users create high-quality article layouts efficiently through a computational approach.

Method: The method involves: (1) Creating or selecting layout templates for conceptualization; (2) Constructing a layout design space to extract eligible layout structures; (3) Using an optimization approach to determine geometry of layout structures; (4) Employing two neural networks for layout assessment; (5) Returning high-quality outputs to users for selection.

Result: The user study confirmed that LayoutShop can effectively help users create high-quality article layouts. The framework was evaluated for usability and output quality.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that LayoutShop is an effective tool for helping users create high-quality article layouts. The framework successfully integrates template-based design, optimization, and neural network assessment to produce satisfactory results.

Abstract: We present LayoutShop, a novel computational framework for designing creative layouts that frame a given article. Inspired by the actual article layout design process, we enable users to create or select layout templates for conceptualization. These templates help construct a layout design space to extract eligible layout structures. Our algorithm then determines the geometry of the extracted layout structures to frame the given article via an optimization approach. We then employ two neural networks for layout assessment, and the high-quality outputs are returned to users for selection. We conducted a user study to evaluate the framework's usability and the quality of the article layouts it produces. The results of the user study confirmed that our framework can effectively help users create high-quality article layouts.

</details>


### [317] [GradRig: Differentiable Weights for Skinned Gaussian Splat Deformation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05127)
*Nina Vesseron,Élie Michel*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a mesh-free deformation pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splats using spatial gradients of skinning weights, enabling real-time deformation without connectivity information while preventing holes during stretching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional skinned deformation relies on mesh connectivity (polygons) to deform shapes, but 3D Gaussian Splats lack this connectivity information. Rigidly transforming points creates holes when stretching shapes, requiring a different approach for proper deformation.

Method: The method uses the spatial gradient of skinning weights to deform Gaussian Splats. When users create a rig structure, the system evaluates these gradients. An optional adaptive resampling scheme is also proposed to split splats that still produce artifacts.

Result: The pipeline enables accurate stretching of splats while maintaining full compatibility with real-time rendering capabilities, demonstrated through a WebGL viewer implementation.

Conclusion: The proposed mesh-free deformation approach successfully adapts skinned deformation to 3D Gaussian Splats, solving the hole problem during stretching while preserving real-time performance.

Abstract: Skinned deformation is a common framework to turn a 3D shape from its rest pose into a dynamic pose through the deformation of a coarser kinematic structure, called rig. When applied to a 3D mesh, this rig only needs to displace vertices to deform the polygons that connect them. However, when deforming 3D Gaussian Splats, which do not provide connectivity information, rigidly transforming points is not enough to prevent the creation of holes when stretching shapes. In this paper, we use the spatial gradient of skinning weights to provide a full mesh-free deformation pipeline for Gaussian Splats, that more accurately stretches splats while remaining fully compatible with real-time rendering capabilities, which we demonstrate in a WebGL viewer. We present how we evaluate these gradients when the user creates the rig structure and propose an optional adaptive resampling scheme to split up splats that still produce artifacts.

</details>
